The Bṛhannīlatantra. First Chapter. Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. Salutations to Tārā.
Seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, the Goddess, resting against his chest, spoke with reverence to Bhairava, who is known as Kāla.
O Lord Sadāśiva, you previously promised to reveal the Kālītantra; now, for the sake of revealing the Nīlatantra, please speak that.
By the mere knowledge of which one becomes victorious on earth;
knowing which, all practitioners move about as they please. (1.3)
O Mahādeva, tell me that reality by the mere knowledge of which poetry that delights the mind is born. (1.4)
The illustrious Mahākālabhairava said:
Listen, O virtuous one, O lady of excellent hips, bestower of all goals!
Out of affection for you, O Mistress of the Gaṇas, I shall declare that reality (tattva) to you. 1–5.
"O my beloved, I have made a vow to reveal the Nīlatantra;
therefore, O Maheśānī, listen, O lotus-faced one, as it is told. (1–6)
This tantra is more secret than the secret; it must never be disclosed.
From the disclosure of this tantra, there is a loss of accomplishment—of this there is no doubt. (1.7)
In whatever house one dwells, there the *tantra* shall cause Lakṣmī to abide firmly—even at the king’s gate, in the cremation ground, in an assembly, or in the midst of battle. (1–8)
And in a lonely, terrible forest filled with beasts of prey, O Goddess of the Gods, O Beloved, by his majesty there shall be a miracle. (1.9)
Therefore, with every effort, it must be guarded with great care;
[especially so, according to the Kha manuscript reading] this *Tantrarāja*, the *Nīlatantra*, is being revealed out of affection for you. (1–10)
O Goddess Pārvatī, O fair-faced one, this supreme distinction of the King of Mantras must be told [to you], for it is most secret, like one's own womb. 1-11.
O Goddess, by knowing which all practitioners shall attain all forms of sovereignty—
this [teaching] is the most essential of the essential, bestowing the essence of all eloquence.
The daily worship, the king of mantras, the ritual procedure for the practice of mantra,
the preliminary service (puraścaryā), and likewise the rules for occasional and optional rites.
O Goddess of the gods, [I shall explain] the rule for the secrets, the procedure for the worship of the Virgin (kumārī), other mantras, and especially the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).

O fair-faced one, the fruit [of practice] and the specific praise must be told; likewise, the determination of the states of being and the procedure for the internal worship should be explained. (1.15)
The rule for the fire-oblation (homa) shall be declared, as well as the determination of the reality of latent impressions (vāsanā-tattva),
secret worship, secret mantra, and likewise the sequence of secret recitation (japa).

The preparation of gold, silver, and so forth, as well as the ash of mercury (sūtabhasma); the definitive determination of mercury (sūtasya nirṇaya) must be stated, as well as the characteristics of the six ritual acts (ṣaṭkarmalakṣaṇa).
"I shall describe the arising of the Vidyā with its specific characteristics; listen to that.
The Goddess said:
"Now I wish to hear about Tāriṇī together with her divisions."
Śrī Śiva said: O Great Goddess, [I shall describe] the perfected lore (siddhavidyā) which destroys great sins, consists of various forms of worship, and causes the delusion of Māyā. (1.19)
Listen, O fair-limbed Mistress of the Gods, to that which bestows all eloquence;
having extracted the seed-syllable of all, listen now to the second seed-syllable. (1.20)

It ends with a *jṛmbhaṇa*, is devoid of the side-vowels (*pārśva*), is joined with the impediment to departure (*prasthānavāraka*), is conjoined with the fourth vowel (*turīyasvara*), and is adorned by the lunar drop (*candrabindu*). || 1-21 ||
O Bhairavī, hear now the seed-syllable of Nīlasarasvatī, the third [mantra].
Having taken the first of all [the letters], one should join the first of that [group] to it. (1–22)
O Maheśvarī, one should apply the prevention of the journey there;
one should make it endowed with two syllables and adorned with the Nāda and Bindu.
Having joined [the syllable] *kūrca* at the end of the *astra*, one should extract the King of Mantras;
this is the five-syllabled Great Vidyā, the illustrious Nīlasarasvatī. (1-24)
A science such as this is extremely rare even in the three worlds;
by mere recitation, it bestows liberation upon all practitioners. (1.25)
Indeed, there is no excessive exertion required here, O Goddess worshipped by the gods! This is the essence of essences, O Devi, hidden within all the tantras. (1-26)
Vasiṣṭha is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and the Bṛhatī is said to be its meter (chandas);
Nīlasarasvatī is declared to be the deity for the accomplishment of one's purpose. (1–27)

The application for the sake of poetic composition bestows the abundance of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*). *Hūṃ* is the seed-syllable, and the weapon (*astra*) is the power (*śakti*); such is the conceptualization of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the other [limbs]. (1.28)
And having risen during the final watch of the night, one should contemplate the supreme Tāriṇī, who is subtler than a lotus fiber, extending from the root-center up to the aperture of Brahmā. (1–29)
Consisting of the root mantra, manifest as the very form of nectar and bliss,
resembling ten million suns in brilliance yet as cool as ten million moons.
His appearance was like ten million flashes of lightning above the crest of the fire of time;
his body was marked by a mass of spreading light that pervaded the entire circle of its radiance.
Endowed with all auspiciousness, one should commence the rite of bathing;
having taken up earth and *kuśa* grass, one should then go to the water’s edge.
Having performed the removal of impurities, one should perform the mantra-bath.
Having submerged himself again in the water, he should perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
For the sake of worshipping one's chosen deity, one should perform a bath in a body of water;
[one should offer] bilva, unbroken rice grains, moḍra flowers, family-specific flowers, kuśa grass, and water.
Having prepared the *arghya* offering in a copper vessel with a capacity of one *prastha*,
he should present it at the end of the root mantra, [addressing the goddess] who resides within the orb of the rising sun.
"O Śivā [the reading 'nitya' is found in the Kha manuscript], [the mantra] 'to her who consists of consciousness, svāhā' is remembered as that mantra.
O Maheśānī, O beloved, hear now of another bath for the different forms."

Having risen during the latter watch of the night, while recollecting the Guru within the lotus of the head, one should contemplate the root-mantra from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 1.37 ||
[He saw] the Supreme Goddess, adorned with earrings, resembling the rising sun,
her form rendered immortal by the very process of the movement of inhalation and exhalation.
Having meditated, one should recite the root-mantra one hundred and eight times in sequence;
then, taking earth and kuśa grass, one should go to the edge of the water.
At dawn, having performed reflection upon the Guru, one should perform the ritual bath;
having approached a river or similar body of water, O Maheśvarī, one should bathe in the waters.
Having meditated upon the water as having the form of goddesses and having taken up water and *darbha* grass,
one should perform the removal of impurities and then carry out the ritual bath with mantras.
O Supreme Goddess, for the sake of pleasing Her, one should perform the bath with a concentrated mind;
having first performed the Vedic *saṃdhyā* rite, one should then carry out the bath.
Thereafter, he should perform the Tantric twilight ritual as proclaimed in the Āgamas.
Having performed that twilight rite, the hero shall then deliver ten million of his family lineages.
Having brought earth for the purpose of bathing and having rubbed it with both hands, the preceptor should apply it as an ointment to his limbs while reciting the Astra-mantra. (1.44)
First, one should show it to the Sun, and then perform the smearing:
cow dung on the nose and [the syllable] "vaṃ" on the two nostrils with the mantra. (1.45)
Then, having offered a handful of water and performed an ablution upon the head,
one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with the right hand within a triangle.
O Goddess, having taken hold of the hand [of the preceptor] in the manner of a conch-spiral,
one should stir [the water] therein and immerse oneself three times while reciting the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn.
Having recited the seed-syllable of the *kūrca* mantra three times, one should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa*;
thereafter, one should indeed offer three handfuls of water to Varuṇa.
Having risen from the water toward the west for Soma Bhānu, and having put on two garments,
the practitioner of mantra should then perform the rites according to the prescribed rule.

One should apply a *tilaka* on the foreheads of the cowherd girls with red sandalwood paste, while for the goddesses it should be with white sandalwood; one should then inscribe the weapon-mantra (*astra*) on the forehead and the seed-syllable of Tārā (*tārābīja*) upon the heart.
One should place [the breath] within the *śakti* and perform *prāṇāyāma*;
having sipped water (*ācamana*), facing the east, and being seated, the knower of mantras should proceed. (1.51)
The best of practitioners should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with the principles of Self-knowledge and Śiva;
reciting the root mantra within the triangle while muttering the *haṃsaka* for Savitṛ.
Having established [the posture], O Goddess, one should recite; listen, O beautiful one:
"To Tārā we pay homage (vidmahe)," having spoken thus, and "to Mahogrā we meditate (dhīmahi). (1.53)
At the end of the words "tanno devī," [one recites] "dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt.
This is declared to be the Gāyatrī, which cuts away all sins. (1.54)
Then, O Maheśvarī, one should place the left foot upon the right foot;
having performed the prostration, one should then recite the *haṃsa* mantra three times with the arms raised upward.
Facing the northern direction, one should offer libations to the Goddess alone with water from a sacred ford, ground sesame seeds, milk, and unbroken grains of rice. (1.56)
Having uttered the word "Tāriṇī" at the end of the root mantra, one should satisfy the beloved of Agni (the Fire-goddess) with a vessel made of gold,
silver, or copper.
Having offered libations with devotion using three straight blades of *darbha* grass, the wise man,
facing the southern direction, should then take up a *moṭaka* (funeral cake).
Having said, "May the ancestors be satisfied," one should perform this libation;
and likewise, O Maheśvarī, there is the salutation of the Sun and the realization of non-duality.
The wise man should mutter the Gāyatrī preceded by the Aghamarṣaṇa;
this alone constitutes the salutation during the three periods of twilight, both by day and by night.
Even during the great night, the best of teachers should always perform [the rites];
however, the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) must necessarily be performed three times a day by one endowed with faith.
He who is devoid of the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) shall not obtain the fruit of initiation;
[this applies to the time] after midnight and for two muhūrtas [before it].
That is designated as the "Great Night"; having performed [the rite] there, it becomes inexhaustible.
Then, having meditated on the Vidyā in the heart, one should recite it one hundred and eight times.
In that very place, one should perform the Tantric bath according to the stated sequence;
thereafter, with a concentrated mind, one should perform both the Vedic and Tantric Sandhyā prayers.
O Pārvatī, among the duties prescribed by the Vedas, know that there are four kinds of actions; however, do not regard them as such, for my word alone is truly one.
O beloved, one should perform the evening twilight rite even on the twelfth day and other such occasions;
for by failing to do so, one goes to hell, since this is a daily scriptural duty.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Twilight Devotions (Sandhyā-vidhi), preceded by the Extraction of the Root Mantra," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī within the glorious Bṛhannīlatantra. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter:
Listen now, O lady of beautiful limbs, to the worship proclaimed in all the Agamas.
Having performed which, O Supreme Goddess, one shall therefore attain the state of Śiva. || 2-1 ||
O lady of pure smiles, one should perform worship with every effort at a solitary liṅga, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, or at a crossroads. (2.2)
Staying there, the yogi should accomplish the Vidyā who is the Mistress of the Three Worlds,
at a place within a radius of five krośas where no other linga is seen.
That is declared to be the single liṅga; therein lies unsurpassed accomplishment, whether on Mount Ujjata, or on a mountain, or in a desolate place, or at a crossroads.
Or one may accomplish the practice of the Goddess, the bestower of all desired objects, in a palace;
likewise [one should worship] Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, the Yoginīs, and Vaṭuka.
O Maheśvarī, those seeds for the village and the cow-pen have been described;
having worshipped them at the door of the house, one should then worship Brahmā.
Then, with his mind, the wise one should first [worship] the deity of the site (Vāstudeva) to the east;
thereafter, he should ward off the malevolent spirits and those in the form of obstacles.
Having resorted to the station of yoga, one should contemplate the seat there;
having visualized the cremation ground there, one should remember the wish-fulfilling tree there. (2-8)
At its base was a jeweled pedestal adorned with various gems,
enriched with diverse ornaments and decorations, and graced by sages and gods.
O Great Goddess, it was surrounded on all four sides by auspicious jackals rejoicing in flesh and bones, and it was adorned with corpses, skulls, and bones.
In the center of that, one should contemplate the Goddess through the yoga of meditation as previously described.
O Maheśānī, O lady of pure smiles, one should thus perform this meditation within the heart. (2-11)
One shall obtain the fruit of worship performed for a hundred thousand years;
one should offer the five types of perfumes and present a red garland. (2.12)
Adorned with golden ornaments, he should hold the syllable *hrīṃ* in his hand;
clothed in two red garments, he must be free from anger and malice. (2.13)
Having first uttered the Praṇava, then the Vajrodaka, then the Kūrca, O Great Goddess, and immediately after that, Phaṭ Svāhā. (2.14)
O Goddess of the gods, one should purify the excellent water with this mantra:
first the Praṇava, then Māyā, and immediately after that, Viśuddhā. (2.15)
After that, pacify all evils;
immediately thereafter, remove every last conceptual construction. (2-16)
"Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā" is considered the *vadhimantra* for washing the hands;
then the *praṇava*, followed by "kūrca," and immediately after that, "phaṭ svāhā. (2-17)
O Goddess of the gods, the most excellent practitioner should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with this mantra:
the Praṇava, followed by the word "Maṇidhari," and then the word "Vajriṇī. (2-18)
The mantra ending with "vaśakarī," followed by "hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," is the incantation;
O Goddess of the Gods, one should perform the binding of the topknot (śikhābandhana) with this mantra. (2-19)
Having first uttered the syllable Oṃ, then the words "protect, protect," one should perform the purification of the ground with the mantra: "Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā. (2-20)
One should sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion with water purified by mantras;
O Great Goddess, [one should likewise worship] Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka at the four gates.
One should worship the Lord of the Field and the Yoginīs with great effort;
likewise, O Great Goddess, one should especially perform the mudrā known as the Nārāca.
Listen to the mantra, O lady of excellent hips, which bestows all eloquence:
having first uttered the *praṇava*, one should command away all obstacles. (2.23)
And after that, O Goddess, remove it once more;
immediately following that, the mantra ending with "kūrcaḥ svāhā" bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.
Having first uttered the *praṇava* (oṃ), followed at the end by the word *pavitra*, then the word *vajrabhūme*, and ending with *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, such is the mantra. (2-25)
O Goddess of the Gods, one should perform the consecration of the ground with this mantra:
first uttering the *praṇava* (oṃ), followed by the word *āḥ*. (2.26)
The mantra begins with *surekhe* and *vajrarekhe*, and ends with *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having worshipped the seat with red sandalwood and flowers, the wise practitioner [should proceed]. (2.27)
O Goddess, one should sit upon that seat and then begin the worship;
with the mantra for binding the topknot, one should tie the knot of the garment.

O Maheśānī, O auspicious one, one should perform the purification of the mind and the other faculties with the very mantra previously mentioned, using red sandalwood paste and other such substances. (2.29)
Having inscribed [the diagram] in a vessel of gold or other precious materials, the wise practitioner should then inscribe the syllables therein:
"Āḥ surekhe vajrarekhe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā namaḥ. (2–30)
O Goddess of the gods, with this mantra one should draw an eight-petaled lotus;
O Goddess of the gods, with that very same mantra, one should draw a beautiful eight-petaled [lotus].
O auspicious Goddess of gods, one should write the seed-syllable of Māyā in the eastern triangle;
one should write Vadhū in the south, and Phaṃ, ending with Dviṭha, in the north.
And then, O Great Goddess, one should write the syllable *Ṭaṃ* in the west;
in the center of that, O Supreme Sovereign, one should write the *Kūrca* mantra with a concentrated mind. (2-33)
Alternatively, O Gaṇeśvarī, listen to the Yantra in another manner;
by it, a seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge that illuminates all scriptures. (2-34)

Likewise, by the grace of this machine, one who seeks knowledge shall obtain knowledge, one who seeks liberation shall obtain liberation itself, and one who seeks all things shall obtain everything. (2.35)
[The mandala] whose pericarp consists of the syllables *vyoma* (kha), *indu* (u), *aurasana* (la), and *arṇa* (ra); whose filaments quiver with pairs of vowels;
whose petals shine with the unfolding of the consonant groups (*varga*); which is encircled by the abode of the earth (the letter *va*);
and which is beautified by the turning of the directions and corners, shining with the syllables *tārādhīśvara* (m) and *vāri* (va).
The yantra of the Blue-bodied One is declared to be supreme, bestowing the accomplishment of all aims.
O Goddess of the gods, having fashioned the yantra, one should perform the worship of the seat (pīṭha-pūjā);
thereafter, one should worship the enclosures (āvṛtis) according to the method described by Gandharva.
Then, having formed the *yonimudrā*, one should worship within the center of the wheel;
having worshipped Gaṇapati in the east, and Vaṭubhairava in the south.
One should worship Kṣetrapāla in the west and the Yoginīs in the north;
all of them, beginning with Dhruva and Dīrgha, are preceded by their respective Śaktis and Bījas.
Then, one should worship Lakṣmī and the others in the middle of the eight petals;
one should likewise sacrifice to Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, and Prīti.
One should worship Kīrti, Śakti (or Kānti, as in the Kha manuscript), Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi;
these are declared to be the Pīṭha-śaktis of the goddess Nīlasarasvatī.
The wise one should worship with effort, beginning with the syllable Om and ending with "Namaḥ";
thereafter, he should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) by means of the sequence of breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should then contemplate the universe as empty, [and] one's own self as untainted, devoid of qualities, pure, and consisting of Tāriṇī. (2.43)
Then, one should meditate on a red lotus arising from the syllable *ĀḤ* in the intermediate space;
furthermore, one should meditate upon a white lotus above that, arising from the syllable *ṬĀṂ*.

Above that, one should again meditate upon the syllable *hūṃ*, resembling the color blue; then, from that seed-syllable *hūṃ*, [one should visualize] a curved knife adorned with the seed-syllable. (2.45)
One should meditate upon oneself as being identical with Tāriṇī, standing upon a curved knife, fierce, and adorned with a garland of severed heads, in the pratyālīḍha posture. (2.46)
She is short-statured, pot-bellied, and formidable, with a tiger skin draped around her waist;
she is endowed with the bloom of fresh youth and adorned with the five mudrās.
The Sumukha, the Caturasra, the Vṛtta, and the Gomukha—these five mudrās are renowned as the Yonimudrā for the purpose of salutation. (2.48)
Four-armed, with a protruding tongue, most terrifying, and bestowing boons;
her two right and left hands are equipped with a sword and a razor.
One should meditate on her as possessing a pair of right hands joined with a skull and a blue lotus, with a single tawny and fierce matted lock, and adorned with Akṣobhya upon her crown.
She has a mass of matted hair adorned with blue serpents, earrings made of white snakes, bracelets of yellow snakes, and her arms are decorated with smoke-colored snakes. (2.51)
She has a dark-blue serpent as her sacred thread, is adorned with bright white serpents as necklaces,
wears a girdle of white serpents, and has two feet marked by pale-red serpents.
With garlands of blue lotuses hanging from both her sides,
she stood amidst the blazing realm of the ancestors, her appearance made formidable by her fangs.

O Goddess of the Gods, having meditated upon Nīlā (Sarasvatī) in this sequence—she whose two left and right feet rest upon the two shoulders and two feet of Śiva; her face smiling with intense absorption; bestowing fearlessness upon her devotees—(2-54).
One should meditate upon oneself as being composed of that; this is declared to be the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Now I shall describe the placement of the *arghya* (offering water), by which the mantra becomes effective;
having drawn a triangular mandala to one's left, O Supreme Goddess. (2.56)
There, O beautiful one, having placed the tripod and washed the conch,
O Goddess of gods, one should fill it with excellent water in three parts.
Having placed the skull-bowl there, one should then offer red sandalwood paste and so forth;
thereafter, one should present a red flower, and the deity will become well-pleased. (2.58)
Having recited the root mantra ten times, one should perform the sprinkling;
thereafter, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) accompanied by the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga). || 2.59 ||
The sage of this [mantra] is Akṣobhya, and its meter is said to be Bṛhatī;
the goddess is Nīlāsarasvatī, well-guarded throughout the three worlds. (2.60)
The seed-syllable *hūṃ* is the weapon (*astra*) and the power (*śakti*), which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
one should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) using [the syllable] joined with the *māyā* and the six long vowels. (2.61)
Having thus performed the rite of placement (nyāsa), one should perform the sixteen-fold placement of Tārā;
having encased it with the Vidyā, one should then place the sixteen-fold Mātṛkā.
O lady of excellent hips, the sixfold Tārā is proclaimed [to be recited] in direct and reverse order;
the practitioner who performs it in this manner is himself proclaimed as Tārā. (2.63)
In this world, he has no superior; he is the teacher of all yogis.
At the end of the seed-syllable, "ekajaṭāyai" is proclaimed as the heart-mantra. (2.64)
"To Tāriṇī, svāhā to the head; likewise, [svāhā] to Vajrodakā for the crest-lock; [svāhā] to Ugrajaṭā for the armor; and likewise [svāhā] to Mahāpratisarā. (2.65)
Likewise, Piṅgogrā and Ekajaṭā are proclaimed as the weapons of the eyes;
just as Kālī is, so too is Nīlā—one should install the Mātṛkās in that sequence. (2.66)
O Goddess of gods, who are easily accessible through devotion and accompanied by your retinue,
remain perfectly steady for as long as I worship you.
Having made everything consist of mantra, one should offer it to the deity;
one should worship with the sixteen services, beginning with perfumes and flowers. (2.68)
Water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), bathing water, garments, and ornaments;
then fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), and again water for sipping. (2.69)
One should employ betel, worship, hymns of praise, libations, and prostrations;
these are the sixteen services to be utilized in the act of worship. (2.70)
The fivefold worship consists of offerings beginning with fragrance and ending with food.
O Goddess, my beloved, listen with a one-pointed mind to the rules regarding the flower. (2.71)
The *kokanada*, the *bandhūka*, the two kinds of *karṇikāra*, as well as the red *vaka*, *mandāra*, and *karavīra* flowers are recommended. (2.72)
The three types of *mallikā*, jasmine, *kṣaumapuṣpa*, *jayantikā*, bilva leaves, *kurubaka*, *munipuṣpa*, and *kesara*. (2.73)
Vāsantī, Saugandha, the charming Kāśa flower, Āmalaka, Kādamba, Bakula, and likewise Muthikā. || 2-74 ||
It was adorned with auspicious bilva leaves, maruvaka and other flowers— excluding tulasī— as well as especially with oḍra flowers and vajrapuṣpa.
One should offer every kind of flower with a mind endowed with devotion;
O Maheśānī, one should especially offer the japā flower to the Goddess. (2-76)
The lotus is most dear to the Goddess, as are the śephālī and the bakula;
O Queen of the Gods, one should worship the supreme Śivā with the red lotus. (2.77)
One shall obtain the fruit of worship performed for a hundred thousand years;
the Śirīṣa flower is supremely pleasing to the Goddess, as is the Tagara.
O Maheśānī, O Sureśvarī, if one should give a land-lotus that is most excellent and follows the sequence of a hundred thousand [repetitions], all perfections (siddhis) will be attained. (2.79)
At that very moment, the perfection of the mantra shall be attained; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
[One should offer] a beautiful *tulasī* of a different species, which is supremely pleasing to Her. (2.80)
O Maheśānī, one who is endowed with devotion should offer all flowers—whether golden, red-colored, or those that are exceedingly dear and abundant. (2.81)
One should offer this most excellent, delightful, delicious, and captivating food-oblation to the Great Goddess with a mind filled with devotion. (2.82)
One should especially offer madhuparka, which is supremely pleasing to the Goddess, along with a warm message and accompanied by sweets such as laḍḍukas. (2.83)
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) and rice mixed with sesame (kṛsara), combined with sugar and jaggery;
likewise, one should present oblations of food mixed with clarified butter, curd, and honey.
The knower of mantras should also diligently offer the śāla fish, the pāṭhīna fish, the excellent flesh of the iguana, and food mixed with honey. (2.85)
O Goddess, having likewise offered goat meat and roasted Rohita fish,
and having displayed the Yoni-mudrā, one should then receive the command according to the prescribed rite.
O Mother Goddess, Mahāmāyā, who brings about both bondage and liberation! Command us, O Great Goddess, regarding the unsurpassed triad of gurus.
"I worship you, O Great Illusion, who bestows all eloquence.
Thus the Goddess spoke with reverence to the Blessed Lord Adhokṣaja.
"O Mahādeva, I desire to hear with diligence about the three gurus.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Without knowing the guru as a deity, one will lose the path. (2.89)
If there is no succession of lineage among gurus and their disciples, then mantra and vidyā are lost to the path; they do not come within the sphere of accomplishment in such a case. (2.90)
Their mantras and vidyās will be fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
Without knowing the lineage of the gurus, the disciple’s spiritual succession is destroyed. (2.91)
One should know that the lineage of the Guru, which brings about auspiciousness, is superior to one's own lineage.
O Goddess, there are the Gurus of the Siddha-stream as well as the Gurus of the Divine-stream.
With hair standing erect, sky-haired, blue-throated, and bull-bannered—O Bhairavī, hear now the definitive teaching concerning the supreme and subordinate gurus. (2.93)
O Goddess of the gods, at the beginning of all [practices], the giver of mantra is the supreme guru;
in all tantras and mantras, she herself is the embodiment of primordial nature. (2.94)
O Goddess of gods, O Supreme Sovereign, one should worship the retinue on the eight petals starting from the east; one should worship Vairocana and the others.
Having first uttered the Praṇava (Oṃ), then the name [of the deity], followed by "vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha" (accept the vajra-flower), the mantra concludes with "huṃ phaṭ svāhā. (2.96)
O Goddess, with this mantra one should worship the retinue;
likewise at the doors, starting from the east, are Padmāntaka and Yamāntaka.
Then, having worshipped Vighnāntaka, one should worship Narakāntaka.
A mantra is not perfected through mere recitation, nor does it grant fruit without burnt offerings. (2.98)
And since one grants desired objects through sacrifice, therefore one should perform this triad.
I shall now proclaim the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) by which everything is accomplished for all purposes. (2.99)
Having properly performed the worship, one should first carry out the ritual according to the procedure of Bali;
thereafter, the best of practitioners, performing the recitation and the libation, should proceed. (2.100)
A Brahmin should also perform rites for subduing Bala and other such purposes;
having duly brought the fire, he should say, "Homage to the flesh-eaters. (2.101)
Having recited the root mantra, one should spread the fire upon the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or even on the ground, with the three Vyāhṛtis.
Having offered oblations three times with [mantras] ending in *svāhā*, one should likewise perform the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) oblation;
then, having invoked the Goddess, one should offer sixteen oblations with the root mantra.
Having offered oblations, praised, and recited [the mantra], and having paid homage, one should dismiss [the deity] within the lunar disc;
then, being well-composed, one should offer the sacrificial portion (*bali*) consisting of goats and other animals according to the prescribed rite. (2.104)
Having first uttered the Praṇava, then the Māyā-bīja, followed by the word "Ekajaṭe," and then "Mahāyakṣādhipa. (2-105)
The two words *baliṃ gṛhṇa*, the two words *gṛhṇāpaya*, then the word *mama*, followed by *śāntiṃ kurukuru* and then the word *paravidyām*. (2-106)
Then, O Maheśānī, having drawn in the pair of feet, thereafter the pair of *truṭi*s, and immediately after that the pair of *chindi*s, [one should proceed with] all the words.
O Maheśānī, bring that supreme state of the world under control;
O Goddess, having offered the oblation with this mantra, one should perform the recitation.
O Maheśvarī, one should recite the mantra a thousand times, or even a hundred times, or twenty times; one should not perform less than that.
O Sarasvatī, as far as the pervasion of knowledge is described by the heart [mantra], I shall now proclaim the meditation on the mantra, which bestows all success through recitation. (2.110)

O Great Goddess, since even a slayer of a Brahmin is purified through mantra and meditation, one should contemplate the *hṛllekhā* at the root-cakra, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns. (2-111)
One should visualize the second syllable, yellow in color, at the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
and at the navel, the Kūrca seed-syllable, resembling a cloud and possessing great luster. (2.112)
One should meditate on the seed-syllable of the weapon in the heart, possessing a radiance like the fire of time;
one should contemplate the entire Vidyā extending from the root [cakra] to the aperture of Brahmā at the crown of the head. (2.113)
Resembling ten million suns and previously beheld by yogis—or else, a tuft on the head with the luster of the full moon, drenched in nectar. (2.114)
Alternatively, one should contemplate that entire vidyā in the form of a lamp upon the tongue, and likewise contemplate the tongue as being pervaded by the mass of its radiance. (2.115)
O Goddess, by placing [this mantra] upon the tongue, even a mute becomes a skilled poet;
you, the protector of the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us. (2-116)
"O Goddess, O Great Sovereign, may success be mine through your grace!
O Supreme Self, if one should perform this sequence of worship at night," (2.117)
At that very moment, one attains perfection; this is the truth, the truth, most certainly so.
O Maheśānī, with a pure mind, one should offer praise in the presence of the Goddess. (2-118)

O Goddess of terrible form and great roar, who brings all enemies under control [the reading *kṣayaṅkari* is also found], O bestower of boons upon your devotees, protect me, who have come to you for refuge! (2.119)
O Goddess worshipped by the Suras and Asuras, served by the Siddhas and Gandharvas;
O Goddess who removes the sin of dullness, protect me who have come to you for refuge. (2-120)
O Goddess, who are endowed with a mass of matted locks, who resemble a flickering tongue,
and who bestow swift intelligence— protect me, who have come to you for refuge!
Homage be to you, O gentle-formed one, O fierce-formed one, O wrathful one (as per the *Krodha* recension), O violent-formed one (as per the *Sṛṣṭi* recension)!
Homage to you whose form is vision; protect me, who have come to you for refuge!
You destroy the dullness of the dull-witted, yet [you grant it to] those devotees who take on that dullness (as per the *Kha* recension).
O Goddess, who art affectionate toward your devotees, remove my delusion; protect me, who have come to you for refuge.
O Goddess, whose nature consists of the syllables *hūṃ* and *hūṃ*, who are fond of offerings and oblations, homage to you!
O Ugratārā, homage to you; protect me, who have come to you for refuge. (2.124)
Grant me intelligence, grant me fame, grant me poetic skill, grant it to me!
O Goddess, take away my evil intellect [the reading "mūḍhatvaṃ" (delusion) appears in manuscript kha]; protect me, who have come to you for refuge.
O Tārā, composed of compassion, saluted by the excellent hosts of gods beginning with Indra, you whose face is like the lord of stars—save me, who have come to you for refuge! (2.126)

On the eighth, the fourteenth, and the ninth day, the person who recites this with a single-pointed mind attains accomplishment within six months; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (2.127)
One seeking liberation attains liberation; one seeking wealth shall obtain wealth;
and one seeking knowledge attains knowledge, such as logic and grammar. (2.128)
The person who recites this hymn constantly obtains wealth;
his enemies go to ruin, and great wisdom arises within him. (2-129)
Whether in suffering, in battle, during recitation, in giving, or likewise in fear of a great portent—he who recites this auspicious hymn, for him there is no doubt. (2-130)
O Goddess of the gods, by praising the Sovereign Goddess with this hymn, one obtains all desires and becomes a treasury of all knowledge. (2.131)
Thus has this divine hymn, which bestows the power of Sarasvatī, been told to you;
O Maheśvarī, there is no hymn superior to this within the Tantra.
Having thus praised the Great Goddess and prostrated like a staff,
and having then offered himself, he should display the yoni-mudrā.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall proclaim this supreme Tārāṣṭaka;
by reciting it, O Deveśī, I attained the state of Śiva, O beloved. (2-134)
By reciting it six times, the destruction of enemies will certainly occur;
and by reciting it twenty-eight times, even a king shall become a servant. (2.135)
By reciting it eight times, one becomes a master of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhiśvara*).
Listen, O lady of excellent limbs, to this hymn by which one shall become a king. (2.136)
O Mother Nīlasarasvatī, bestower of the wealth of good fortune upon those who bow to you,
standing in the pratyālīḍha posture upon the heart of Śiva, with a smiling lotus-face,
endowed with three eyes like blossoming blue lotuses, and holding a skull and a blue lotus in your hands.
Wielding the sword, you alone are my refuge; I take shelter in you, the Sovereign Goddess.
O Mistress of Speech, O Wish-fulfilling Vine for devotees, O Sovereign of the Accomplishment of All Aims! [An alternative reading is "O Bestower of Siddhis.
[The reading "gadyaprākṛtapadyajātiracanā" (the composition consisting of prose, Prākṛt, and verse) appears everywhere in manuscript *kha*.]
O bestower of the accomplishment of all goals in composition,
O you who possess three eyes with blue lotus-like pupils, O ocean of compassion, please sprinkle those like us with your grace by raining down the nectar of good fortune. (2.138)
O you whose body is filled with a multitude of haughtinesses, radiant in the guise of a serpent and the like,
with a beautiful waist encircled by a tiger skin and marked by swinging bells,
and with the hair from two skulls— freshly severed and dripping with dust— intermingling [with yours];...
O terrifying one, beautiful with a garland of human heads and a string of knots, destroy my fear! 2-139 ||

O Lalanā, whose form consists of the transformations of the limbs of Māyā, whose nature is the Bindu and the Half-moon, and who are composed of the syllables HŪṂ and PHAṬ—O you who are the essence of mantra, you alone are the refuge for one such as I. O Mother, your form is fashioned from the three abodes; it is gross, exceedingly subtle, and supreme.
I take refuge in her who is not within the range of the Vedas in any way, yet has been attained [by me]. (2.140)
O Śrī Parameśvarī, through service to Your lotus feet, the virtuous attain union with Him,
whose nature is equal to the three-eyed Lord Śiva, Brahmā, and the other gods.
O Mother, what person of dull intellect— who is averse to serving Your feet— would serve the gods, headed by Indra, whose bodies are incapable of sinking in the ocean of saṃsāra?
O Mother, [he alone would serve You] who bears upon his head the imprint of the dust from the two lotus-feet of Yours.

These gods, victorious in the battle for conquest, have come without hesitation into my lap; yet others, bearing the rivalry that "I am the god in this world, there is no one equal to me," surely meet their destruction by themselves, just as those who are like them [perish] through their own impurities (or, according to the reading *yathāsuśucibhiḥ*, by their own excessive purity).

The hosts of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and yakṣas, as well as the lords of the nāgas, the foremost of the daityas and dānavas, the sky-dwellers, and creatures such as tigers, are all incapable of even looking at you, intent as they are on fleeing upon remembering your name.
O Mother, on this earth, the ḍākinīs and even the enraged Antaka [the God of Death] are but for a moment among men. (2.143)
(20) Prosperity, the host of supernatural powers (*siddhi*), the paralyzing of the mouths of opponents in debate, as well as the paralyzing of enemies (*vairiṇaḥ*—
variant reading *vāriṇaḥ*) on the field of battle, the immobilization of elephant herds, and likewise the power of delusion (*mohana*).
O Mother, by serving your feet, indeed those various virtues of men are perfected;
[by your grace] even a lowly person becomes as radiant as the mind-born god of love and attains the status of Vācaspati. 2-144.
The man who, full of devotion, recites this meritorious *Tārāṣṭaka*—whether at dawn, at midday, or in the evening—being self-controlled and pure, [attains the beautiful state]. (2.145)
One obtains divine poetic skill and becomes a knower of the meaning of all scriptures; having attained imperishable fortune and enjoyed pleasures as desired, || 2.146 ||
One shall attain fame, beauty, freedom from disease, and become beloved by all;
having also achieved renown throughout the worlds, one shall finally attain liberation. (2.147)
Having praised the goddess Sarasvatī with this king of hymns,
one shall indeed enjoy all desires right here and attain liberation.
O Goddess praised by the gods, there is nothing superior to this among hymns;
therefore, in the Kali age, one should abandon everything else and recite this hymn with every effort. (2.149)
Having first prostrated with the eight limbs, one becomes manifest as Sadāśiva himself:
with the two feet, the two hands, the two knees, the chest, the head, and the eyes. (2.150)
Prostration with both mind and speech is declared to be the eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga) salutation;
and that which takes the form of a triangle is proclaimed as belonging to Tārā. (2.151)
Having thus offered salutation, one should then apply fragrant unguents;
then, by means of the path of the Suṣumṇā alone, one should lead [the deity] to the heart with the mantra "Forgive me" (kṣamasva).
Having performed breath control once more, one should contemplate one's own self;
and listen with a single-minded focus, O beloved, to the mantra for taking up the flower. (2-153)
One should first utter the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], followed by the word "nirmālya";
then, at the end of the word "vāsinyai," one should pronounce "namaḥ" and perform worship.
By the command of Śrī Śiva, I offer to you food to be chewed, licked, eaten, and drunk, as well as betel, garlands, and ointments—the remnants of offerings—to be consumed by you. (2.155)
Then, having placed the remaining *nirmālya* upon his head,
he should give the *naivedya* to a Brahmin and likewise to young maidens;
and having himself partaken of a small portion, he should always wander upon the earth.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Sixteen-Part Worship, Hymns, and So Forth," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī within the illustrious *Bṛhannīlatantra*.
Now begins the third chapter.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who show compassion to the helpless!
O Mahādeva, please explain the procedure for initiation in brief.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O beautiful one, sovereign of all, sinless one, as it is being told by me;
for without her, O Great Goddess, there is no authority over ritual action.
O Goddess of excellent vows, among all stages of life, all beings, and all gods, everything becomes futile for one who lacks initiation, O Great Goddess. (3-3)
Therefore, with every effort, one should be initiated by a Guru;
for the entire world has initiation as its root, and supreme austerity has initiation as its root. (3–4)
Supreme accomplishment has initiation as its root; therefore, one should perform initiation.
O Great Goddess, one devoid of initiation shall go to the Raurava hell. (3–5)

If one should give food to those who are uninitiated after taking even a small portion of the auspicious [substance], all that drinking becomes in vain; therefore, one should avoid it entirely. || 3-6 ||
From association with families that have not received initiation, the loss of spiritual accomplishment arises;
their food is considered equal to excrement, and their water equal to urine. (3.7)
Therefore, with every effort, one should receive initiation from a true guru;
having received initiation from a true guru, one should perform all ritual actions.
O Great Goddess, without a guru, initiation becomes futile;
for that lowest of men who receives a mantra after merely seeing it in a ritual manual (kalpa).
Even throughout thousands of Manvantaras, no atonement ever arises;
yet from the mouth of the Guru comes the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), which destroys all sins. (3.10)
O Great Goddess, listen as I describe the true Guru;
a Guru who withdraws the external senses is difficult to find anywhere. (3.11)
A teacher who has withdrawn his inner senses is auspicious in every respect;
he wears blameless attire and is free from deceit. (3.12)
One who possesses proper conduct, is devoted to the propitiation of the Great Vidyās, and is capable of following the ritual procedures prescribed in their manuals, is designated as a Guru. (3.13)
The knower of Kaula wisdom, the great yogi, is indeed the guru and the deity;
he is the one established in the lineage (kūlīna) of all mantras and the giver [of them] among all, O beautiful one. (3-14)

He alone is the master of initiation—the Self, and no other, even one who has mastered the Vedas; the leader of the Kaula tradition is superior to both the progenitor and the giver of the Veda. (3-15)
Therefore, one should always consider [the teacher] to be even more venerable than one's father;
the form of the teacher is the root of meditation (*dhyāna*), the ritual action of the teacher is the root of worship,
and the word of the teacher is the root of mantra— therefore, one should first worship the teacher.
Śiva, moreover, is undoubtedly the instructor of the higher knowledges (paravidyās). (3-17)

O Goddess of the Gods, the Vaiṣṇava [initiation] is for those established in that doctrine, the Saura for the virtuous who know the solar [path], and the Gāṇapatya is for the initiators of the Gaṇa-initiation.
Whether a follower of Śiva or a follower of Śakti, he is everywhere the master of initiation; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in a guru of noble lineage.
Having observed the student's fitness for one, two, three, four, or five years, he should examine whether he is truly fit; otherwise, he will encounter suffering. (3.20)
Then, having performed the *vṛddhiśrāddha* and having satisfied the Brahmins, one should receive initiation; otherwise, one will not obtain the fruit.

The fruit of [rites performed] in Caitra and the other months is to be known; one should avoid the intercalary month (malamāsa), as well as the equinoxes, the two solstices, the solar transits (saṃkrānti), and the festival of Madana.
Initiation should be performed with great effort during the purifying festival of the Guru;
[specifically] on the sixth lunar day in the month of Bhādrapada, or on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āṣāḍha.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight in Kārttika, the third day of the bright fortnight in Mārgaśīrṣa, the ninth day of the bright fortnight in Pauṣa, and the excellent fourth day in Māgha. (3.24)
The ninth day of the bright fortnight in Phālguna, the Kāma-trayodaśī in Caitra,
the Akṣaya-tithi in Vaiśākha, and the Daśaharā lunar day in Jyeṣṭha are all auspicious.

The fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha and the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa—these are the festivals of the gods; on these, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacred fords (tīrthas).
Even during times considered censurable, initiation is declared auspicious during an eclipse;
there is nothing on earth equal to the time of a solar eclipse.
On a day pure in its five components, auspicious in both the moon and the stars, and during the rising of Jupiter and Venus, the consecration of mantras is highly recommended.
Listen, O lady of excellent limbs, to the place by which one succeeds without doubt:
in a cow-pen, in a holy temple of Śiva, in a cremation ground, or on the bank of a river. (3.29)
When the planet is in an empty house and on a meritorious mountain, one who desires to attain success should know it to be an auspicious time for the undertaking of a mantra. (3.30)
Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Ārdrā, Dhaniṣṭhā, the three Uttarās,
Puṣyā, and Śatabhiṣak are said to be the lunar mansions for initiation (dīkṣā).
Having duly set the ritual sequence in motion and performed the worship and fire-offering,
the knower of reality should correctly impart that Vidyā into the ear of the living disciple.
Without knowing the Kullukā goddess, without bowing to the sandals of the Guru, without giving the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and without properly performing the Kula-worship; 3-33.
Whoever engages in this tantra, you shall certainly not harm them—
especially during the month of Āśvina— for the sake of accomplishing dharma, desire, and wealth.
In this matter, there is no consideration of time and so forth, nor is there any purification of the lunar mansions;
one should perform one hundred and eight oblations with bilva leaves.
One should prepare eight, eighteen, or even twenty-eight [offerings];
one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa), rice mixed with sesame (kṛsara), and the most excellent meat of the monitor lizard (godhā).
One should diligently offer oblations of *rambhā* flowers and *śālamatsya* fish;
thereafter, one should present barley-milk along with rice cooked in milk and mixed with honey.
One should offer a coconut fruit as well as ornaments made of gold and other materials; one should satisfy one's own guru with gifts such as cows, land, gold, and clothing. (3.38)
And a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should especially be given, O Maheśvarī;
one should give the fee to the Guru, who is Śiva himself manifest before one’s eyes. (3.39)
If this power were not mobile, how could he give away his entire possession as a sacrificial fee, or give a milch cow? (3.40)
When he gives with contentment and a cheerful countenance, he should offer a seat to the Guru, provided with a red woolen blanket. (3.41)
One should give ornaments such as necklaces and the like, and one should give a milch cow;
one should give land that provides a livelihood, which shall be inherited by sons and grandsons. (3-42)
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru, consisting of gold accompanied by a garment;
through the mere satisfaction of the guru, eternal success (siddhi) is attained. (3.43)
Otherwise, there would be no success at all; it would instead lead to malevolent magic.
One should give food to the Brahmins preceded by great respect. (3-44)
One should feed a married woman and a maiden with sweet foods;
one should follow her shadow and dwell near her for three days.
Afterwards, the mobile power (saṃcāriṇī śakti) undoubtedly comes to the guru;
there is nothing higher than the guru, especially within the three worlds.
O Supreme Goddess, one should contemplate the identity of the deity with the Guru;
Mahādeva is the Guru manifest, and the Śrī-guru is all the deities. (3-47)
In the presence of the Guru, one should not worship any other deity; O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the Guru alone in his presence.
O Goddess, I shall describe to you exactly the fruit of worshiping the guru;
and I shall also describe the procedure for the worship of the guru, O lady of beautiful countenance.
First one should offer a comfortable seat (bhadrāsana), and after that, one should offer water for the feet (pādya);
one should especially offer the guest-offering (arghya) as well as water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
One should offer incense of guggulu and present a most beautiful lamp; likewise, one should offer delightful foods to be chewed, sucked, licked, and drunk. (3–51)
One should offer various kinds of fruit endowed with diverse flavors;
O fair-faced one, one should especially offer food that is both chewed and eaten. (3.52)
One should offer a handful of flowers combined with sandalwood;
O Maheśānī, one should offer a bed that is variegated and all-enchanting. (3.53)
O Maheśānī, one should offer a couch adorned with variegated garments;
O Sundarī, one should perform service at the feet of the Guru with great diligence. (3.54)
One should behave toward the sons of the guru as toward the guru himself, and likewise toward their children and so forth;
one should especially honor the wife of the guru with all kinds of offerings of food.

Furthermore, the wife of the guru, even if she is young, should not be saluted at her feet by one who has completed twenty years of age and understands virtues and faults; for this very reason, O Maheśānī, one should not perform service at her feet. (3.56)
Thus ends the third chapter, concerning the description of the procedure for initiation, in the glorious Bṛhannīlatantra, within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Now, O Maheśānī, O Śivā, I shall describe the procedure for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).
But one who recites the mantra daily without having first performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), [attains no fruit].
Even by reciting it ten million times over the course of an eon, its accomplishment does not arise;
for like a body deprived of life, it is incapable of performing any ritual action. (4.2)
Even a mantra that is devoid of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is thus proclaimed [to be effective].
Recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), libation (tarpaṇa), consecration (abhiṣeka), and feeding the twice-born (dvijabhojana)—[these constitute the ritual]. 4-3.
In this world, five duties are said to constitute *puraścaraṇa*:
whatever number [of recitations] may be omitted, the *japa* must be twice that number. (4-4)
O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips, it is taught that this procedure applies to all;
at its conclusion, the best of practitioners should perform a great worship. (4–5)
One should satisfy an unprecedented maiden with ornaments;
one should perform the preliminary rite for the worship of the mantra, making it the "stake" (kīlaka) of the mantras.
O Maheśvarī, O Great Goddess, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) for the sages and others;
listen, O Queen of the Gods, as I shall explain the sequence of mantras from the Kālītantra.
The *bindu* is the ear, the *nāda* is the mouth, and from that, the letter *ka* is the heart;
O Priyaṃvadā, the fire is the eye, while the long vowel *ā* is the *kīlaka*.
Know, O Pārvatī, that the syllable *tā* is the heart-mantra in the *Tāriṇītantra*;
know, O Sovereign of the Gods, that the letter *ha* is present everywhere on the side of Śakti.
Having done thus, one who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with undistracted mind;
thereafter, one may perform the ritual applications for all purposes, such as subjugation and the like.
The practitioner of mantra, intent on acting according to his own will,
should always recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), having donned a secret garland.
When this has been performed, O Great Goddess, one will become a master of the mantra;
through one hundred thousand recitations of the mantra, one obtains the illustrious power of speech.
For those who lack devotion, who are base, and whose minds are petty, it is declared that the recitation must be fourfold for success; otherwise, it will not come to pass.
Even Brahmins, though unable to follow the Mahācīna-krama,
perform the supreme recitation (japa) by means of the fourfold method for the purpose of enchantment.
Whether one is dull-witted or mute, if they are intent upon the power of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā),
all castes are twice-born (dvijātayaḥ) when devoted to the secret path.
Thereafter, by my grace, all the social classes (varṇas) will individually abstain from performing those [prescribed duties], especially in the Kali Yuga. (4.16)
O Gaṇeśvarī, there is no mantra for attaining success superior to this.
One who eats at night, subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya), and remains pure by day, should recite the vidyā. (4.17)
Having performed that, one attains success; one should recite the mantra steadily with the mind, sleep on the ground at that time, and avoid women during the day.
One should perform the morning recitation (prātarjapa); thereafter, one's mouth becomes purified.
Then, having partaken of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), one should offer the "Brahma-flower" (brahmapuṣpa) into the fire.
O Maheśānī, during the time of recitation, one should carefully avoid one’s wife;
one should avoid the Viṣṇukalpa plant and likewise avoid Tulasī.
One who possesses devotion should avoid the *mālatī* flower and the worship of other deities; he should perform the washing of hands, purification, and proper conduct. 4-21.
Likewise, one should place the flowers for the goddesses in separate vessels;
indeed, they must be brought together as one if one desires one's own welfare. (4.22)
One should know that the Lord alone is the enjoyer of offerings such as fruit, water, various kinds of oblations, perfumes, milk-rice, sweetmeats, and so forth. (4.23)
In this manner, one should consume curd and likewise milk in succession;
O Maheśānī, O Bhairavī, hear now the rule regarding the garlands.
Success in one's endeavors comes spontaneously through a rosary known as Mahāśaṅkha;
a garland fashioned from fifty beads grants all desires.
O Goddess of the Gods, a skull from the head of even a Cāṇḍāla who has died in battle is especially proclaimed as a "Great Conch" (mahāśaṅkha). || 4-26 ||
O Goddess, by means of this garland, the Tārā mantra becomes perfected.
O beloved of excellent form, listen with a one-pointed mind to its consecration, my dear. (4.27)
A garland strung with thread made by a brahmin woman, or one fashioned from silk threads, serves for the subjugation of the world. (4.28)
A garland made of golden thread becomes Vaiśravaṇa in person. One should join mouth to mouth and attach tail to tail. (4-29)
The garland should be like a cow’s tail or it may take the form of a serpent;
one should fashion the knots according to the prescribed rule, interspersed with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
One should fashion a single bead of that same kind as the Meru;
in this manner, a garland strung in sequence is beautiful in every respect. (4.31)
Thus, that strung garland bestows the accomplishment of mantra;
taking each individual jewel, one should designate a Brahma-knot.
One should recite that which is contained within the *mātṛkā* both in direct and reverse order;
by that, one becomes endowed with all virtues and a partaker of accomplishment. || 4-33 ||
Then, having bowed to the *kullukā* and performed the worship with the garland,
one should receive it with the right hand and not touch it with the left.
One should fashion a *kullukā* at the navel and the region of the head;
a garland made of silk thread is always pleasing to the Goddess. (4.35)
Even in the absence of a conch shell, one should perform the recitation with a rosary made of crystal;
such is the specific type of rosary, O Goddess of Gods, O Bhairavī, beloved of my life.
O Goddess of gods, by the recitation of which one becomes perfected in that very instant;
O beautiful one, there is no knowledge equal to this in the three worlds.
Out of compassion, O Supreme Goddess, and out of affection for you, it is being revealed.
Listen to the supreme, O lady of beautiful limbs; listen, O Pārvatī, according to the ultimate truth. (4.38)
By which mere consciousness mantras are accomplished at that very moment, through the forward and reverse order of the arrangement of the mantra's syllables. (4.39)
One should form a rosary consisting of mantra, which illuminates all mantras, by interspersing the syllables with the mantra and the mantra with the syllables. (4.40)
One should never transgress the final letter, which has the form of Mount Meru.
This supreme secret has been told to you by me, O illustrious lady. (4.41)
This must be kept strictly secret by you and not disclosed to anyone;
[this was done] at an auspicious time, under an auspicious ascendant, in an auspicious lunar mansion, and on an auspicious lunar day.
A wise person should perform the consecration ceremony either personally or through a preceptor;
one should arrange nine *aśvattha* leaves in the shape of a lotus.
There, the practitioner of mantra should establish [the fire] and recite the Mātṛkā-mantra;
having consecrated the fire, O Goddess worshipped by the hosts of gods, he should perform the oblation.
One should offer the remnants of the oblation (*hutaśeṣa*) during the counter-oblation (*pratihuti*) with the thought that they are for the deities;
having worshipped the Goddess there, one should also worship her during an eclipse.
One should consecrate it with the letters of the Mātṛkā in both forward and reverse order;
having consecrated the Meru with the *preta* syllable, one should lead it to the nature of the deity.
Thus, endowed with all virtues, she is born for the sake of all accomplishments.
Then follows the Smṛtisūtra, Vītihotra, and the triple repetition.

Day and night are said to be the sun and the moon; therefore, this auspicious triad of lights should be constantly protected while reciting the mantra according to the Sūtra for the attainment of one's desired goals. (4.48)
O Dear One, having refined it through the yoga of Kuṇḍalinī, one should utter [the mantra] consisting of bindu, nāda, and kalā, by means of the mother, the object, and the means of knowledge. 4-49.
One shall obtain accomplishment through this tenfold vidyā; no deliberation is required here.
The mantras, existing solely in the form of letters, reside in the region of the throat.
For those [mantras] uttered upon the path of the Suṣumṇā indeed attain sovereignty;
and he who performs the supreme recitation with such a garland— || 4-51 ||
One is liberated from untimely death and the Kali age; of this there is no doubt.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the determination of the fingers.
One should perform two joints of the ring finger (*anāmā*) in sequence by rotation, three joints of the middle finger (*madhyamā*), and one joint of the index finger (*tarjanī*). (4.53)
This is declared to be the Śaktimālā, which illuminates all mantras; whatever is recited with a distracted mind, and whatever is recited while overstepping the *meru*, [is rendered fruitless]. (4-54)
"O Supreme Goddess, they say that all of that becomes fruitless;
know, O Pārvatī, that the two joints of the index finger are indeed Meru. (4-55)
For the sake of attaining success, the practitioner should bow repeatedly to Mount Meru before reciting his prayers;
he who recites while pointing with the tip of his index finger or his middle finger is likewise a doer of evil.
One should always perform the recitation with the hands, but never for the sake of a specific desire;
then, having bowed to Kullukā and performed the worship of the rosary... (4-57)
Having meditated upon the feet of the venerable Guru, one should recite the mantra of the rosary;
even if a person does not know the *kullukā*, they may mutter the great mantra. (4–58)
Upon his death he will be reborn as one of the five elements, or else he will become a madman [the variant reading in manuscript *kha* is *mūḍhakolakaḥ*].
Furthermore, the mantra of Tāriṇī Caṇḍikā is devoid of the *kulluka*. (4–59)
Even one who is not at all acceptable among the twice-born, if he is wise, shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices by wearing a skull upon his head. (4.60)
No other deliberation is approved by Virūpākṣa in any case, provided that no woman is present when men are excluded from the *kulluka*. (4.61)
My worship is always in vain, and likewise my sacrifice;
one should know the Tārā mantra, the supreme three-syllabled mantra.
And that fool who does not know how to recite the *kullukā* which enables one to cross over—O Maheśānī, he shall never attain success as long as he lives. (4.63)
He who abandons the Great Mantra and worships Tāriṇī instead will meet his death or become insane. (4.64)
That goddess named Kullukā is the very embodiment of sovereign power;
she possesses four arms, with her left hand raised as a weapon. (4.65)
One should draw that three-syllable mantra on a dark-complexioned woman with a body like a blue lotus, adorned with all ornaments, using either turmeric or sandalwood paste. (4.66)
One should always wear the syllable of the mantra on the crest-lock for as long as one lives;
having received it through the Great Vidyā, one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times.
One should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) and having conquered the senses;
O Goddess of Gods, then the establishment of its seat occurs in elevated places.
Having performed the previously mentioned worship and being intent upon propitiating the Brahmins,
one should thereafter perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites in sequence, using a tenth part [of the materials].

At the end of the daily recitation, the practitioner of mantra should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) consisting of one-tenth of that number; likewise, he should perform libations (tarpaṇa) and ritual ablutions (abhiṣeka) for the mantra at one-tenth of those respective amounts.
Every day one should feed Brahmins for the sake of pacifying any deficiency or excess;
then, when everything is thus complete, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites.
At night, the *bali* offering should be presented by those desiring all accomplishments;
one should not worship an empty space before [the deity] without the lamp-mantra. (4.72)
O Great Goddess, without this lamp consisting of the three colors, and without the shedding of blood and pain, she is called a *mantriṇī*. (4.73)

O fair-faced one, how can there be accomplishment even through a hundred million recitations for one who does not know the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the yonimudrā? (4.74)
O beloved, those mantras whose life is hidden will not yield fruit;
however, mantras endowed with consciousness always grant all accomplishments.

Whatever manifestation of one's true nature occurs when the mantra is uttered—even after a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, or ten million recitations—that fruit is not attained [by those other means]. (4.76)
O Mistress of the Kula, there is the breaking of the knot in the heart and the piercing of all the bodily centers; there are tears of bliss, horripilation, and the possession of the body. (4.77)
And a faltering of speech arises suddenly; of this there is no doubt.
When the mantra endowed with consciousness has been thus uttered even once— || 4.78 ||
And it is seen, O Great Goddess, that this is called the lineage tradition;
thus, having performed the recitation in this manner, one should perform the ten-part offering with blue lotuses.

The practitioner of mantras should offer oblations with substances smeared with clarified butter, and perform a libation (tarpaṇa) with one-tenth that amount using pure fragrant waters mixed with the liquid of black aloe-wood.

One should satisfy that supreme goddess; the manner of doing so is stated here: having invoked her in water according to the rule, one should offer water-based offerings such as the foot-washing water (pādya) and the rest.
Having worshipped the Goddess and her retinue according to the rules, offering oblations to each one individually,
he should then, with devotion, satisfy them according to the ritual by offering a tenth part as libations.
Furthermore, having again satisfied each one along with their retinue,
one should sprinkle Tāriṇī and utter "Namo" while placing it upon the head.
This consecration has been described as the destroyer of all sins;
and for the practitioners, there shall be a feast equal to one-tenth of the number of those consecrated.
Immediately thereafter, one should feed a married woman and a maiden with foods consisting of milk, sugar-candy, and ghee; by this, the accomplishment of the mantra will certainly occur. 4-85.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru preceded by great respect.
In the case of the fire-oblation (homa) and the libation (tarpaṇa), the mantra is "svāhā"; in the case of the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship (pūjana), it is "namaḥ."

Having uttered the name at the end of the mantra, one should then say "I satiate" (tarpayāmi); after that, at the end of "svāhā," the satiation (tarpaṇa) is performed. Now hear from me regarding the consecration (abhiṣeka).
Having uttered the name at the end of the mantra, one should then say the word "I sprinkle";
thereafter, one should perform the feeding of Brahmins to the extent of one-tenth of that [mantra recitation].
Thus, having become one whose mantra is perfected, one shall accomplish all desires;
then, O Maheśānī, one should offer oblations of bilva leaves ten times [the number of recitations]. (4.89)
Moreover, O beautiful one, one may likewise perform oblations with sesame seeds and clarified butter;
then one should give all one's possessions to the guru, or half of that, or half of that again.
Without knowing the goddess Kullukā, without reciting the Guru-pādukā mantra, without properly giving the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and without performing the worship of the Cakra; || 4.91 ||
Whoever should engage in this tantra certainly torments his own self.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
O Supreme Lord, you have explained to me the procedure regarding another’s wife.
O fair-browed one, no sin arises for me in the act of approaching another's wife.
If practitioners touch the wife of another and recite [the mantra], then at that very moment great accomplishment is attained; there is no need for deliberation in this matter. (4.93)
And it is said in the Kālīkalpaprakāśa: "O Maheśvara, O beloved of my heart, give a complete exposition right here. (4.94)
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess of great fortune, you who deliver from calamity;
that which is not to be told, O Great Goddess, is revealed to you out of affection.
In the act of violating another's wife, one incurs the censure of the Vedas;
O Great Goddess, from union with them, the Tāmisra hell shall ensue. (4.96)
Having understood this to be the meaning of the Veda, how should the practitioner act?
"One must never approach another's wife; if one does so, one should recite [the mantra]"—thus says the Veda. (4.97)
Because they would contradict two Vedic injunctions, one should not approach the wives of others;
therefore, O lady of excellent hips, listen as I explain the meaning of the Vedas to you.
The Śrī Devī said: (p. 35) Which Veda is it? From where does it come? Or who is its illuminator?
Who is the author of that Veda? Tell me all of that. 4.99.
The illustrious Bhairava said: "O daughter of the mountain, I know for certain that the single Veda became fourfold—the Yajus, Sāman, Ṛk, and so forth; the Veda is indeed Brahman itself. (4.100)
The Veda proceeds of its own accord; there is no author of it, O beautiful one.
The Lord is self-existent; the Veda was sung by Him as it was in the past.
From Śiva down to the sages, these are the rememberers of this [text], not its authors;
Kṛṣṇa and the other inhabitants of heaven are its revealers. (4.102)
O Maheśānī, that which is propounded by the Vedas is proclaimed as Dharma; its opposite, O beloved, becomes Adharma. (4.103)
O Goddess of the gods, I shall speak of approaching another's wife; that which is prohibited, O Devi, is indeed forbidden, O Maheśvarī, when it is contrary to the Vedic injunctions.

O Great Goddess, if one recites the mantra while contemplating another's wife even in the mind, at that very moment all perfections (siddhis) shall be attained; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Thus, those who know the established doctrine should understand that which is taught in the Tantra: the fruit that arises from being entwined by the great cīna-tree and its creepers. (4.106)
O Goddess of the gods, O you who are worshipped by the deities, there is no fruit in the three worlds that does not exist;
whatever conduct is found in a mantra, such is the dharma therein.
By means of that, one becomes one who has accomplished the goal—attaining either heaven or even liberation.
One should not entertain doubt in this matter; success will certainly come to pass. (4-108)
Therefore, O Goddess of gods, O Maheśvarī, there is no sin for him;
thus, O auspicious one, the best of practitioners should approach the wives of others.
Now I shall further explain the characteristics of mantra-siddhi:
having encapsulated one's own mantra with the *mātṛkā*, the wise practitioner should recite it. (4.110)
By reciting it one hundred times in both direct and reverse order, at the end of that [sequence], one should recite the mantra alone.
In this manner, one should mutter it every day until one hundred thousand [recitations] are completed. (4-111)
"It is certain that mantra-siddhi will be attained," so it has been stated by those who know the tantras;
even through a hundred preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) and likewise through the ritual of application (*prayoga*). (4.112)
O fair-browed one! Even by reciting [the mantra] ten million times for ten million eons, and even by performing a hundredfold worship, success is not attained if the right disposition does not arise.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for Puraścaryā," in the Śrī-Bṛhannīlatantra, within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. || 4 ||
Now begins the fifth chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
The practitioner of mantra, devoted to daily worship, should perform occasional worship;
through occasional worship one attains perfection, and one should perform optional worship without interruption.
For half a month, or a month, or likewise for double or triple that time, the yogi should practice in this manner until he has attained the portion of the fruit. (5.2)
In rites performed for specific signs or for desired objects, the attainment of the fruit extends as far as the maṇḍala;
however, if one does not double [the practice], how could the wise person become a partaker of the fruit? (5-3)
On the eighth and the fourteenth [lunar days], one should worship with diligence;
whatever the mantra-practitioner prays for, that he obtains constantly.
One obtains charming speech; therefore, one should recite [the mantra] on the eighth day.
At the time of midday, the worship of the Goddess bestows accomplishment. (5-5)
O Great Goddess, worship should be performed according to the prescribed rite at dawn;
O Great Goddess, worship is also praised by the wise in the evening.
On the eighth day, the worship of the Goddess bestows the fruit of all desires;
[one should offer] the *rambhā* flower and the *bījapūra*, well-blended with fragrances. (5–7)
Having mixed [the ingredients], one should offer the bali, especially on the eighth day;
one should offer a golden garland to Mahādevī, especially with fragrant perfumes.
One should likewise offer fruit and milk, with an abundance of sugar;
therefore, with every effort, one should worship Śivā for the sake of prosperity.
One should diligently offer fine rice grains and white mustard seeds to the Goddess;
and on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, one should worship her according to the prescribed rule.
One attains the accomplishment of command (*ājñāsiddhi*) by offering *japā* flowers, *varvara*, sandalwood, *arka* flowers, and white *aparājitā*. (5.11)
One should especially offer the *arghya* at all times during daily worship;
the mantra should be recited one hundred and eight times for as long as one lives. (5.12)
But he who would worship Durgā with diligence on the Mahāṣṭamī day shall destroy, at that very moment, the sin accumulated over three lifetimes. (5.13)
Those who recite the Mahāmāyā mantra, having understood Bhairava according to reality, [should offer] honey, milk-rice, milk, clarified butter, and sugar. (5.14)
One should offer the bali-oblation, and indeed the lizard and the liquor (āsava) are praised;
here, the liquor must certainly be offered, especially by a Brāhmaṇa.
"And [regarding] the *āsava*, O Great Goddess, listen with a one-pointed mind, my dear. Śrī Bhairavī said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, [who is proficient] in all the scriptures, traditions, and so forth..."
In what form, O Lord of Gods, should a Brahmin then offer the liquor? (5.16)
Tell me the distinction before me, for it is the most essential of the essential;
abandon all deceit if you have any affection for me. (5.17)
"By whom is this liquor to be drunk, and by whom is it not to be drunk? Tell me.
Is it not to be drunk, O mighty-armed one, or is it to be drunk? Tell me that. (5.18)
O Supreme Lord, O Goddess, since my doubt has been dispelled by this supreme essence of the three crore tantras. (5.19)
Therefore, O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods, I shall proclaim the truth to you here.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O illustrious Goddess, you who have mastered the meaning of all the scriptures.
The supreme reality that you desired to know has been declared by me; listen to it.
"Intoxicating liquor is not to be given, it is not to be drunk, and it is not to be accepted; however, it may be given during the recitation of mantras (japa).
Indeed, liquor is the impurity of living beings, and evil is said to be impurity.
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink liquor. (5.21)
In this regard, O lady of excellent hips, hear about *surā*, which is worshipped by the hosts of gods:
*surā* is to be known as threefold—*gauḍī*, *paiṣṭī*, and likewise *mādhvī*. (5.22)
Indeed, O illustrious lady, these should be drunk by certain of the best of the twice-born:
the fruit of the jackfruit tree, grapes, madhūka, dates, palmyra palm, and sugarcane juice. (5.23)
Honey-wine, *tāla*-wine, *madhvīka*-wine, *maireya*-wine, and that produced from coconut—one should know these to be equal; indeed, there are eleven other types of intoxicants. (5.24)
O Goddess, regarding the ritual of drinking liquor, whose censure is approved?
Listen to the distinction, O Mistress of the Gods; it is revealed out of affection for you. (5-25)
O Great Goddess, that which is prohibited and distinct from the Vedic [practice]—the drinking of wine without having been consecrated by mantra—is for which an expiation is prescribed. (5-26)
Listen, O illustrious goddess, to this captivating account of the past:
in former times, Śukra, the preceptor of the Daityas, performed japa for the sake of attaining perfection. (5.27)

O Great Goddess, even by reciting [the mantra] ten million times over the course of many eons, one will never achieve success unless one drinks the *āsava* while remaining devoted to the daily recitation.
Then, a state of mental intoxication and supreme curiosity arose within him;
he became distracted from his recitation there and remembered his auspicious wife.
Likewise, Urvaśī, the celestial courtesan, having gone there to that delightful place, spoke these words, sweet with all aesthetic flavors, O beautiful one! (5.30)
O Goddess of the gods, Urvaśī took her pleasure with Śukra;
from that union, the birth of Śukra occurred, and thereafter knowledge was born.
Having realized the truth, Śukra then cursed the excellent *āsava*;
by that curse, O Goddess of the Gods, the excellent *āsava* was cursed. (5.32)
From that time forward, O Goddess, it did not lead to success;
thus, O Mistress of the Gods, a hundred years passed by in this manner, my dear.
Then that blessed goddess Kālī, who is the very embodiment of Time, spoke these words with reverence to the preceptor of the Daityas.
Listen, my child, to these weighty words; attend to them with careful attention.
O illustrious one, how was the vital breath, so difficult even for the gods to attain, cursed?
Śrī Śukra said:
