O Sovereign of all, O Mistress of all beings, O You who are encompassed by all beings, O Śivā who are saluted by Brahmā, Īśa, and Viṣṇu—I bow to You eternally. (5.36)
O Goddess who is the source of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, O embodiment of compassion; O Goddess who bestows knowledge upon the ignorant, protect me, who have come to you for refuge! (5.37)
O Great Goddess, you are the savior here at the arrival of the full [age] of the Yuga;
O Mother of Viṣṇu, you are the giver of knowledge to us—salutations be to you! (5.38)
You are Śrī, you are Sāvitrī, and you are Satī, O Sovereign of the Gods! O Primordial One, O First, O Source of all, O Mother of the Universe—salutations be unto you!
O Auspicious One, whose nature is auspiciousness, O Terrible One, treasury of all knowledge, O Blessed One!
Be gracious, O Omniscient One, who reveals all mantras. (5.40)
"Be gracious to us, O Goddess, you who consist of compassion for all beings!
Thus, Mahākālī Karālinī was praised with this hymn.
Having first prostrated like a staff, he spoke again these weighty words:
"O Bhairavī, hear the reason why the liquor was cursed by me."
"O Great Goddess, having drunk the liquor, no success has arisen for me.
Therefore, O Maheśānī, I am cursed; hear everything that has been said. (5.43)
That great virtuous lady Kālī, whose nature is Time itself, spoke as if smiling toward Śukra, the preceptor of the Daityas.
The gods were invited, yet the supreme nectar so difficult to obtain was not drunk;
for that very reason, O handsome one, success has not been achieved by you.
The expiation for drinking liquor when invited is prescribed,
O auspicious lady, whether it be in an iron vessel, or likewise in one of gold or silver.
A Brāhmaṇa who possesses the Vedas may drink the auspicious Vāruṇī;
he may also drink heated liquor, for otherwise he shall not attain success.
Thus has this divine and supreme account of the essence been told to you;
she is, in due order, unfit to be drunk, forbidden, and likewise unfit to be smelled.
And that goddess who is other than Vaidha is indeed ungraspable;
therefore, in the rite of recitation, she should be known as the goddess considered to be the bestower of success.
O Maheśānī, the three kinds of liquor may be offered by members of all castes;
or else, for the sake of those who have consumed liquor, one should give molasses and fresh ginger.
One should diligently offer buttermilk mixed with jaggery to the Goddess;
or one may pour coconut water, or honey, into a vessel of bell-metal or copper.
With the Tārā mantra and likewise with that of Kālī,
one should offer an extremely captivating *āsava* liquor as a substitute during this full ritual procedure.
The best of those who know mantras should offer oblations of rambhā fruit and śāla fish;
having attained all supernatural powers (siddhi) in succession, he shall finally attain liberation (mokṣa). || 5.53 ||
By the oblation of bilva leaves with clarified butter, the world comes under one's control;
by a thousand oblations, O Goddess of Gods, one attains the highest perfection.

On the great eighth day (mahāṣṭamī), on a day of the week corresponding to his family (kulavāra), and especially on the eighth and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight, the practitioner obtains charming speech.
Therein lies the worship of the Yoginīs, the practice, and the worship of the Kula;
just as Viṣṇu, when worshipped on his own lunar day, bestows all that is desired.
Likewise, when the lunar day (tithi) corresponds to one's own family lineage (kulatithi), Śakti, when worshipped, bestows boons;
especially so on the day of one's own planetary week-day (kulavāra), as well as on the fourteenth and the eighth days of the lunar fortnight.
A conch filled with water, a hibiscus flower and *barbara* grass, sandalwood, an *arka* flower, and white *aparājitā* [are required]. (5-58)
The offering of water for the feet (arghya) is especially prescribed as the sequence for daily worship;
it should be recited one hundred and eight times for as long as one lives. (5.59)
O Dear One, one should recite the mantra a thousand times during the ritual of daily worship;
the Mahoprāyas should always be honored, and in the act of worship, the supreme Kullukā is to be worshipped.
Listen, O beloved, to the performance of hymns, mantras, vows, and so forth;
through the non-performance of that [initiation], all of it becomes fruitless. (5–61)
Whoever worships the Great Vidyā of Sundarī and Vāsudeva obtains all that fruit and shall attain union with Hari. (5.62)
Vāsudeva, Hari, Brahmā, and Tāriṇī Prakṛti are always one single form; they should always be meditated upon as a single form, for they abide eternally as a single form.
The Goddess bestows heaven and liberation; she grants wealth and knowledge.
She increases wealth, knowledge, fame, fortune, longevity, and health. (5-64)
Therefore, one should worship that goddess with perfumes, flowers, and incenses;
one should always worship Tāriṇī with various food offerings and with devotion. (5–65)
In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should perform the reclining; in Siṃha, the turning over;
and in Āśvina, one should awaken the Goddess with offerings of milk-rice for the nourishment of the cattle.
O beautiful goddess, a boon is obtained through the purifying rite at night;
it is never so during the day, whether in a state of wakefulness or even in a dream.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, specifically on the Ghaṭāṣṭamī, the wise man should worship the jar and the Moon during the night in the month of Māgha.
O Great Goddess, the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) is where unsurpassed accomplishment is found;
among all sacred seats, Kāmarūpa is the supreme seat, yielding great fruit.
In that regard, O Maheśvarī, if worship is performed even once, I shall dwell within the body of that person, having abandoned all other sacred seats (pīṭhas). (5.70)
Therefore, the Kāmākhyā-yonimaṇḍala is said to be a hundred times superior to those;
O Maheśānī, how could I possibly describe its fruit?
There, the primordial Tāriṇī dwells together with those who possess ten million-fold merits;
my seat is the mouth of Brahmā, secret and bestowing all happiness.
Since the gods, the Vedas,
and even the sages are all born of this being and manifest from it, you must always keep it protected.
O Maheśvarī, that seat (*pīṭha*) which is of two kinds must be protected— the manifest and the secret;
the secret is more meritorious than the manifest and is difficult to attain.
By the lowest of practitioners [the best, according to the reading in manuscript kha]. || 5-74 ||
O Kulasaundarī, it is found hidden everywhere in every land, O Mistress of the Gods.
O Bhairavī, in connection with the *pīṭhas*, listen now to the *pīṭhas*, O Mistress of the Gods. (5–75)
Listen, O highly wise one, to those most excellent places which bestow success upon the virtuous and have been frequented by the great. (5.76)
Puṣkara and the sacred field of Gayā, as well as Akṣayavaṭa, Varāhaparvata, and the auspicious Amarakaṇṭaka. || 5.77 ||
O beloved, [these are] the Narmadā, Yamunā, Piṅgā, Gaṅgādvāra,
as well as the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, Kuśāvarta, and Bilvaka.
And likewise Śrī Nīlaparvata, as well as Kalamba and Kubjaka;
Bhṛgutuṅga (an alternative reading is Bhṛgubhraṅga), Kedāra,
and Sarvapriya Mahālaya.
Lalitā, Sugandhā, the beloved city of Śākambharī,
Kaṇatīrtha, Mahāgaṅgā, and Tilikāśrama.
And [the places called] Kumāra and Prabhāsa, as well as Dhanyā and Sarasvatī;
Agastya’s hermitage is dear to me, and beyond that, the hermitage of Kāṇva.
The beautiful and beloved Kāmodaka, preceded by the Kauśikī, Sarayū, Śoṇa, Jyotis, and Sara lakes, as well as the lovely Uttaramānasa.
Mataṅgavāpī, Saptārcis, the great Viṣṇupada, the great holy site of Vaidyanātha, and the beloved mountain Kālañjara. || 5.83 ||
Vāmoccheda, Haroccheda, Gargoccheda, Mahānala,
the great sacred ford Bhadreśvara, and Lakṣmaṇoccheda as well.
Know that the Kāverī, beloved by the gods, has waters like those of the Kapilā;
there is Someśvara, Śuklatīrtha, and the source where the Kṛṣṇaveṇī flows forth.
Pāṭalā, Mahābodhi, Nāgatīrtha, Madantikā, the meritorious Rāmeśvara, O Goddess, and likewise Meghavana of Hari. (5.86)
Aila, Ramaṇaka, and the very dear Govardhana; Hariścandra, Puraścandra, and the very dear Pṛthūdaka.
Indranīla, Mahānāda, and likewise Priyamena;
Pampā lake, Pañcavaṭī, and the Vaṭī mountain. || 5.88 ||
Gaṅgābilva, Prāsaṅga, Priyanāda, Vaṭa,
Gaṅgāvāmācala, and likewise Ṛṇamocana.
And Gautameśvara-tīrtha, as well as Vasiṣṭha-tīrtha,
likewise Hārītaka, O Goddess, and Brahmāvarta, which bestows auspiciousness.
Kuśāvarta, the most excellent, and likewise Haṃsatīrtha;
the famous Piṇḍāvakaraṇa and likewise Haridvāra. || 5.91 ||
Likewise, O beloved, there are Badarītīrtha and Vāmatīrtha, as well as Jayanta and Vijayanta, which bestow all auspiciousness.
Vijayā, Śāradātīrtha, and likewise Bhadrakālīśvara;
the highly renowned Aśvatīrtha, and Vedaśiras, which is dear [to him].
The river Oghavatī, the sacred ford Atripada, the Chāgaliṅga, the Mātṛgaṇa, and likewise Karavīrapura. || 5.94 ||
The holy ford of Saptagodāvara bestows the fruits of all dharmas;
so too do Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, Durgā, and Dvārāvatī of Hari.
Vidyāpura, Avantī, Kāñcī, Maṅgalakoṭaka [with alternative readings: Śakulakoṭhara, Nakulakoṭhara, or Maṅgalakuṭṭaka];
Kālīghaṭṭa, Guptatīrtha, and the one called Siddha [with the alternative reading: Liṅga].
The deluder of all. || 5-96 ||
Kirīṭa, Uttarātīrtha, the supreme Dakṣiṇātīrtha, Viśālātīrtha, Kālī’s grove, and likewise Vṛndāvana. (5.97)
O beautiful one, know that Jvālāmukhī, Hiṅgulā, Mahātīrtha, and Gaṇeśvara are the causal sites for all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). 5-98.
Here, all the gods, great seers, ancestors, and those who are devoted to yoga and intent upon spiritual perfection are eternally present.
O Dear One, the tasks of those possessed of faith and devotion are swiftly accomplished;
whoever recites this during an auspicious time, their merit shall become inexhaustible. (5.100)
Whoever recites this at the time of a śrāddha ceremony, or even listens to it with devotion,
that speech shall become inexhaustible, and it will bring supreme happiness to the ancestors.

Whoever recites [the mantra] in this place—[the reading is either "peṭhedyastu" or "japedyastu"]—attains accomplishment at that very moment. Now, O Maheśānī, I shall speak of where each deity resides; listen. (5–102)
Listen as I shall recount those names which belong to you;
I am submerged in the ocean of the nectar of your story, which is supreme bliss.
Puṣkarā is at Puṣkara, Kamalākṣī at Gayā, and Gayeśvarī at Gayā; Akṣayā is at Akṣayavaṭa, and Amareśā at Amarakaṇṭaka.
On Mount Varāha you are Vārāhī, the beloved of the Earth;
you are Durmadā in the Narmadā, and Kālindī in the waters of the Yamunā.
Śivāmṛtā is in Gaṅgā, Ambā in Tilikāśrama,
Kaumārī in Kumāradhāma, and Surapūjitā in Prabhāsa.
In Kāśī she is Annapūrṇā, and in Draviḍa she is Sarasvatī;
likewise, she is Mahāvidyā and Mattamedhā in Agastya’s hermitage.
Kauśikī is her beloved name; she is Kauśikā at Amṛtakauśika (or, according to another reading, Ghṛtakauśika);
she is Śāradā on the bank of the Sarayū, and Kanakeśvarī on the Śoṇa. || 5.108 ||
O Goddess, by virtue of self-luminosity, she is Jyotiṣmatī here at the confluence;
likewise, she is Śrīvahā on Śrīgiri and Kālī in Kāloda. (5.109)
O Great Queen! Mahābuddhi is at Uttaramānasa, Mātaṅgī is at Mataṅga, and Guptārcis is at Viṣṇupādaka.
Svargaṅgā is on the path to heaven, Gaveśvarī is in the Godāvarī,
Vimukti is in the Gomati, and Mahābalā is through the power of the Brahmins.
Śataprabhā, Śatarūpā, and Candrabhāgā are indeed there;
and at Siddhitīraka, the one named Īrā is the bestower of success in Airāvatī.
At Dakṣapañcanada you are proclaimed as Dakṣiṇā;
at Oujisa you are Vīryadā, and at the confluence of sacred fords you are Saṅgamā.
You are the Bāhudā flowing through Kurukṣetra, the one who watches over it;
you are the ascetic, most meritorious Bhāratī, in the hermitage of Bharata. (5.114)
She is Sukathā in the Naimiṣa forest, Ananā among the Pāṇḍavas,
Viśālākṣī in Viśālā, and Śivātmikā on Muṇḍapṛṣṭha.
Śraddhā is at the Kanakhala holy ford; Śuddhabuddhi is with the Lord of Sages; Suveśā and Sumanā are with Gaurī; and [Gaurī] is at the Mānasa lake. (5.116)
Mahānandā is in Nandāpura; Lalitā is in Lalitāpura;
Brahmāṇī, the destroyer of great sins, is on the head of Brahmā.
Pūrṇimā is always the beloved who sprinkles [the world] with Indumatī and others;
at the confluence of the Jāhnavī, you are Tṛpti and Svadhā, who grant satisfaction to the ancestors.
Puṇyāhā is at Veṇuvatī, Pāpanāśinī is at the water-shed (prapā), Śaṅkhasaṃhāriṇī, Ghorarūpā, and Mahodarī [are likewise located there]. (5.119)
At the destruction of Garga is Mahārātri, powerful in the great forest;
she is Bhadrā, Bhadrakālī, and Bhadreśvarī, the beloved of the Lord.
At Bhadreśvara is Ramā, the beloved of Viṣṇu; likewise at Viṣṇupada is Dāruṇā; and at the confluence of the Narmadā is Kapileśvarī on the Kāverī. (5.121)
She is Bhedinī at the confluence of the Kṛṣṇaveṇī, Śubhavāsinī at the confluence,
Śuddhā at the Śuklatīrtha, and likewise Prabhā at Rāmeśvara.
At Mahābodhi she is Mahābuddhi; at Pāṭala she is Pāṭaleśvarī; at Surasā and Nāgatīrtha she is Nāgeśī, who is worshipped by the nāgas.
Madantī, Madantī, Pramadā, and Madantikā;
Merusvanā [Meghabalā, with "Maghavane" as an alternative reading], Meghavane, Vidyut, and Saudāminīcchaṭā. (5-124)
At Rāmeśvara she is Mahāsiddhi; at Cailāpura she is Satī;
at Priyāramaṇaka she is Durgā; and at Surasundarī she is Suveśā. (5.125)
Kātyāyanī is the great goddess, and likewise Ambikā is at Govardhana;
Śubheśvarī is at Hariścandra, and Pureśvarī is in Puraścandra.
In Pṛthūdaka she is Mahāvega; in Menāka she is Akhilavardhinī;
in Indranīla she is Mahākāntā; and in Ratnaveśa she is Suśobhanā.
Māheśvarī is at Mahānāda; she of great splendor and great strength is at Pampāsaras;
Śāraṅgā is at Pañcavaṭī; and Tapasvinī is at Pañcavaṭī.
At Vaṭīparvata she is Surangiṇī, together with her five attendants;
at the confluence of the Vindhya-saṅgā she is Vindhyaśrī and Vindhyavāsinī.
On the banks of the Nanda you are Mahānandā; on the mountain where the Gaṅgā flows, you are Śivā; in Āryāvarta you are Mahāryā; and at Ṛṇamocana, you are Vimukti.
Cāmuṇḍā is at Aṭṭahāsa, the Mistress of Tantra at Gautameśvara;
she is Vedamayī, the Knowledge of Brahman, at Vāśiṣṭha, while Arundhatī is at Amarakaṇṭaka. (5.131)
In Hārīta she is Hariṇākṣī, and in Brahmāvarta she is Vrateśvarī;
she is Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī, and in Kuśāvarta she is Kuśapriyā.
Haṃsīśvarī is at Haṃsatīrtha, and she is also known as Parahaṃsīśvarī; at Piṇḍāvakaraṇa, she is Dhanyā, Surasā, and Sukhadāyinī. (5.133)
She is indeed Nārāyaṇī and Vaiṣṇavī at Gaṅgādvāra, the bestower of liberation;
she is Śrīvidyā at the sacred ford of Badarī and Mahādhṛti at Vāmatīrtha.
When [the moon] is in the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, you are Jayantī; when it is in Viśākhā, you are Aparājitā.
When it is in Uttarāṣāḍhā, you are Mahāśuddhi; and when it is in Śravaṇā, you are Śāradā.
Subhadrā at Bhadradā, Bhavyā likewise at Bhadrakālīśvara;
Mahābhadre is Bhadrakālī, and Girīśvarī is at Hayatīrtha.
She is the giver of the Vedas, the mother of the Vedas, the mistress of the Vedas, and at the pinnacle of the Vedas;
she is the one of great heroism in the Oghavatī and the one of great prosperity in the Mahānadī.
Caṇḍā is at Atripada, and Balipriyā is at Chāgaliṅga; Jaganmātā is at Mātṛdarśa, and Satī is at Karavīrapura.
Malinī, Raṅgiṇī, Vāmā, Paramā, Parameśvarī,
Devaśīrṣā, and Akhileśvarī are at the sacred ford of Saptagodāvara.
In Ayodhyā she is Bhavānī, the bestower of victory and the auspiciousness of victory;
and in Mathurā she is Mādhavī, Devakī, the sovereign of the Yādavas.
Vṛndā, Gopeśvarī, Rādhā, she who delights in the rasa of the Vṛndāvana forest;
Kātyāyanī, Mahāmāyā, Bhadrakālī, and Kalāvatī. (5.141)
Candramālā, Mahāśānti, the sovereign of the great yoginīs, Vajreśvarī, Yaśodā, the glory of Vraja, and the mistress of Gokula. (5.142)
In Kāñcī she is Kanakakāñcī; in Avantī she is Atipāvanī; in Vidyāpura she is Vidyā; and on Mount Nīla she is Vimalā. (5.143)
Vimalā is at Rājeśa, Śvetagaṅgeśī is at Puruṣottama,
Virajā is at Yāgapurī, and Bhadrakarṇikā is at Bhadreśa.
In Tamolipta, she is Tamoghnī Svāhā; at the confluence of the ocean, she is Kulaśrī, Vaṃśavṛddhi, Mādhavī, and the beloved of Mādhava. (5.145)
Maṅgalā is at Maṅgalakoṭa; Maṅgalacaṇḍikā is at Rāḍha;
Jvālāmukhī is at Śivapīṭha; and Bhuvaneśvarī is at Mandāra.
Guhyakālī is at Kālīghaṭṭa, and Maheśvarī is at Kirīṭa;
the Great Goddess Kirīṭeśvarī is at Kirīṭa, and Liṅgavāhinī is at the place called Liṅga.
He is manifest everywhere for his devotees, but never so for those who are not devotees. Now, O beautiful one, I shall further describe the places of spiritual accomplishment (siddhisthāna).
Those places of accomplishment (*siddhisthāna*) which have been fashioned here by Śiva for the purpose of destroying all evils and bestowing all supernatural powers (*siddhi*). (5.149)
Having heard that which is to be meditated upon in the mind as manifest among those who hold authority,
O Lord, at the great seat (mahāpīṭha) of Amareśa, there is the one known as Oṃkāra.
Therein, the two named Durgās are Caṇḍikā and Maheśvarī;
and at Prabhāsa, Somanātha, and other sites, there is the goddess Puṣkarekṣaṇā.
Śambhu, the lord of the gods of gods, and Maheśvara are in Naimiṣa;
there also is the goddess Prajñā, Bhavānī, who bears the linga.
In Puṣkara is Puruhūtā Maheśvarī, who has the fragrance of royalty;
on Śrīparvata is the one named Priyā, and Śaṅkara, the destroyer of Tripura.
There, at the great sacred site of Japyeśvara, Māyā is Śaṅkarī, who grants all desires to her devotees; she is both Śaṅkarī and the wielder of the trident.
There is Triśūla, Śaṅkara, the liberator from all sins;
in Āmrātakapura is Sūkṣma, and the Supreme Goddess is known as Sūkṣmā. (5.155)
In Mahākāla there is Mahākāla, and Maheśvarī is Mahākālī;
in the center is Śiva, and everywhere is Śarvāṇī, the Supreme Goddess.
At Kedāreśvara, the Lord is Īśāna; the Goddess is Sanmārgadāyinī.
At Bhairava, the Lord is Bhairava Śambhu; the Goddess is Parameśvarī Bhairavī. (5.157)
In Gaṇakṣetra, I am Śiva named Maṅgala, the great-grandfather;
in Kurukṣetra, I am Śiva Sthāṇu, and Śivā is the supreme Sthāṇupriyā.
Svayambhū is considered the goddess at Iṣṭalābha, and she is regarded as Svāyambhavā;
Ugra is proclaimed [to reside] at Kanakhala, while Śivogrā is the beloved of Śiva.
In Vimaleśvara, she is Viśvastā, Viśvā, and always Viśvapriyā;
in Aṭṭahāsa, she is Mahānanda, Mahānandā, and Maheśvarī.
Mahāntaka and Mahendrā, as well as Mahāntakā and Pārvatī;
Bhīmeśvara in the Bhīma-pīṭha, and likewise Śivā and Bhīmeśvarī.
On Vastrapāda she is named Bhavā, Bhavānī, and Bhuvaneśvarī;
on Adrikūṭa she is Mahāyoginī, Rudrāṇī, and Parameśvarī. (5.162)
In Avimukta is Mahādeva and the supreme Śivā Viśālākṣī;
likewise, in Mahālaya is Hara Rudra and the highly fortunate Śivā.
And at Gokarṇa, Mahābala is to be known as Śiva, and Caṇḍikā as Bhadrā (according to another reading).
At Bhadravarṇa, Mahādeva is present, and likewise Bhadrā and Karṇikā.
In Suvarṇākhyā, O Thousand-eyed One, is Utpalā, the Supreme Goddess;
at Sthāṇusaṅga is Śiva as Sthāṇviśvara, and the auspicious Śivā is Sthāṇvīśvarā. (5.165)
In the abode of Kamalā (the Lotus), the Great Lord Maheśvara is the lotus-eyed one;
the Great Goddess Maheśānī is the lotus-eyed one, the bestower of all goals. (5.166)
In Chagalāṇḍa is Kapardin and Prasara, the Great Goddess Maheśvarī;
in Dviraṇḍa is Ūrdhvaretas and the Supreme Goddess known as Sandhyā.
In the place called Mākoṭa, Mahākoṭa and Śivā are Muṇḍakeśvarī;
and in the Maṇḍaleśvara-pīṭha, Śaṅkara and Śivā are Khāṇḍavī.
At Kālañjara, Nīlakaṇṭha is considered to be Hara and Kālī is Śivā;
at Sthāṇvīśvara, the Supreme Goddess is known by the name Sthalā. (5.169)
In the illustrious city of Vyāghrapura, the presiding lord of the assembly was Śiva himself, known by the name Dhara;
there, Śaṅkara dances under the title "Sabhāpati."
There, the Goddess of Gods beholds the Lord of Gods dancing in the great ocean of bliss, which is filled with the supreme joy of the bliss of the Self.
Where Mahādeva swiftly becomes the bestower of boons upon his devotees;
where, by beholding the Lord of Gods dancing, the world is liberated. (5.172)
Among all sacred places of merit, this place is the most excellent;
for indeed, all actions performed here become truly inexhaustible.
In this most excellent place, there is a wonderful tank named Śivagaṅgā;
on its southern bank, the Lord dances.
Dwelling by this pond, having bathed and beheld the Lord of the Assembly,
one should, endowed with faith, recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times.
Those deities whom you have mentioned here always abide here,
as do the ancestors, the Siddhas, the Gandharvas, and the Siddhis that bestow all accomplishments.
Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, recited as a mantra, or used for bathing here bestows imperishable merit;
having worshipped with whatever name has been proclaimed, one should perform these acts.
By [worshipping] from the Praṇava to the end of the Hṛdaya-mantra, one obtains the highest desired object;
he who feeds Brāhmaṇas here enjoys inexhaustible fruit. (5.178)
Having enjoyed various pleasures here, one shall go to the city of Hara-Gaurī;
for the destruction of grief and suffering, the Lord is a treasure-house of compassion. (5.179)
He fashioned fields of merit upon the earth for the sake of all prosperity,
through many purifications of merit and practices performed over many ages.

The residence of the believers shall be here; the means is the sacred revelation (*śruti*)—[an alternative reading is *rati* (delight)—therefore, the best of men should strive with effort to practice the means here. (5.181)
Now listen, O lady of beautiful limbs, to the seat that is lovely in every part;
know, O Supreme Goddess, this seat of mine to be composed of a rosary of beads. (5.182)
O Maheśvarī, that wherein all tasks are accomplished is the abode of Śaṅkara and of Viṣṇu, whose wisdom is unfathomable; it is the locus of his activity.
Indeed, there is also swift grace from other gods who dwell at your feet; in that regard, my joy is supreme.
"O beloved, I shall tell you about the supreme [rosary] consisting of akṣa beads, in which there is the presence of all the gods, beginning with Brahmā. (5.185)
O beloved, whatever place has been adorned by us or by the great ones, each of those is declared to be most excellent and bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
O beloved, wherever great beings reside and accomplish the supreme state, each such place is most excellent and bestows all that is auspicious.
Amareśapura and likewise the city of Asurāntaka—
each of those is a most excellent place that bestows all spiritual perfections upon men.
O beloved, whatever place has been adorned by virtuous and chaste women—
the seat of Ambikā and likewise the city of Ananta— is exceedingly so.
You know the city of Aniruddha, as well as the supreme city of Aditi,
the city of Aṇimā and the others, and the supreme city of Aśvamedha.
The great seat of Annapūrṇā, as well as the city called Aṃbuja;
the Ādi-pīṭha and Ānanda-pīṭha, and Cāmoda, Vādi, and Sūkara. (5.191)
Āśusiddhipura and Yathādyantapura as the mouth;
Akampādityapīṭha and the two seats of Ādyādinātha. (5.192)
O beloved, there is the city named iṣṭa, as well as Indirāpura; and Ilodayagiri, and Ilāntendupura. (5.193)
Indrāṇī and Indreśvara, as well as Indrānandapura; the city named Induvatī and likewise the city Induvijaya.
O Goddess, the union of the Lord and the Mistress, as well as Īśānanda and the city of Īśvarī,
and the city of Aiśa for Īśānī— this is declared to be the supreme sacred seat (pīṭha).
Kāmarūpa, Priya, Vārāṇasī, and Naipāla; Pauṇḍravardhana-pīṭha, Paurakya, and Kānyakubjaka. (5.196)
Puṇyādri, Arbuda, Ekāgra, Āmrātakeśvara,
Trisrotas [Traipura according to the Kha manuscript], Kāmakoṭa, and likewise the excellent Bhṛgupura;
Kailāsapīṭha, Kedāra, and the auspicious Candrapura.
And likewise Śrīpura, Kanyāpura, and Jālandhara.
Mālava, Bilvapīṭha, and Kulānta (variant reading: Kha), as well as Devīkoṭa;
Gokarṇa, Māruteśa, and likewise Aṭṭahāsa. || 5-199 ||
The lineage named Kollāna, and Elāpura which is very dear, as well as Mahāpathapura and Oṃkārapura. || 5-200 ||
Jayada and Jayapura, as well as Ujjayinīpura,
Haridrāpīṭhaka, and the beloved Kṣīrapura, which is dear.
Gajāhvaya-pura, Uḍḍīśa-pura,
Prayāga, and likewise Ṣaṣṭhī-pura, which bestows auspiciousness.
Māyāpura, the most excellent city, and Saurabheśvara; Parameśvara, Jaleśvara, Śrīśaila, Merupīṭha, and the great mountain Malaya.
And the seat of Mahendrapura, as well as the beloved Balipura,
the seat of Hiraṇyapura, and likewise Mahālakṣmīpura.
"O beloved goddess, having recognized Caṇḍīpuram as most excellent, as well as Chāyāpura—this sacred seat (pīṭha)—reveal it among my devotees. (5.205)
Lift up these worlds from their connection with me—worlds scorched by the fire of saṃsāra and tossed about by the wind of anxiety. (5.206)
O beloved, sprinkle me and uplift me, consecrating me with your compassion that rains down nectar!
O dear one, there is great merit, and there is also great fame and happiness.
There is great favor toward the people, my delight in protecting the world, my association with them, my conversation with them, my festival for them, and my grace toward them. (5.208)
My action, my relationship, my name, my contemplation, my story, my meditation, my absorption, and my worship. (5.209)
Beholding me, becoming one with me, my thought, my devotion, and praise;
singing of me, dancing in my city, and indeed exerting oneself in my service. (5.210)
Truly, let them know me as Manu, the Manava; let them have devotion to me and a longing for what is dear to me.
By this alone, one shall have achieved his purpose and become a partaker of my grace. (5.211)
Whatever one desires at sacred fords and seats, that beloved object one quickly obtains;
moreover, by the mere reception of my mantra, one becomes free from sin. (5.212)
Through practice, one attains accomplishment in the sacred fields (*siddhakṣetra*) without delay;
my grace is indeed the supreme cause for my satisfaction. (5.213)
I know not what becomes of him who, having taken [it], does not worship it;
even the celestial wish-granting tree (kalpavṛkṣa) that has descended to heaven does not indeed grant desires. || 5-214 ||
If one does not rely upon that which is its root, O beloved, what fault is there for him?
Even if a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) is in his house, he has no desire for it whatsoever. (5.215)
What fault is there in that, for by means of effort all ritual actions are accomplished?
Therefore, regarding that which has been told to you, effort therein yields fruit. (5.216)
"Without effort, what might not be achieved? I do not know, O friend Vijayā!
All sacred fords are present here; this sun is the sacrificial fire. (5.217)
The stars, the moon, the light, the clouds, and the water itself;
the earth, the other planets, as well as the cardinal and intermediate directions. (5.218)
Tulasī, the Brāhmaṇas, and the many Purāṇas, as well as the Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas—these are the essence of the eternal Dharma. (5.219)
Those who take refuge in me with devotion and unfailing faith have various means that serve as constant causes for their own protection. (5.220)
Nevertheless, alas, they do not strive [for virtue], yet they desire such evil; for those who seek that [power], what indeed would they not do to appease the king's wrath? (5.221)
And likewise, the experience of pleasure and pain from one place to another;
similarly, the attainment and non-attainment of objects, as well as day and night. (5.222)
The enjoyment of sensory contact and the perception of the pure and the impure;
action performed with effort and without effort; the great ocean that is both filled and unfilled. (5.223)
One may have a body that has eaten or not eaten, be well-dressed or poorly dressed, speak kindly or unkindly, and be far away or indeed near. (5.224)

Happiness and suffering, as well as various pleasant and unpleasant karmic results, the increase and decrease of all things, and the emergence and dissolution of bodies—[all these arise from karma]. (5.225)
The stability and destruction of riches, the decay and persistence of fragrances, and the entire progression of age, youth, and physical forms. (5.226)
Even while seeing, the ignorant do not see, whereas the wise always see;
therefore, every mantra consists of faith, for faith indeed bestows the accomplishment of one's being.
He who has an intention toward us acts accordingly toward us;
therefore, the virtuous should proceed with great care upon the path of the good. (5.228)
"Even through negligence, one should not [stray] onto the path of the unwholesome by means of the vision of knowledge.
Having thus reflected upon everything according to its true meaning with an intelligent mind, O wise one, [one should act accordingly]. (5-229)
Practice your own beloved dharma and carry out your pure vows;
let them come into my presence through service to my lotus feet. (5.230)
May they sport with the waters and attain supreme bliss;
O high-minded one, listen to this news through these instructions of mine. (5.231)
"O most beloved one, by your grace these worlds shall become wise;
O daughter of the mountain, hear here your dear names. (5.232)
You are Kāmeśā in Kāmarūpa; you are Pūrṇā in Kāśī, the bestower of liberation;
you are Puṇyadā in Nepāla, the meritorious one; and you are Suveśā in Pauṇḍravardhana.
Dharmabuddhi and Sudhā are indeed the givers of happiness and the liberators from sin;
Paurakyā is supreme bliss, while Brahmāṇī resides in Kānyakubja. (5.234)
On Mount Puṇya she is Mahāpuṇyā; at Pūrṇa she is Yajñaphaleśvarī;
at Arbuda, O Goddess, she is Kātyāyanī, the giver of wealth, and the beloved of Śiva. (5.235)
And Ekā resides in the region of Ekāmraka as Surūpeśāmrakeśvarī;
in Tripura she is Sundarī, possessing a divine form that captivates the hearts of all. (5.236)
At the great seat (pīṭha) of Kāmakoṭi is Pramadā, who is languid with passion;
she is Kāmeśvarī and Rati, while at Bhṛgupurī she is Vrajeśvarī.
Vṛkṣeśā is the Fortune of Austerity, Bhuvaneśvarī is in Kailāsa;
Varadā is in Kedāra, and Amṛtā is white in Candrapura.
Kalāvatī and Prabheshā are the beloved Śrī-Ramā in Śrīpura;
Kumārī and Brahmacaryā are in Kanyakāpura. (5.239)
In the great sacred seat (pīṭha) of Jālandhara, there is the auspicious Nāgarī Agnimukhī;
she is Jvālāmukhī, Lolajihvā, Suveśā, and Suraṅgiṇī.
In Mālava is Mahāvidyā, and in Bilvapīṭha is Rūpiṇī;
the Great Goddess Rūpavatī is in Devīkoṭa, and Akhileśvarī is in [Devīkoṭa]. (5.241)
In Gokarṇa, the dear seat, you are Rudrāṇī, the all-auspicious one;
and in Pavana, the seat of Hara, you are Gandhaśrī and Sugandhikā.
At the great seat Aṭṭahāsa are Bhīmakālī and Kālikā;
at Viraja is Muktihetu; salutations to Sudhāmayī, who brings well-being. (5.243)
Jayaśrī and Rājalakṣmī are at Rājaparvata;
Suveśā is at Elāpura; Mahāsampat is at Māheśvarī on the Great Path (Mahāpatha).
Gāyatrī is the form of Brahman, and her seat is the syllable Om;
the goddess Jayā resides in Jayapura, the bestower of victory and the auspiciousness of victory.
Vijayā, Maṅgalā, and Gaurī are always Śivā in Ujjayinī;
Gaurīśvarī, the Great Goddess, and Śivā are at the Hāradrā-pīṭha.
Kṣīrapīṭha, Yugādyā, Kṣīrā, Niyamaprabhā, Rājeśvarī, Mahālakṣmī, and she who dwells in Hastināpura. (5.247)
Kamalā, Vimalā, and Bhakti are on Mount Nīla;
Yāgeśvarī is at Triveṇī, and Triḥsrotas, whose form is Brahman, is there as well.
O Dear One, Kāmadhenu is in Sindhu, and Ṣaṣṭhī is in Ṣaṣṭhipura.
Māyā is the goddess in Māyāpura; Surabhī is in Saurabheśvara. || 5-249 ||
Vilāsinī is at Mahānanda on Mount Priyacandana;
Mahāvrajeśvarī is the most excellent at the Śamaneśvara seat.
Bhavānī is devoted to Bhava on Śrīśaila,
while she who is the beloved of Śiva is the goddess Svargalakṣmī on the Kanakāmara mountain.
Umā, Gaurī, Satī, Satyā, Pārvatī on the Himavat mountain;
Indreśvarī, the one worshipped by the gods, and Jagadīśvarī in Māhendra. (5.252)
Allābhogeśvarī is the eternal Śivā in the illustrious city of Vali;
Suvarṇā, Kanakā, and Vāmā reside in the sacred seat of Hiraṇyapura. (5.253)
Mahālakṣmī is Maheśānī; Ambikā is in Mahālakṣmīpura;
in Caṇḍīpura she is Pracaṇḍā, and Śivā is Caṇḍā and Caṇḍavatī. (5.254)
At Kālīghaṭṭa, the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha), there are Chatrā, Meghasvanā, Māyā, Chatreśvarī, as well as Kālī, who is the very soul of Time (kālātmikā). || 5-255 ||
The Vidyā Bhairavī is at Liṅgākhya, and Vijayā is on the bank of the Jāhnavī.
Thus has this divine sequence of the sacred seats (pīṭhakrama) been declared to you. (5.256)
O Maheśānī, worshipped by the gods (or, according to another reading, "honored by the hosts of deities"), this which is extremely secret has been told;
O Maheśānī, make it manifest to my devotees.
"By the power of their good fortune alone,
O auspicious Śivā, my dearest beloved, that which was not to be told has been spoken by me from my own mouth."
"O beautiful one, everything that is the most essential of the essential has been told to you.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Occasional Worship, the Sacred Seats (Pīṭhas), and Their Goddesses," in the Śrī-Bṛhannīlatantra, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
The Holy Goddess said:
O Blessed One, knower of all phenomena, skilled in all treatises,
I now wish to hear about worship and the worship of the family.

"O Bhairava, by performing what does the heroic practitioner (sādhaka) immediately attain liberation? If there is but one person who knows the Kula scriptures and is worthy of worship therein, tell me, O Mahādeva, if you have affection for me. (6-2)
The illustrious Bhairava said: O you whose wealth is austerity, it must be told in detail that [this] is of great merit;
O Śivā, all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are indeed worthy of worship—this is the truth.
O Kulabhairavī, if even a single young woman there is honored and gazed upon,
then all the supreme goddesses are indeed honored.

For she is to be honored especially at the beginning, the end, and the middle—at the completion of the hundred thousand [recitations]. If one does not honor the beloved, then one is besmeared by many obstacles. (6.5)
There is no fruit from what was previously acquired; what talk can there be of accomplishing or worshipping another?
O Maheśānī, there is the ninefold power (navaśakti), and the fivefold power (pañcaśakti), O Bhairavī.
Since honoring [the worthy] transforms everything that is deficient into that which possesses all virtues,
one should bestow upon a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas land abounding in crops.
The fruit that one obtains by giving [these gifts] is obtained from the worship of the Kaulika;
it is superior even to a thousand or a hundred gifts of food and sacrifices performed by other sacrificers.
By giving them food, one obtains that same fruit as from the worship of the Kaulikas;
and by constructing ponds, wells, and tanks for Śiva and Kṛṣṇa.
Whatever fruit one obtains from giving, that same fruit is obtained from the worship of the Kaulika, provided one worships him even once by the power of fortune. (6.10)
For they have accomplished their purpose; having crossed over [the obstacles], they go of their own accord to the City of the Goddess.
Even at the time of the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa), if there should be worship of the sacred seat (pīṭha), [it is likewise effective]. (6.11)
In that very place, the worship of the sacred seat (pīṭha) is not lacking even when performed mentally;
[therein dwell] the highly fortunate Devīkoṭa and Bhairavī in Oḍḍiyāna.
Yonimudrā, in Kāmarūpa she is Mahiṣāsuramardinī;
in Kāmabhūmi she is Kātyāyanī, and she is Kāmākhyā, the one whose form is desire. (6.13)
Jālandharī, Pūrṇeśī on Mount Pūrṇa, Caṇḍikā, and then the Goddess residing in Dikkaravāsinī at Kāmarūpa are to be worshipped. (6.14)
Alternatively, if by good fortune there is a vision of Kāmarūpa, then the worship of the goddesses Bhaga and the others is performed there. (6.15)
If, by the power of destiny alone, the vision of the lineage arises, then at that very moment one should mentally project them there. (6.16)
Bhaginī, Bhagajihvā, Bhagāsyā, and Bhagamālinī;
Bhaginī, Bhagākṣī, Bhagakarṇā, and Bhagatvac.

Having worshipped there with perfumes and other offerings, as well as mentally, the one who has a vulva-like nose, vulva-like breasts, stands upon a vulva, and glides upon a vulva, and likewise the Guru; (6.18)
Having performed the salutation according to the prescribed rite, the wise man himself, remaining unperturbed,
should worship Viṣṇu on the twelfth lunar day and the Lord of Umā on the fourteenth.
On the eighth day, one should indeed worship Śakti, the bestower of all accomplishments;
O beloved, one should always have the rites for the grooming of the hair performed.
O Goddess of the gods, having first brought either one's own wife or another's woman,
one should first offer a seat and thereafter give water for the feet (pādya).
O Maheśānī, O Śivā, one should offer the *arghya* according to the prescribed rite;
likewise, O Dear One, one should offer the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) with the nectar of immortality (*sudhā*). (6.22)
O Supreme Goddess, one should offer the bathing water with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*;
O Great Goddess, one should likewise offer perfume, specifically the eight types of fragrances.
O lady of excellent hips, one should offer beautiful flowers endowed with fragrance;
one should offer pleasing incense made of guggulu to the Great Goddess.
One should offer a lamp with ghee in a very beautiful copper vessel;
one should present the supreme food offering, which is delicious and most enchanting.
One should offer it together with various substances, as well as with coconuts,
plantains, citron fruits, and bilva fruits, which are the abode of Śrī.
O Maheśānī, O auspicious one, one should give honey measuring two palas;
O Maheśānī, one should give fresh ghee in the measure of one pala.
One should likewise offer supreme betel, accompanied by various offerings, along with curd and milk, which is very sweet and well-perfumed.
O Maheśvarī, one should offer that which is to be chewed, sucked, licked, and drunk, combined with camphor and other ingredients, and accompanied by betel nut.
O lady of excellent hips, one should offer water scented with camphor and other fragrances at whatever time one desires during that worship of the hosts of gods.
One should especially give that by which the beautiful woman—whether she be seven, eight, or nine years of age—is satisfied. (6.31)
O Maheśānī, she reached ten years, and likewise eleven;
she attained twelve years, and similarly thirteen auspicious years. (6.32)
Likewise, O Goddess, in the fourteenth year, and likewise in the fifteenth;
likewise, O Goddess, she who is sixteen years of age is most excellent and bestows the fruits of action.
One should perform the adornment of the hair with various delightful substances; thereafter, one should offer a great gift by which the human woman is satisfied. (6.34)
O Supreme Goddess, one should write the seed-syllable of Ramā on the pair of breasts, the two Bhagas on the pair of jaws,
and the two Gaṅgādharas below the armpits.
O beloved, one should draw the vulva below and a pair of lotuses upon the two thighs; on the soles of the lotus-feet, one should write the Viśvabīja, which is most difficult to obtain.
Having drawn it according to the rules with devotion using a *śirīṣa* stalk, O Maheśānī, one should write the *bālā*-seed syllable upon the vulva, O Maheśvarī. (6.37)
The *bhaga* should be drawn on both lips with a golden stylus,
and the *kākinī* should be drawn on both hands by the instructors.
O Maheśānī, one should offer a beautiful and pleasing red garment;
O Sureśvarī, one should write the seed-syllable with sandalwood known as "red."
Having offered a handful of flowers at the bhaga, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff;
one should do this three times until vision arises. (6.40)
O Maheśānī, one should recite the root mantra on a mountain peak;
O Maheśvarī, one should recite it there to the measure of one thousand times.
O Dear One, one should recite [the mantra] twenty-eight times upon its face;
O Dear One, one should recite it one hundred and eight times within the cavity of the yoni.
For the sake of accomplishing their desired goal, one should perform the "crushing of the mountain";
O Great Goddess, one should recite the root mantra and strike the circle of the yoni.
Then, having cast that reality before him, the practitioner becomes a perfected one (siddha).
Know this, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, to be the ritual application of Kālī. (6.44)
Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Tripurā, Ārṇā, and Maheśvarī—
by the practice of these Bhairavīs, one shall attain perfection.
O Maheśānī, one should offer the bali-oblation at the time of twilight in a temple of Śiva;
for without offering the bali, O Mahādevī, beloved, it does not bring benefit to all. (6-46)
And one should offer a bali-oblation to Śivā with every possible effort;
otherwise, there will be a loss of accomplishment—of this there is no doubt. (6.47)
In a wilderness, at the foot of a bilva tree, or even in a cremation ground; or in a lonely forest, a terrible place, a palace, or even in a courtyard—the practitioner [should practice]. (6.48)
O Maheśānī, one should offer the bali according to the prescribed rite either below the wall;
at the time of twilight, one should present the food offering (naivedya) consisting primarily of meat.
When it was to be said, "Kālī, Kālī," she, in the form of Śiva, arrived there in the form of a bound soul (paśu), accompanied by her hosts of attendants. (6.50)

O Goddess worshipped by the gods, when it cries out while eating toward the northeast or the northwest, there is the attainment of happiness in the northeast, and the northwest bestows both enjoyment and liberation. (6.51)
At that very moment, their auspiciousness is assured; of this there is no doubt.
By the gift of food, one must certainly and constantly satisfy Śivā.
Just as the daily *śrāddha*, the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*), and the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*) are obligatory,
so too is this daily regularity in the worship of the family deities (*kuladevī*) within the family tradition.

Whoever does not worship the goddess Śivā in the form of a goat in a secluded place, [his] recitations, rites of worship, and whatever meritorious deeds he may have performed [are all in vain]. (6.54)
Having taken and received the curse, Śivā weeps in solitude;
by her howling as a jackal, everything is certainly destroyed instantly. (6.55)
O Goddess Bhairavī, where one is enjoyed by Śivā alone, there indeed lies the supreme and most difficult-to-attain delight of all the gods. (6.56)

O Bhairavī, O Supreme Goddess, the power of beasts, the power of men, and the power of birds— when worshipped, they certainly bring about the accomplishment of even a defective rite, making it doubly effective and endowed with qualities. (6.57)
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the great worship when faced with dangers such as those from kings and so forth, or fears regarding other lands and the like. (6.58)
Having reflected upon the inauspicious karmas, one should offer the bali-oblation.
I shall proclaim the mantra for the bali; listen attentively. (6.59)
By which all is accomplished, O Sovereign of All; there is no fixed rule regarding time.
Having first extracted the syllable *Kālī*, and then [the syllable] *Śive* thereafter. (6.60)
Then the two words "O bearer of all forms, come hither," followed by the word "mama" (of me), and after that the word "bali" (offering). || 6.61 ||
"Grasp, grasp!"—this mantra, ending with the fire-born consort (svāhā) and the dual form [dvandvam], is for the offering;
O Goddess of Gods, having given a charming *bali* offering with this mantra... (6.62)
One shall be liberated from all sins; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Maheśvarī!
I shall now proclaim another mantra, which is captivating for the purpose of offering oblations (bali).
Accept it, O Goddess, highly fortunate Śivā, whose form is like the fire of time!
Reveal clearly the fruit of good and evil; accept this offering for you.
Having uttered this, the *bali* offering dear to the family members should be given;
O Goddess, if it is not consumed, then no auspiciousness shall come to pass. (6.65)
If there is anything auspicious therein, it is consumed entirely;
knowing this, O Great Goddess, one should perform rites for peace and well-being.
Thus, O Goddess Śivā, I have explained to you the ritual for the occasional occasion;
by performing which the heroic practitioner becomes free from all calamity.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the auspicious sequence of the Śākta conduct (ācāra).
Know it, O daughter of the mountain, to be the entire essence of the Kula for the Śāktas. (6.68)

Having risen in the morning, the knower of mantras, after bowing to the family tree and meditating on the Guru within the lotus of his head, should contemplate him as being bathed in that nectar. (6.69)
Having propitiated him with mental offerings, one who is free from affliction should contemplate the root-mantra from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
One should contemplate one's own body as resembling ten million suns, its form drenched in nectar, and pervaded by a mass of that radiance.
The śleṣmātaka, karañja, akṣa, nimba, aśvattha, kadambaka, bilva, or aśoka—these are the eight family trees (kulapādapa). || 6.72 ||
Thus it has been told to you, O auspicious Maheśvarī, in another tantra:
[regarding] a girl, or one intoxicated with youth, or an old woman, or a beautiful woman of noble family.
Or, having paid homage to one who is contemptible or extremely wicked, one should meditate [upon her];
likewise, striking them, reviling them, as well as being deceitful or unpleasant toward them. (6.74)
Under no circumstances should one act otherwise, for it would obstruct success:
women are gods, women are life-breaths, and women alone are the ornament.
One should always remain attached to women; otherwise, even toward one's own wife, she will become inclined toward perverse pleasure, having been cultivated in that way within the heart. (6.76)
One should offer to the deities the substance gathered by that hand, the water gathered by that hand, and the food gathered by that hand. (6.77)
One should avoid honoring other mantras and likewise refrain from disparaging them;
this is Brahman, this alone is it—neither I am that, nor is he that.
One should not practice various improper conducts, nor should one wander here and there without proper conduct;
likewise, one must perform penance, undergo the fall from Mount Bhṛgu, and visit sacred pilgrimage sites.
One should avoid the ritual offering of the *piṇḍa*, the Vedic injunctions, and the ritual assignments (*nyāsa*)—these five—in the Kaula tradition.
One must not commit violence against living beings, and especially not violence against sacrificial animals (*paśu*).
One should avoid violence toward the Goddess in all circumstances except for the offering of a sacrificial oblation (*balidāna*).
For that violence which is committed for the sake of the sacrificial offering is proclaimed to be without fault. (6.81)
"O Goddess, one should always slaughter great sacrificial animals for the offering of the *bali*;
O Goddess, this is the conclusion of those who know the Vedas, agreed upon by all. (6.82)
That which is the doctrine approved by the Vedas is also approved by me;
O Great Goddess, one should kill the sacrificial animal in the animal sacrifice—of this there is no doubt. (6.83)
For that violence is censured by the Vedas which is other than what is prescribed by the Veda; however, violence prescribed by the Veda must be performed—of this there is no doubt whatsoever. (6.84)
Now listen, O lady of beautiful limbs, to this most wonderful secret—
the secret of all goddesses, characterized by the conduct of the *samaya*.
O Great Goddess, without which the supreme mantra would not be accomplished—even by reciting it ten million times, its success does not arise. (6.86)
Those men who follow the family traditions of the Kula scriptures and are devoted to the conduct of the Vaiṣṇavas will undoubtedly attain perfection. (6.87)
One should be patient with the censure of others and always intent on helping them, whether in the mountains, in a secluded place, or in a deserted, empty region. (6.88)
O Maheśvarī, if by chance one should be at a crossroads or in the midst of a marketplace,
one should meditate for a moment, recite the mantra, bow down, and then depart as one pleases.
Having beheld the vulture, one should reverently pay homage to Mahākālī;
likewise, having beheld Kṣemaṅkarī, Jambukī, and Yamadūtī.
O Kurarī, Śyenī, Bhūkākī, Kṛṣṇamārjārī, O slender-waisted one, O highly fierce one, O you with disheveled hair, O you who are fond of offerings! 6.91
Salutations to you, whose face is radiant with noble conduct, O beloved of Śaṅkara!
Having seen a corpse in a cremation ground, one should circumambulate it while following behind.
Having prostrated with this mantra, the practitioner shall attain happiness:
"O you with terrible fangs, with a gaping mouth, with fierce eyes, O you who resound with the cry 'kiṭi'! (6.93)
Salutations to you who dwell in the cremation ground, O Mother Tripura, upon seeing whom— clad in red garments and adorned with red flowers— the fierce roar of the guru resounds.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, a person should recite this mantra:
"O Tripura, who resembles the bandhūka flower, O destroyer of fear! (6.95)
Salutations to you, O lady of excellent complexion, who have arisen from the dawning of good fortune;
likewise, [salutations to] the black-colored flower, the king, and the prince.

Having seen the elephant, horse, chariot, and weapons, as well as Karavīra and Śiva, the buffalo, the lord of the clan, and Mahiṣamardinī; (6.97) [The variant reading in manuscript *kha* is "phalakān vīrapūruṣān"].
Or by bowing to Jayadurgā, one is not defiled by obstacles:
"Victory to you, O Goddess, Mother of the World, Primordial One of the Triple City, O Triple Deity! (6.98)
O Goddess, bestower of boons upon your devotees, O slayer of Mahiṣa, salutations be unto you!
Having beheld a vessel of wine, fish, meat, and a beautiful woman—
Having beheld the goddess Bhairavī and prostrated before her, one should apply the mantra for the destruction of terrible obstacles and for the fulfillment of the Kula tradition. (6-100)
I bow to you, O boon-granting Goddess, adorned with a garland of severed heads, drenched in streams of blood; I bow to you, O boon-granting one, whose face is radiant.
O Goddess who removes all obstacles, salutations to you, the beloved of Hara.
If, upon merely seeing these, one does not act in such a manner; || 6-102 ||
If one prioritizes the mantra of power (śakti-mantra), its accomplishment does not arise;
for [the accomplishment of] harming, driving away, or killing these [beings] by means of snares and the like [is required]. (6.103)
By what means is a sinful soul made into one devoted to me?
O beloved of the noble people, these [qualities] arise from the portion of primordial matter (pradhāna). (6.104)
And the ḍākinīs, O Great Goddess, are your own portions in every direction;
if there is a vision of a ḍākinī, it is the attainment of the union of accomplished siddhis. (6-105)
Alternatively, success is attained by the Dānavas, and especially by those devoted to me,
as well as by the Vaṭukas and the deities.
Upon beholding another's wife—sixteen years of age, captivating, dressed in red garments, and with eyes like a deer’s—one should bow and recite the mantra. (6.107)
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one certainly attains success;
thereafter, the practitioner whose mantra is perfected shall accomplish all rites.
O Goddess of the gods, in the month of Vaiśākha, there is the third lunar day known as Akṣayā;
on that day, one should duly invoke Kālikā, the Mistress of the World.
The wise one should cause the recitation to be performed, which bestows the fruit of all desires;
having praised and invoked with effort, he should worship the Supreme Deity.
The supreme Great Goddess has four arms, is adorned with a garland of severed heads,
and holds the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, as well as a sword and a garland of severed heads.
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, who has reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures,
[please explain] the worship of the Great Goddess Kālikā in detail."
O Śaṅkara, tell me in brief about the secret seed-syllable, the secret mantra, and the process of externalizing [the energy] from the mūlādhāra, so that I may be satisfied.
(Śrī Bhairava said:
Having performed the ritual placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*), one should perform the ritual placement of the seer and the other [limbs] (*ṛṣyādinyāsa*).
First, having offered a seat, one should worship the Supreme Deity. (6.114)
O Great Goddess, whoever worships Kālikā on this lunar day shall achieve success in all their aims and the destruction of all enemies. (6.115)
O Maheśānī, O Bhairavī, other kings would swiftly fall into servitude if they do not worship Kālī, whether out of deceit or otherwise. (6.116)
When she becomes angry, Kālikā swiftly brings about total destruction;
therefore, with every effort and through extensive displays of great wealth, [one should worship her]. (6.117)
One should worship the Supreme Goddess, who bestows the fulfillment of all desires;
O Great Goddess, O fair-faced one, if one should perform the great worship (mahāpūjā). (6.118)
At that very moment, great accomplishment (siddhi) surely occurs; of this there is no doubt.
One who desires the four aims of life (caturvarga) should indeed worship Kālikā with joy.
The wise one should establish the vital breaths with the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra,
having indeed deposited the entire network of ritual placements (*nyāsa*) upon the body of the Great Goddess.
In this manner, one should establish the network of placements within one's own body;
then one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) three times.
May those beings depart who dwell upon the earth;
may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva.
Having dispelled the obstacles, O Goddess of gods, the knower of sacrifice, having fashioned a lotus, should then commence the worship facing the Goddess, O Goddess. (6.123)
When the first watch of the night has passed, O Goddess worshipped by the gods (or:
honored by the hosts of gods), one should first offer a seat, and immediately thereafter, a welcome. (6.124)
Then [he offers] water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping; after that, the honey-mixture (madhuparka);
likewise, further water for sipping and then water for bathing.
One should offer a red garment and likewise silver ornaments;
then, O Great Goddess, perfume and flowers, followed by incense and a lamp. (6.126)
One should offer three kinds of food-offerings that are delicious and very pleasing;
one should also give to the Goddess excellent betel-leaf, which is most heart-pleasing and captivating.
The most excellent practitioner should perform the offering of sacrifice (*balidāna*) for Mahādevī;
he should offer a goat, as well as a ram, a buffalo, and likewise a monitor lizard. (6.128)
And one should offer a charming pigeon to the Goddess, O Maheśānī,
as well as honey-water prepared with sugar and other ingredients to the Great Goddess.
Then the king should offer a bali-oblation to the enemies made of milk;
he himself should cut it with a wrathful gaze and with a weapon that inflicts a blow. (6.130)
O Goddess, O Gaṇeśvarī, O Maheśvarī, by merely uttering [the name] once— truly, truly— having performed the consecration of life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) with the name of the enemy, [he shall be destroyed].

O Great Goddess, O lady of pure smiles, by reciting the mantra according to the prescribed rite and offering salutations, the destruction of enemies will surely occur; of this there is no doubt. (6.132)
Having offered the musical instruments with every effort, the teacher [is perfected];
thereafter, that practitioner becomes a hero—of this there is no doubt. (6.133)
One should offer the supreme *sandaṃśa* (tongs) together with fried substances,
as well as jaggery, milk, honey, grapes, and aged sugarcane.
O Maheśvarī, one should offer the fruit of the *rambhā*, the *bījapūra*, and likewise the coconut; the coconut mixed with honey is especially recommended as a gift.
One must certainly cause that to be given; great will be the satisfaction of the Goddess.
Know this, O Maheśānī, daughter of the Mountain, to be the secret mantra. (6.136)
The mantra is: Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ krīṃ krīṃ, Dakṣiṇe Kālike, krīṃ krīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā.
O auspicious lady, there are two Bhuvaneśīs, followed by a pair of Kūrca-syllables.
O Goddess, there are two of one's own seed-syllables, and [the word] "Kālikā" on the right.
One should utter the preceding seed-syllables by means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal;
this great mantra, beginning with the Vedas and ending with the wife of Fire (svāhā), is thus remembered.
There is nothing higher than this; the mantra of Kālī is supreme beyond the supreme.
This mantra is named the "Wish-Fulfilling Tree" (Kalpapādapa); it grants all desires to those who worship it. (6.139)
Because it is so exceedingly dear, O fair-faced one, it has not been revealed;
this secret seed-syllable of Kālī is concealed within all the tantras. (6.140)
O Great Goddess, by means of this [mantra], subjugation and other such feats are accomplished without delay;
even with one hundred and eight recitations, the externalization from the *mūlādhāra* occurs. (6.141)
And it can be accomplished, O Goddess; one becomes perfected at that very moment.
In the Kali age, Kālī, Tārā, Annapūrṇā, and Sundarī [are likewise effective]. (6.142)
O fair-browed one, even by merely receiving the glorious mantra of these perfected vidyās, the state of Śiva arises; of this there is no doubt whatsoever. (6.143)
The mantras are quickly perfected; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Maheśvarī!
On the fourteenth day known as Raṭantī, in the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha.
In that [mandala], one should worship Tārā with extensive displays of great wealth;
one will undoubtedly become a great king, a universal monarch (cakravartin). (6.145)
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the bright fortnight, on the seventh lunar day favored by the Sun,
one accompanied by sons and grandsons should worship Annadā with devotion.
Fortune will certainly remain stable for as long as the world of moving and non-moving beings endures;
and in his house, Fortune shall abide, entirely free from any deformity.
And she shall become motionless, O Goddess; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Gaṇeśvarī!
And her worship, O Maheśānī, has been described here in your presence. (6.148)
O Gaṇasundarī, understand correctly from the *Annadākalpaka*:
that which is the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, when it falls on a Monday (sitā).
O Maheśānī, the beautiful Supreme Goddess is to be worshipped there;
O auspicious one, the worship of Sundarī has been fully described in her chapter.
Thus, O Goddess of the Gods, I have told you something of the most auspicious omens; I shall speak of others as well, by which people become free from calamity. (6.151)
Now I shall describe the supreme performance of rites for desired ends, by which alone, O Goddess, one may become composed of all vidyās. (6.152)
The fire-oblation, the libation, the worship, the meditative cultivation, and the recitation—these constitute the practice of the mantra, as well as the rites of slaying and expulsion. (6.153)
The practitioner should always perform these rites for the fulfillment of desires:
at midnight during the autumn season, and at dawn during the winter.
Spring occurs during the forenoon, and summer at midday;
the rainy season falls in the afternoon, and the cool season is recorded as occurring at dusk.
At the conjunction of dawn comes Hemanta; at daybreak, the arrival of Śiśira;
at half a watch, Vasanta; and at the interval of midday, Grīṣma. (6.156)
In the fourth watch [of the night], it is called the rainy season; when the sun has set, it is autumn.
This has been told to you, O fair-browed one; now hear the rule regarding the divisions of time.

O Great Goddess, having understood this, one should perform all rites, such as pacification (śānti), nourishment (puṣṭi), subjugation (vaśya), attraction (ākarṣaṇa), eradication (uccāṭana), and so forth. (6.158)
The six rites employed include subjugation as well as killing; the removal of diseases, malevolent spells, and exhaustion, and so forth, is declared to be pacification (śānti). (6.159)

The nourishment of wealth, people, and so forth, as well as subjugation and other such rites, and the winning over of people and the attraction [of others] performed by oneself, are described [here]. (6.160)
The performance of rites such as eradication (uccāṭana) and so forth is proclaimed as suppression (nigraha);
the taking of the lives of people is proclaimed as killing (māraṇa). || 6.161 ||
Starting from sunrise, ten successive ghaṭikās constitute the seasons beginning with spring, occurring day after day throughout the day and night.
Spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the cool season—
winter is prescribed for rites of pacification (śāntika), while spring is for the rite of subjugation (vaśya).
Stambhana is prescribed for the winter season; Grīṣma is declared for vidveṣa; Prāvṛṣ is recommended for uccāṭana; and Śarad for the rite of māraṇa. (6.164)
For subjugation and attraction, one should visualize [the deity] as red in color;
for neutralizing poison, pacification, nourishment, and replenishment, one should visualize [him] as white. (6.165)

Yellow [light] is for acts of immobilization; smoky [light] occurs in the rite of expulsion; that which resembles the *śakragopa* insect is for driving mad; and that which has the appearance of black color is for death. (6.166)
One should meditate on [the deity] standing for the purpose of killing; it is taught that he is sleeping for the purpose of eradication;
O Queen of the Gods, one should contemplate him seated for subjugation and other such rites. (6.167)
One who is seated and white in color should be known as belonging to the peaceful (Sāttvika) and auspicious [state];
one situated on the left side and black is proclaimed to be Tāmasa.
The *sāttvika* [type] is for those desiring liberation; the *rājasa* is for those desiring sovereignty;
the *tāmasa* is for the purpose of destroying enemies and warding off all diseases. (6.169)
For killing, the neutralization of poison, the warding off of spirits and planetary seizures, expulsion, and causing enmity, the five-colored [mantra] is employed. (6.170)
The placement of the name at the end of the mantra is designated as "yoga";
[it is used] in rites for pacification, nourishment, subjugation, and the purification of expiatory rites. (6.171)
Wise men employ the yoga for enchantment and illumination;
it is also said to be used for paralyzing, driving away, destroying, and creating enmity. (6.172)
The manifestation of the mantra is said to occur at the beginning, middle, and end of the name;
it brings about the presence of the mantra and destroys all sins. (6.173)
This fever is said to be the pacification of the rite of poison;
it is also [the remedy] for the closing [of the eyes], as well as for the syllables of the mantras.

That which is proclaimed as the "interleaved" (ekaikāntarita) arrangement of mantras is that which should be employed in rites for pacification (śāntika), when the mantra is placed at the beginning and end of the name. (6.175)

That [mantra] becomes a "saṃpuṭa" (encased), which is defined as a "kīlaka" (stake); it is used for paralyzing, overcoming death, subduing enemies, protection, and so forth, while the *saṃpuṭa* is used for these same purposes. (6.176)

Where two mantra-syllables are interspersed with each single syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished, this is to be known as *vidarbha* by the sages who are knowers of the tantras. (6.177)
One should recite "svāhā" in rites pertaining to fire, and "namaḥ" everywhere during worship;
likewise, in rites for peace, nourishment, subjugation, hatred, killing, and expulsion.
One should sequentially place *sudhā*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*.
O Great Goddess, the *padmāsana* is proclaimed for rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*).
O Maheśānī, O Śivā, for the rites of subjugation as well as for those of pacification, the svastika posture is prescribed; it is indeed the direct bestower of accomplishment.
And for attraction, O Great Goddess, the *kambala* posture is prescribed;
for causing enmity, O Great Goddess, the *vīrāsana* posture is prescribed. (6.181)
For the rites of eradication and killing, the heroic posture (vīrāsana) is recommended;
for the rites of pacification, nourishment, and subjugation, the beautiful woman with auspicious intentions is praised.
Blazing with all ornaments, having attained the desires of her heart,
the deity should be properly meditated upon with a face as serene as a lotus.
It should be the same for summoning, and it is praised for eradication;
it is proclaimed by those who know the tantras as being effective for the attraction and the hatred of the subject. (6.184)
It is woven by self-controlled people who avoid [forbidden things], and it is bound together by Takṣaka;
it is entered by the letter *u* and the bird (*vaya*), and likewise by the Yakṣa in the act of eradication.
One should contemplate the reality [of the practice] through the act of treading upon stone, as in the case of grass, water, and so forth.
Now listen, O lady of beautiful limbs, O auspicious one, to the rule regarding the lunar days (tithis).
The fifth, second, third, and likewise the seventh lunar days,
when conjoined with the weekdays of Mercury and Jupiter, are highly esteemed for rites of pacification.
The seventh day is recommended for rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), as are the eighth and ninth;
likewise the tenth and eleventh, when conjoined with the sun, Venus, and so forth. (6.188)
For the rite of attraction, the new moon, the ninth day, and likewise the first day [of the lunar fortnight] are suitable;
for the rite of causing hatred, the full moon joined with Saturn is prescribed.
Likewise, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the eighth day,
and a Sunday are auspicious lunar days for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), especially at the time of dusk.
The fourteenth and eighth days of the dark fortnight, as well as the new moon day,
when joined with a Saturday or a Sunday, are commended for rites of killing.
The fifth lunar day (pañcamī) joined with the day of Mercury and the Moon, as well as the tenth (daśamī) and the full moon (paurṇamāsī),
should be known as the appropriate dates for the rite of immobilization (stambhana).

One should perform auspicious deeds when auspicious planets are rising, and inauspicious deeds when inauspicious ones are rising; one should perform fierce rites during the *riktā* lunar days and the sun's transit, and carry out lethal magic during the *mṛtyu-yoga*.
The fire-oblation, the satiation, the worship, as well as meditative cultivation, the recitation, and the retention of the mantra, as also killing and destruction. || 6.194 ||
One should perform these rites for specific desires, offering other [substances] during the ritual application.
Now, I shall further explain another supreme method of subjugation.
By the mere knowledge of which mantras are accomplished at that very moment;
one should have an image made, O Goddess, out of a pala of silver. (6.196)
O Maheśānī, O Śivā, [one should fashion] an image of the person to be accomplished using half a *pala* of yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), and likewise half a *pala* of turmeric powder.
Having dug a pit measuring one and a half cubits and having placed [the object] therein, O beautiful one,
one should dwell there with a mind fixed upon that, after providing a red seat.
O Great Goddess, one should place banners in the four directions;
then, sitting upon a red seat and facing the east, one should perform the recitation.
O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, know the rule for the worship:
there, O Goddess, the preceptor should place a jar filled with sesame seeds. (6.200)
Then, having placed the copper vessel there, one should perform the consecration;
the wise practitioner should then establish the vital breaths by means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra.
Having placed it below and worshipped it with a rosary of coral, one should perform the recitation;
by ten thousand recitations, one then becomes fit for the ritual application.
First, having uttered the Praṇava, the second is the Māyā-bīja; then the letter 'ka' joined with Lākinī, adorned with the left ear [the letter 'u'] and the moon [the bindu]. (6.203)
Then one should utter the word "raktapada," and immediately after that, "cāmuṇḍe.
Then, having placed the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), one should follow that with "vaśamānaya. (6-204)
One should recite the mantra ending with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā) ten thousand times;
one should likewise perform the fire-oblations and other rites according to the measure of one-tenth or other proportions.
Having bathed in the morning, become pure, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), and with his senses subdued,
he should recite [the mantra] starting from the morning until midday.
O Goddess of the gods, when the recitation is completed, one should perform oblations day after day on an auspicious day;
by means of an oblation of jasmine flowers, one shall bring [others] under control—of this there is no doubt.
One should satisfy the Supreme Deity with waters mixed with camphor;
first uttering the *praṇava*, one should then pronounce the name of Cāmuṇḍā.
"O Bhairavī, know this mantra which ends with 'agnijāyā' (svāhā).
Having satisfied the Supreme Deity by means of this very procedure," (6.209)
O Goddess of the gods, the application for attaining success arises; there is no doubt about this.
Then, O Bhairavī, beloved of life, one should perform the consecration. (6.210)
O Maheśānī, [one should recite] the Praṇava and then Cāmuṇḍā;
after that, one should consecrate [the disciple], and then one should perform the consecration with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
O Goddess of gods, one should then feed Brahmins with a tenth part of that [number].
When this is done, O Maheśānī, there is supreme subjugation. (6.212)
This shall come to pass, there is no doubt here; it is the truth, O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods!
He will be equal to Kāma to women and like a destroyer of enemies to his foes. (6.213)
O Goddess worshipped by the hosts of gods, as long as one lives, [this] becomes like the arrow of Smara; there is no doubt in this—it is the truth. (6.214)
One should grind the root of white Aparājitā mixed with yellow pigment (rocanā),
empower it one hundred times with the mantra, and then apply it as a tilaka mark.
One shall bring [them] under control; of this there is no doubt, O Maheśvarī, truth, truth!
If the moon and sun were otherwise, then they would be fruitless. (6.216)
One should propitiate Cāmuṇḍā with great effort by means of a red garment;
O Dear One, a gold dakṣiṇā should be given according to one's wealth.
O fair-faced one, one should perform a great worship at its beginning and end;
by practicing this for five days, one shall bring even a king under one's control.
O Great Goddess, for your pleasure I have related that which is difficult to find on earth;
listen with a single-minded focus, O beloved, especially regarding this incantation for causing enmity. (6-219)
O Maheśvarī, the raven and the owl should always be drawn upon a birch-bark leaf using the poison of the karañjaka plant as well as dhattūraka.
Having written down the mantra together with the names of those to be accomplished, the practitioner [should say]:
"May there be between these two such enmity as exists between these two. (6.221)
The mantra ending with the wife of Vahni (svāhā) causes enmity among all;
Mahākālī is its deity, and worship of her bestows auspiciousness. (6-222)
Thus, O lady of pure smiles, one should perform the recitation with a count of one thousand;
now listen with a single-minded focus, my dear, to the specific method for the rite of killing.
Having killed a black cat, the best of practitioners should bring its head there and anoint it with vermilion. (6.224)
O Great Goddess, O Śivā, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished upon the tongue;
having written the name of the person to be accomplished, one should joyfully recite the Kālī mantra.
Then one should recite the syllable formed with its own seed-syllable;
by ten thousand recitations, one shall slay the enemy before oneself.
Having invoked Śmaśānakālikā there, one should worship her in that auspicious place;
one should cause a garment adorned with iron ornaments to be offered to the Goddess.
Facing south, one should recite the mantra; then the mantra will become perfected.
Having cooked food, O Great Goddess, O Beloved, one should cause it to be given in a secluded place. (6.228)
If one offers a bali-oblation at midnight and digs [the ground] at the enemy's house,
O Goddess of Gods, within seven days the enemy goes to the abode of Yama.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you that which is considered the essence of essences;
out of affection for you, O lady of noble limbs, this has been revealed before you. (6.230)
O Omniscient One, hear now the rite of pacification (*śāntika*) by which the practitioner lives;
first, having brought forth Urvaśī, [one recites] the supreme mantra that brings about the end of the eon.
Joined with the two breasts, then the triad of *dhūminī*;
O Goddess of the Gods, this mantra [is recited] to the extent of one thousand and eight [times].
O Maheśānī, one should perform the recitation (japa), with Annapūrṇā as the presiding deity;
one should worship her with various kinds of edible foods endowed with diverse flavors. (6.233)
One should offer delightful substances to be chewed, sucked, and licked,
and perform the fire-oblations (homa) and other rites according to the prescribed proportions, such as one-tenth [of the total offerings].
O beautiful one, through the oblation of lotus flowers, peace is attained;
one should satisfy the Goddess with honey, for she is the supreme goal who is full of food.
On the first day, O Goddess of gods, one should fill a jar with water;
in that jar one should worship the Goddess, having invoked the Mistress of the Gods after performing the ritual worship. (6.236)
O Goddess of the Gods, if one performs a ritual application with this mantra, every disease shall be destroyed; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. (6.237)
Listen to the secret, O Mistress of the Gods, by which one may attain direct manifestation—[an alternative reading says: "by which one may go to the City of Truth"].
O Great Goddess, the means of accomplishment and so forth have been described by me in many ways. (6.238)
Furthermore, O Varārohā, O Supreme Goddess, listen with favor to me as to by what method one should behold that which has the form of light. (6.239)
Listen, O virtuous and highly fortunate lady, to that which resides within all knowledge—
whether in the Vaiṣṇava, the Gāṇapatya, the Śaiva, or even the Śāmbhava [traditions].
Whether in yoga or in the dharma of renunciation, the Kaula dharma is praised;
O Śivā, having resorted to the dharma of the Kulīna, one should recite [mantras] day and night.
One should worship her with a pure disposition in a river or similar place, in a solitary empty house, at the foot of a bilva tree, on a riverbank, or in a place entwined by creepers. (6.242)

The beautiful woman always dwells in a cremation ground or even in a desolate place; if those seeking spiritual accomplishment worship you while remaining free from emotional disturbances, [they shall succeed]. (6.243)
Then you shall become visible to the sight of practitioners; and I shall proclaim the means of accomplishment (sādhana) which was taught, O lady rich in austerity.
O Goddess Śivā, whether by way of being an ascetic or by way of being a king, the practitioner, having become one who perceives no difference, beholds you. (6.245)
If the eighth lunar day falls on a Tuesday, one should place a new jar filled with water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) there,
and having performed worship according to the rules and the prescribed ritual.
Having sprinkled water there upon the altar, and having spread an auspicious seat upon it,
one should dwell there, preceded by the *jyotis* mantra.
O Goddess, while uttering that mantra with a hissing sound in the four directions, one should constantly and diligently meditate upon your form with the mind. (6.248)
Two-armed, beautiful, and dark-complexioned, adorned with various jewels,
wearing red garments, with a smiling face, she protects like a mother.
Then, O Bhairavī, one knows you, Bhairavī, who are of terrible form;
one should meditate upon your splendor with one's own eyes above the nostrils.
Or else, one may perceive within the center of the *kūrca* your stainless light—
cool with the radiance of ten million moons, yet as scorching as ten million suns.
And on the lofty [peak], one should, with a steady mind, meditate at the proper times according to the prescribed rule upon Mahākāla and the Guru Svaprakāśācala. (6.252)
"In an empty house, in a courtyard, or on the pavements of the streets; at crossroads, in marketplaces, or in halls—he may perform [the rite] according to his preference. (6.253)
But, O Goddess, why does the mind become serene without a cause? How could internal purity and mental purity exist without a cause? (6.254)
Affection is not carried away by improper conduct, nor do I have any taste for what is censured;
therefore, having established the underlying reason and keeping it well concealed, one should perform the recitation (japa).
Surā is the cause and the means, and she is indeed the supreme nectar;
she is the giver of knowledge, the bestower of auspiciousness, the sacred ford, the intoxicating wine, and the virtuous one.
Śuṇḍā, Prabāhukulyāṅgā, Pāvanī, and Tāriṇī—know these to be your secret names, O Kulabhairavī. (6.257)

One should meditate upon her, who is identical in form [to the previous deity], intoxicated with passion, holding wine, adorned with a conch shell, facing the practitioner, smiling with beautiful teeth, auspicious, and the bestower of welfare. (6.258)
And do not speak ill of me, always with a peaceful mind;
for through your support, both my state as a monk and my kingship shall endure in age after age.
Action is devoid of cause and destroyed; there is neither internal purity nor new happiness.
O Goddess, know the body to be useless without your sādhana. (6.260)
O Goddess, practice is indeed in vain; likewise, hear now the doctrine of causality.
