O Śaṅkarī, it is to be pursued through the paths of the Bhairavas, the lords of causes.

Having gathered on the mountain in the forest, he who has indeed restrained his self should not drink alone, nor [eat] food, nor [be with] women; [he should perform] the well-praised hymn of praise. (6.262)
O Goddess, for one who is well-restrained, the reciter should perform the recitation with five or ten [breaths]; when in a state of equanimity, he should certainly recite together with two or three.
Whatever is [perceived] through meditation, all that is not twofold; having remembered that which is pervasive and consists of Brahman, no delusion arises therein. (6.264)
Having accepted this, you too should meditate; then, O beautiful one, you shall see [it].
Having meditated thus, O Great Goddess, if my mind is propitious, [then you shall see it].
I shall now fully explain the purification that bestows omniscience through knowledge:
first, having placed a water-pot before oneself, one should recite the root mantra three times while chanting it. (6.266)
Then, having displayed the *yonimudrā*, one should utter this auspicious [verse]:
"Homage to you, O bestower of knowledge, pure one, who are firmly established in the state of purity. (6.267)
O you who are the form of light, the dispeller of darkness, the giver of boons, and the embodiment of nectar;
O you who abide within ignorance and destroy great sins!
O source of all merit, O essence of the nectar of immortality for all, homage to you, homage to you; be gracious, O Supreme Goddess!

Grant me supernatural power; grant me purity of mind—homage to you! O you who support the moving and the unmoving, O meritorious one, O bestower of fortitude, O destroyer of [worldly] attachment! || 6.270 ||
O sinless one, worthy of being served by gods, demons, and men, remove my delusion; O red-eyed one, large-eyed one, you who are yourself the witness in the midst of those who are bewildered!
May she who is clothed in divine conch-shells, who is easily pleased, who destroys the mass of darkness, who assumes the form of Śivā, and who is supreme, be gratified with me. (6.272)
Salutations to you, O Kālikā, who embodies the dharma of the lineage; hail, O Power!
Aiṃ Strīṃ Hūṃ Hrīṃ! O You of divine form, O Great Illusion, O Sovereign Goddess! (6.273)
From the syllable *hrīṃ*, one attains perfection; O illustrious one, grant me intelligence!
Attain immortality here and bestow upon me the supreme accomplishment.
O you who are beyond the shore, in this essence-less saṃsāra; O savior, O wish-fulfilling cow, O sinless one;
O you who delight all the hosts of gods; O refuge of immeasurable virtues! || 6.275 ||
Obeisance to you again and again, O Supreme Bliss of Brahman!
O Goddess, Sovereign of the Gods, dispel the darkness of my eyes and the darkness of my mind.
O you who are pleased by the conduct of noble families, purify me, O expounder of Brahman!
O Śrī, O Goddess Kamalā, O wielder of the trident, you who consist of truth and bliss! 6-277.
O Pūtakratu, who are served by all, O source of inspiration in the minds of sages—salutations eternally to you, Jayā; I bow down to you, the Supreme.
O you who delight in pure conduct, O secret one, O necklace of the hosts of cattle,
O you worshipped by the gods, act in such a way that I may be liberated from darkness.
Having praised thus, O Great Goddess, one should purify with the root mantra itself:
"Oṃ, there is only the one Supreme Brahman, consisting of the gross and the subtle, eternal."
Therefore, I shall destroy for you the sin of killing a Brahmin that has arisen from your hair.
Oṃ! O Goddess, born from the solar disc, arisen from the abode of Varuṇa, consisting of the seed-syllable Amā—may [this] be released from the curse of Śukra. 6-281.
Oṃ! If the Praṇava is the seed of the Vedas and consists of the bliss of Brahman, by that truth, O Goddess of Gods, may it remove the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa. (6.282)
Then, having placed her before him, he should perform the recitation as prescribed;
indeed, O Great Goddess, if he performs the worship day after day.
The supreme practitioner must certainly recognize that form.
O Goddess, the practice with corpses has been described by me in many ways. (6.284)
O Goddess, that which came to pass was fruitless and devoid of cause due to your heroic nature;
O Śivā, one should now constantly meditate upon you in the form of a corpse.
Then, filled with shame, she plays with her own form upon the corpse;
thereafter, through constant passion, you manifest according to whatever state [is required].
At the dead of night or during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one intent on meditation will certainly behold your form, which is supreme bliss. (6.287)
O Goddess, when you have been propitiated by means of night worship, recitation, and meditation, cultivated many times as causes,
then you shall become firmly established there.
Having seen the Satī, one should pay homage; having touched her, one becomes pure.
And having drunk [from her], one attains supreme bliss and the liberation of the vital breaths.
Having placed a jar filled with wine and adorned with bilva branches and other ornaments before him, and having performed worship according to the prescribed rules with mantras; || 6.290 ||
With incense, lamps, food offerings, oblations, and purifications,
one should constantly recite [the mantra] one hundred and twenty-two times upon the altar.
Or else, one should perform the recitation (japa) with great concentration for one hundred thousand times according to one's ability;
then, having risen from that, one should offer oblations according to the rule with sesame seeds, clarified butter, and bilva fruits.
O Goddess, one should satisfy [the deities] with that liquor according to the prescribed rite;
when the mandala is satisfied, O Goddess, it then becomes satisfied and bestows spiritual accomplishments (siddhi).
Therein, the supreme mind becomes free from obstacles, fearless, undisturbed, sorrowless, and changeless, and it attains clarity. (6.294)
One should offer salutations to the food offering (naivedya), for He will accept it with the thought that it is you;
one should never, even in the mind, entertain a deluded notion [regarding this]. (6.295)
If anyone reviles that food offering even in their mind, then Kālī shall devour him, or he shall be utterly destroyed. (6.296)
Therefore, having seen and heard this, one should never be censured anywhere by men, cats, buffaloes, goats, or rams. (6.297)
With pigeons, sparrows, and the like; with swans, water-fowls, and cocks; and with birds such as the śāla-saja, the śakula, and the rohita.
With various other offerings, and with fruits soaked in honey,
with sugarcane stalks that are moistened, ripened, or roasted, and stripped of their bark.
Having placed Tāriṇī before him, the instructor, with a pure mind,
must not strike the hearts of women, and especially those of his own female disciples.
For your manifestation, O beautiful one, exists everywhere in the form of power;
there is the power of the bound soul (*paśu*), the power of the bird (*pakṣin*), and the power of man (*nara*), O beautiful one. (6.301)
An action performed with defects always becomes endowed with qualities when [the deities] are worshipped;
O auspicious one, their worship should be performed with devotion according to the prescribed rite.
One should not strike the auspicious Kaulinī Śakti even with a flower;
O Śivā, if the Śakti is pleased, know her to be truly pleased.
Devoted to recitation and fire-offerings according to the rules for daily worship,
one should perform the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) while relying on the company of those of the same lineage (kula).
Having seen Kṣemaṅkarī, Jambukī, Kākola, and the excellent Gṛdhra, and having heard their cries, one should bow down preceded by the mantra.
O Maheśānī, if the sound of these [beings] is heard at the time of recitation, then know that success has been attained; one should not recite further, but rather perform a hymn of praise.

Having fashioned a house with garlands of severed heads, one should perform the recitation (japa), O slender-waisted one, O most fierce one, O you with disheveled hair, O you who are fond of offerings! (6.307)
Salutations to you, whose face is pleased by the family traditions, O beloved of Śaṅkara!
Having caused [the lamps] to be illuminated with lights, and dwelling again in their midst— || 6.308 ||
With a mind of supreme bliss, one should perform the recitation of that form;
by reciting it one hundred thousand times, one shall accomplish the highest siddhi.
If one does not perform recitation at night, as well as worship and the consumption of the secret nectar, how can he be a Kaulika who accomplishes the bliss of the Kula? (6.310)
O Goddess, I have spoken in many ways; know my word to be true.
O Goddess, without the nectar of the lineage (kulāmṛta), why would the mind find peace?
Then, O Goddess, having taken up the worshiped Kula-purifying [mantra] and relying on undivided devotion, my self becomes perfectly serene. (6.312)
The Śrī Devī said: For what reason, O Lord, has the praise of Modinī been proclaimed in many ways?
How is it that it has been stated that without her, there can be no accomplishment at all?
Tell me that, O Maheśāna, by which its sādhana may always be performed with a peaceful mind, so that its form is seen with joy. (6.314)
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, the cause of the very cause; by the knowledge of which, O Maheśvarī, [the suffering] of the body and the mind [is destroyed]. (6.315)
Great delusion perishes, and one shall obtain a divine body;
[one obtains] the essence of the meaning of all scriptures and the mother of all yoga. (6.316)
Know the body to be impure and the mind to be indeed fickle;
since there is no removal of impurity, how can there be meditation, O Maheśvarī? (6.317)
O auspicious one, since there are many bodily states consisting of pleasure and pain among living beings, by what means can your mental union with them be known? (6.318)
Fear, shame, disgust, and the like; sleep, drowsiness, delusion, and so forth; indigestion, confusion, and others such as grief and anxiety. (6.319)
Various states arise for living beings who possess bodies;
upon the departure of the body, there is the leading away of those beings, and [likewise] during the maintenance of the body.
In that very state, I am the mind itself, the eternal one who delights in the Self;
therefore, O Goddess, you are my savior, whose nature is splendor.
Know her to be endowed with devotion; take refuge in her according to the prescribed rite.
When the body has been cleansed of impurities and its vital energy has been perfectly kindled, [perform the practice].
Stability and strength are attained in the yoga of meditation;
one who is indigestible, weak, diseased, timid, or overwhelmed by anxiety [does not attain them]. (6.323)
O Goddess, indeed these faults do not arise from the consumption of liquor;
moreover, many other faults are destroyed through the yoga of liberation.
The curses pronounced here against Brahmā and others of unsteady mind have been uttered;
therefore, aiming at them with this mantra, become intent upon my worship.
O Great Goddess, O Beloved, know her always to be of your own nature;
without her, the mind will never abandon its impurity. (6.326)
But once impurity has been cast off, the mind assumes a body endowed with form;
therefore, having taken recourse to a woman, perform the practice with diligence.
Now listen, O lady of beautiful limbs and lovely countenance, to the Śākta conduct (śāktācāra), without which no success can be attained even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. (6.328)
Honey, meat, fish, sexual intercourse, and likewise women—
of these five, she who is the fifth is identical in form to you.
Having bowed to and praised that Goddess, and having worshipped her while always remaining pure, she shall become my Śakti, born of the gods and possessing a nature identical to my own form.
Relying upon that, accomplishment shall be attained; there is no need for deliberation here.
One should pay homage to a vessel of liquor and to a woman dressed in red garments. (6.331)
A tawny cow, a red cow, a small cow, a cow-pen, and a milch cow;
worship with the fruits of the family tree, and offerings of meat and flavorful food.
You alone are the one among all the gods, and yet you are the very soul of all the gods;
you are manifestly composed of all bliss and are the ultimate refuge of all desires.
Devoted to recitation at crossroads, pure, and occasionally dwelling in cremation grounds,
having thus meditated upon the Self, one then becomes a worshiper of Śakti.
The bliss of Brahman is the essence of Brahman; it is adorned with flowers and bones, and the seat of the gods, garlanded with spirits, is borne by the deities who are Śaktis.
At night, the worshipper of Śakti, who delights in the bliss of the essence of the Supreme Brahman, performs worship with white, potent flowers of his own body.
The night worship should be performed especially by the best of practitioners with offerings of the five groups of sacrificial foods (*pañcamīvarga*) and various kinds of flour-based cakes.
With offerings of food weighed out, moistened and mixed with meat broth,
as well as with flowers, incense, lamps, sacrificial food, and ritual oblations.
Together with the Śaktis and the practitioners, and with joyful dancing, singing, and so forth,
one who has taken refuge in the [spiritual] group should worship with supreme devotion and satisfy [the deities].
Those of noble birth, related by family ties, well-known, free from dualistic thoughts,
possessed of great being, who have seen the path, and who are devoted solely to me alone.
The Śaktis are to be worshipped everywhere, especially with the thought "I am [the deity]";
and the Śakti is to be worshipped with flowers, vermilion, perfumes, and sandalwood.
Then, out of pure maternal affection, one should constantly worship a maiden with garlands and ornaments, or otherwise worship another Śakti.
Thus, when one is capable, the worship of Śakti brings liberation from worldly existence; [otherwise there may be] censure, humiliation, or the forcible abduction of a woman. (6.343)
O Goddess, if you desire success (*siddhi*), you must not even mentally perform [these acts]:
wandering at night, O Goddess, and the worship of the *śakti* at night. (6.344)
When the Kaulika practitioner does not perform [harm] in the world, how could he be otherwise?
He is free from reviling any living beings and is endowed with compassion toward all. (6.345)
Without an offering to the Great Goddess, violence is indeed avoided everywhere;
[he remains] always with a joyful mind, devoted to my desire.
He pays homage at crossroads, worships those who roam the cremation grounds,
dwells in darkness, and is intent on frequenting mountain caves.
With his soul purified by the supreme nectar and devoted to my love,
he should utterly avoid censuring the Śāligrāma stone and the Brāhmaṇa.
O Śaṅkarī, the Brāhmaṇa performs their worship especially well, as does the Kṣatriya, each according to his own nature— through the state of Brahman and through the Kṣatriya nature respectively.
And the Vaiśya shall wander about with a mind purified by his Vaiśya nature;
by day he shall eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) and shall not touch another man.
O Śivā, at night, joined by his own group, he should resort to the fifth [day],
being intent on your worship along with the Śaktis and the practitioners (sādhakas).
Whatever is danced or sung is your hymn of praise and worship;
yet, O Bhairavī, without bathing at a sacred site (tīrtha), the inner self is not purified. (6.352)
He shall no longer experience sorrows and shall partake in liberation in the next world;
O Goddess, there is no doubt whatsoever regarding the vision of his form. (6.353)
O Maheśānī, having performed this worship, one shall dwell in the city of the Goddess;
O Maheśvarī, O Goddess, there is nothing superior to this in the Tantra.
This is indeed the worship of the Goddess, O you who are praised by the gods;
for he who abandons all other dharmas and performs this worship— (6.355)
He is a yogi and a great soul who delivers one from cyclic existence in an instant;
O fair-faced one, for him there is no sin in approaching those women who should not be approached.
O Goddess of gods, O lady of beautiful countenance, whatever discourse is yours is your hymn of praise;
and moving here and there is declared to be circumambulation. (6.357)
Beyond that, O Great Goddess, neither merit nor demerit arises.
It is not to be disclosed, O Maheśānī; yet it has been revealed out of affection for you. (6.358)
O Maheśānī, having brought forth this light for My devotees, one must not give it to those who are not devotees; for by giving it to them, one incurs death.
Thus has the propitiation of the Goddess been described to you; listen, O Bhairavī!
One who desires knowledge should offer oblations of sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter and honey.
By offering oblations of *bilva* leaves smeared with ghee, as well as *kiṃśuka*, *bakula*,
and *bandhūka* flowers, even a king shall fall into servitude.
By an oblation of clarified butter and salt, one attracts a woman who desires him;
by an oblation of *karṇikāra* flowers, a man obtains good fortune.
With *karavīra* and *puṃnāga* flowers, one undoubtedly attains nourishment;
by means of a fire-oblation (*homa*) of *rājavṛkṣa*, one shall possess all prosperity.
By offering oblations of durvā grass, sesame seeds, and clarified butter, one shall attain long life;
likewise, by worshipping with bilva leaves smeared with ghee while reciting the root mantra. (6.364)
By offering a thousand oblations every day, one attains the supreme goal;
through the homa of *mālatī* flowers smeared with clarified butter, one becomes a swift poet.
O Śivā, in connection with the rite of libation (tarpaṇa), this fire-oblation (homa) has been described;
one should perform the libation with honey, which bestows the fruit of all desires. (6.366)
O Great Goddess, for the sake of attaining the power of mantras and destroying great sins, one should offer libations for a full month with water mixed with camphor. (6.367)
Having brought all kings under his control, he shall be an enjoyer of pleasures for as long as he lives;
by [offering] ghee, glory full of fame is accomplished, and through milk, one attains health. (6.368)
O Goddess, by mixing it with aguru, one shall be happy at all times;
by using water mixed with coconut water, one shall attain all goals.
One should destroy all enemies with water mixed with *marīca* (black pepper);
and with hot water alone, one may cause an enemy to vanish in an instant.
One who is afflicted by fever shall find relief through the sprinkling of milk;
eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), with hair disheveled, one should perform the recitation of ten thousand [mantras].
His speech in the assembly becomes composed of both prose and verse;
the tawny-eyed woman causes expulsion, while the squinting-eyed woman brings honor.
When released, she causes [the enemy] to flee; when agitated, she causes him to whirl;
when disturbed, she causes him to tremble; and when appearing faint, she causes him to suffer intense torment.
One should contract [the breath] when it is obstructed and awaken it when it is completely blocked;
all this should be performed as a mere mental visualization.
In all rites of eradication (*uccāṭana*), the wise man should recite it ten thousand times;
by merely consecrating it one hundred times, a person [should apply] a mark (*tilaka*) with yellow pigment (*rocanā*).
O Dear One, having performed this, whatever the mantra-practitioner beholds, he should treat that person like a servant;
by means of a tooth, one should bring forth powder, and with that, one should fashion a ritual peg (kīlaka).
Just as one might write a series of lines within a mere lotus leaf smeared with honey and ghee, so should one write the root mantra interlaced [with the name]. (6.377)
Having cast those [flowers] into the square sacrificial pit,
one should also offer oblations of a thousand red-hued lotuses soaked in milk and water.
Listen to the mantra, O lady of excellent hips, by which one certainly attains accomplishment:
*oṃ padme padme mahāpadme padmāvati māye tathā*. (6.379)
This great mantra, ending with *svāhā*, bestows occasional fruits;
he who performs the rite in this manner shall immediately become a swift poet. (6.380)
By means of a specific ritual application, one may bring the king's wife under one's control, using *rambhā*, jasmine, and *bījapūra* mixed with fragrant substances. (6.381)
Having mixed [these], one should offer the bali, especially on the eighth day;
this is the mantra for the bali of ritual application, which accomplishes all applications if used.
Then, at midnight, one should always offer an oblation at a crossroads;
this wards off enemy armies, planetary afflictions, misfortune, disease, and malevolent spells.
Having first uttered the *praṇava*, then after that "Ugratāre," one should utter the pair: "O you with formidable fangs, delude the enemy faction" (or "agitate," according to the Kha manuscript).
Having uttered the pair "devour," one should again speak the pair "cook."
"Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Strike down those who are intent on harming me with the circles of yoginīs!
Svāhā! Attract the enemy’s magic spell, 2! Cut it, 2! Slay it, 2! Seize it in the skull, 2! Svāhā!
O Goddess of gods, O Maheśvarī, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) with this very [mantra].
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā, [one should say] "Kālī Kālī," O beautiful one. (6.385)
After worshipping with the word "Vajreśvarī," one should then worship with the word "Salutation to Lohadaṇḍā.
O Goddess of the Gods, having thus worshipped, one should then worship Śakti.
HŪṂ! Salutation to Vāgīśvarī and Brahmā; HŪṂ! And to Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. Then, O Goddess Caṇḍā Maheśvarī, one should utter the word "namaḥ. (6.387)
Then one should worship with "Obeisance to Umā and Maheśvara," and so forth;
and after that, the Praṇava followed by "Obeisance to Kārttikeya and Īśvara."
With this very mantra, a person should worship the Śakti;
having thus worshipped the sword, one should worship it with special care. (6.389)
Oṃ! To the sword, the destroyer of the harsh; you who are intent on the purpose of the task of power—the animal must be sacrificed by you; O Lord of the Sword, homage be to you! (6.390)
With this very mantra, one should prostrate before the supreme sword;
having taken a copper vessel filled with water, one should face the north.
Desiring joy, he should perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) for the Great Goddess and for the sacrificial animal;
having performed the sprinkling of the animal, he should release it with the thought that it is a deity.
Let this offering be presented to you according to the prescribed rite;
growth occurs when [the branch] is cut and falls, while its falling on the left side is censured.
The wise one should remember the breakage as having fallen in the middle of the deity’s [form] and characterized by wretchedness;
then, having gone near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), an oblation (āhuti) should be offered fifteen times.
Thus, having cast away the defect by this means, one should observe the sacrificial offering (bali) for its auspicious marks;
then, having prepared blood, one should worship Vaṭuka and the others.
And in the southwest, O Great Goddess, one should worship Vaṭukabhairava with "Hūṃ Vāṃ," and in the northwest with "Hūṃ Yāṃ, obeisance to the Yoginīs," and so forth. || 6.396 ||
And in the northeast, O Maheśānī, [one should worship] with "Hūṃ Kṣau! Homage to Kṣetrapāla!
and so forth, O Goddess, one should properly worship with perfumes and flowers. (6-397)
In the southeast, one should worship with "Hūṃ! Oṃ, salutation to Gaṇeśa," and so forth.
Having worshipped thoroughly with perfumes and flowers, one should perform the offering of the *bali*.
Thus, O Goddess, the determination regarding the *balidāna* has been told to you. (6.398)

Thus ends the sixth chapter in the illustrious Bṛhannīlatantra, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, concerning the description of the rules for the Kula-worship, Śākta conduct, and other rites. || 6 ||
Now begins the seventh chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the supreme method for subjugation;
likewise, the ritual application and its accomplishment must certainly be performed.
On an auspicious Saturday, one should collect charcoal from a cremation ground;
having wrapped it in a black cloth, one should bind it with a red thread.
Having consecrated it one hundred times with mantras, one should cast it into the house of the enemy;
within seven days, this shall bring about their eradication.
One should inscribe the mantra upon human bone using turmeric mixed with alkali;
then, having recited it one thousand times on a Saturday at night.
In whose house it is deposited, death shall come to him within three months;
in the case of a field, there will be loss of crops, and in the case of a horse, loss of speed.

If there is loss of wealth, one should write the mantra on a cloth from a corpse in the house of wealth; if there is destruction in the midst of the village, the wise man should likewise write it on a cloth from a corpse in the place of enmity.
By means of the names of the one who hates and the one who is hated, his hatred shall become great.
Listen to the mantra, O lady of excellent hips, for it is fit for ritual application.
One should cause such-and-such a person to die; first the word "cause to die," and then this mantra, O Maheśvarī, having recited it a thousand times.
But listen with one-pointed mind, O beloved, to this specific mantra for inciting hatred:
immediately after [the seed syllable], say, "Create hatred between so-and-so and so-and-so; create it! (7–9).
O Queen of the Gods, having uttered the mantra, O Goddess, one should recite it a thousand times;
thereafter, O Piṅgākṣī, one should utter the pair of words "uccāṭaya."
Having again uttered the *phaṭ* mantra accompanied by the name of the one to be acted upon (*sādhya*), the enemy goes from place to place like another crow. (7.11)
Having written the enemy's mantra on a leaf within a fire-pouch,
one should recite the mantra in a cremation ground, fold it up, and then pierce it with a needle.
Even if recited for a thousand lifetimes, this vidyā does not bestow its fruit;
even the accomplishments (siddhis) that are difficult for the gods to attain will perish.
The nectar should be written within the circle of the Mothers (mātṛcakra) and enclosed in a vessel of powdered collyrium;
having cast it into water while reciting the mantra "punarnava," it is so described. (7.14)
Manu, though born with his brilliance eclipsed, was as affectionate as the newly risen moon;
he remained radiant moment by moment, even when coming within the sight of his enemies.
Now I shall speak of a single mantra; one should always maintain it, O Dear One.
One should write the root mantra within the pair of yonis using a golden stylus. (7.16)
Then, one should write the six syllables, excluding the neuter ones and those that are long or split, within the hexagon;
the eight syllables on the eight petals; and outside of that, two enclosures of squares (bhūpura).
The most excellent practitioner should draw the eight vajras and the city-gate (bhūpura) on a golden plate, or on birch bark, or on silver, O lady of virtuous vows. (7.18)
One should draw [the design] with a golden stylus combined with the eight fragrant substances;
or alternatively, having drawn it with a stalk of dūrvā grass or with the root of kuśa grass.
One should carefully wrap it with a yellow cloth;
one should tie it with a yellow cloth as an ornament for the necks of children.
In this manner, for women it is on the left arm, and for others on the right arm;
thus a barren woman obtains a son, and one who is destitute becomes wealthy.
This protection was formerly established by Gautama and others for the sake of knowledge, and by other kings for the sake of fame, desiring victory in battle. (7.22)
The Vāgbhava [syllable], the Kula-deity, the Tāraka, the Vāgbhava likewise, the Hṛllekhā, and the Astra-mantra—this mantra ends with the wife of Fire (svāhā). (7.23)
The eight-syllable mantra is proclaimed; it is declared to be the essence of all mantras.
One should perform only those ritual applications (prayoga) taught in the Kālikā-mantra-tantra.
One should perform here the ritual applications (prayoga) taught in the mantras of the Kālikā-tantra;
for as is Kālī, so is Nīlā—there is no difference between them, O Maheśvarī. (7-25)
Truth has been declared by me as something to be practiced without distinction.
Listen to another [instruction], O lady of excellent limbs, regarding the supreme method of subjugation. (7.26)
O Great Goddess, on a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism, the heroic practitioner will certainly become blessed; at that time, he should procure the root of a vīra.
O Śivā, having purified it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should dry it in the heat of the sun;
then, taking it up, one should grind it with a ram's horn.
O Goddess of the gods, having drawn the most beautiful yantra known as Mātṛkā, listen, O lady of excellent hips, to the mantra which bestows omniscience through meditation. (7.29)

The lotus has the sky, moon, earth, and the letter *ra* as its pericarp; it possesses shimmering filaments formed by pairs of vowels, petals that shine with the [consonant] groups, and is encircled by the abode of the earth (*vasumatī*).
It is accompanied by the letters ending in *la* and *ṭa* in the three directions, and is surrounded by the city of the earth (*kṣoṇīpura*).
The Yantra of the Blue-bodied One is declared to be supreme, bestowing the accomplishment of all aims.
O Goddess of the gods, having carefully drawn the yantra with that powder upon an earthen vessel,
one should place it atop the water-pot (kumbhaka).
O Goddess praised by the gods, one should place a jar filled with sesame seeds there;
one should worship Cāmuṇḍā with a silk cloth and with water mixed with sugar.
O Supreme Goddess, by reciting that mantra one may bring the three worlds under control;
having extracted Kapardin, Kalaha is the second [syllable]. (7.33)
"O Khaḍga! O Supreme Goddess! O Cāmuṇḍā!"—after uttering these words, one should then pronounce the word "Victory! and say "vaśam ānaya ṭha ṭha. (7.34)
With this king of mantras, one should perform the supreme rite of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*);
one should offer food and edibles to Mahādevī, who is worshipped by the hosts of gods. (7.35)
Having sat upon a red seat, one should joyfully recite [the mantra] sixteen thousand times;
then one should perform the fire oblations (homa) and other rites according to the measure of one-tenth or other such proportions.
When the recitation is completed, O Goddess of Gods, one should give a silver dakṣiṇā—
either a pala, or half of that, or even half of that, according to one's capacity.
O Goddess of pure smiles, one should perform the recitation with a garland of coral;
O Beloved, a red turban and likewise a red upper garment are prescribed.
Having put on red garments, one should recite [the mantra] with the mind focused upon it;
O fair-browed one, poetic skill arises through the grace of this mantra. (7.39)
Poetry comes under one's control; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Now listen, O lady of beautiful limbs, to the supreme means of producing poetry. (7.40)
Out of affection for you, this practice—which is to be concealed from all—is now revealed:
it concerns the Naṭī and Caṇḍālinī, and the Yogin who deludes all. (7.41)
One should recite the three seed-syllables at night, specifically at midnight on a Sunday;
one should perform the recitation with a count of one thousand and eight.
Having consecrated it one hundred times with mantras, one should drink that excellent water;
by practicing this for seven days, poetic talent that delights the mind will arise.
This shall come to pass, there is no doubt about it; this is the truth, O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods!
With her right hand alone, she should offer honey and parched grain.

O Goddess praised by the gods, the practitioner should perform the consecration of the child even before the severing of the umbilical cord; through that, poetic skill arises as his second [attainment]. (7.45)
Having cleansed the tongue, O Goddess of gods, one should draw [the lines] with a golden needle;
or else, O Great Goddess, one should draw them on the tongue and the lips with *dūrvā* grass. (7.46)
Having written it out in two rows, one should perform the purificatory rite for the child on the eleventh day,
O Goddess of Gods, or alternatively on the twelfth day.
According to the distinctions of caste, birth, and so forth, [the practice] will occur for up to one month;
one should worship the deity before oneself with offerings according to one's capacity.
O Maheśvarī, having worshipped the deity with devotion,
one should write the mantra when the father is not present in the country, or likewise the paternal uncle or maternal uncle.
Having written it, O Supreme Goddess, one should perform the sacrament for the child;
the practitioner of mantra should write the root-mantra upon the child's lip with white dūrvā grass.
A child devoted to the utterance of speech shall become eloquent and a swift poet.
When a son is born, it is recommended that he be given a name that effects his purification at birth.
One should write the mantra upon the tongue using a sacrificial wood splinter or a blade of *kuśa* grass;
having thoroughly wiped it three times with the right hand alone.
Having recited the mantra, one should form each line very beautifully;
first the consecration (saṃskāra) should be performed, and at its end one should write the mantra.
One should worship the auspicious Tāriṇī with fragrant sandalwood and flowers;
facing north, one should establish the excellent pedestal.
One should worship the goddess Tāriṇī with various beautiful edibles and should worship her with devotion through the sixteen types of ritual offerings.
One should offer incense made of guggulu, which bestows the fruits of all rites;
likewise, one should offer coconut, plantain, jujube, and bakula flowers. (7.56)
Bijapura, karṇikāra, sugar combined with fragrant substances,
honey-water, peas, and prepared food soaked in milk-rice (pāyasa).
If one offers meat, fish, and flour-cakes—which are greatly and most beloved—the son shall become a poet and an eloquent speaker, capable of performing all types of tasks. (7.58)
One who has conquered his senses, speaks the truth, and is righteous is born as a great man;
likewise, he becomes a father, a father’s brother, and also a mother’s brother.
O Maheśānī, worshipped by the hosts of gods, no one else should write the mantra;
however, even a brother may write the mantra that bestows the fruits of all desires. (7.60)
Having taken the child onto his mother’s lap and carefully spread out a cloth,
he, joined by Brāhmaṇas [or practitioners, according to the Kha manuscript], should perform a rite of pacification for the child. (7.61)
O Maheśānī, desire this son right here as one born of desire; he shall nourish the intermediate space between the gods.

"O Maheśvarī, at the conclusion of writing the mantra, one should perform the rite of pacification (śānti) for Tārā with the words 'śivaśāntis tārāyai', for the filaments [of the lotus] with 'tārāyai', and for Śiva with 'śivāya śivayaśase'.
This has been explained in detail in the Matsyasūkta. (7.63)
One should joyfully recite the Śāntistotra into the mother’s left ear:
"O Mother, O Goddess, salutations to you, the sinless one who bears the form of Brahman."
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me all accomplishments. (Mantra, as read in manuscript Kha) || 7-64 ||
O Great Goddess, bestower of boons, whose form is supreme bliss!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me all perfections.
O Kaumāri, sovereign of all vidyās, supreme in youthful play,
out of compassion remove my obstacles and grant me all accomplishments.
O Goddess who bears the form of Viṣṇu, O carrier of the son of Vinatā!
By your grace, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of the mantra.
O Vārāhī, O goddess who grants boons, you who have lifted up the earth with your tusk!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and bestow upon me all spiritual accomplishments.
O Goddess who assumes the form of Śakra, worshipped by the gods beginning with Śakra:
out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me all accomplishments.
O Cāmuṇḍā, adorned with a garland of severed heads and smeared with blood, O destroyer of obstacles!
Out of compassion, remove my obstacle and grant me all spiritual accomplishments.
O Mahālakṣmī, you of great energy, who removes the torment of sorrow;
out of compassion, take away my obstacles and grant me all success.
O Goddess, who consist of both the measure and the measurer, yet are beyond the measure and the measurer; O Goddess, who are one and yet manifold, whose form is the universe—salutations be to you!
O Maheśvarī, for one who recites this hymn at the commencement of an undertaking,
or upon seeing a clever woman, no obstacle shall arise.
O beautiful one, these have been described to you as the door-deities of a person of noble birth;
if one does not worship them at the time of initiation or during the occasion of daily worship, [the rite is flawed].
O Goddess, the fruit of his worship is carried away by yakṣas and rākṣasas;
O beloved, even from a hundred years of recitation, no success arises, O Goddess.
During a great calamity or sudden misfortune, one should recite this hymn to Gaṇeśvarī;
then all adversities flee away—of this there is no doubt whatsoever. (7.76)
O Goddess of gods, one who desires knowledge should recite this hymn a hundred times.
Thus has been told to you this hymn to the Mother, which is an ornament for the neck.
O Great Goddess, bring this into light for my devotees;
this hymn is not to be disclosed to just anyone. (7.78)
Indeed, one who is endowed with devotion and faith should always give to him who is of noble birth, peaceful, upright, and free from hypocrisy. (7.79)
O Maheśānī, one should offer this hymn; otherwise, one shall not partake of the fruit.
It was proclaimed by Vedavyāsa within the eighteen Purāṇas. (7–80)
The Goddess said:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O cause of maintenance and destruction,
O you of noble vows, I ask one question here in your presence."
Abandoning all deceit, O destroyer of worldly existence,
tell me that which has not been revealed, even though it was spoken— the Great Cīna-krama, O Lord. Tell me that now, if you have affection for me.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess, the Mahācīnakrama is concealed within all the tantras;
by performing it, all practitioners attain the state of Śiva at that very moment. (7–83)
O Maheśānī, O Śivā, one must not speak [of this] within the three worlds;
O Queen of the Gods, it should be spoken with a pure disposition within your sphere of perception.
O Goddess praised by the gods, there is no one else dear to me other than you;
now, O Supreme Sovereign, O Auspicious One, fix your mind [on this].
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, the Mahācīnakrama must be told;
O Great Mistress, I am the body and you are the embodied one who perceives all forms.
Just as a fish, O Great Goddess, is struck within the water, so too are you, the True Self, O Maheśānī; there is nothing that cannot be told, O beautiful one. (7-87)
Some were gods, some humans, some dānavas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas;
there were also those from the world of the nāgas, kinnaras, and hosts of gandharvas and apsarases.
Whether they be domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, or whatever else exists within the world—all these are utterly insentient and by nature mutually hostile. (7-89)
All of them are devoted to evil deeds and are eager for the vision of false paths.
O Great Goddess, even Brahmā does not know the consciousness of these beings—the Brahman that is bliss, the consciousness-bliss; how then can I tell it to you?
This [reality] has the nature of being eternally liberated; it is for that purpose that this has been stated.
"Forgive me, O lady of beautiful limbs; if it must be so, O Maheśvarī, you need not speak.
The Goddess said:
"Salutations to you who are the form of Śiva; salutations to you who are the form of the Guru. (7.92)
Salutations to you, O Lord who grants boons; salutations to the treasury of compassion.
Even those who are devoted to other deities all desire your feet.
For those very devotees of mine, a superior fruit is established;
as for lions, tigers, and others, as well as those who follow after obstacles (or those who cause them).
Likewise, transformations, serpents, and other wicked creatures—all of them go to destruction like moths in a fire. (7.95)
O Lord, O All-pervading One, it is only through your own affection that this body is seen by wicked beings as having the form of a lamp-flame within the house.
Or else, having become composed of a corpse, the five deities on the seat cause the earth to attain the state of water, and the water becomes composed of fire. (7.97)
Fire [entered] Vāyu, and likewise Vāyu [entered] Ākāśa, which is its illuminator;
so too did all the Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and whatever other hosts of deities there were.

Kings and all others likewise abide at your feet; even the Gandharvas obey your command, so what need be said of the mere insects of hell? [The variant reading "kinnarāḥ" is found in manuscript *kha*.]
Wherever there may be a desire, that very thing is held in the hand as an accomplished success;
speech that always follows him certainly attends upon him. (7.100)
Having abandoned the state of duality, what is the use of further talk?
One who seeks liberation attains liberation; one who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth.
But first, one is born in the world of Gaurī like another Śiva;
tell me before me how her devotees become perfected beings (siddhas). || 7.102 ||
The illustrious Bhairava said:

"O Goddess Śivā, this Mahācīnakrama, which has been described to you in its various forms, must not be spoken of to one who is not a devotee, nor to one devoted to another [deity], nor to a sinner. (7–103)
Bathing and other rites are mental purification; recitation is preeminent when mental;
worship is divine when mental; and even ritual construction and the like are mental. (7.104)
Every moment is indeed auspicious; nowhere does an inauspicious time exist.
There is no distinction between day and night, nor between the twilights and the dead of night. (7.105)
One should not perform purification here with water for clothes, seats, dwellings, the body, touch, and so forth; rather, one should practice the mind free from conceptual construction. (7.106)
In this, there is no requirement for purity and the like, nor is there any defect such as impurity;
the practitioner who contemplates in this way bestows the fruit of all desires. (7.107)
His speech, consisting of both prose and verse, arises in the assembly;
by the mere sight of him, the disputants are considered shorn of their luster.
Even kings attain the state of servitude; what then of other people?
One should always worship the Goddess, even if one has not bathed or has already eaten. (7.109)
At midnight, one should cause an offering to be presented with the mantra in a pure place;
one should not utter disparagement of women, but rather increase affection for them. (7.110)
Even when her offense is extremely grave, one should not harbor hatred toward her;
one must never practice hatred toward women, but rather especially honor them. (7.111)
Having placed a great conch shell at the place of recitation, one should perform the recitation while facing upwards;
even while approaching, touching, or looking at a woman, wherever the teacher may be.
Chewing betel leaf and other edible substances according to his pleasure, as well as meat, fish, curd, honey, and other edible substances according to his pleasure. (7.113)
Having eaten all the remaining food from one's meal, one should perform the entire recitation (*japa*).
There is no restriction regarding direction or time, nor is there any restriction regarding posture and so forth. (7.114)

There is no restriction regarding time for recitation, nor for worship and the like, nor even for the offerings; here, in the practice of the Great Mantra, it is said that one may follow whatever rules accord with one's own inclination. (7.115)
O fair-browed one, no unrighteousness exists; there would be only great dharma.
Established in the conduct of one's own will, O Goddess, one should act with a joyful mind. (7.116)
Considering himself one who has achieved his purpose, being contented and having conquered his mind,
he should perform recitation especially, and he should also perform recitation with a woman.
Listen to the description of the seat, O Goddess of gods; by means of it, the supreme recitation will first be perfected.
This is the most excellent of all seats, and through its recitation, it bestows omniscience. (7.118)
Having placed [the penis] upon the vulva-pīṭha at the hips, O lotus-eyed one, with the liṅga inserted into the vulva, he should mutter [the mantra] with his mind fixed upon that. (7.119)
By reciting this a thousand times every day, a man becomes like Kandarpa;
of this there is no doubt, O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods—this is the truth.
O Supreme Goddess, the specific conduct of China has indeed been described;
O Great Mistress, it has been revealed in detail in the Tārākalpa.
And here, O Great Goddess, I have described a special rule:
having taken the hair from the vulva, one should take the undergarment.
Thus, with the mind fixed upon them, one should recite [the mantra] for the duration of a year;
[the deities are] Nīlāsarasvatī, Kālī, Annapūrṇā, and Bhairavī. (7.123)
She becomes gracious toward the joyful practitioner, of this there is no doubt;
and the practitioner, O Great Goddess, beholds her after one year.
In this matter, O Maheśvarī, you have no doubt; this is the truth, the absolute truth.
Out of great affection for you, O best of goddesses, this has been revealed to you.
Listen to the secret, O lady of beautiful limbs, by which one attains success, O fair one:
if, upon seeing a woman in her menses, one should mutter [the mantra] a thousand times. (7.126)
At that very moment, the accomplishment of the mantra shall occur; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
O Goddess, within sixteen days, the practitioner attains perfection. (7.127)
Placing his hand upon the mountain, free from fear and with a disciplined mind, he too attains poetic inspiration and goes to the state of immortality. (7.128)
A blue lotus, a bimba fruit, a wagtail, a mountain peak, a fly-whisk, the solar disc, a sesame flower, and a lake (or, according to the Kha manuscript reading, a lotus). || 7-129 ||

Having beheld the trident (the reading *triśūla* is found in manuscript *kha*) and constantly recited [the mantra] with a pure disposition, one attains a state of blissful serenity— [a deity] with a gracious face, beautiful eyes, and a smiling countenance.
One obtains beautiful hair, a good rebirth, a bulbous root, a pleasant fragrance, and happiness itself; listen with respect, O Pārvatī, according to their respective order. (7.131)
Having meditated upon the Goddess there at the great Chinese tree and having worshipped her there,
one should worship her with devotion using a flower produced from that tree.
He shall become a family deity, pure and following the lineage tradition;
having meditated upon the Goddess according to the ritual at the great root of the Tree of Brahman.
One should satisfy [the deities] in the forest of the Mātṛkās with the essence of that nectar;
he shall become the best of practitioners and dear to the Mothers. (7-134)
Enveloped by great Chinese trees and creepers, the supreme practitioner, if he recites the mantra at night, shall become a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*). (7.135)
O Goddess of gods, when one is encircled by the creeper according to the sequence of lunar days,
then success shall be attained within a month through ten thousand recitations.
If it is recited twice as much on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days,
then at that very moment one attains a great accomplishment difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Having written the seed-syllable with saffron on a great Chinese tree,
and having inscribed the name of the target beside it, one should strike it with glances and showers [of mantras].
Afflicted by desire, she goes wherever she may find him;
having prepared a bolus smeared with the juice of the great *cīna* tree. (7.139)
O Goddess, he by whose name [the offering] is given shall attain liberation before long, [by means of] the marrow from the root of the great *cīna* tree and *bilva* leaves. (7.140)
Having worshipped the Goddess a thousand times in the cremation ground, the best of practitioners then attains a kingdom, provided that she does not flee. (7.141)
Those corpses do not equal even a sixteenth part of that [merit];
entering a house of creepers yields a fruit far greater than sitting upon a corpse-seat.
But that wise man who desires wealth, who longs for great sovereignty,
and who wishes to become equal to Bṛhaspati— (7.143)
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and having summoned the *kula*, he who, knowing the mantra,
engages in sexual union in this manner shall obtain all fruits.
One should recite [the mantra] upon the vines for the sake of liberation from great sins;
if there is no contact with the vine, then one must carefully [dispose of] the semen. (7.145)
Having driven [the obstacles] away, one should recite the mantra for the accomplishment of dharma, kāma, and artha;
it should be recited during sexual unions for liberation from great sins.
Having beheld his chosen deity at the base of that [tree] seated upon an excellent throne,
and having worshipped [the deity], one should worship the mantra for three days during the deep of night.
O Goddess, one obtains the fruit of a hundred thousand seats; of this there is no doubt.
The accomplishment of the Vetāla, the accomplishment of the sandals, and the accomplishment of the sword arise.
Having secretly recited [the mantra] one thousand times over collyrium and a forehead mark (tilaka),
[one should offer] one thousand bilva leaves smeared with the blood from one's own body.
Having worshipped the Goddess in a cremation ground, one attains equality with Vāgīśa;
the mantra-practitioner, having worshipped a virtuous woman who has reached her fertile season in a cremation ground, [attains the same]. (7.150)
Having recited the mantra, one should then meditate upon the beautiful woman, her limbs smeared with red sandalwood and adorned with red garments and lovely flowers. (7.151)
Having enjoyed her, he shall obtain the kingdom if he does not flee from this place;
by means of the blood of a ram or a buffalo, eloquence arises for him.
Wealth arises for him, and all accomplishments (siddhis) are produced.
And by speech one may become a living being, and by wealth, a lord of wealth.
By his command he is the king of the gods; by his very form he is the god of love; by his strength he is indeed the wind-god, the accomplisher of the meaning of all principles.
One should always offer meat together with bones as a bali-oblation that has been purified and prepared;
likewise, everything should be offered along with bones and accompanied by hair.
O Goddess, such a practitioner is always difficult to find on earth;
for whatever kind of sight or whatever recitation is seen among men on this earth, [it is rare]. (7.156)
O Goddess, by revealing this, death occurs and not otherwise;
likewise, by reviling this practitioner or, again, this mantra. (7.157)
Together with the hosts of great elements, I take away everything belonging to him; accompanied by the circle of Yoginīs, I myself am the one who brings about his destruction.
Listen to the secret, O Goddess of gods, by which one shall always become eloquent;
for there is nothing superior to this within the tantras, O Mistress of the Gods. (7.159)
This application of Sarasvatī has been described for the enchantment of the universe;
I shall now explain its specific details—listen with careful attention. (7.160)
It has been taught to you in the Vīratantra by which one may become identical with all things:
he who meditates upon Tāriṇī in the form of a lamp upon his tongue. (7.161)
Having recited the Vidyā together with the Mātṛkā three times, one should drink water;
by this method of drinking water, even a mute becomes a skilled poet. (7.162)
Through the constant practice of cultivation, the practitioner—virtuous and wise—becomes a poet, an eloquent speaker, a great yogi, and one who partakes in liberation. (7.163)
Within a year, his fourfold scholarship arises.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the most wonderful secret. (7.164)
One should write enchanting mantras upon the vulva of young women; having recited the great mantra that bestows all eloquence, [one should apply it]. (7.165)
One should perform the ritual application by means of a thousand recitations;
thereafter, one should strike the yoni-maṇḍala through the yoga of circumambulation.
One should recite it a thousand times until semen is produced;
with that essence, O Goddess of Gods, one should satisfy [the deity] with a restrained mind. (7.167)
O fair-browed one, poetic skill and eloquence likewise arise;
scholarship and greatness are born—of this there is no doubt. (7.168)
O Maheśānī, one should perform the worship of the *yoni* with red flowers;
assuming the form of a young woman, one should worship it with great effort. (7.169)
O Maheśānī, casting aside all aversion, one should worship the Yonimaṇḍala;
listen to this secret, O lady of beautiful limbs, by which the mantra becomes perfected. (7.170)
(The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, Sovereign of beings, of great power!
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods of gods, you who are devoted to the welfare of all living creatures. (7.171)
"O Lord, tell me that means by which success will inevitably be attained.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme knowledge, the most excellent among all knowledges."
By means of which mere consciousness, the vidyā quickly becomes propitious. || 7-172 ||
The power within the root tuber that takes the form of the support of the universe—the wind of its whirling vortex—is called "prāṇa" by the wise. (7.173)
The sound of the cricket, more distinct, warbling and constantly rising, goes through the aperture of Brahmā and enters its own abode. (7.174)
One should effect the dissolution of the mind there through the very process of going and returning;
by that, the crest-lock (śikhā) is born within the mantra, serving as the illuminator of all mantras.
Just as nothing at all appears in a house filled with darkness, so too mantras devoid of the crest-syllable (śikhā) never attain success. (7.176)
O Supreme Goddess, the instruction on the crest (śikhā) is concealed everywhere;
without it, there can be no accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of years.
Therefore, O Girijā, you too must guard [this] with great effort;
she is asleep, slumbering, intoxicated, and intent on putting others to flight.
O Kulasundarī, [she who is] bound by the entire web of defects [or, according to the Kha manuscript, she who is free from them].

During sleep, at the watch of the dead of night, there is the movement of the wind through the left channel (vāmanāḍī); likewise, when the wind arises in the right channel, there is movement during the day; however, the movement during the twilights (saṃdhyā) is as follows:
The flow through both channels; the night practice, the day practice, and the twilight practice are the "sprout."

Having understood the difficult-to-obtain union of the seed-syllable, as well as the convention of entities and the very conjunction of entities, the hero, the guru, should awaken [the disciple]; he alone is the cause therein. (7.180)
O Great Goddess, I shall tell you the specific rule regarding the night-walk;
O Goddess, it concerns the actual rising [of the breath] in the left and right nostrils according to reality.
However, the recitation of mantras during the time of sleep yields fruitless results;
the time of sleep is the flow of the left (vāma), while waking is the flow of the right (dakṣiṇa). || 7.182 ||
One should know that the time for awakening both of these mantras—the fiery mantra of Manu and the lunar mantra—is the reverse of this. (7.183)

In the two karmas, [the mantras] beginning with Vahni and Tārā are declared to consist mostly of the letter *vi* (the sky); those belonging to Agni and Soma likewise consist for the most part of the syllables of the nectar of the moon (*amṛta*).
Thus, fifty *vidyās* are proclaimed as belonging to Agni and Soma;
when the wind flows through the left [nostril], that is the application of the long vowels. (7.185)
When the wind is in the south, then the short [vowel] is applied;
when the wind is situated in both, then they would be of a dual nature.
The Praṇava, the Goddess Mātṛkā, and Hṛllekhā constitute the triad of nectars (amṛtatraya).
Through the conjunction of this triad of nectars, even a corrupt mantra becomes effective.
Listen thus, O lady of excellent hips, to this supreme mantra which is the essence of all;
the observance must be understood by men, never by women.
By whatever means or in whatever manner, and from every direction whatsoever, the accomplishments (siddhis) shall undoubtedly arise for women through mere meditation alone. (7.189)
Just as iron pierced by a hidden stone [magnet] comes forth of its own accord merely by the presence of a magnet, or as [metal is drawn out] by the heat of the sun; || 7.190 ||
Just as the sun-gem clearly shines by the rays of the moon, and just as the moon-gem melts during the rains due to the clouds; || 7.191 ||
The earth, thoroughly satiated by the sprinkling of water, is said to be filled with essence;
just as one afflicted by hunger becomes satisfied by drinking milk. (7.192)
Merely by seeing the flower, the Gandharva becomes happy;
by the offering of the family-flower, Śakti is thoroughly pleased according to one's capacity.
Just as the accomplishment of mantra may come about through service to the guru alone,
so too one becomes a master of accomplishment by meditating upon the Great Lotus Grove.
By the mere meditation upon Tripurā, may there be both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
and by the grace of Mahādurgā, may one become a lord of supernatural powers (siddhis). || 7.195 ||
Just as one becomes a patriarch merely by meditating upon a young woman,
so too does one become free from sin merely by recollecting the Gaṅgā.
In the same way, by mere ploughing, Śiva himself is produced;
O Bhairavī, just as he is pleased by the worship of the womb at Kāmākhya. (7.197)
Merely by thinking of her as a woman, she likewise bestows boons;
therefore, with every effort, one should initiate a woman of the Kula lineage.
From association with families that have not received initiation, the loss of spiritual accomplishment arises.
By this very sequence, he who performs auspicious ritual action [attains success]. (7.199)
In his lineage, O Great Goddess, a man equal to Bṛhaspati shall be born;
there is no doubt in this, it is the truth, the absolute truth, O you who are worshipped by the gods. (7.200)
Once, having approached Nārada, Gaurī, endowed with all happiness and devoted to seeking Śaṅkara, questioned him in sweet speech.
The celestial sage spoke these words: "Listen, O daughter of the mountain!
This is indeed the application of Tārā, by which success shall be attained. (7.202)
Nārada said: Once Indra, having fallen from his prosperity, left Amarāvatī and went to the city of Hiraṇyākṣa accompanied by the hosts of the gods’ army.
A very great conflict arose there between the gods and their enemies;
the king of the gods was defeated by those who had Bṛhaspati as their domestic priest.
Having returned once more to the hermitage and reflected deeply upon various auspicious matters, Indra approached his preceptor,
the teacher of the world, and spoke these words with reverence:
(Indra said:)
For you are indeed the purifier of all that exists in this world of moving and unmoving beings;
O God, I go to you for refuge; protect me, O Blessed One, from whatever [evil] arises.
"O Lord of Gods, tell me the means by which the status of Indra is attained;
in what form, O Lord of Gods, will my protection come to pass? (7.207)
Bṛhaspati said:
"O Lord of the Gods, listen to my words, by which protection shall be found.
O God, in the city of Hiraṇyākṣa dwell the Daityas, the crushers of all enemies. (7.208)
I am not capable of bringing about their defeat upon the surface of the earth;
hear the reason, O Lord of Gods, and listen to my words.
O King, in former times during the Tretā Yuga, you performed the Nīla-sādhana;
by the very fruit of that merit, O dear one, you attained the status of Indra. (7.210)
And that son of a Daitya composed the *Kālītārāsādhana* in various forms and at length; therefore, from this [work], may there be the fruit of merit and so forth. (7.211)
O Great King, with full attention, consider that means by which you yourself shall attain the status of Indra, O Lord of the Gods. (7.212)
He always prospers through righteousness and does not increase through unrighteousness;
yet, in a certain form, that Daitya quickly abandons righteousness.
Listen to my truthful words regarding that means, O Lord of the Gods: I shall deceive you by assuming the form of an aged Brahmin. (7.214)
Then, having become a great brahmin— an elder who purifies the learned and one who knows the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures— he went to the city of Hiraṇyākṣa.
Listen, my child, to these weighty words by which prosperity shall come to pass:
I am a knower of all the scriptures, yet I have come here because of my poverty.
"By providing a livelihood, I have performed the act of teaching;
for he who, having provided a livelihood to a teacher, causes the twice-born to study. (7.217)
What could there be that has not been given by him who desires virtue, pleasure, and wealth?
Know that this merit is more meritorious than any other merit, and is universally esteemed. (7.218)
Having accepted the words "So be it," he provided excellent means of subsistence;
having granted delightful livelihoods, he caused the twice-born to study.
O Goddess, hundreds of fallacious arguments were made by that most eminent one;
yet, O Great Goddess, this [present] fallacious argument, though great, is surpassed by that [former] fallacious argument. (7.220)
The lord of the Daityas, that foremost of Dānavas, was deluded by this thought:
"Once a deed has been performed by those dwelling on earth, how can there be satisfaction in heaven? (7.221)
Tāriṇī, Mahākālī, Bhavānī, and Maheśvarī—the worship of these, O Lord, is in vain; for what purpose is this inauspicious rite performed? (7.222)
Thus, by various kinds of fallacious reasoning, even that great king of the Daityas was deluded; having abandoned Dharma, he [sought refuge] with Maheśvarī.
O Maheśvarī, O auspicious one, having abandoned the Dharma, they all became devoted to unrighteousness;
and in the course of time, supreme calamities befell them. (7.224)
Then the god Bṛhaspati went to the palace of the king of the gods and related everything to Indra regarding the bondage of the Daityas through their own actions.
Listen with a one-pointed mind, O King of Gods, Lord of the World, so that great merit may arise for you; there is no doubt in this matter. (7.226)
Having worshipped Tāriṇī, Kālikā, Annapūrṇā, and the supreme Bhairavī according to the prescribed rites with devotion, all perfections (siddhis) shall be attained.
"O Lord of Gods, O handsome one, I wish to hear without doubt the procedure for worship during the middle watch of the night in the month of Phālguna."
O Maheśāna, O Lord of Gods, O beloved, have excellent plantain pillars erected in the four directions and a pavilion constructed in front of yourself.
One should construct a pavilion covered with mango, holy fig, and banyan trees;
one should surround the pavilion with young girls, for it brings total enchantment.
O King of the Gods, O Great Lord, fashion for me that form of Tārā or the form of Kālī, which bestows all accomplishments.
O you who are praised by the gods, fashion this very form of the Giver of Food;
one should diligently cause an offering to be presented to the Great Goddess upon a banyan leaf. (7.232)
One should offer a seat and a woolen blanket, along with a welcome offering made of honey; one should offer water for the feet with milk, and the respectful arghya offering with kusha grass. (7.233)
One should offer the madhuparka with clarified butter alone, the water for rinsing the mouth (ācamanīyaka) with water, and perform the bath with buttermilk; a red garment is prescribed.
One should offer silver ornaments that are enchanting to all the gods;
O dear one, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented to the Goddess without rice.
One should offer delightful foods to be chewed, sucked, licked, and drunk;
then, with seeds of red sandalwood, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times.
Beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, one should complete [the rite] on the eighth day;
one should offer an oblation to Mahādevī with a goat or a buffalo.
One should offer to the Goddess food, fish, meat, most excellent ghee, and flour-cakes—delightful substances that are exceedingly beautiful. (7.238)
O Lord of the gods of gods, one should perform the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rules and to the best of one's ability.
Śrī Bhairava said:
One should worship the Kumārī with diligent efforts and various kinds of ritual substances.
But all rites such as the fire-oblation, without the worship of the maiden, do not yield their full fruit; indeed, the entire worship would not be complete. (7.240)
Then, for the sake of attaining all perfections, one should worship a young girl;
one should bring a suitable maiden who is a virgin or a married woman.
O beautiful one, abandon your doubt regarding a young woman in the full bloom of youth;
I shall tell you of the auspicious worship of the maiden, of this there is no doubt. (7.242)
O Maheśānī, by the mere worship of her, the worship of the three worlds is accomplished; and Kumārī is established as a triple-formed manifestation.
The third [nature] consists of both the supreme and the non-supreme; it is the supreme-non-supreme.
At that time, when nothing whatsoever exists—neither gods, nor asuras, nor great serpents—(7-244).
Neither the three worlds nor you nor I existed then;
she who is the primordial creator of creation manifested visibly in a threefold manner.
That goddess was born as Umākalā, the form of creation in another existence;
Sandhyā shall be one year old, and Sarasvatī two years old. (7.246)
A three-year-old is the threefold form; a four-year-old is Kālikā;
a five-year-old is Subhagā; and a six-year-old shall be Umā. (7.247)
With seven [syllables] she is Mālinī; with eight, Kubjikā;
with nine, Kālasaṅkarṣā; and with ten, Aparājitā. (7.248)
In the eleventh [year], however, she is Rudrāṇī; in the twelfth year, Bhairavī;
in the thirteenth, Mahālakṣmī; and in the twenty-second, she is the Mistress of the Pīṭha.
The Kṣetrajñā is worshipped with fifteen [deities], and Carcikā is considered the sixteenth;
thus they should be worshipped in sequence until the flower arises. (7.250)
One should worship from the first day (pratipad) until the full moon (pūrṇānta) according to the various stages of increase,
on all the great festival days (mahāparvan), and especially during the Pavitraka rite.
O Goddess of gods, on the Mahānavamī day, one should worship Kumārī;
and he who, observing a single meal on the sixteenth day, worships Piṅgalā.
Having worshipped with devotion, one shall become possessed of all prosperity;
one should worship each individual Kulabhairavī of the Kula-vidyās. (7.253)
In this way, one should worship the reality of consciousness through the yoga of the *praṇava*;
indeed, O daughter of the mountain, know the specific significance of the *praṇava*. (7.254)
By the knowledge of which all practitioners become partakers of liberation;
it is the source (yoni) consisting of the bindu, and beyond that is the seed-syllable of Māyā.

Then, having uttered *lakṣmī*, one should perform the *māyā* [mantra], O Maheśvarī: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ*. These are the five *praṇavas*. O auspicious lady, these five *praṇavas* are renowned as destroyers of all sins. (7.256)
The seed-syllable of Bhairavī is declared to be the captivating seed-syllable of the Preta;
it may consist of one, two, three, seven, or even eight [syllables]. (7.257)
O Mistress of the Family, great fears such as famines and other portents, bad dreams, untimely death, and whatever other calamities may arise—[these are all overcome]. (7.258)
Indeed, by the worship of the maiden alone, those [obstacles] do not prevail over him;
O Goddess of Gods, one should worship according to the rule through the daily ritual sequence. (7.259)
When worshipped, they destroy obstacles as well as most formidable enemies; likewise, diseases, all portents of misfortune, and ill omens are undoubtedly destroyed. (7.260)
The planets, yakṣas, bhūtas, vetālas, and pannagas go to destruction; so too the asuras, guhyakas, the proclaimed yoginīs, and the secret ḍākinīs. (7.261)
Indeed, the powers such as aṇimā, as well as the Vetālas and Bhairavas, are pleased; through the worship of the Kumārikā, one becomes a divine Vetāla. (7.262)
Water should be offered with the syllable *aiṃ*; the washing of the feet is performed with the syllable *hrīṃ*.
O Maheśānī, O Maheśvarī, one should offer the *arghya* with the syllable *śrīṃ*.
O Goddess of the gods, one should offer excellent sandalwood with the *kūrca* seed-mantra;
flowers with the *śakti* seed-mantra; and one should cause incense to be offered with all [the seed-mantras]. (7.264)
Then one should place Vāgbhava, then Māyā, and after that Sundarī; then the western face ending in the dative case (ṅe), [all] ending with the Heart-mantra, O beloved. (7.265)

O Goddess worshipped by the gods, having uttered the word *kumārike* joined with the *yoni-bīja*, the syllable of peaceful color (*śa*) joined with the *bindu*, and *śirase* followed by *vahnivallabhā*. (7.266)
Then [one should utter] the beginning of the Veda, followed by Māyā and her own seed-syllable;
then "Vaṣaṭ to the Tuft (śikhā)," O Goddess praised as the life-force of Bhairava. (7.267)
Having uttered the Praṇava, Kākinī, and the eternal [syllable] joined with the Bindu,
one should then utter the word Vāgīśvarī and say "Hūṃ" for the armor (kavaca).
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), followed by "Astrāya Phaṭ," and then the Vāgbhava syllable (Aiṃ) and the word "Siddhi" for the sake of victory. (7.269)
O Goddess of gods, one should worship the eastern face with [the mantra] ending in *hṛt* (namaḥ).
Again, the northern face consists of the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable joined with *ṅe*. (7.270)
O Great Goddess, one should worship Surasundarī with the salutation *namonta*. O Maheśānī, [the mantra consists of] the *praṇava*, then the word *Kālike*, and then the intermediate word.
O beloved of Bhairava, after that, [one should worship] the right face ending with "namaḥ";
by means of the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable], there is the agitation of the city, and in the *māyābīja*, the eight qualities.
Through the seed-syllable *śrī*, there is the attainment of prosperity; through the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, the destruction of enemies;
and through the *bhairava* seed-syllable, one becomes unconquerable with a sword. (7.273)
Or else, you yourself are always the eight Kumārikās;
one should worship either the hundred and eight [Kumārikās] or a single maiden.
When honored, these honor [the worshiper] back; when slighted, they consume [him].
A maiden is a yoginī in person; a maiden is all the deities. (7.275)
The goddess Bhūrbhuvarmūrtikā and Kumārī have been fully worshipped;
so too have the asuras, the wicked nāgas, and whatever malevolent grahas there may be.
O Bhairavī, all the deities— the bhūtas, vetālas, gandharvas, ḍākinīs, yakṣas, and rākṣasas— as well as the worlds of bhūr and bhuvar, are centered in the heart.
All things beginning with the earth, the entire universe with its moving and non-moving beings,
as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva— || 7.278 ||
But those who fully worship the maiden are satisfied and all are satisfied;
likewise, the arrangement beginning with Gaurī extends as far as Kālāgniśiva. (7.279)
The seven continents, the oceans, and the fourteen worlds—by this rite, one should indeed feed the maiden and Bhairavī as well. (7.280)
Having worshipped with a spirit of devotion by offering water for the feet, the arghya-offering, incense, saffron, and sandalwood, one should present all of these to him. (7.281)

One should perform three circumambulations— at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end— and afterwards, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given consisting of silver, gold, and pearls.
If one marries off a maiden oneself, the sin of killing a Brahmin is destroyed;
the sin of killing cows, the sin of killing women, and all other sins are utterly annihilated.
The mother, the father, and especially the brothers—whosoever may be present there—all should perform the rite of giving the daughter in marriage. (7.284)
The fruit of enjoyment and liberation, good fortune, and all riches belong to him;
he shall dwell eternally in the world of Rudra with the three-eyed Lord Hara.
A mortal who marries off a daughter shall obtain this fruit: the merit of sixty thousand horse-sacrifices. (7.286)
O Maheśvarī, for as many years as there are grains of sand in the ocean,
he remains even in the Satya-kalpa, having extracted each individual family [of beings].
He enjoys pleasures for as long as there are inhabitants of the earth and the heavens;
the gift of a daughter is a great gift, the best among all gifts. (7.288)
Misfortune perishes quickly and good fortune increases;
one receives honor at the royal gate, and royal prosperity becomes stable. (7-289)
One should worship all the young maidens with a spirit of devotion;
indeed, he who worships a maiden when a great danger has arisen [is saved]. (7.290)
At that very moment one attains liberation; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Thus, O Goddess, I have described to you the procedure for the worship of the Kumārīs.
I shall also explain the specific characteristics; listen closely.
O Maheśvarī, there is nothing superior to this within the Tantra. (7.292)
Having worshipped the Virgin Goddess, I attained the state of Śiva;
Kṛṣṇa attained the state of Kṛṣṇa, and Brahmā attained the state of Brahmā with joy.

Thus ends the seventh chapter in the glorious Bṛhannīlatantra, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, concerning the description of the sequence for the worship of the Kumārī and the application of rites such as suppression (nigraha). || 7 ||
Now begins the eighth chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Listen, O lady of excellent hips, to the yantra by which success is certainly attained;
thereafter, one should draw the king of yantras, which bestows all human goals.
By the mere knowledge of which one immediately attains the power of moving through the sky;
first, having inscribed a triangle, one should inscribe another triangle outside of it.
Having drawn a triangle outside, one should place a hexagon outside of that;
in the center, however, is the Bindu-cakra adorned with the Māyā-bīja.
One should draw a hexagon outside that, then a circle, and then an eight-petaled lotus;
this is joined with an outer circle and enclosed by a square fortress (bhūpura).
Having known this, one attains liberation through this yantra; of this there is no doubt.
One should inscribe this upon copper smeared with *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*.
One should place [the vessel] before [the deity] on a pure seat, joined with *svayambhū* flowers and mixed with saffron and agallochum, and unseen by ordinary beings (*paśu*).
The wise practitioner should place the materials for the *arghya* offering into the *arghya* vessel before him;
then, the mantra-master should have the *arghya* offered by that well-attired woman.
O fair-browed one, no unrighteousness arises from the substance produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, nor likewise from the *suyaṃbhū* flower, in the accomplishment of the great mantra.
Then, by means of the sequence of the seats (pīṭhakrama), one should perform the worship of the Yantra;
thereafter, [one should contemplate] the Supreme Goddess vibrating within the heart-lotus.
O Maheśvarī, having led [the soul] through the path of the Suṣumṇā to the location of the head,
one should then indeed bring it to the heap of flowers upon one's own lotus-hand.

O Goddess, O Mistress of the Gods, who are easily accessible through devotion and accompanied by Your retinue—the knower of mantras [should worship] with the *nāsa* (nose) and *vāmā* (left) [fingers] using the seed-syllable of Vāyu. 8-11.
With this mantra—"O Mother, O Goddess, come here so that I may worship you"—the wise one should invoke the Goddess. (8-12)
Having invoked that goddess, worshipped her with ritual offerings, and established her there,
[one should worship] Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, and Virodhinī.
One should likewise worship Vipracittā outside in the hexagon, and Ugrā,
Ugraprabhā, and Dīptā within that, in the triangle.
One should worship Mātrā, Mudrā, and Mitā in the other triad;
all of them are dark-complexioned, holding swords in their hands, and adorned with garlands of severed heads.
Holding a threatening gesture with their left hands and being naked, they [should be worshipped];
one should worship Mahākāla on the right side of the deity. (8.16)
Then, having offered praise and performed prostration, one should mentally effect a union before the deity—an enjoyment that brings pleasure to the deity. (8.17)

But having placed the enjoyment [of the consort] foremost and having dismissed the goddess here, the practitioner of mantra becomes one who has accomplished his purpose; there is no need for deliberation in this matter. (8.18)
Now listen, O Goddess of gods, to the specific modes of worship:
first, wine is to be honored, namely both the honey-based (mādhvī) and the molasses-based (gauḍī).
In the absence of that [alcoholic liquor made from flour], one should perform the rite by means of a substitute;
coconut water kept in a bronze vessel, or honey placed in a copper vessel. (8.20)
Cow's products kept in a copper vessel are equal to liquor, with the exception of clarified butter;
likewise, betel leaf with camphor and coconut with sugar [are forbidden].
Milk-rice with ghee, ginger with jaggery, rice with sesame seeds, as well as palmyra fruit and dates; || 8.22 ||
The plantain, the tamarind, the bilva—the most excellent fruit—and other fragrant and delicious fruits as well. (8.23)
The human, the goat, the ram, the buffalo, the hare, the śarabha, and the boar are proclaimed to be the offerings (bali). || 8-24 ||
And the black cat should also be known by those most skilled in mantras;
