their blood, O Supreme Goddess, is to be offered. (8.25)
Well-scented water should be offered, as well as water for washing the feet;
the principal food offerings have thus been described by me, O beloved. (8.26)
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, one should give that with which the fair-complexioned maiden is satisfied; what else do you wish to hear? (8.27)
The practitioner of steady mind who, having touched the family abode of a woman in her menses, recites [the mantra] ten thousand times as the prescribed measure, [attains success]. (8.28)
(121) By means of pure intention alone, he shall become a treasury of knowledge;
[this applies to] refined and vernacular words, as well as worldly and Vedic ones. (8.29)
They all come under the control of the practitioner; it is not otherwise.
With disheveled hair and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), the man should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Having touched another man’s naked wife, one should recite [the mantra] with a steady mind;
by the mere sight of him, the disputants become lusterless. (8.31)
Even kings fall into servitude; what then of other people?
This is true for any learned man who desires wealth or seeks great power. (8.32)
If a man desires to become equal to Bṛhaspati, he should diligently bring a beautiful woman who is intoxicated with youth. (8-33)
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and having summoned the *kula*, he who, knowing the mantra,
engages in sexual union shall indeed become a treasury of knowledge.
But she, the Goddess Śrī, delights in the reverse position upon his heart;
having given a kiss upon her face, one should perform a thousand mental recitations (japa). || 8-35 ||
He shall become the lord of all accomplishments; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
For among all practices, the practice of the Kula is indeed the most excellent. (8.36)
Therefore, with all effort and composed in mind, one should accomplish that;
now listen, O Goddess of Gods, to this supreme secret. (8.37)
Formerly, in the delightful Dāruvana forest, intoxicated and deluded by passion, they would constantly violate the wives of others and consume liquor. (8.38)
Having seen that improper act committed by Viṣṇu, Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O source of compassion for all the gods! (8.39)
In the Devadāru forest, sinful sages, addicted to drinking liquor and deluded by passion, violate the wives of others. (8.40)
"What destination will those foolish Digambaras go to?
Having heard these words of his, I said to him, "O beloved," (8.41).
Kālikā, who is indeed the Great Vidyā, the unceasing Sarasvatī, she who is called the Queen of Vidyās—these are the reciters of her mantra. (8.42)
But they shall become liberated by chanting that Gāyatrī;
indeed, by its power, all the gods were set free.
By the killing of his own mother, that Paraśurāma was also liberated;
and Dattātreya, the son of Atri, was liberated from the drinking of liquor.
By the violation of Gotama’s wife, even Devendra was liberated;
and previously, by approaching a Cāṇḍāla woman, Vasiṣṭha was liberated. (8.45)
The Moon was liberated from the violation of his preceptor’s wife, and Śiva was liberated from the severing of Brahmā’s head; such am I who have been liberated.
Furthermore, through the slaying of Rāvaṇa, Rāmacandra was liberated;
I shall speak of that very [liberation] in secret, which the wise should always hear and keep hidden. (8.47)
Having uttered the word "kālikāyai," one should say "vidmahe" immediately thereafter;
then the word "śmaśānavāsinyai," and after that, "dhīmahī."
Having uttered "Tanno Ghorī Padaṃ," followed by "Kāmaḥ Pracodayāt," this is the Kālīgāyatrī; by reciting it ten times with this [mantra]— || 8.49 ||
Indeed, sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are shattered into pieces by this;
there is no knowledge equal to this, and no recitation equal to this. (8.50)
Knowledge equal to this has never existed, nor will it ever exist.
Listen further, O Goddess of Gods, regarding the practice of drinking and other such rites: || 8-51 ||

O Maheśānī, one should accomplish the rites for the Kumārī and other such practices with this [mantra] during an auspicious time; and by doing so effortlessly, success will certainly be attained. (8.52)
An actress, a female Kāpālika, a courtesan, a washerwoman, an auspicious Brāhmaṇī, a Śūdra girl, a Vaiśya woman, and a Kṣatriya woman who bestows everything [are suitable]. (8.53)
Having brought some of these women there to that circle of wombs and having worshipped the Great Goddess, one should then engage in sexual union.
With the mind as the sacrificial ladle, I perpetually offer the oblation of merit and demerit into the fire of the self through the path of the *suṣumṇā*, while the senses remain withdrawn. (8.55)
This great mantra, ending with "svāhā," has been proclaimed for the commencement [of the rite].
Having grasped the ladle of *unmanī* with the hands of light and space, [one should offer]. (8.56)
"I offer into the fire the entire portion of the fruits of dharma and adharma, filled with affection; svāhā. This great mantra, ending in *svāhā*, is proclaimed for the emission of semen. (8.57)
"Then one should go to the beloved goddess, the sovereign of the three worlds.
Having heard those words, Viṣṇu spoke to me again:
Homage be to you, O Mahādeva, whose essential form is the soul of all tantras;
by your grace, O Lord, this great doubt of mine has vanished.
"Grant me leave, O Lord of Gods; I shall depart as I please.
Then, having been granted permission by me, he prostrated according to the prescribed rite.
Viṣṇu went to his own abode; this has been told to you, O beloved.
Now listen, O Goddess of gods, to the beautiful King of Mantras.
In this regard, O Pārvatī, listen to the majesty of the glorious King of Mantras;
by means of which, O Goddess of Gods, one shall attain supreme liberation through faith. (8.62)
By means of horse-sacrifices, cow-sacrifices, human-sacrifices, and others as well;
by various gifts of material objects, and also by manifold kinds of fire-offerings (homas).
Through austerities performed over many thousands of births,
the supreme Vidyārājñī Ghorakālī Aniruddhasarasvatī is attained.
Having known this, one attains liberation; what more need be said of the supreme?
Indeed, by the power of this knowledge, the eight Siddhis come to be. (8-65)
Merely by knowing this mantra, one becomes victorious on earth;
merely by looking at it, the disputants are considered to be deprived of their luster. (8.66)
Even kings fall into servitude; what then of other people? Can one expect coldness from fire, the solidification of water, or the cessation of the sun's motion? (8.67)
One shall become capable of controlling the reversal of day and night;
one shall be as eloquent as Bṛhaspati and become a great poet like Bhārgava.
In wealth he was like Kubera, in splendor comparable to the sun;
in strength he was equal to Rāma, and his prowess was like that of Viṣṇu.
Through the grace of this mantra, one is instantly freed from the taint of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, or violating the teacher’s wife. (8.70)
Thus I shall speak in brief: there is nothing equal to mantra now, whether in the solar, the Gāṇapatya, the lunar, or the Vaiṣṇava [traditions]. (8.71)
O Supreme Goddess, it cannot be described in detail by anything else— not even with thousands of millions of mouths or hundreds of millions of tongues.
O Goddess of the gods, having extracted one's own [seed-syllable], the second is the transgressor;
O Maheśānī, Vāṇī is also declared—these are the three syllables.
O beloved, there is nothing else equal to this king of mantras;
out of affection for you, O lady of noble hips, it has been revealed here. (8.74)
"It must not be spoken, it must not be spoken, it must not be spoken, O Maheśvarī!
Out of affection for you, O Sureśvarī, this has been told as if it were my very life."

O Goddess, may you be blessed; by the worship of the maiden alone, the supreme procedure for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) has been declared. That which was not to be revealed has now been revealed. 8.76
This ritual of worship has been proclaimed; where is Śivā worshipped?
Or where is the Goddess meditated upon? Listen to that, O Maheśvarī. (8.77)
In Kāmarūpa, at Pūrṇagiri, in Koṅkaṭa and Oḍḍiyāna,
in Vārāṇasī, at Lauhitya, and in the waters of the river Karatoyā.
In Āryāvarta, at Prayāga, and likewise in Brahmāvarta,
worship yields infinite fruit everywhere, whether in water or on land.
In its absence, [one should worship] in an empty house smeared with vermilion and other substances,
[using] a curved knife, a trident, a bow, a sword, a bell, a chowrie, and so forth.
It was crowded with canopies and banners, well-perfumed with black agallochum incense,
and beautified by the songs of courtesans who possessed beautiful teeth and lovely hair.
In a house of spirits filled with the sound of ringing bells and adorned with rows of lamps, one should likewise worship the most beautiful Tārā. (8.82)
She should always be worshipped in the cremation ground, which is considered even superior to the sacred seats (pīṭha).
For Tāriṇī, no place other than the cremation ground is praised.
Therefore, those who desire prosperity should perform worship in the cremation ground;
for that Gāyatrī which was previously proclaimed is the very embodiment of the knowledge of Brahman.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is its seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (chandas);
indeed, the deity is proclaimed to be the very nature of Śiva and Śakti. (8.85)
Hereafter I shall declare that by which one may swiftly obtain the fruit:
having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta with the mouth filled with betel.
With a sword in hand, he should offer a very abundant oblation accompanied by meat;
having worshipped according to the rule, he should then bring forth a beautiful woman.
Upon seeing a woman of noble birth, a young maiden, intoxicated by youth, well-dressed, and possessing a beautiful smile, one should pay homage with a concentrated mind. (8.88)
If, by the power of fortune alone, the vision of the [divine] family arises, then at that very moment one should perform mental worship toward them there. (8.89)
Women are the gods; women are the vital breaths; women alone are the ornament.
One should always seek the company of women, especially those who are beautiful.
Striking them, censuring them, being deceitful, or speaking unpleasantly—none of these should ever be done, as otherwise they will create obstacles to success. (8.91)
One should offer that food prepared by his hands to the deity;
then, having performed the morning rites and bathed for a long time according to the prescribed rule.
Having entered through the practice [of yoga], one should enter into the space within the skull;
there is no restriction of direction or time, nor any restriction regarding the duration of the stay and so forth.

There is no restriction regarding time for the recitation of mantras, nor for worship and other offerings such as the bali; here, in the practice of the great mantra, it is said that one may follow one's own will.
One should worship her with various auspicious flowers, excluding tulasī;
having thus worshipped according to the rules, one should mutter the mantra of the Supreme Goddess.
At night, a man who is self-restrained should worship the Goddess and recite her mantra;
he should always be adorned with vermilion or likewise be naked.
Having made the woman naked, one should engage in inverted sexual union;
one should perform striking and kissing for the sake of attaining one's desired goal. (8-97)
The temple, which is the bow, may be rubbed by the arrow of shameless desire;
at that time, the supreme practitioner, with a completely purified mind, should perform the recitation. (8–98)
While personally performing the enjoyment, one should recite that which bestows eloquence;
therefore, O Great Goddess, it is said to be difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Having attained whose grace I perceive the three worlds—
the Goddess who is the essence of Śiva and Śakti, Aniruddha-Sarasvatī, by knowing whom one attains liberation— what else shall I tell you? (8–100)
(The Śrīdevī said:
"Now, O Lord, tell me, O Sadāśiva, O Supreme Sovereign, who possesses preeminence in this auspicious yet terrible Kali age? (8-101)
Śrī Bhairava said:
O Goddess, O Maheśānī, in the age named Kali, [worship] the preeminent and auspicious Tāriṇī,
as well as Kālī and Aniruddha-Sarasvatī.
Listen, O Bhairavī, to the preeminence of Śmaśānakālikā;
for Aniruddha-Sarasvatī is indeed the cause of all accomplishment.
By means of her mantra, the practitioner shall become a bestower of the fruits of all accomplishments.
The Tārā mantra has been stated previously; now hear from me the Kālī mantra. (8–104)

The pair of *māyās*, the pair of *kūrca*s, and likewise the three of one's own *bīja*s—[three each, according to the *kha* manuscript; O auspicious one, with the words "O Kālikā" on the right]—are arranged according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*).
Having extracted the previous seed-syllables, this mantra is remembered as ending with "svāhā";
it is renowned as the Queen of Knowledge (Vidyārājñī) and is a wish-fulfilling tree of mantras.
There is nothing more excellent than this, the enchanting mantra of Kālī;
therefore, with every effort, listen to me as I recite this king of mantras.
Merely by knowing the mantra, the practitioner becomes liberated while living;
this is the secret knowledge (vidyā) for both worship and recitation. (8-108)
Likewise, meditation is found in the conduct of the clans and in all the scriptures of knowledge;
it includes the rites of eradication, killing, and the supreme subjugation.
Attraction, immobilization, and thereafter incitement to hatred—one should accomplish these by means of this [mantra], O Goddess; it will certainly succeed, there is no doubt. (8-110)
One should perform various kinds of worship according to the sequence prescribed in one's own Vedic branch;
having worshipped with red flowers, one should then perform a thousand oblations.
But that woman, consisting of desire, shameless and deluded by passion, will certainly abandon her husband and go to the practitioner herself. (8.112)
And one should recite ten thousand times, O Goddess, having meditated upon the naked Goddess;
[then] those who are stationary and those who are moving, even those dwelling in the depths of the netherworld, [are subdued].
And having recited the mantra and meditated upon the goddess Digambarī in the cremation ground, the practitioner shall instantly summon those who dwell upon the earth.
One should apply that ash as an unguent; thereafter, he withdraws the universe.
One should worship with white Aparājita flowers with a spirit of devotion. (8.115)
Having offered ten thousand oblations even in a cremation ground, one will certainly cause the destruction of the entire universe;
likewise, by touching a naked woman in a cremation ground and her vulva. (8.116)
And having performed the recitation, one should bring her under control if she does not flee;
having worshipped with black flowers and meditated upon her as naked. (8.117)
Having recited it ten thousand times while staying in a cremation ground, one may perform the slaying of enemies;
thus has the essential nature of the Kālī-kalpa been told, O beautiful beloved.
If kept secret, all accomplishments shall be attained; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
As is Kālī, so is Nīlā and Aniruddha-Sarasvatī.
Therefore, the Vidyā Kālī has been declared [as preeminent] in the Kali Yuga.
Listen to the secret, O fair-limbed one, regarding the determination of the wheels of Kuṇḍalinī. (8.120)
This seat is the nectar of life and the protector of the body;
O Pārvatī, hear now of the threefold Śāmbhava-cakra, which is beyond the guṇas. (8-121)
By which mere consciousness one certainly becomes composed of light;
and between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, the phonemes are also of the nature of light. (8.122)
The wheels are of the nature of light, and Kuṇḍalī is also of the nature of light;
here, from the moon to the sun, there are fourteen wheels.
Here exists the Kuṇḍalinī power, whose form is that of a seed-syllable and which is without external shape;
this supreme Kuṇḍalinī power resides within the lunar orb. (8.124)
O Great Goddess, he who knows this division is a knower of Yoga;
[he knows] the petal, the calyx, as well as the phoneme, and likewise the deities of the wheels.
In this very way, as before, this procedure is to be known for all the wheels (cakras);
from the moon up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), there are fourteen wheels here.
The Kuṇḍalinī, known as the individual soul (jīva), is celebrated as both supreme and inferior;
here, from the sun to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), there are fourteen wheels (cakras).
She is proclaimed as Parameṣṭhī, abiding within the solar disc;
she has the form of a human being and is the nature of the supreme light.
The Goddess residing within the *golaka* is supported by the light-bindu (*jyotirbindu*). Herein lies the *golaka*-cakra, which appears like Goloka. (8.129)
This is Nārāyaṇī, Kālī, Tārā, Śūnyanivāsinī,
Sundarī, Raktakālī, and likewise Mahiṣamardinī.
This form, fashioned by the mind, consists of radiant energy and is yet another [manifestation];
this Rāma is indeed the Supreme Self, the Great Viṣṇu, and the Great Śiva.
She is of the nature of the stainless, and Tāriṇī is of the form of Kṛṣṇa;
she is the eternal illuminator of the self, whose very nature is eternal bliss.
O fortunate one, her mantras— and indeed my own mantras—
bestow the fruit of swift desire when practiced according to the prescriptions of the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya).
The Goddess is the remover of various evils; the hero whose mind is fixed upon her, having attained the state of reality, shall obtain the reality of the fruit. (8.134)
O Goddess of gods, your mantras bestow all goals,
just as the four gods were proclaimed by the Self-born One.
They are to be known and established through traditional instruction;
they are also to be understood by way of their synonyms, according to the distinctions within the body of revealed scripture. (8.136)
Thus, the six Āmnāyas were proclaimed by me to you in his presence;
that Āmnāya is to be known as Śruti, and Śruti is said to be the Veda.
Therefore, O Girijā, you too must keep this secret like your own birth;
henceforth, O fortunate one, hear the supreme secret.
O Goddess, when a great mantra-practitioner becomes a spiritual adept (*sādhaka*) through the turn of fate, whom should he then perform recitation for, as well as worship and other rites? (8.139)
One should always diligently perform salutations to all the gods; however, one should perform recitation (*japa*) and other rites directed toward that very deity in whom doubt arises. (8.140)
O beautiful one, even if a practitioner who has received the mantra from his guru should, through negligence, laziness, or even a lapse in conduct, [violate his vows], || 8.141 ||
O fair-faced one, it is said that if [the mantra] of Śaṅkara is taken up anywhere at all,
the mantra and so forth will become deficient in power.
Now listen to the ritual procedure for the purpose of destroying these and other defects:
the first is called *janana* (birth), and the second is *jīvana* (vivification). (8.143)
O Goddess, the third is striking (tāḍana), the fourth is likewise awakening (bodhana), the fifth is consecration (abhiṣeka), and the sixth is purification (vimalīkaraṇa). || 8.144 ||
The seventh is nourishment (āpyāyana), while the eighth is remembered as satiation (tarpaṇa).
The ninth is declared to be illumination (dīpana), and the tenth is considered concealment (gopana).
The extraction of mantras from the *mātṛkā* yantra is known as their "birth.
A wise person should recite the syllables of the mantra, placing the *praṇava* (oṃ) between each of them. (8.146)
The life-force is said to consist of the distinction between vowels and consonants;
having written down the syllables of the mantra, one should strike them with sandalwood water.
Now listen to that which is called "striking" each [syllable] with the seed-syllable of wind (*vāyu*):
having written the mantra according to the rule, [one should perform this] with *karavīra* flowers. (8.148)

One should perform the awakening with the letter *ra*, equal in number to the syllables of that mantra, according to the procedure taught in the *Svacchanda-tantra*. Then, by the number of the mantra's syllables, [one should perform the rite].
One should consecrate the mantra with the sprouts of the *aśvattha* tree for the sake of purification;
having contemplated the mantra mentally, one should burn it away with the *jyotis* mantra.

O Goddess, the mantra consisting of the three impurities is for the purpose of purification; the *tāra* (oṃ), followed by the sky (ha), fire (ra), and man (u), is considered the *daṇḍī-jyotirmantra*. (8.151)
One should sprinkle water consecrated by the recitation of the mantra over every syllable;
this is considered the ritual nourishment (*āpyāyana*) performed according to the rules with that very mantra. (8.152)
The libation performed with water from the vessel becomes a true *tarpaṇa*;
through the conjunction of the *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā* [syllables], it is called the "illumination" (*dīpana*) of the mantra. (8.153)
The concealment and non-disclosure of the mantra being recited—these ten consecrations are kept secret in all tantras. (8.154)
Having performed these, O beloved, one should always recite the mantra for the benefit of others—that Supreme Brahman which is devoid of qualities, whose form is light, and which is formless. (8.155)
If the deity were to arise with form within all bodies, it would always exist as three forms according to the distinctions between the bodies of embodied beings. (8.156)
O fortunate one, some always worship that Brahman which is of the form of the female organ (bhaga) by means of the essential nature of the male organ (liṅga). 8-157.
Various types of wise ones always cultivate the form of the *bhaga*, knowing it to be the female nature present everywhere within all bodies. (8.158)

That which is of the nature of Śakti is to be known as Vijñeyā, while Puruṣa assumes the form of Śiva. O fair-faced one, for the sake of distinguishing them therein, [they reside] within the human body. (8.159)
Śakti and Śiva are to be known as my supreme convention; O fortunate one, the vulva is the sacrificial pit, and the phallus is proclaimed to be the wooden ladle. (8.160)

O fortunate one, the season is the fire, and its casting into the middle of the pit is considered to be the form of clarified butter; semen is declared to be the oblation, and the mind is proclaimed to be the priest. (8.161)

And having understood that the fruit-form is right there, as well as the various desires of saṃsāra—just as a practitioner of mantra and a human being [understand] the Brahmā-seat (pīṭha)—[he attains it]. (8.162)
O Goddess, one should perform the fire-oblation constantly; his form is infinite.
Whatever desire or other object one contemplates in the mind, O Goddess, that one shall accomplish.
One should not be concerned with faults or virtues; one shall obtain whatever desire one seeks and enjoy the fruit as described for the deity as prescribed. (8.164)
O Goddess, one shall obtain long life, prosperity, fame, renown, and liberation.
This must be guarded with effort and should not be given to just anyone. (8.165)
"It must be hidden, hidden, and hidden again, like the pregnancy of one's mother's paramour.
Thus has this excellent sequence of purificatory rites been fully explained to you. (8.166)
Now listen, O Pārvatī, to the threefold Śāmbhava-cakra, by the mere knowledge of which one will certainly become composed of light. (8.167)
Between the iḍā and piṅgalā [nāḍīs], the phonemes are of the nature of light;
the cakras are of the nature of light, and Kuṇḍalinī is of the nature of light.
From the moon to the sun, there are fourteen wheels here;
therein resides the Kuṇḍalinī power, which is in the form of a seed-syllable (bīja) and yet formless.
The Kuṇḍalinī power, residing within the lunar orb, is to be brought across;
O Great Goddess, he who knows this distinction is a knower of Yoga.
The petals, the calyx, as well as the color, and likewise the deities of the [moon/sun]—this procedure is to be understood as being exactly as before in all the cakras. (8.171)
From the moon up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), there are fourteen wheels (*cakras*) here;
the Kuṇḍalinī, known as the *jīva*, is celebrated as both the supreme (*parā*) and the non-supreme (*aparā*). (8.172)
From the sun up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), there are fourteen wheels here;
she who resides within the solar orb is known as Parameṣṭhī.
This goddess, whose nature is the form of man and whose essence is the supreme light, resides within the spheres of the senses, supported by the points of light. (8.174)
Here there is a sphere-like wheel that appears like Goloka;
this is Nārāyaṇī Kālī, who may be Tārā, the dweller in the Void. (8.175)
Sundarī, Raktakālī, Bhairavī, and likewise Nādinī— this form, fashioned by the mind, consists of radiant energy and is both supreme and non-supreme.
This Rāma is indeed the Supreme Self, Mahāviṣṇu, and Mahāśiva;
he is of the nature of the stainless (nirañjana), and Tāriṇī is of the form of Kṛṣṇa.
The Goddess who illuminates the Self, whose nature is eternal bliss—thus, O Goddess, has this most wonderful secret been told to you. (8.178)
O Mistress of the Gods, there is nothing superior to this within the Tantra.
Now, O Goddess of the Gods, hear [the teaching on] the supreme nature of Brahman. (8.179)
But the vital breath (prāṇa), O Supreme Goddess, is the knowledge of the Self, O lady of pure smiles;
that which is the vital breath, O Great Goddess, is proclaimed to be the individual soul (jīva). (8.180)
O beloved, the form of a lamp-flame exists within the heart;
O Maheśānī, the Supreme Brahman has the shape of a lamp-flame. (8.181)
O Goddess of gods, the Inner Self (antarātman) exists in the hearts of all;
the Inner Self is the Supreme Brahman, which remains pervading the body. (8.182)
O lady of excellent hips, at the time of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one sees a wonder within the two [eyes]: the energy (śakti) whose form is primordial nature (prakṛti), O fair-faced one. (8.183)
O Yoginī, listen to that which was seen as the supreme secret;
O Supreme Goddess, that which was seen by one who has become equal to Brahman through the Self. (8.184)
O Maheśānī, that syllable, when seen, produces wondrous bliss;
O Pārvatī, O Maheśānī, having fixed my mind right there, [I beheld it].
O Maheśānī, O fair-faced one, having become submerged in the ocean of nectar for a hundred thousand years, O Parameśvarī, [the time] has passed, O Maheśānī.
O Goddess, during the moment of my breath-control (prāṇāyāma), a hundred thousand years passed for me.
O Supreme Sovereign, listen, my beloved, to that which was seen and now described by me.
O Supreme Goddess, there is nothing beyond this within my range of perception;
this paryanka is a supreme and most wonderful marvel.
O Supreme Goddess, that bed which resembles the foam of milk and is adorned with various jewels—that very bed is Śrī Sadāśiva himself. (8.189)
There above, O Maheśānī, is the subtle Tripurasundarī,
whose form and appearance resemble the hibiscus flower, liquid lac, and vermilion.
Four-armed and three-eyed, bearing five arrows and a bow,
with hands granting boons and fearlessness, she is the Sustainer, the Supreme Goddess.
O Supreme Goddess, when he who was filled with bliss and fickle came within the range of my vision after a hundred thousand years had passed,
[I beheld him].
At that very moment, O Maheśānī, O beautiful one, he suddenly assumed a subtle form there as soon as my meditation was interrupted.
Right there, O Maheśānī, my beloved, the universe and the dwellers of heaven beginning with Brahmā were seen; without Śakti, nothing exists for me.
For Śakti is the form of Brahman; O fair-faced one, she is the very nature of power.
Without Śakti, O Great Goddess, nothing at all comes within my range of perception. (8.195)
Thus, O Goddess, having performed the supreme installation of the Mātṛkās in this sequential manner, O Maheśānī, the Mātṛkā becomes the enchantress of the universe. (8.196)
Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should perform the Śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa;
by the mere performance of the Śrīkaṇṭha-nyāsa, O lotus-faced one, I am Śiva. (8.197)

O Parameśānī, O lady of pure smiles, one should perform everything regarding Śrīkaṇṭha— who is exceedingly difficult to attain in the three worlds— exactly according to the sequence previously described.
O Maheśānī, O Supreme Goddess, one should perform everything with diligence;
O lotus-eyed one, one should meditate upon Śivā, the lady of excellent hips, within the lotus of the heart.
The lotus of the heart is the supreme abode, the station of Brahman, O goddess worshipped by the gods;
this heart is indeed the dwelling place of the individual soul, the highest state.
The heart-lotus has twelve petals and possesses the brilliance of a thousand suns;
in its center, O beloved, one should meditate upon the Lord Śiva, the conqueror of death.
Resembling pure crystal, five-faced, and of great luster;
with arms reaching to his knees, O Mistress of the Gods, lotus-faced and with beautiful eyes.
Wearing a crown and earrings, adorned with armlets and bracelets,
he was ever accompanied by smiles and graced by a row of brilliant teeth.
His chest was adorned with rudrākṣa beads, his head was graced with matted locks,
he was clothed in a tiger skin, and he shone with ten arms.
Having meditated thus, O Great Goddess, O Beloved, one should always [meditate upon] Mahādeva as Mṛtyuñjaya,
endowed with Śakti, the Great God who deludes all limbs and everything.
Having performed contemplation on all the limbs, one should then contemplate a single limb;
by relinquishing even that single limb, meditative absorption (samādhi) is thereafter born.
O Goddess of the Gods, listen to that splendor which arises at the time of meditative absorption—knowledge that is most difficult to attain. (8.207)
But when all the limbs have been relinquished, that splendor which arises—O Parameśānī, O beloved, that alone is Śiva, the conqueror of death. (8.208)
Know, O Pārvatī, that the primordial nature (prakṛti) has the form of a lamp-flame;
within that light, O Goddess of Gods, the inner self (antarātman) is eternally situated. (8.209)
The inner self, O Maheśānī, is devoid of cause and effect;
having bound the female bee to the male bee within the heart-lotus, O Parameśvarī. (8-210)
"O Great Goddess, a hundred thousand years have passed for me while established in yoga.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for the Application of Yantras and Mantras and Their Purificatory Rites," from the *Śrī-Bṛhannīlatantra*, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. 8.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim another supreme means of accomplishment;
by performing which, O Supreme Sovereign, one’s purpose is fulfilled—of this there is no doubt. (9.1)
O Goddess, near the palace there should be a plantain pillar;
there, O Maheśānī, one should construct an altar and plant a tree. (9-2)
Having sat upon a red seat, one should accomplish the heroic practice (vīrasādhana);
having performed the deposition of the Mātṛkās, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
One should worship the Supreme Deity with the sixteen types of offerings.
One should offer water mixed with cow's urine as *pādya* (water for the feet) to Mahādevī.
O Maheśānī, having placed honey in a copper vessel along with milk and sacrificial oblation, one should offer curd that has become thickened and mixed with sugar. (9.5)
O Goddess of the gods, one should cause the water for sipping (ācamanīya) to be offered using a vessel of bell-metal;
one should present the supreme food offering (naivedya), which is delicious and most enchanting.
O Maheśānī, by offering a coconut mixed with honey and buttermilk mixed with sugar to the Goddess, one will certainly become liberated while living. (9.7)
O Maheśānī, O most auspicious one, one should offer food together with meat;
for seven days, one should recite [the mantra] right there with a mind focused on that.
O Goddess, having begun in the first watch of the night and continuing until the second watch,
one should always recite the mantra with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, free from fear.
Within seven days, O Goddess, the person becomes a perfected one (siddha),
provided he then installs the vidyā conjoined with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
Becoming intent on mantra and meditation, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind;
if it be a single-syllable mantra, then one should recite it a thousand times.
For mantras of two syllables, there are eight thousand; for those of three syllables, fifty thousand;
beyond that, for mantras, there are ten thousand eight hundred.
Beginning the recitation at night, one should perform it until sunrise;
having offered the *bali* offering at the beginning of the recitation, one should offer the *bali* again afterwards.
If, either at the end of the recitation or during the recitation, [the deity] says, "Give!
Give!", then one should offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) consisting of either goat or buffalo meat.
There was no looking about in any direction, nor was there any meeting with kinsmen;
likewise, there were elephants, enemies, wicked serpents, wild beasts, and fanged predators.
Whatever is present in the minds of birds, insects, and spirits—all that one should perceive as being like a dream and avoid it everywhere without fear. (9.16)
Having completed the ritual practice, O Goddess, one should cause the teacher, the teacher’s son, and also the teacher’s wife to receive a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's means. (9.17)

For one who has correctly mastered the mantra, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished; what need is there to mention a man who possesses both the guru and the mantra? He is Rudra himself. (9.18)
For this reason, O Goddess of the Gods, the worship of the Guru is most weighty in every respect;
one should never engage in the discussion of mantras and tantras in his presence. (9-19)
When the feet of the Guru are indeed worshipped, one shall always be happy;
for that Supreme Lord is the father of all Tantras and Mantras.
O Goddess, whether it be the worship of another deity or the glorification of another deity, if performed without the Guru-deity, one's standing before him is in hell. (9-21)
If one should be mounted upon a corpse, that specific [practice] is described here:
in an empty house, at the root of a bilva tree, on a riverbank, or at a crossroads. (9-22)

Seated upon a corpse, the practitioner of mantra should contemplate the heroic practice (vīrasādhana), [using] either a Caṇḍāla or one who has been overcome [by disease], which bestows the fruit of swift accomplishment. (9-23)
Having brought [the deity] and established [him] at the outset, one should perform the network of ritual placements (nyāsajāla).
Having inscribed the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra), one should worship it with scents, flowers, and other offerings.
Having worshipped [the deity] and offered a seat, one should perform self-protection;
then, according to the rule, one should perform the nourishment of the deity within the mouth of the corpse.
At the end of the mantra should be Bhuvaneśī; thus the mantra is said to end with the letter *ra*.
O Goddess, this is the Mahānīlakrama, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhis*). (9.26)
It must not be imparted to anyone, but kept secret for my pleasure,
regarding all living beings who have been deprived of life during the hero’s accomplishment.
Having abandoned the *brāhmaṇa* and the *gomaya*, one should accomplish the *vīrasādhana*;
great corpses (*mahāśava*) are recommended, for one should accomplish the primary [practice], O Dear One. (9.28)
For the preliminary practice (*puraścaryā*) taught in the cremation ground is difficult to find on earth.
O Goddess, the *sādhana* of the cremation ground is considered the supreme *sādhana*. (9-29)
If one stays in a cremation ground reciting the mantra with undistracted mind, having performed all the means of accomplishment, he is glorified in the world of the Goddess. (9.30)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, [the Ritual for the Practice of Heroes], in the glorious Bṛhannīlatantra, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. || 9 ||
Now begins the tenth chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now listen, O lady of beautiful limbs, by what means the mantra becomes perfected:
having taken a corpse and a skull on a Tuesday at night, [one should proceed]. (10.1)
Combined with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and mixed with sandalwood paste,
[this should be placed] in a pit measuring half a cubit, containing turmeric and yellow pigment (rocanā).
One should cast a human skull there together with silver;
having filled it all with earth and performed the consecration, one should purify it. (10.3)
Thereupon, O Goddess, one should enter [the state] above, duly following the sequence;
with a concentrated mind, one should perform the recitation (japa) to the measure of a thousand.
When the recitation is completed, one should worship the Supreme Goddess there;
in this way, within three days, the person becomes perfected. || 10-5 ||
Thus, O auspicious one, I have explained to you this practice which bestows accomplishment;
one should recite it one hundred and eight times at the junction of the eighth lunar day. (10.6)
Through practice for seven days, a person attains accomplishment;
on a Saturday at the time of twilight, one should worship the deity named Latā in the house.
One should recite [the mantra] alone in a secluded place, intent upon the practice of the creeper-sādhana;
when this is done, O Great Goddess, the practitioner attains perfection.
Having adopted the previously mentioned ritual procedure and performing the worship and other rites,
that Kāmadeva alone, having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, [attains his goal].
Within seven days, O Goddess, one shall attain great sovereignty.
Listen to the special instruction, O lady of beautiful limbs, which grants all desires according to the tantras. (10.10)
By means of which mere consciousness the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) indeed arise;
at the root of those, O Goddess of Gods, the practitioner, having worshipped Ugrā— || 10-11 ||
O Goddess, O fair-faced one, great accomplishment shall truly, truly come to pass, once the mantra has been written in a bower of creepers drawn according to the Kula tradition. 10-12.
Having worshipped there and performed the consecration, he should offer it to her;
then, intent upon the state of the deity, he should take the mantra that has been recited a certain number of times.

Having worshipped her and paid homage, and having himself recited the mantra with great self-restraint, a man shall achieve mastery over the mantra by offering a bali-oblation to women in the morning. (10.14)
The new moon day conjoined with the Bhūmiputra [Mars] bestows auspiciousness;
on that day in the month of Bhādrapada, during the Puṣkara yoga, the most excellent of heroes [performed his deed]. || 10-15 ||
Having brought Viṣṇukrāntā, one should place it upon the ground where the deceased lies;
having made it conscious there on that very day at the marketplace for the dead (mṛtahaṭṭaka), [one should perform the rite].
Having spread it there, one should cause it to be applied with the oil of fish-skin;
and with that water, one should perform an aspersion over the corpse as before.
Having placed the victorious *vijayā* mixed with mercury into his belly by way of the mouth, he remained right there, his eyes anointed with that same fish-mercury (*matsyamañjana*). (10.18)
Having applied the *tilaka* with the previously mentioned substance, one should likewise recite the mantra constantly;
then the Blessed Lord Bhairava, whose arms are formidable, will come of his own accord. (10.19)
Then, having seen him, the hero, free from fear, should recite the mantra;
O Goddess, if by the power of fortune a staff is perceived there.
Then that Bhairava himself becomes manifest as Vīreśvara;
O Goddess of gods, having brought a fish, one should cast it into the cemetery of the ancestors.
Having recited [the mantra] there repeatedly, there occurs a meeting with the deity;
and at night, in the marketplace of the dead, [one encounters] Unmattānandabhairava.
Clad in the directions (naked), pure, adorned with ashes, with disheveled hair, and holding a sword and a dagger in his hands—if he should recite the Mātṛkā [mantra]... 10.23.
Then, O Great Goddess, all accomplishments (siddhi) will be held in his hand;
whether it be a ḍākinī, a yoginī, or another beautiful attendant of the Gaṇas. (10.24)
Having brought him there and honored him, one shall become the lord of all siddhis; having brought the Guru and established him, one should worship that omnipresent Lord as a deity.
One should personally satisfy the guru with garments, ornaments, gold, and other such gifts;
and especially so his son, his daughter, or his wife.
Having performed worship and recited the mantra, one becomes the master of all supernatural powers (siddhis);
and having meditated upon the lotus feet of the Guru within the thousand-petaled [cakra] and worshipped them [there]. (10.27)
By reciting [the mantra] solely with a divine disposition, one becomes a master of supernatural powers (siddhi);
even a wicked mantra is perfected merely by the permission of the guru. (10.28)
Even for the gods, there is no authority in this scripture if they bypass the Guru;
so too if the application of these mantras and tantras is performed [without him]. (10.29)
"O Goddess, without the mouth of the Guru, the loss of accomplishment arises.
One should not bestow this Tantra and these mantras even upon disciples;
otherwise, one will certainly go to the abode of the King of the Pretas. (10.30)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for Other Means of Accomplishment," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī within the glorious Bṛhannīlatantra.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Listen to the specific instructions that I shall declare, by which the three worlds may be perfected;
there is no doubt that among all tantras, there is none superior to this. (11.1)
Consisting of all languages, pure, and saluted by all the sacred traditions; having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā, which is the savior joined with fire. (11.2)

The second seed-syllable is extracted as joined with Māyā (the letter *i*), Bindu (the nasal *m*), and Īśvara (the letter *r*). [A gap is seen here. Then there is Ramā (*hrīṃ*) and Phaṭ; these constitute the five supreme seed-syllables. || 11-3 ||
I shall explain its extraction—the lamp that consumes the fuel of ignorance, pervaded by five rays; listen to this cause of omniscience. (11.4)
First, having uttered the *praṇava* (Om) adorned with the fourth vowel, mounted upon the letter *ra*, throbbing and radiant, and graced by the lunar drop (*bindu*). || 11-5 ||
And likewise, O Great Goddess, one should join Bhaga conjoined with the fourth vowel, mounted upon Dāha, and joined with Raya and Śakti. || 11-6 ||
Then one should join the syllable *hūṃ* together with *nāda* and *bindu*;
thereafter, one should add the syllable *phaṭ*, which, when complete, bestows accomplishment. || 11-7 ||
Because she bestows speech through her divine play, she is Nīlasarasvatī;
because she always delivers [beings] from saṃsāra, she is Tārā, the bestower of bliss and liberation. (11.8)
Because she delivers from fierce calamities, she is celebrated as Ugratārā;
she is also Vitāraikajaṭā, and she always grants great liberation. (11.9)
The three-syllabled Mahānīla-Sarasvatī is devoid of the Tārā-mantra;
this Śrīman-Nīla-Sarasvatī begins with Tārā and consists of five syllables.
O Goddess of gods, when preceded by the seed-syllable of Śrī, then Śrī becomes all-pervading;
for this very Mahāvidyā, beginning with Māyā, grants all desired objects. (11.11)
When the Vidyā, whose nature is speech and which comprises all speech, begins with the syllable *Vāgbhava*,
it attains these various forms (*mata-bhedas*) that follow its sequence and pervade the entire universe.
This is the five-syllabled vidyā that illuminates the five elements;
it consists of the seed-syllable of the bride (Vadhū), the middle seed-syllable, and the final of all seed-syllables.
This knowledge is the fruit-bearer of all sciences, the victorious for those desiring victory;
it is the science that destroys poison and bestows immortality.
Merely by knowing the mantra, one becomes victorious on earth.
One should write the letter Kha (khaṃ) joined with the Kūrca (the letter Ra), as well as the Raudra and the Traiguṇya.
This auspicious Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), which bestows all perfections, is considered to be the respective power of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, according to their sequence. (11–16)
Consisting of all mantras, pure, and hidden within all tantras, it swiftly bestows accomplishment upon those who worship it according to the traditional injunctions. (11.17)
The best of practitioners should perform all [rites], such as meditation and worship.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain Tārā, the savior of the world. (11.18)
Merely by remembering it, one’s fear is swiftly destroyed.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, one should extract the Hṛllekhā seed-syllable.

One should extract the sky (ha) conjoined with the remainder (kṣa), adorned with the bindu and nāda; then the kūrca seed-syllable (hūṃ) and the heart-mantra (namaḥ); and finally, [the word] "to Tārā" (tārāyai). || 11-20 ||
Having extracted the Great Lotus, it was likewise extracted for Tārā; "O Tārā, deliver us from all that is difficult to cross," so it was said again.
This mantra, consisting of two *tara*s (oṃ) and the wife of fire (svāhā), is the celestial tree;
eloquent speech, both in prose and verse, arises for him in the assembly. (11.22)
Indeed, by reciting this [mantra] four hundred thousand times, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) are attained;
one should perform all the preliminary rites, such as meditation and worship, as previously described. (11.23)
Having first extracted the Praṇava, then "Tāre uttāraya," and "Māyā svāhā"— this mantra is declared to consist of ten syllables.
Through remembrance, one shall swiftly destroy the fear of all sentient beings;
O Goddess of the Gods, all practices such as meditation and worship have been previously described. (11.25)
I shall proclaim the jewel of knowledge; listen, O daughter of the mountain!
[It consists of] Vāgbhava, Kuladevī, Tāraka, and likewise Vāgbhava. (11.26)

The mantra ending with the weapon-mantra (astra) and concluding with the consort of fire (vahnijāyā), preceded by Hṛllekhā, is declared to be the unsurpassed eight-syllabled mantra of the Mother of the Vedas (Gāyatrī). (11.27)
One should arrange the five limbs of this mantra using the five seed-syllables;
having assigned the weapon-mantra with the remaining syllables, the person becomes one who has accomplished his purpose.
O Maheśvarī, all [the practices] such as meditation and worship have been previously described.
Kālikā is the perfected vidyā; she is considered the supreme Mahākālī. (11.29)
In her Tantra, this Great Vidyā is to be known by the most excellent practitioners;
she is the Vidyā consisting of all the Vedas, saluted by all the Āmnāyas. (11.30)
She is proclaimed as the protectress, and she should be served by practitioners when they recite the Praṇava first, followed likewise by the pair of lotuses.
One should place *pada* in *mahāpadme*, and then *pada* in *padmāvati*;
"māye svāhā"—this is declared to be the mantra consisting of seventeen syllables.
The worship is prescribed as before at midnight at a crossroads;
whoever performs its recitation shall quickly become a swift poet.
The seed-mantras of Tāriṇī are independent and bestow all accomplishments;
these are the divisions of Mahogrā that set in motion the goals of human existence. (11.34)
It bestows longevity, prosperity, beauty, eloquence, knowledge, and good fortune;
in the end, it grants the state of Brahma free from all affliction and the liberation while living.
O Maheśānī, [the mantra consists of] the seed-syllable of Śiva, followed by the seed-syllable of Śakti;
it is joined with all the *bindus*, beginning with the first of the Vedas (*oṃ*), placed below that in due order. (11.36)
*Māyā* (Hrīṃ), followed by the woman (*strīṃ*), then the armor-seed (*vaṃ*), and finally *haṃsaḥ*, which is declared to be the *jīva*—
this eight-syllabled *vidyā* has been revealed to you out of affection.
One attains the perfection of command (*ājñāsiddhi*) and brings the three worlds under one's control.
The fourteen branches of Vedic knowledge come under one's control instantly.
The great vidyā Haṃsatārā has been revealed out of affection for you;
it brings poetic talent to men, and one who desires wealth shall obtain wealth. (11.39)
One who seeks liberation attains liberation; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Ugratārā is the Great Vidyā, and she is declared to be my own power.

And this five-syllabled vidyā, which begins and ends with *haṃsa* and brings great prosperity, has been proclaimed solely through your exertion—and by your grace (as per the Kha manuscript)—out of affection for you. (11.41)
One should perform the recitation, worship, and other rites for this [goddess] just as for the Five-Syllable [Mantra].
The Great Vidyā, joined with the seed-syllables and preceded by the Three Tārās, is applied individually for each. (11.42)

She is declared throughout the three worlds as the bestower of accomplishment and the giver of supreme prosperity; one should perform the six-limbed ritual with the six long vowels and the syllable *māyā*. (11.43)

The worship is prescribed as before, or else the ritual applications are similar to those; the seed-syllables are Vāc (Aiṃ), Māyā (Hrīṃ), and Kamalā (Śrīṃ), with Īśa (Ha) served by Bhṛgu (S). || 11-44 ||
"Joined with the fourteenth moon, followed by Bhṛgu together with the Lord;
enriched with fourteen visargas—tell me the dual [form] and the word for speech. (11.45)
The word *vādinī* follows, then the three-fold *klīm* mantra, and then the word *nīlasarasvatī*, which is repeated three times for speech and mind. (11.46)
After the two syllables *kāhi*, there is *kalarīmagnivallabhā*.
This mantra of Nīlasārasvata consists of thirty-four syllables: [Explicitly:
*aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hasauṃ shauṃḥ vada vada vāgvādini klīṃ klīṃ klīṃ nīlasarasvati aiṃ aiṃ aiṃ*.]
kāhikāhi kalarīṃ svāhā || 11-34 || 11-47 ||
This [mantra] should be known as having six sheaths, since it is composed of six mantras;
O Pārvatī, hear now the division of the sages, meters, and deities. (11.48)
The sage named Gaṅgāpravāha is Janārdana in the form of a fish;
the meter is called Atyaṣṭi, and the goddess is Nīlasarasvatī. (11.49)
Consisting of the sovereignty of all speech and bestowing all desired objects,
the seed-syllable *aiṃ* is to be known as the *kīlaka*, and *hsauṃ* is declared to be the *śakti*.
The color should be known as blue, and the fruit of poetry is attained swiftly;
the mudrā for those who reside [there] is declared to be the face-mudrā. || 11-51 ||
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the *hṛllekhā* mantra conjoined with the six long vowels.
[She is] auspicious, wearing blue garments, adorned with jewels, and clad in a tiger skin. (11.52)
One should diligently pay homage to Vidyā, whose nature is that of Brahman, who bestows the fruits of all desires, and who is the sovereign lady of all desired boons. (11.53)
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the nature of Nīla first.
Formerly, in a battle between the gods and the asuras, [the gods fought] with the Dānavas, the sons of Diti. (11.54)
Severed by the discus of the wielder of the discus, those wicked Daityas fled in all directions; having gathered together, they entered the depths of the ocean's interior.
Created by the Wielder of the Discus for the subjugation of the former gods, the Blessed Lady is divine in form, auspicious, and composed of all mantras. (11.56)
In that very place, the sacrificial section for all the Brahmins proceeds;
by means of the oblations produced in those sacrifices, the gods become powerful.
"Surā indeed oppresses us; therefore, we have become weak. (11.58)
Having heard these words of those dejected sons of Diti,
Hayagrīva and Somaka fell into a state of profound despondency.
Those two wicked brothers, Turaṅgagrīva and Somaka,
performed austerities directed toward the goddess Śabdākarṣaṇikā.
Pleased by their formidable asceticism, the goddess who attracts sounds said to them: "O beloved of boons, choose here whatever you desire."
Addressed by those two for the purpose of requesting a boon, the Blessed Lady said:
"Let a boon be granted to us for the sake of attracting all sounds. (11.62)
When she replied, "So be it," those two Dānavas, exceedingly arrogant,
arrived in the world of mortals through his power.
All the sounds of the twice-born, drawn forth in the form of mantras, are that goddess Sarasvatī, whose form is sound and who possesses a radiant white appearance. (11.64)
Having abandoned the faces of all the brahmins and assumed a divine form, she came and entered the house of the two wicked and excellent Daityas. (11.65)
Having led her away, helpless and wailing, to the hollow of Pātāla,
he fashioned a pit with Hālāhala poisons that possessed the luster of dark blue water.
Having submerged her there and bound her with ropes made of serpents,
he enclosed her tightly with mountains, once again desiring to conquer the gods.
Having approached that auspicious one of great luster,
they two praised her with arrows capable of attracting sound from the Daityas upon the surface of the earth.
And the twice-born, having forgotten the Vedas because of the arrow, became silent;
indeed, by that very forgetting of the mantras, the science of sacrifice was cast aside.
Due to that destruction, deprived of their sacrificial portions and suffering from a loss of strength,
the gods were rendered powerless and devoid of effort, thus cast out by those two.
Having thus routed the awakened ones, those two— Hayagrīva and Somaka— remained within a house situated inside the ocean, marked with the discus of Viṣṇu.
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, the eternal Lord Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a great fish, made an effort for the sake of her rescue.
Then the supreme Lord Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a thousand-tusked fish named Pāṭhīna,
entered the ocean with effort to rescue the gods;
just as in age after age he had lifted up the earth submerged in the ocean by means of the boar-form.
In that very manner, the lotus-eyed one, having taken the form of a fish, churned the flood of the ocean.
From the body of the glorious Hari in the form of a fish, four arms manifested;
in his four arms appeared a sword, as well as a discus, the Śārṅga bow, and the Kaumodakī mace. (11.75)
A battle took place between Janārdana in his form as a fish and [Hiraṇyakaśipu] for a thousand autumns;
then, for the sake of investigating the meaning of words, he forcibly seized him with the wind of his breath. (11.76)
Seized, cut by the discus of Hari, and rendered unconscious by the blow of the Kaumodakī mace, those two Daityas named Hayagrīva and Somaka met their destruction in that great battle. (11.77)

Then the Blessed Lord Ananta, in the form of a fish, [rescued] her who had been cast into the midst of a pit of poison within the city of Garta in the ocean, and who had nothing remaining of her body but her very breath.
Hari comforted her with words of song and, smiling, spoke to Sarasvatī;
he first uttered the *tritāravidyā*, the root of the entire collection of mantras.
Even by that he did not obtain her consent; the Goddess spoke again the mantra of the palace.
Even by that she did not obtain his consent; then Viṣṇu spoke to Kāmeśvarī.
Having thus awakened that six-syllable mantra, the progenitor of all speech, he addressed that consciousness:
"O Nīlā, you have been born from the midst of the poison-pot, your every limb complete, with a lotus-face smiling. (11.81)
"Just as in the past you entered effortlessly into the mouths of all the great Asuras,
so now recite the Vedas and destroy them!"— thus did the Goddess speak these words to Hari.
Protected by the Fish Incarnation, I have no fear and my purpose is fulfilled;
yet, I am deeply troubled by the thought that its beautiful form has otherwise turned blue for me. (11.83)
"Just as I am cast into the midst of a pit of poison, so act with your renowned means before I vanish in an instant"— when addressed thus, even the Lord spoke to Lakṣmī.
"Do not grieve, O Savitrī; long ago I was of a complexion as pure as the moon.
I have attained this blueness through the extraction of the fierce Hālāhala poison—what fault is there in this? (11.85)
The indigo plants nourish the beauty of the marketplace and of the world; indeed, the God himself is blue.
Mṛḍānī, the progenitor of the worlds, is blue, as is the throat of the Subduer of Cities (Śiva). (11.86)
Mahendra is blue, the sovereign of the gods; the clouds that give life to the world are blue;
the sky is blue, providing space for all people; and the dark spot is blue, serving as the cause for the moon’s radiance. (11.87)
I too am blue and a locus of the quality of goodness; so how can there be any fault in the color blue?
For those whose limbs are adorned with every kind of jewel, what need is there for collyrium applied to the eyes? (11.88)
They will not be beautiful, nor young, nor full of grace, nor in the prime of youth;
yet your fame as "Nīlasarasvatī" shall become renowned throughout the three worlds.
O noble one, O fawn-eyed girl, it was for your sake alone that I constantly practiced the sixfold medicinal herbs (*ṣāṭkauṣikī*);
for by means of the yoga of the six syllables, you were restored to life when you had lost all movement within the midst of a pit of poison. (11.90)
Having thus consoled the Primordial Goddess with these words, and having bowed to her and received that Sarasvatī,
he set her forth again into the mouths of the twice-born for the sake of obtaining the ocean of sacrificial offerings that brings happiness to the gods.
From that time forth, she became renowned throughout the world as Nīlasarasvatī, the bestower of liberation.
(p. 152) Her secret great mantra grants the fruit of all desires;
by the mere recollection of which one becomes victorious upon the earth. (11.93)
Listen, O Goddess of gods, beloved; I shall explain the means for accomplishment, by which, O Goddess of gods, welfare will certainly be yours. (11.94)
Listen to the mantra, O lady of excellent hips, which bestows omniscience through its recitation:
it consists of the power of Viṣṇu, the Great Power (Mahāśakti), and the seed-syllable of fire, ending with *phaṭ*. (11.95)
This great fivefold set of syllables is the cause of omniscience; O Goddess, when one recites the mantra a thousand times with a rosary of *akṣa* seeds, [this result is attained].
One attains the perfection of command; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
After six months, O Goddess, one shall attain the status of a great king.
There is no knowledge equal to this, nor is there any austerity equal to this; O Mahāmāyā, O Sovereign of the Gods, such a thing does not exist within the Tantras.
By means of this king of mantras, one should perform rites such as subjugation (*vaśya*);
then a mortal shall become accomplished—no doubt or ritual procedure is prescribed in this matter. (11.99)

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Extraction of Mantras and the Description of the Blue State through Alternative Methods," in the *Śrī-Bṛhannīlatantra*, within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Now listen, O fair-faced one, as I shall describe the origin of the Vidyā:
Mahākālī is the sustainer of the world, whose form is splendor and who consists of the universe. (12.1)
The Great Goddess, whose form is Brahman, is the cause of all auspiciousness;
her abode, adorned with jewels, pearls, and other gems, is situated above Goloka.
It has four doors and four sections, is square and beautiful,
adorned with four walls, and is exceedingly radiant with pearl necklaces.
O Supreme Goddess, that which is reflected in crystal pillars and joined with dance, song, and so forth, is liberated; there is no doubt about this supreme state.
Thus has the divine and supreme abode of Kailāsa been described to you;
when the entire world has passed away in the ultimate, sinless dissolution.
O Bhairavī, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva dwelt there;
there was a great king named Bhīma, a righteous and supreme man.
At his gate, O Great Goddess, were Śivā and the others, who grant all desires;
and they were pleased by his asceticism, O Great Goddess, toward that Bhadrakaikaya.
And when the dissolution had arrived, O Goddess Śivā, Brahmā and the other gods, O Supreme Sovereign Śivā, devised a means to protect the king.
Having observed the inner reality and the means, O fair-faced one,
they assumed the charming form of goddesses and dwelt there.
O Supreme Goddess, remaining within the hollow of a banyan leaf and meditating upon the state of the Blessed Lady, one hundred thousand years then passed.
(p. 154) O Bhairavī, Kālī was born there as the supreme, eternal, and manifest one.
She said: "O Great God, who is it that is being praised here by you? (12.11)
Then, perceiving her within the range of their vision, the gods headed by Brahmā offered a supreme hymn of praise there and took refuge at the feet of the Blessed Lady.
Salutations to you, O Great Sovereign, whose form is supreme bliss;
you have come upon the waters for the sake of protecting our lives.
Salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations again and again!
Homage be to you, O Mahāraudrī; O Kālarātri, homage be to you!
Without you, O Supreme Raudrī, Bhava has fallen into the state of a ghost;
protect, protect us, O Supreme Vidyā, within the belly of the three worlds and the universe! (12-15)
O slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, O crusher of the demon Niśumbha, O Goddess who bestows sovereignty upon the gods, salutations to you, O beloved of Śaṅkara! (12–16)
O Goddess, who consists of the moon and sun, whose nature is the supreme light, you who have become the very essence of this hymn—be gracious, O Supreme Sovereign! (12-17)
Having spoken thus and prostrating themselves, bowing again and again,
O beloved, they touched Kālī’s feet with their sun-colored crowns.
"Choose a boon, O highly fortunate one," was the excellent word spoken by the Blessed One.
"Protect us, O Great Illusion; salutations to you, beloved of Śaṅkara! (12.19)
"Let it be so," having spoken these words, O sinless ones, perform the creation and other [cosmic acts]!
Brahmā said:
"O Goddess of gods, by what form shall the creation, maintenance, and so forth, come to be?"
Having heard these words of his, Bhavānī, the deluder of Bhava, [spoke].
He spoke to all those excellent Asuras:
"Take the dust from my feet, which is auspicious and constitutes the very essence of material existence. (12.21)
O wise ones, perform the rites of emanation and so forth, by which accomplishment will be attained; O Goddess Śivā, auspicious one, take the dust originating from his feet. (12.22)
Then Brahmā set forth to perform creation, Viṣṇu was the promoter of its maintenance,
and Rudra himself swiftly initiated the process of dissolution.
Then creation appeared through the most excellent of all the gods;
Sanaka and the others, Sananda and the others, and Sandhyā were also born.
The Lord of gods created auspicious progeny consisting of all beings;
the illustrious and all-pervading Viṣṇu established the stability of the worlds. (12.25)
And Rudra brings about the dissolution; now hear the sequence of creation.
O Great Goddess, in heaven the gods reside, and Indra is indeed the king there. (12.26)
The Lord Manu, the sovereign of the worlds, made the mortal realm rich with its protectors and the netherworld (pātāla) abounding with all the nāgas.
There, a king named Virādha was devoted to the protection of his subjects;
then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Sadāśiva [appeared]. (12.28)
O Goddess of the Gaṇas, they whirl about in their respective activities and exert their power;
therefore, O Supreme Goddess, that night is declared to be Raudrī.
There, O Goddess of the gods, the Asuras fled in great terror;
afflicted by a most fearsome dread, they were driven out from heaven by them.
Indra and the other hosts of gods, seeking to accomplish their respective purposes, approached the Great Goddess, who is the very essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
You alone are the Lord of the worlds; everything is established in you.
You alone are the oblation (and the priest), the object of enjoyment, and the eternal enjoyer.
You are the object of knowledge and the knower; you are the meditator and the object of meditation, devoted to that [Supreme].
You are the father even of the ancestors, and the deity even of the gods.
You are higher than the high, the ordainer even of the ordainers;
you are the very nature of the Supreme Brahman. Be gracious, O Supreme Goddess! (12.34)
Having heard these words of those born of Aditi, the Goddess said: "O gods! There is a supreme dharma, even higher than the highest."
"What is the reason, O illustrious ones? Make an effort with devotion!
Having heard this, Brahmā, the best among speakers, then spoke.
The sovereignty of Mahendra is not pacified by him, nor is she [pacified] by him;
however, there is no doubt that she would be pacified by a great being such as Viṣṇu or others.
Accompanied by Mahendra, Brahmā went joyfully to Goloka;
and with various kinds of words, O Maheśānī, he [praised] the Supreme Lord.
And he praised the Supreme Bliss for the sake of rescuing his own task.
Having heard these words of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, [he spoke]. (12.39)
Viṣṇu spoke respectfully: "O All-pervading Lord, O Maheśānī, it is not possible for me [to prevent this], for Brahmā and Viṣṇu have come within my range of vision. (12.40)
O auspicious one, they praised the Supreme with many kinds of divine hymns.
I said, "O Supreme Goddess, it is not possible to kill these. (12.41)
Having heard these words of mine, Brahmā and Viṣṇu became composed;
then, joining their palms in reverence, they praised me for a long time.
Thereafter, O Great Goddess, that which deludes all was told;
I have no power there to be capable of crushing it. (12.43)
There exists Kālī at the great sacred site of Kailāsa, the dweller in Bhava;
the supreme goddess Śivā is established there, the enchantress of the universe.
She alone is Kālī, the Great Vidyā who kindles the fuel of ignorance;
from her arise Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and I, O Supreme Goddess. (12.45)
"O auspicious one, O goddess who bears a form of splendor, O Great Mistress beloved of Hara, we have gone there to behold Mahākālī. (12.46)
O Supreme Goddess, for the benefit of the gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, be gracious, O source of all auspiciousness; salutations to you, O sinless Śāradā! (12.47)
Having heard these words of theirs, O Goddess, Mahākālī, the Great Śivā, assumed a manifest form for the pleasure of the gods. (12.48)
The Goddess said: "O all you gods, rich in ascetic merit, what boon do you request? O immortals, declare everything that you desire! (12.49)
The gods said:
"O Goddess, terrified by the great asuras, the sacrificial rite has been interrupted.
For their destruction, O Goddess who pervades all, be gracious. (12.50)
Having heard these words of those born of Aditi,
that great goddess, the excellent woman of blue form, was pleased.
She is renowned as Nīlasarasvatī, the creator of universal delusion;
rising from her, that goddess is called Nīlavāṇī.
"O Goddess, what do you command? I shall perform that with ease.
Having heard those words of hers, Mahākālī, who is composed of pure consciousness, [spoke].
She spoke with reverence, O Goddess, in a voice faltering with affection:
"Because she bestows speech through her effortless play (līlā), she is therefore called Nīlasarasvatī. (12.54)
O Goddess, you are renowned as the virtuous Nīlavāṇī (the Blue-Voiced One), the future Savior;
by the multitude of her powers, the entire threefold world is pervaded.
Go, O Supreme Goddess, you who are my own form, O fair-faced one;
you were created for the sake of the welfare of the gods' mission, O lady of pure smiles.
Having heard these words of hers, Tāriṇī, the enchantress of the universe, said to the gods: "O highly fortunate ones! Go to where those asuras are. (12.57)
"I shall go there, O gods, being present in every way," having spoken thus, that great goddess Tāriṇī, who moves at will— || 12.58 ||
The Great Illusion vanished, she who possesses an illusory form;
the auspicious Mahāmāyā, ever-blissful and composed of all the gods.
And that which is the Gāyatrī of all the gods, delightful to the mind—that very Gāyatrī is Sāvitrī; she is the very embodiment of Brahman.
Having attained her, O beautiful one, those great-souled ones considered nothing unattainable within the three worlds regarding virtue, pleasure, wealth, or liberation.
Through the grace of the Great Goddess, Indra attained supreme poetic power and sovereignty, and Hari attained the state of Viṣṇu. (12.62)
"Rudra has attained the state of Śiva, the great one endowed with all sovereignty.
Having heard these words, the gods were saluted by everyone. (12.63)
Touching her lotus feet with their sun-colored crowns,
they bowed down again and again, repeatedly prostrating before the Great Goddess.
O Great Goddess, every task is accomplished; nothing whatsoever remains unfinished.
O Goddess, whenever you are remembered, you shall surely destroy even the most dire calamities.
Having thus bowed to the Great Goddess, the sovereign lady who grants all desires and boons,
they returned once more to that place where Śivā resided upon the mountain.
Five years passed there for those gods of divine birth, who,
having lost their kingdom, were filled with supreme terror like mortals upon a mountain.
Indra and the hosts of gods again called the Goddess to mind;
they all went to the pure mountain where the beautiful Śivā resides.
A seat, a welcome, water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, the honey-mixture, further water for sipping, bathing materials, garments, and ornaments. (12.69)
O Śivā, one should worship the goddess Nīlasarasvatī with sixteen types of offerings: perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and prostrations. (12.70)
Having worshipped and offered various auspicious oblations to Śivā,
O Goddess of gods, that best of deities performed his recitation (japa) amidst the host of gods.
O Maheśvarī, having first recited the great mantra one hundred thousand times,
one should offer ten thousand oblations with delightful lotus flowers.

They performed the *homa* with offerings mixed with sesame seeds and also with sugar. Having thus offered the oblations, O Great Goddess, they performed the consecration (*abhiṣecana*) with a tenth part [of the total].
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, the libation was performed by all with one-tenth parts;
then, at the conclusion, the Goddess was worshipped during the dead of night.
Having offered the oblation to Mahādevī, the gods, who subsist on nectar,
likewise performed this delightful rite according to the prescribed rule.
Then the Blessed Goddess Maheśvarī was remembered by the gods;
that Great Goddess, blue-hued and large-bellied, was well-pleased.
"O Supreme Goddess, you have appeared before the gods in person.
O gods, tell me in this assembly: what shall I do, and where shall I go? (12.77)
The gods said:
"We bow down, O Great Goddess; be gracious, O Sovereign.
Then the Blessed Goddess appeared in a beautiful blue form.
Having seen the hosts of gods, that Tāriṇī, who grants all desires,
created from her own body twelve supreme Vidyās, as they are proclaimed.
Kālī and Mahādevī, likewise Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśānī, Bhairavī, and Chinnamastakā. (12.80)
Dhūmāvatī, Bagalā, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalātmikā—O Great Goddess, these vidyās are proclaimed as the vidyās of accomplishment. (12.81)
O fair-faced one, [these] were born from the body of the Great Goddess Sarasvatī;
and other Mothers as well, O fair-faced one, were born from her body. (12.82)
All the goddesses dance at the feet of Parānanda;
then, O Maheśvarī, having indeed slain the asuras, [they restore] the gods once more.
He then established them, and they returned to their respective places;
O Bhairavī, mistress of the gods, hear this manner from my own mouth. (12.84)
Out of affection for you, O lady of excellent limbs, this has been made manifest;
thus, O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, the origin of the Vidyā has been told to you.
O Goddess of the gods, O Sovereign of the Suras, this must be kept secret in all tantras;
O Maheśvarī, there is nothing more supreme than this among the tantras.
This knowledge, the most excellent of all essences, has been told to you.
Now listen, O Goddess of Gods, to what is considered the cause of omniscience. (12.87)
During the first watch of the night, on an auspicious and propitious day,
one should indeed construct a beautiful altar measuring four cubits in size.
O Great Goddess, having fashioned the yantra with vermilion,
the practitioner should place it upon copper and encircle it with a red cloth.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should place there a jar filled with sesame seeds;
one should perform the recitation using that very seed-mantra previously mentioned. (12.90)
Facing the east, the wise practitioner should perform the recitation while seated upon a red seat;
O Goddess of the gods, having inscribed the name of the target person, interlaced with mantras, upon birch bark.
O Goddess, one should place that below and enter above it, O Beloved;
having put on a red garment and a red turban, O Śivā.
O Goddess, facing the east, one should mutter [the mantra] and worship the Supreme Goddess,
whose body is as red as vermilion, who holds a severed head in her left palm,
and who, on her right ear, is joined with a mass of matted hair and a corpse-lord.

One should meditate upon her who possesses a loud, boisterous laugh, who is distinguished by streams of blood, known as Raktā, whose root is full, who bestows excellent boons, who can assume any form at will, and who is of beautiful limbs. || 12-93 ||
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Great Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign;
O lady of pure smiles, one should perform the recitation with ten thousand repetitions.
One should perform the fire-oblation with a tenth part of that [number], and one should perform the libation with a tenth part of that;
O Great Goddess, one should perform the consecration with a tenth part of that.
Then, O highly fortunate goddess, one should perform the recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites;
by practicing for five days, the practitioner becomes accomplished.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this supreme essence of the ritual practice, which bestows all accomplishments and wards off all calamities. (12.97)
If the two possessors of flowers (the sun and moon) were in vain, then [the world] would become fruitless;
there is nothing superior to this, O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods—this is the truth.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the illustrious Bṛhannīlatantra, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, concerning the description of the origin of the Vidyā, the sequence of creation, worship, and the means of accomplishment. || 12 ||
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Now I shall speak, O Maheśānī; listen with careful attention, to the supreme mantra of Mahākālī, which bestows all eloquence.
Her whom they call the primordial Prakṛti, the excellent woman, the first of all perceivers, the complete Fourth State (Turīyā),
the Mother who is both supreme and non-supreme, the bestower of boons, the most worthy of choice—
Vīreśvarī, the bestower of accomplishment upon the practitioner.
O Dear One, they call her the primordial nature, Kālī, whose very form is Time; her mantra is the great mantra, this essence of all mantras. (13-3)
Having known which, all practitioners and great seers attained perfection—she who is the form of Śiva, mounted upon a corpse, the bestower of boons, and the destroyer of fear. (13.4)
The Goddess bestows all desires and causes all wonders; herein there is no need for the purification of the mind and so forth, nor is there any defect caused by enemies and the like. (13.5)
In the accomplishment of that great mantra, there is no restriction of time; nor is there any concern for the day of the week, the lunar mansion, or the defects of the lunar date and so forth. (13.6)
In this practice of Mahākālī, there is no concern regarding a guru.
Listen to the mantra, O lady of excellent hips, which bestows all eloquence. (13.7)
O Goddess, there are two great powers (mahāśakti), then two seed-syllables of sound (śabdabīja), and likewise three of one's own seed-syllables; and on the right is the word "Kālike."
O Śivā, one should utter the initial seed-syllables by means of the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama),
beginning with the circle and ending with the beloved of Fire (the syllable *svā*), which constitutes the great mantra.
This most excellent mantra consists of twenty-three syllables.
By means of this king of mantras, one is Śiva; of this there is no doubt. (13.10)
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), Uṣṇik is cited as its meter (chandas), Mahākālī is its deity, and the seed-syllable of Lañjā is its seed-mantra (bīja). || 13-11 ||
The seed-syllable *hūṃ* is the power of the mantra; thus its application has been proclaimed.
Listen, O lady of excellent hips, to the meditation that bestows success through recitation, by the power of whose practice, O Goddess, even bound souls attain the state of heroes. (13–12)
[One should meditate upon] the Supreme Goddess (Parā), whose body is like a cloud, who is naked, mounted upon a corpse and a jackal, and possesses three eyes;
she bestows auspiciousness with a pair of young elephants' ears suspended from her ears, wears a garland of severed heads,
and holds a human head and a sword in her left upper and lower lotus-hands respectively.
I bow to Mahāsundarī, who bestows fearlessness through her gift and whose mass of hair is loosened.
Having thus worshipped with meditation, one should satisfy the Supreme Goddess.
Listen, O fair-limbed one, to the Gāyatrī which bestows omniscience through its recitation.
Having uttered the word "kālikāyai," one should then say the word "vidmahe";
thereafter, the word "dhīmahī" follows [the phrase] "vāsinyai" at the end of the cremation ground (śmaśāna). || 13-15 ||
"Then, O Goddess of gods, may Ghorā impel us immediately;
having been recited twenty times, the Goddess bestows all prosperity. (13–16)
One should recite the mantra twenty thousand times for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa);
