one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that number, and satisfy [the deity] with a tenth part of that. || 13-17 ||
One should perform the consecration with a tenth part [of the total], and then feed the Brahmins;
at the conclusion of that, having performed a great worship, one should carry out everything.
Then, O Goddess, one should dismiss [the deity] and cast the jar into the water.
I shall now describe that ritual application, which bestows both seen and unseen fruits. (13–19)
When this ritual application has been accomplished, the mantras become effective, and not otherwise;
[this occurs] when the first watch has passed, up until the third watch. (13–20)
Or else, O Maheśvarī, one should accomplish the *vīrasādhana* in a courtyard or on the ground, having erected a pillar of plantain and a sacrificial altar. (13.21)
Having placed a water-pot there, provided with vermilion,
one should likewise place mango sprouts, as well as those from the breadfruit tree and the catechu tree, within it.
O Goddess of the Gaṇas, one should cast leaves of the Aśvattha and Badarī trees into the pitcher,
as well as gold, silver, pearl, coral, and crystal.
Having set all this aside, one should accomplish the *vīrasādhana*;
having drawn the *mātṛkā* yantra, one should enter there with joy. (13–24)
The practitioner, facing the northern direction, should lie down upon a woolen blanket after having worshipped with various substances provided with food and side dishes. (13.25)
O Goddess, one should cause goat meat, as well as rice with condiments, delightful *paramānna*,
and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), to be offered to Mahādevī.
Having brought a beautiful young woman adorned with various ornaments, one should perform the grooming of her hair and cause betel to be offered to her. || 13-27 ||
O Goddess, one should write the seed-syllable of Ramā on the two breasts, the seed-syllable of Vāgbhava in the mouth, and the two Kāma-syllables on both sides of the vulva, O Śivā.
O lady of pure smiles, one should pull her hair while first massaging her breasts; then, withdrawing the penis, one should strike it against her yoni.
O fair-faced one, one should perform the recitation with a measure of one thousand;
O beloved, through practice for seven days, the accomplishment of the mantra will occur.
Alternatively, one should recite the mantra until the leaf is seen;
O Maheśānī, once the leaf has appeared, there is no doubt that the mantra is perfected. (13.31)
Thus, O Goddess, this secret that grants all desires has been told to you;
it must not be disclosed, O Maheśānī, it must never be disclosed.
O Great Goddess, O Daughter of the Mountain, there is no fear of worldly existence;
this practice, O Great Goddess, bestows all accomplishments. (13.33)
The greatness of the root mantra cannot be fully described, even by thousands of millions of mouths or hundreds of millions of tongues. (13.34)
Nevertheless, O Supreme Goddess, I am unable to speak [of it];
there exists a most secret place in the three worlds that is exceedingly difficult to attain.
Kāmarūpa is a great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha) that bestows the fruits of all desires;
when recited in this manner, O Great Goddess, it becomes the giver of infinite fruit. (13.36)
If a person reaches a sacred seat (pīṭha) solely by the power of fortune, O Maheśānī, that which is chanted there shall yield infinite fruit. (13.37)
O Great Goddess, wherever there is accomplishment (siddhi), there Bhairavī resides;
therefore, there is no doubt that in this Tantra there is no place higher than this. || 13-38 ||

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Vīrasādhana, Including the Mantra of Mahākālī and its Purification Rituals," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī within the illustrious Bṛhannīlatantra. || 13 ||
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall declare the supreme mantra of Kāmākhyā, the embodiment of the five Bhairavas corresponding to the five forms of Kāmākhyā. (14.1)

One who possesses desire should desire that which abides in desire, which stands in the midst of desire, and which is made into the hollow interior of desire; one who possesses desire should desire desire by means of desire. (14.2)
The elder consonant is Brahmā, while the other is said to be Śakra;
one should place the first [vowel] in front, joined with that which consists of the earth (the consonant). (14.3)

The seed-syllable of Kāmākhyā is said to consist of Prajāpati (the letter *ka*), likewise Śakra (the letter *i*), joined with the eye (the vowel *i*), and accompanied by half of the moon (the bindu). 14-4.
This bestows the Dharma and conveys the goals of both desire and liberation;
this is the supreme secret, which is otherwise extremely difficult to obtain. (14.5)
Whoever hears this supreme and excellent praise from the mouth of a guru,
having attained all desires, is glorified in the highest world.
Just as I have previously described the mantra of the Kālītantra,
so too [is there] the mandala and the sequence of the abode through its practice.
That very same [rite] should first be performed upon a stone slab with flowers and sandalwood paste;
likewise, one should apply it here as well for the purpose of consecrating vessels and other such items. (14.8)
There, all those [mantras] are to be taken; the worship of the seats and so forth [should be performed], and first one should offer arghya to the Sun with white mustard seeds.

With red sandalwood and flowers, one should worship the great-souled Lord along with his retinue; at the conclusion of the worship of the seat, all the deities mentioned for the pedestal are to be honored.
Having worshipped by means of the name of the *pīṭha* in the center of the mandala,
O fair-faced one, the nature of meditation is indeed distinct from that of Mahākālī.
O Supreme Goddess, when there is complete identity with Kāmākhyā, one should worship the sixty-four Yoginīs arising from the Mahāmāyā-stava.
O Goddess, one should then worship Guha, Manobhava, Mahocchvāsā, and likewise her companion, followed by the guardians of the directions and the nine planets. (14.13)
Having designated them by their forms, he should worship them before the Lord of the Gaṇas;
O Śivā, he should first worship Gaṇapati at the eastern gate.
One should worship Nandin and Hanūmat at the western gate;
Bhṛṅgin is to be worshipped in the north, and Mahākāla in the south.
One should worship these gatekeepers of mine at your door;
indeed, one should perform the rite of transforming the vessel into nectar by means of the Kāmamudrā.
One should first perform the expulsion of the elemental spirits by means of three claps;
one should execute the clap with the right hand upon the left hand. (14–17)
One should cause the Vetālas and others to tremble with the mantra "hūḥ hūḥ phaṭ.
Here, one should perform the practice ending with breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the form described in this context.
The worshipper should first install the Goddess with the root mantra, using honey, milk, clarified butter, curd, cow urine, and likewise cow dung. (14–19)
With jewel-water, with water containing sugar and other substances, jaggery, gems, and *kuśa* grass;
likewise with white mustard seeds, mung beans, sesame seeds, milk, and barley.
With red sandalwood flowers combined with dūrvā grass and gorocanā,
one should offer the arghya nine times in the vicinity of the womb of the stone.
A seat, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and then water for sipping;
honey-mixture (madhuparka), water for bathing, clothing, sandalwood paste, and ornaments. (14.22)
Flowers, incense, and a lamp; thereafter, collyrium for the eyes; then the food offering and water for sipping; and finally, circumambulation and prostration. (14.23)
O beautiful one, these sixteen services have been described;
O Great Goddess, one should invoke [the deity] with the Gāyatrī mantra whose form is desire.
Know her to be thus [endowed] with Vetālas, Guhyakas, Daivatās, and Bhairavas;
O Kāmākhyā, come here duly into my presence.
O passionate one, manifest your presence here for the rite of worship;
and at the conclusion of the worship, one should offer a bali-oblation for the pleasure of the Goddess.
Having performed the recitation with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, one should conclude it;
one should worship [the deity] with the three syllables of the root mantra repeated three times.
Likewise, the six limbs of Mahākālī are within one's own limbs;
as are those of the Nīla mantra, the mantra itself, and the ritual assignments of the hands and limbs.
O Great Goddess, [the syllables] are pronounced with the vowels, along with the half-moon (anusvāra) and the bindu;
one should simultaneously join them with the first two syllables of the root mantra upon the ground.
One should perform the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) precisely in the order beginning with the little finger;
having performed both the aṅganyāsa and the karanyāsa, the practitioner [should proceed] afterwards.
One should place [the mantras] on the heart, the head, the crest (śikhā), the armor (varma), and then on the eyes, the mouth, the belly, and the back;
furthermore, one should place them on the two arms, the two sides, the two shanks, and the two feet.

O Goddess of the gods, one should worship Śiva, Sūrya, and likewise Śivā and the lunar digits (candrakalās), [visualizing him] with hands granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, and holding a rosary.
A red lotus and an arrow, as well as a red *brahmaputraka* flower;
there [he saw] Manobhavā, slender-waisted, holding a spear in her hand. (14.33)
The devotee should worship the sword at the side of the Goddess;
there, one should also worship the presiding deities of the pedestal and the auspicious Kāmeśvarī.
One should worship Tripurā, the tutelary deity (pratyadhidevatā), in the center of the pedestal;
likewise, one should worship Śāradā and Mahocchvāsā in the very center.
Caṇḍeśvarī, the Great Goddess, who wears the remains of the offerings of the Goddess,
is declared to be the Yonimudrā for the disposal of the *nirmālya*.
This substance is vermilion, while the body-unguent is with saffron;
such is the specific detail regarding worship that has been declared by me here. (14.37)
Accompanied by these special features, having mastered the entire ritual manual, one should worship Kālikā in the propitiation of the Great Goddess. (14.38)
Within the cave of the mind's arising, he attains the supreme goal;
[there dwell] Brahmāṇī, Caṇḍikā, Raudrī, Gaurī, and likewise Indrāṇī.
Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Durgā, Nārasiṃhī, Kālikā, Cāmuṇḍā, Śivadūtī, Vārāhī, and likewise Kārtikī.
Māheśvarī, Śaṅkarī, Jayantī, Sarvamaṅgalā, Kālī, Kapālinī, Medhā, Śivā, and likewise Śākambharī. (14.41)
Bhīmā, Śāntā, Bhrāmarī, Rudrāṇī, and Ambikā;
likewise Kṣemā, Dhātrī, Svāhā, Svadhā, Aparṇā, and Mahodarī. (14.42)
Ghorarūpā, Mahākālī, Bhadrakālī, Bhayaṅkarī,
Kṣemaṅkarī, Ugracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā, and Caṇḍanāyikā.
Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Caṇḍī, and likewise Mahāpriyaṅkarī;
the goddess Balavikaraṇī and likewise Balapramathanī. (14.44)
Manonmathanī, Sarvabhūtasudamanī, Umā, Tārā, Mahānidrā, Vijayā, and likewise Jayā; || 14-45 ||
The eight yoginīs previously mentioned, beginning with Śailaputrī, are likewise [to be worshipped] in their proper order;
together with these, one should worship the sixty-four yoginīs.
One should worship within the mandala for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims, offering various kinds of food, drinks, and even milk-rice (pāyasa). (14.47)
One should properly offer sweetmeats, cakes, flour-based foods, and so forth to the Goddess;
in this manner, one should worship the Goddess Kālikā, the bestower of desires. (14.48)
Having become endowed with devotion, a man obtains all that is dear;
she is remembered as Mahocchvāsā, Mahādevī, and Mahāmāyā.
Having worshipped in the vulva-mandala with the mantra of the Kālikātantra, that very mandala belongs to her, and the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) is likewise that same one. (14.50)
That very sequence of worship is that meditation; she herself is the deity.
From the mandala to the final emission, all is for the propitiation of Mahāmāyā.
As was previously stated by him, one should worship that goddess in the mandala with great breath,
preceded by bathing, using honey, clarified butter, and other such intoxicating drinks.
Listen with a one-pointed mind, O beloved, to the worship of Tripurā;
her root mantra was previously [taught] in the Uttaratantra. (14.53)
The Vāgbhava, the Kāmabīja, and the Ḍāmara—this triad, joined with Kuṇḍalinī, is the means for accomplishing all goals of dharma, artha, kāma, and so forth. (14.54)
One should offer three things in her worship; she is the Great Goddess meditated upon as heaven.
Therefore she is renowned as Tripurā, known as Kāmākhyā, whose form is desire.
The practitioner should perform the bathing of that [image] with the very same procedure as that prescribed for Mahākālī, using the root mantra. (14.56)
Her maṇḍala is a triangle, her city is Tripura with three lines, her mantra is to be known as having three syllables, and likewise, she possesses three forms. (14.57)
The power Kuṇḍalinī is threefold for the prosperity of the three deities;
because everything is a triad, she is therefore considered Tripurā. (14.58)
In the mandala, lines should be drawn from north to east and so forth;
three lines each should be made, and they should be further adorned with flowers and sandalwood paste.
Having constructed the yantra starting from the northeast and ending at the southwest, one should draw it with focused attention;
then, proceeding from the southwest to the northwest, and thereafter again to the northeast. (14.60)
In this manner, one should again draw a triangle within the mandala;
O Goddess of Gods, that which is in the northeast is the Supreme Goddess Śakti. (14.61)
(171) Thus, O Goddess of the Gods, one should worship the Vetālas and others in this sequence.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kāmākhyā Mantra and the Worship of the Tripurā Maṇḍala," in the Śrī-Bṛhannīlatantra, within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. 14.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the supreme place of practice, wherein that which is recited, O Maheśānī, bestows accomplishment by its very power. (15.1)
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, O Auspicious One, there is a mountain named Darpaṇa where Kubera dwells together with the world-protectors.
O Maheśvarī, Rohita dwells in that Middle Country;
O Maheśānī, he is red in color, like another form of iron. (15.3)
O Maheśānī, by virtue of Parvata’s greatness, he attained the state of heaven;
he became equal to Himālaya and a accomplisher of all rites. (15.4)
Once Lauhitya had been born, Hari, together with all the hosts of gods,
duly bathed that son with the waters of all the sacred fords.
O Maheśānī, because he bathed there and because his pride was shattered,
this place was named Darpaṇa by all the hosts of gods.
O Great Goddess, when that has been recited, one attains accomplishment at that very moment. That Daitya named Rohita recited the mantra of the Goddess. (15.7)
There, having obtained a boon from the goddess, he went to heaven at that very moment;
however, in the sacred precinct of the goddess, there was then one named Darpaṇa.
In the eastern direction from the mirror, a mountain consisting of flames of fire is recorded as having been fashioned, long in shape with hundreds of serpent-like flames. || 15.9 ||
O Maheśvarī, there indeed the Fire-god resides upon the upper portion,
on the surface of a beautiful wooden slab that resembles a mass of vermilion.
On that excellent mountain, the fire shines eternally even today;
and for the benefit of Bhairava, Mahākālī is exceedingly radiant.
There, O Goddess of gods, dwells she who is red in color and most radiant;
even before her, the most radiant Fire himself stands there in person. (15.12)
Near the Lauhitya is the Kuṇḍa, which bestows all the benefits of the Sarasvatī;
having bathed there, O Maheśānī, one becomes manifest as the embodiment of the Divine. (15.13)
To the east of the site of the fire-altar is a small pool named Varuṇa;
on its bank stood in ancient times an excellent mountain called Kaṃśavara.
Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, dwells there eternally.
Having properly worshipped Pracetas at that excellent Kaṃśa [lake], [one attains his favor]. || 15-15 ||
Having bathed in the Vāruṇa pool, one shall attain the world of Varuṇa;
here, the first consonant is indeed joined with the fifth vowel. (15–16)
The seed-syllable of Kubera is said to be joined with the crest of the moon;
it is the seventh [letter] of the letter *pa*, conjoined with the dot (*bindu*) and the half-moon. (15–17)
It is known as the seed-syllable of fire; with it, one should worship the Fire-god.
The fifth letter of the group beginning with *ma*, conjoined with the moon-drop (*bindu*), is remembered as the syllable of Varuṇa.
One should worship these deities constantly with these mantras.
To the east of Vāruṇācala is the mountain named Vāyukūṭa. (15–19)
Endowed with the mandala of the sword-bearing Lord (Khaḍgīśa) and the seed-syllable of wind, the world of wind is situated there, from which the wind issues forth. || 15-20 ||
Reaching the upper and lower regions, it flows constantly upon the surface of the earth;
by worshipping the wind there, one shall attain the world of Vāyu. || 15-21 ||
To the east of Vāyugiri is the mountain known as Aśvakūṭa;
it is triangular and resembles a horse, and above it is the lunar disc.
O beautiful one, having recited the mantra consisting of the letter *kūrma* joined with the *bindu*, know that it is known as the seed-syllable of the Moon, O Supreme Goddess. (15.23)
Even today, O Great Goddess, at every new moon, the Moon, the lord of the night, circumambulates him and proceeds on his course, O Great Goddess. (15.24)
O beautiful one, O Goddess of the gods, Mahākālī of terrible form dwells there together with Śiva, engaged in play during the dead of night. (15–25)
Having gone there and recited the mantra, the practitioner becomes accomplished.
Listen, O Goddess of gods, to the supreme secret that brings delight to all. (15–26)
To the east of that very place is a lake named Somakuṇḍa;
by bathing and drinking there, a human being attains liberation. || 15-27 ||
O Goddess, O Beloved, Candra and Mahendra, together with Rohiṇī, are at the feet of the Blessed Lady; they are honored there as the bestowers of liberation.
O Great Goddess, when the task had been accomplished by the Blessed One Maholkā, O Goddess, the Moon, the illuminator of all, was joined with Rohiṇī. (15.29)
O Supreme Goddess, he prepared an abundance for Mahākālī;
O Great Sovereign, with curd and indeed with milk, O Maheśvarī. (15-30)
With the mantra "Tejo 'si," O Maheśānī, [one should offer] ghee together with sugar-candy, as well as fruit-water accompanied by *śrīpuṣpa* flowers. (15.31)
Immediately thereafter, one should consecrate [the disciple] with the waters of various sacred fords; that bathing-pool, together with those waters, bestows the fruit of great merit. (15.32)
On the bank of the Candra-kunda, O Maheśvarī, there is one of great majesty and white form; by worshipping him on every new moon day, one shall attain liberation.
O Goddess, in the very vicinity of that [place] is the great mountain Bhasmakūṭa, where the high-minded Mahādeva, the Lord of Beings, resides. (15.34)
To the south of that peak is the goddess Pīyūṣadhāriṇī,
renowned by the name Urvaśī, where Mahendra resides.
O Great Goddess, Mahākālī’s Urvaśī resides there;
O Great Queen, wherever the auspicious Mahākālī dwells, [Urvaśī is also present].
And that very heap of nectar, having been gathered little by little,
is constantly presented within the circle of the womb called Kāmākhya.
But Urvaśī, residing within the Sudhāśilā stone, dwells in the Kuṇḍa;
in the center of the peak of Urvaśīkuṇḍa is the pool fashioned from nectar.
Thirty-two bow-lengths wide and fifty bow-lengths long; having bathed there and drunk [the water], a man shall become able to assume any form at will. || 15.39 ||
To the northeast of Candra Kuṇḍa is the great mountain Maṇikūṭa;
there, O beautiful one, the great Maṇikarṇeśa always resides.
It is known as Sadyojāta; Kālikā resides there.
One should perform recitation, worship, and the excellent practice, as well as the supreme sādhana. (15.41)
Sadāśiva should always be worshipped with the Sadyojāta mantra;
by beholding Maṇikarṇeśvara, the practitioner attains liberation. (15.42)
Among the rivers, the one named Maṅgalā, which flows from the Himavat mountain,
always issues forth beautifully toward the east of Maṇikūṭa.
He who, having ascended Maṇikūṭa, beholds the auspicious river,
shall attain the merit born of bathing in the Gaṅgā and proceed to the third heaven.
To the east of Mount Maṇikūṭa is the Kulācala known as Matsyadhvaja,
where Madana was once again consumed by the fire from Hara’s eye.
Having attained a body and propitiated the bull-bannered Lord through austerity,
he remained there in the form of a fish, together with Kāmadeva. Indeed,
the earth was being beheld from the plateau in its infinite extent.
There flows a river named Śāśvatī, which runs toward the south.
On that mountain resides Śiva, known as Kāmadhara;
having bathed in various ways in the eternal [waters] and having drunk from the waters of the Kāmadharā, [he remains there].
Freed from sin and pure in soul, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
thus, O Supreme Goddess, is he who knows the supreme reality. (15.49)
That man, liberated from great sin, shall become truly, truly real.
Now listen, O lady of beautiful limbs, to the secret that deludes all.
To the east of Gandhamādana is the mountain named Sukānta;
at its edge is the Vāsava pool, where the food of Indra’s nectar is found.
Standing there in the south in ancient times, Śakra, the lord of Śacī,
his body exhausted, drank the nectar within the Kāmarūpa region.
O Supreme Goddess, having worshipped Mahādevī on that mountain and having performed one *puraścaraṇa*, one shall attain liberation.
In the east, however, is the mountain called Rakṣaḥkūṭa belonging to Sukānta, where the god Nirṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas, dwells perpetually. (15.54)
With a sword in his hand and a massive body, likewise holding a shield in his left, he is endowed with a mass of matted hair, tall, and resembles a black mountain. (15.55)
Two-armed and black in color, he stands upon a corpse, having ascended the peak of a *rakṣas*—Nirṛti, the lord of the *rākṣasas*. (15.56)
O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods, for one who worships the Great Goddess Kālikā, whose form is Time itself, there is no fear from demons.
Rākṣasas, piśācas, vetālas, and vināyakas—upon seeing that Mahākālī, one is liberated from all sins. (15.58)
To the east of Rakṣaḥkūṭa is the mountain named Bhairava (or the *sādhaka* mountain), renowned as Pāṇḍunātha, which stands according to its true form. (15.59)
In that very place, one should worship the deity named Pāṇḍunātha on the mountain;
he is dark-complexioned like a rain cloud, and holds a mace and a lotus in his hands.
To the right is Goddess Kamalā, who supports him with her two arms;
he has four arms, is seated upon a red lotus, and is adorned with a crown.
Wearing pure earrings, with the excellent Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest—one should worship Hari with the root seed-syllable "Namo Nārāyaṇāya. (15.62)
In this manner, one should worship the God for the attainment of the four aims of life.
To the north of Pāṇḍunātha is the mountain named Brahmakūṭa. (15.63)
Formerly created by Brahmā for the residence of the inhabitants of heaven,
it is one hundred vyāmas in length and half of that in width.
This merit, which removes all sins, has come from the divine sprinkling;
it arises from the water-pot and is the interior nectar of the Brahma-pool.
"Take away all my sins and accomplish pure merit"—in this manner, O Goddess, [he addressed] the great mountain Brahmakūṭa. (15.66)
By worshipping it with circumambulation, one attains union with the Goddess.
To the east of Pāṇḍunātha is the mountain Citramaha, which is Hari. (15.67)
Where Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a boar, dwells eternally—
that supreme abode of Kāmākhyā is known as Nīlakūṭa.
To the east of that dwells Brahmā, and furthermore is Brahmagiri;
to the east of the Brahma-mountain is situated Bhūmipīṭha.
The beautiful linga is white in color, the sacred circle named Kāmākhyā;
there the Supreme Goddess delights in the form of Ugratārā. (15.70)
In that regard, she whose nature is auspicious should be worshipped in that very form.
Listen to her form, O lady of excellent hips: Sadāśivā is to be meditated upon there. (15.71)
She is black, pot-bellied, tall, agitated, and has red teeth;
she has four arms and a slender body, and in her [right] hands she holds a knife and a skull-cup.
He holds a sword and a blue lotus in his left hands, and his matted hair is upon his head;
having placed his left foot upon the thighs of the corpse, he stands with his excellent right foot raised.
Placing [her foot] upon the heart of a corpse and laughing with a loud roar, she wears necklaces and a garland of serpents; she is the supreme bestower of prosperity and the fulfiller of desires.
Her maṇḍala is a triangle with the seed-syllable *hūṃ* in its center;
the names of the various yoginīs at the gates are as follows in the tantra: || 15-75 ||
These things should be known by the tigers among men, as they have been declared within its sphere:
having bathed according to the rules at Urvaśī and likewise having touched the Pāṇḍuśilā rocks. (15.76)
Having ascended Nīlakūṭa, one is not born again in a womb;
having worshipped the Goddess there, one becomes a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 15-77 ||
O you who have gone to the city of Purandara, which is filled with throngs of celestial damsels;
O infallible one, overflowing with nectar; O captivating one, remove my sin! 15.78
"O Goddess Urvaśī, grant me today nectar through nectar!
O Goddess beloved of Purandara, you who are superior to the assembly of celestial courtesans! (15.79)
"O Urvaśī, who are mingled with the Lauhitya lake, take away my sin!"—
having bathed in the holy forest of Urvaśī with these hymns of praise, [one attains merit].
Completely liberated from all sins, he shines resplendent in the world of Viṣṇu;
Urvaśī is said to have two arms and to wear golden bracelets.
Clad in white garments, fair-complexioned, with full and elevated breasts, beautiful in every limb, pure, and adorned with all ornaments. || 15-82 ||
Indra then recited the mantra proclaimed for her;
Gaṇeśa was situated in the eastern region of the mountain known as Kāmākhyā. (15.83)
And right there at the door stands the captivating Agnivetāla;
O Maheśvarī, their form and their mantra are exactly as described. (15.84)
Therefore, O beloved, I shall reply; listen with a one-pointed mind.
O Supreme Goddess, [the first is] the Praṇava, and immediately after that, the Heart.
Then, joined with its own seed-syllable and so forth, this is proclaimed as the mantra of the perfected Gaṇeśa stationed at the door, addressed as "O Elephant-faced One. (15.86)
I shall describe his form: he has the face of an elephant, three eyes, a protruding belly, four arms, and wears a serpent as a sacred thread.
[He has] ears like winnowing baskets, a large snout, a single tusk, and a broad belly;
on the right [he holds] an elephant tusk, and likewise a blue lotus in the other [hand]. (15.88)
One should describe him as holding a sweetmeat ball and an axe in his left hands;
he has a broad chest, three eyes, and thick shoulders, limbs, and feet.
It is joined on both sides by two female deer, with a mouse situated in the middle;
the mantra for the worship of the Five-Faced One is declared to be as follows. (15.90)
That very mantra should be taken up, and such a ritual practice should be observed:
[the deity] has two arms, a full face, red eyes, and is terrifying. (15.91)
In his right hand he holds a knife, and in his left a vessel of blood;
his face is terrifying with bared fangs, and he is emaciated, covered with visible veins.
He who bears long matted locks upon his head and is endowed with a terrible roar is supreme;
for him who worships him, there shall be no fear again from spirits and the like.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the supreme *yoginī-tattva* and the eight-syllable mantras of those headed by Śailaputrī.
And those Vaiṣṇava tantric mantras previously mentioned, as well as the limb-mantra of Śailaputrī explained earlier. (15.95)
Especially for yoginīs whose complexions resemble that of Rūpa,
[one should proceed] with each individual seed-syllable (bīja) according to the path taught in the Durgātantra.
O Maheśvarī, the Yoginīs should be worshipped with their own respective seed-syllables;
one should worship the pair of feet of Kātyāyanī according to the Durgā-tantra.
That very form of worship has been previously explained;
having first extracted the Praṇava, one should then prescribe the letter *cha*. (15.98)

O Śivā, the mantra joined with the left cheek (the letter *v*), adorned with the lunar drop (*bindu*), and ending with the *visarga* of the remainder of the *haṃsa* (the letter *ḥ*), is dear to all. (15.99)
Having worshipped Kālarātri, one shall be endowed with all sovereign powers;
by this very procedure, one should worship Bhuvaneśvarī.
Having extracted the Mahāśakti, and immediately after that the Vāgbhava,
and again having reached the Yoni, the triad of seed-syllables (bījas) is thus proclaimed.
With this king of mantras, one should worship Bhuvaneśvarī;
all these yoginīs, like Kāmākhyā, bestow their fruits. (15.102)
Where no specific distinction is stated regarding the form, the tantra, or the worship, one should perform the worship there according to the form described in the Nīlatantra. (15.103)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, whoever worships each Yoginī individually obtains the fruit of all sacrifices; there is no doubt in this matter. || 15-104 ||
The essential nature of the form of Nīlaśaila has been explained;
it lies to the east of the navel-mandala and to the south of Bhasmakūṭa. (15.105)
To the east is the mountain named Kapaṭa, which assumes its own form;
there is a southern stone there, black, with a luster like that of blue collyrium.
On the plateau, one should always worship the Lord of Kings, Vyāsa, Pañcasura, Antaka, Śamana, Pāśa, and Daṇḍa. (15.107)
He always holds in his hand the instrument for punishing living beings;
he is black in color, two-armed, and radiant with a crown and diadem. (15.108)
He always holds a sword and a leaf in his left hand;
he is black in color, has thick feet, and protruding teeth. (15.109)
O beautiful one, one should worship with supreme devotion the Lord who eternally bestows fear and fearlessness upon men, whose vehicle is a buffalo, by means of the seed-syllable of Yama.
The syllable at the end of the penultimate group, joined with a bindu and an anusvāra, is known as the seed-syllable of Yama; it brings pleasure to Yama. (15.111)
Indeed, by worshipping Yama with this very mantra at Śiva on the excellent mountain named Kapaṭa, one shall not meet an untimely death. (15.112)
To the east of the one named Kapaṭa is the mountain known as Arciṣ;
it was obtained through former merits and is situated to the southeast of Bhṛṅgeśī. (15.113)
The planets dwell here constantly according to their own will;
he who worships them shall never encounter misfortune anywhere. (15.114)
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall declare the mantra of the Sun as well;
listen to the form, the mantra, and the tantra of the Sun. (15.115)
Now hear from me the mantra-forms of the other seven:
he who holds a red lotus, the trident-bearer, the wielder of the spear, and the bearer of the mace. (15.116)
May this four-armed Sun-god be my boon-granter and bring me auspiciousness.
Having first uttered the Praṇava (Om), one should then place the letter at the end of the consonants (Ha). (15.117)
The seed-syllable encased by the Moon is the second, most excellent seed-syllable.
Listen now to the third, O lady of beautiful limbs: it is the great-souled seed-syllable of Fire. (15.118)
By means of this king of mantras, the worship of the Sun shall take place.
Now I shall describe the supreme collyrium-mountain (kajjalācala). || 15-119 ||
There, Gaurī, the Great Durgā, being virtuous, dwells together with Śiva;
and all the divine beings, such as the Vidyādharas and others, reside here. (15.120)
And having beheld that mountain of divine form, one should recite ten thousand times the mantra declared for the range of all things and all states of being. (15.121)
Having extracted the seed-syllable at the end of the position (thānta), adorned by the left cheek (the letter *v*),
and encapsulated by a half-moon, this first seed-syllable is the bringer of what is dear.
O lady of excellent hips, the second seed-syllable, ending with the wife of fire (svāhā), is extracted as the mantra of Mahāśakti;
it is the supreme seed-syllable of Durgā. (15.123)
O Goddess of the gods, O Auspicious One, one should worship Kālikā with that seed-syllable;
O lady of pure smiles, one should perform the recitation (japa) to the measure of a thousand.
O Maheśānī, when that has been recited, the practitioner attains liberation;
and when one *puraścaraṇa* has been performed, O Maheśānī, [the goal is achieved]. (15.125)
There, O Maheśānī, the fruit of hundreds of thousands of *puraścaraṇas* will be attained; to its east, O auspicious one, lies the beautiful Śubhaparvataka. (15.126)
In ancient times, Śakra, the lord of the gods, took his pleasure there together with Śacī;
formerly, O Great Goddess, that river was known by the name Kapilā. (15.127)
Having bathed in it and drunk its water, one is glorified in the world of the Goddess.
Likewise, in the south-eastern direction from the abode of Kālikā— || 15.128 ||
O Gaṇeśvarī, there exists a great, pure, and vast subterranean cavern, measuring twenty-five yojanas in extent.
From him came the river, who is saluted by all the gods;
for he is remembered as the father of that one whom the gods call Brahmā. || 15.130 ||
Because she bestows fruit like the Gaṅgā, she is therefore known by the name Kapilā;
having bathed in the Kapila-Gaṅgā and previously in other [sacred waters], [one obtains the results].
Having first attained heaven, a man shall thereafter go to the world of the goddesses;
on the eastern bank of the river is the one called Damanikā, which grants all desires.
Then there was the river Mahāhṛṣṭatoyā, which likewise pacifies sins;
after that came another, most excellent river, called Brahmāhvayā.
On the eastern side of that river, it bestows fruits like the Gaṅgā;
O Maheśvarī, having bathed in the river for the entire month of Māgha, [one attains the results].
Likewise, by means of *damanikā*, one shall attain supreme *nirvāṇa*.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Other Places for Practice," in the *Śrī-Bṛhannīlatantra* from the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. 15.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the conduct that bestows the state of Sarasvatī; listen with a one-pointed mind, O Parameśānī, for it is essential. (16-1)
O Maheśānī, those things which must necessarily be performed have been determined;
they are the virtuous ones, whose defects are exhausted, who are self-reliant, and who utter words of praise. (16-2)
Whatever constitutes their conduct is called "right conduct" (sadācāra).
One should adopt the prescribed right conduct as if it were the interior of one's own home. (16.3)
The king should likewise establish prohibitions and injunctions through [the application of] injunctions and prohibitions; he should employ the Brahmins in all respects within the six duties.
In the same way, one should employ the Kṣatriyas and others each in their own respective duties;
for he who abandons his own dharma and practices the dharma of another [falls]. (16.5)
O Supreme Goddess, he is to be punished; one should punish him with a fine of a hundred [coins].
In rites performed annually, one should treat these [offenses] specifically.
O Maheśvarī, the king must certainly perform those specific rites,
including the complete worship of Durgā on the Mahāṣṭamī day during the autumn season.
One should indeed perform the Nīrājana rite on the tenth day for the increase of strength;
O Maheśvarī, this occurs on the third day of the dark fortnight in the month of Pauṣa.
O Goddess of gods, by worshipping the Goddess there when [the moon] is conjoined with the Puṣya asterism, one attains all desires; everything certainly comes to pass. || 16-9 ||
O Maheśvarī, on the tenth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha,
one should perform the worship of Kālikā and likewise of Nīlasarasvatī according to the prescribed rite.
These must necessarily be performed by kings; otherwise, [the kingdom] will certainly perish.
Through these duties, the army, the realm, and the treasury also increase. (16.11)
O Great Goddess, if this is not performed, there will be famine and pestilence; all living beings will suffer, so one should practice these [rites] with particular care. (16.12)
The procedure for the worship of Nīlā on the Mahāṣṭamī in the autumn season has been previously declared; by that very procedure, the worship should be performed. (16.13)
O daughter of the mountain, listen to the ritual for the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), by performing which there shall be prosperity even for our elephants. (16.14)
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina, the Yoginī bathes;
she herself, together with the gods, accepts that supreme bath in the northeast.
Then, when the eighth day of the deity has arrived, one should perform the *nīrājana* rite;
the proper time for the *nīrājana*, however, was previously explained by me to you.
O Goddess of gods, O beloved, listen with a one-pointed mind to the mere procedure:
[one should offer] a single horse of great courage or indeed one that is very beautiful.

One should worship [the deity] for seven days with perfumes, flowers, garments, and other offerings; having worshipped him on the third day and thereafter, one should lead him to the sacrificial mandala.
One should determine its auspicious or inauspicious nature by observing its movements;
if the horse flees, there will be a crushing defeat of the enemy kingdom.
If the prince dies when he spits out the *leḍāni* [seeds],
or if he does not proceed while being led away, there will likewise be the death of the queen.
In the same way, if a horse makes sounds from its mouth, nose, or eyes while facing a particular direction, one shall conquer the enemies in that very direction. (16–21)
"Thus, O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, I have told you this practice, which bestows sovereignty; know it to be my very essence. (16–22)
Listen to another [method], O lady of excellent limbs, by which the practitioner attains success:
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the bright fortnight, O beautiful one, when it is joined with the asterism Jyeṣṭhā.
O Maheśānī, the full moon day (Paurṇamāsī) is [auspicious]; bathing on that day yields great fruit.
[One should bathe] with sandalwood, agallochum, kakkola, dūrvā grass, and white mustard seeds.
O Maheśānī, with *āmalaka* fruit, with the powder of turmeric, with sesame oils, with Viṣṇu oils, and with other fragrant substances; || 16-25 ||
One should bathe the Supreme Goddess with Nārāyaṇa oil;
likewise, one should bathe Kālikā with coconut water.
And for a hundred thousand years, O Supreme Goddess, one is honored in the world of the gods after having bathed the Queen of the Gods with curd.
Even after a hundred crores of kalpas, one does not fall away from union [with the deity].
One should bathe the goddess Mahākālī, who is most radiant, with milk. (16.28)
His prosperity shall be especially stable; of this there is no doubt.
One should bathe the Goddess with ghee for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. (16–29)
Likewise, O Goddess, the practitioner obtains fruit by bathing the Mistress of all desires and boons with sugar, and by bathing her with honey. (16.30)
O Supreme Goddess, by [worshipping] Kālikā and likewise Sarasvatī,
one is liberated from all suffering and is glorified in the heavenly world.
One should bathe the Supreme Goddess with fragrant flowers and water;
O Goddess, O beloved, listen with a one-pointed mind to the fruit of that merit.
Through thousands of millions of kalpas, one shall attain union with the Goddess and enjoy various pleasures until the dissolution of all beings.
Having bathed the Queen of the Gods with sandalwood water alone, one shall abandon the realm of Yama and dwell upon Kailāsa. (16.34)
O Goddess of the Gods, in the month of Vaiśākha, one should bathe [the deity] with cool waters;
one should offer her divine and enchanting coconut water. (16.35)
One should worship the Goddess in the morning and reveal [the ritual] in the evening;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, O best of gods, one should likewise offer Mallikā and Mālatī flowers.
O Supreme Goddess, one should cause [the offerings] to be given and perform a bath with curd;
likewise, one should bathe Śivā with waters mixed with camphor. (16.37)
Having thus bathed the Goddess of the Gods in due order, there shall be happiness.
In the month of Śuci, one should offer curd mixed with sugar to Mahādevī.
And one should give [the offering], O Supreme Goddess; one should bathe [the deity] with white mustard seeds.
One should cause parched grain mixed with sugar to be offered to Mahādevī. (16–39)
In this manner, O Goddess of the gods, one shall gradually obtain the fruit of the *puraścaryā*. O Supreme Sovereign, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should bathe Śivā with clarified butter.
Likewise, having bathed Maheśvarī with lentil flour and enjoyed various pleasures, one is glorified in the world of Durgā. || 16-41 ||
O Goddess, one should satisfy the Supreme Sovereign with flour-cakes mixed with jaggery;
O Supreme Mistress, in the month of Nabhasya, one should bathe the Beautiful One of the Gods.
O beautiful one, O beloved, one should offer milk mixed with sugar to Mahādevī, having stirred it with turmeric and myrobalan.
One should offer goat meat and rice mixed with vegetables, along with fine food,
and also offer cakes made of mung beans, adorned with milk and clarified butter.
He who gives in this manner in succession shall attain the world of the Goddess;
specifically, when the month of Īṣa has begun, one should worship the Great Goddess Sarasvatī.
And one should bathe [the image] with a decoction, with the nectar-like essence of the Kalpa-tree, or again with Nārāyaṇa oil or Viṣṇu oil. (16.46)
One should bathe the one who deludes worldly existence with another fragrant oil,
and offer her a most pleasing message that brings delight to the sense of taste.
O leader of the gods, one should cause a supreme sweetmeat ball (laḍḍuka) to be given to her;
and one should worship Śivā, the consort of Śaṅkara, with various kinds of offerings.
Having performed such worship, a person shall dwell in heaven for ten thousand kalpas;
O Goddess of gods, in the month of Kārttika, one should bathe [the deity] with warm milk.

Or one may bathe [the deity] with yakṣakardama paste during the auspicious month of Kārtika, O Great Goddess; as for the offering substance, it should consist of preparations made from wheat and similar grains.
One should offer these together with milk, which is pleasing to Mahādevī:
coconut, plantain, breadfruit, and sugarcane. (16.51)
One should offer a very beautiful jambhīra and nāgaraṅga fruit to the Goddess,
along with lukewarm paramānna mixed with flour.
O Śivā, one should diligently cause fallen fish and other such items to be given to her;
by doing so, a man shall immediately become liberated while living. (16.53)
For him, neither sin nor merit arises; of this there is no doubt.
O Great Goddess, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the best of months, [one should worship] Sundarī.
One should bathe [the deity] with fragrant, warm water filtered through cloth, combined with saffron and other substances, and with beautiful garlands of flowers. (16.55)
One should bathe the Supreme Goddess with the seeds of Āragvadha mixed with turmeric and sugar, and offer excellent food smeared with ghee.
One should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with side dishes smeared with ghee, accompanied by jaggery and vinegar, along with fried vegetables. (16.57)
O Śivā, one should diligently cause radish to be offered to her, O Goddess, along with various kinds of food offerings adorned with chickpeas and other items. (16.58)
O Goddess, O most beautiful one, one should offer fine cloth together with plantain fruits to Mahādevī,
and one should offer a very splendid bedstead.
O Maheśānī, O Goddess praised by the gods, one should cause a bed to be given;
he who, O Goddess, should cause these to be given in this sequence during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa—‖ 16-60 ‖
O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, hear now the fruit of his merit:
having enjoyed happiness in this world, he shall attain the status of a great king. (16.61)
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you that which bestows all accomplishments;
one should bathe the Great Goddess in the month of Pauṣa according to the prescribed method.
O enchantress of the gods, one should cause cakes, parched grain, and other such substances to be offered;
during both day and night, one should cause excellent food to be offered to Mahādevī.
O beloved, the best practitioners, with diligent effort, should offer the supreme oblation (naivedya), which is most heart-pleasing, accompanied by ghee and betel leaves and other such items. 16-64.
In the month of Māgha, O Great Goddess, one should bathe [the image] with ghee and milk-rice;
having also bathed the supreme Śivā with water mixed with perfumes.
In this matter, one shall attain union (sāyujya) with the Goddess; of this there is no doubt.
One should offer delightful food to be chewed, sucked, licked, and drunk. (16.66)
One should offer food such as flour-cakes and other items that are pleasing to Mahādevī;
in this manner, one should satisfy the Goddess of the Gods with great effort through this sequence.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, one shall attain liberation in the next;
O Goddess of gods, one should bathe the Supreme Goddess in the month of Phālguna.
One should bathe the Supreme Goddess with either ghee or milk;
[one should offer] the supreme, divine, delicious, and most enchanting food offering (naivedya).

O auspicious one, O Great Goddess, the practitioner should offer to the Goddess all the most beautiful substances combined with various other materials; thus the practitioner attains happiness. (16.70)
O Maheśānī, in the month of Caitra, one should offer ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa),
as well as curd, milk, honey, and likewise sugar with the milk-rice.
O Maheśānī, one should offer most excellent and beautiful substances to the Goddess;
O Deveśī, the practitioner who worships in this sequence [attains success]. (16–72)
"He shall certainly attain liberation; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Maheśvarī.
Thus has been told to you this divine [teaching], which liberates one from all sins. (16.73)
Whoever performs the practice in this manner shall be happy; there is no doubt about this.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Twelve Months (as another application)," in the glorious Bṛhannīlatantra, in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. 16.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the supreme cause of omniscience.
O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips, when the first watch of the night has passed.
If the practitioner, being composed and with supreme devotion, should especially recite this mantra a thousand times at midnight; 17-2.

One should first recite the *yoni* mantra, then again the *yoni* mantra, and the *manu* consisting of a pair of seed-syllables; one should perform this recitation at midnight and sprinkle water consecrated by the mantra.
Within six months, O Goddess, one shall attain omniscience;
this is the truth, O Great Goddess, there is no doubt whatsoever. (17.4)
If the moon and sun were in vain, then everything would become fruitless.
Listen to the secret, O lady of beautiful limbs, which brings delight to Mahākālī. (17.5)
O Goddess of the Gods, by this the practitioner free from envy attains success;
O Goddess of the Gods, it is on the lunar day of the new moon in the month of Kārttika.
On that night, one should especially worship the supreme Kālikā. During the first watch of the night, the goddesses [approach] the Supreme Goddess for her bath. 7.
O Great Goddess, having propitiated [the deity], one should thereafter form a resolution;
O beautiful one, having fashioned a lotus near that [deity]—specifically within the pavilion—[one should proceed]. (17.8)
Alternatively, O Supreme Goddess, having fashioned an auspicious mandala that is beneficial in every respect,
one should establish the Great Goddess upon a noble seat.
O Supreme Goddess, O beautiful one, he should bathe [the deity] in a bright mirror with turmeric and sour gruel, and with scented oil, O fair lady.
One should joyfully bathe the goddess Kālikā with cool, pure waters;
and in the manner thus described, the wise person should worship her like Nīla.
Listen, O lady of excellent hips, to the meditation that bestows eloquence;
by means of which meditation, O Goddess of gods, one may achieve the highest perfection. (17-12)
Cloud-colored, with a smiling face, her hair disheveled and naked,
her countenance laughing with loud, boisterous laughter, her lotus-like face radiant with a gentle smile.
Three-eyed, bestowing boons, eternal, seated upon Mahādeva, adorned with a garland of severed heads and rich with young ears suspended from her ears. || 17-14 ||
In her upper left hand she holds a divine flaying-knife, and below that she holds a severed head;
with her right hands, she displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
One should thus meditate upon the auspicious Mahākālī, whose face is serene, as she beautifully bears a divine garland that deludes the three worlds. (17.16)
O Parameśānī, O Śivā, having constructed a pavilion according to the rules—quadrangular, with four doors, and its upper part marked by a crown—[one should proceed]. (17–17)
O Goddess, one should worship the Supreme Goddess in the supreme pavilion with various ritual substances, such as flowers, incense, seats, and so forth. (17–18)
One should present the supreme food offering (naivedya), adorned with various ingredients—divine, excellent cooked food endowed with manifold flavors. (17–19)
O Maheśānī, this supreme message—the heart’s duty—is most delicious and captivating; it is inexhaustible, reaching even to the depth of one's navel.
At every watch of the day, one should perform worship and recitation;
and with various kinds of offerings, one should worship the auspicious Kālikā. (17–21)
O Supreme Goddess, one should perform the fire-oblation for Sundarī with milk-rice and clarified butter;
O Great Goddess, one should also perform the oblation for Maheśvarī with bilva leaves. (17–22)
O Maheśānī, one should recite the hymn that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
thereafter, the wise one should bid farewell to the captivating Mahādevī. (17–23)
Thus has been told to you the divine worship of Kālikā;
O Great Goddess, he who performs it shall certainly attain liberation. (17–24)
O Goddess, O beloved, there shall be happiness in this world through the rite of Nīlā;
now, O Great Goddess, I shall likewise declare the determination of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
O Supreme Goddess, O Sarasvatī, beloved of Śiva!
For the sake of the fire-oblation (homa), I shall describe the procedure for the oblation itself, along with the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), O Śivā.
At the outset, one intent on the characteristics of the site (vāstu) should examine the ground;
or else, O Supreme Goddess, one should perform the extraction of any embedded obstacles (śalya).
O Great Goddess, worshipped by the hosts of gods, one should fashion a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the eastern direction of the site (vāstu), digging it according to the human measurement. || 17-28 ||
Or, O Maheśānī, one should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the rules in the northeast;
it may be seven cubits, nine, or five, according to the various divisions.
One should fashion it as square with four doors and free from gaps;
one should spread it with *darbha* grass and arrange it with thread alone.
In a square measuring one *kuṇḍa*, there should be no other room larger than five cubits; O Great Goddess, one should accomplish all rites within this square. (17–31)
Listen, O Goddess of gods, to the measurement by which the mantra becomes perfected:
it is the length of the middle joint of the middle finger of the right hand of the practitioner. (17–32)
O Goddess, the measurement of one finger-breadth (aṅguli) for the middle [finger] is defined by its length as eight barley-corns (yava); this is what is traditionally taught.
Having struck each individual thread, one should effect purification in the middle of it;
and having likewise divided that middle into three parts, O Pārvatī, [one should proceed]. (17.34)
One should draw a pair of fish at the two cardinal directions; from those two fish, one should drop a thread extending north-south according to the desired length. (17.35)
Having fixed that [line] at the tips of the threads, one should draw crocodiles (makara) in the corners;
from the positions of those crocodiles in the corners, one should drop threads toward the cardinal directions.
When this is done, a square consisting of four compartments arises;
O Maheśānī, this is the quadrangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with excellent characteristics.
O Supreme Goddess, the measurement of the width of the *kuṇḍa* is indeed such;
O Supreme Sovereign, its measurement is likewise, and the girdle (*mekhalā*) is of that same form. (17.38)
The excellent practitioner who knows the tantra should fashion five triple-girdles;
indeed, O Maheśvarī, there should be three girdles in the great fire-sacrifice (mahāhoma).
The height and width of the eye, which consists of three fires, is one cubit;
its internal height is nine finger-breadths, and its width is likewise nine finger-breadths. (17.40)
In every case, such is the field according to the dimensions of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas);
leaving aside one finger-breadth, there shall be a girdle (mekhalā) within the pit.
In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of one cubit, one should indeed avoid making another;
however, the knower of mantras should construct a pit measuring half a finger-breadth [in depth]. 17-42.
The first girdle is said to be *sāttvika*, the second *rājasa*, and the third *tāmasic*; such is the determination regarding the girdles.
Thus I have told you the divine determination regarding the girdle;
now, O Great Goddess, I shall declare the supreme determination regarding the womb.
In the first case, the knower of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should fashion the yoni in the pit itself—
[according to the Kha-pāṭha reading, "in the first girdle" (mekhalā)]— to the east of the inner girdle;
it should have the color of an elephant's lip and possess all the required characteristics.
The *yoni* is said by the wise to be six fingers in length, four fingers in width,
and two fingers in height in a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit.
The wise man should fashion the navel like an eight-petaled lotus below the *kuṇḍa* (or, according to the Kha manuscript, below the *kuṇḍa*),
or the learned practitioner should fashion the navel there in accordance with the specific dimensions of that particular *kuṇḍa*.
In this case, the navel indeed has a height and width of four fingers;
in sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) of two cubits and so forth, one should increase the yoni proportionally.
One should likewise increase the navel by the measure of one finger-width each;
O Maheśvarī, know that the area outside the site of the pit is the *sthala*. (17.49)
Commencing from a four-cornered base, with a perforation in the middle of its stalk, it should have a thick root and a slender tip; such an elevation is truly captivating. (17.50)
One should construct it starting from the position of the outer girdle (*mekhalā*) on the exterior [the variant reading *bāhyasthamekhalābāhyasthānam* is found in manuscript Kha].
One should make a cavity in the middle of the womb (*yoni*), and outside of that, the part known as the "grasper" (*grāhin*). || 17-51 ||
The wise man should increase the length of the vulva; the navel should be circular in shape.
It is taught that with a span [of the hand] there are ten thousand [recitations], while with two spans it is said to be ten thousand times ten thousand.

O Maheśānī, one should perform a hundred thousand oblations (lakṣahoma) at a sacrificial pit of four cubits, a million oblations (daśalakṣa) at one of six cubits, and ten million oblations (koṭihoma) at one of ten cubits.
O Supreme Goddess, in this tantra there is nothing beyond ten cubits;
if it exceeds the measurement of the sky (the prescribed depth), one becomes diseased, and if it is deficient, there is loss of cattle and wealth. (17.54)
In a curved pit there is suffering; in one lacking a girdle, the destruction of kinsmen;
in one devoid of a girdle, grief; and in one that is excessive in size, the loss of wealth. (17.55)
O Maheśvarī, a *kuṇḍa* that is empty of the vulva (*yoni*) causes the destruction of one’s wife;
if it is devoid of a neck, that *kuṇḍa* brings about the ruin of one’s offspring. (17.56)
If it is cracked or filled with fissures, there will be eradication or death;
therefore, O Supreme Goddess, one should prepare the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) only after having examined it.
The pool that brings delight to the Goddess is saluted by all the gods;
it is the pool that grants success in mantra and bestows all eloquence.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the most beautiful fire-rite (agnikārya),
by performing oblations in which, O lady of excellent hips, one becomes composed of all vidyās.

Having constructed the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) as prescribed on the northern side of the pavilion, one should perform there the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) for the obligatory, occasional, and optional ceremonies.
There should be eighteen consecrations for the sacrificial pits according to the method of the Tantra:
one should perform the inspection with the root mantra and the sprinkling with the *śara* mantra.

Striking with that same [mantra] is prescribed, sprinkling with darbha grass with the armor-mantra (varma), digging and lifting up with the weapon-mantra (astra), and filling with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya). (17.62)
Sprinkling with the Samīkaraṇa mantra is prescribed, while warding off with the Varman mantra; pounding with the Heti mantra and cleansing with the Varman mantra. (17.63)

The application of ointment and the fashioning of the artistic forms follow immediately after that; subsequently, the drawing of the three lines and worship with the heart-mantra should take place. (17.64)
O Goddess of gods, the best of practitioners should consecrate the yoni-pits with the Astra-mantra for the vajrīkaraṇa (vajrification) and with auspicious waters using the Hṛdaya-mantra. (17-35)
O Maheśānī, one should draw three lines upon that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
then, one should write three lines with their tips pointing either eastward or northward.
The deities of the lines with tips pointing eastward are traditionally held to be Mukunda, Īśa, and Purandara;
those of the lines with tips pointing northward are Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu. (17.67)
Alternatively, O beloved of Prāṇa, one should draw a triangle, a circle, and a square; therein, one should worship the Yoga-pīṭha of Vahni.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Ambikā are the Śaktis in sequence;
thereafter, O highly fortunate Goddess, one should worship the Tārākuṇḍa.
In the center of that, one should worship the supreme sovereign goddess Nīlā Vāgīśvarī;
thereafter, the learned priest should draw forth the fire using her seed-syllable alone.

O Goddess of the gods, one should then recite the mantra for the kindling of the fire, beginning with *hūṃ phaṭ* and ending with the wife of fire (*svāhā*), directed toward the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*). (71)
One should purify that fire there with the *dhenumudrā* and the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*);
the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) is considered to be performed with the *vāruṇa* mantra alone. (72)
Having lifted it with both hands, one should whirl it three times above;
O Supreme Goddess, with the thought that it is the seed of Śiva, [one should cast it] into its womb.
Having first recited the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* and the form of Fire (*vahnimūrti*) joined with the suffix *ṅe*,
and having thus worshipped [it], O Great Goddess, O beautiful one, draw [the breath] in through the *iḍā*.

Then, by means of the *kumbhaka* breath-retention while reciting the *kūrca* seed-syllable (*hrūm*), O Supreme Goddess, at the conclusion of bringing about the consciousness of the fire, [one should join it] with the suffix *-ṅe*. (17.75)
Then, O Maheśvarī, one should kindle the fire with the *cinmantra*;
O Parameśānī, O beloved, listen with a single-minded focus to the *cinmantra*. (17.76)
*Cit piṅgala hana hana daha daha paca paca sarvajñājñāpaya svāhā*.

O fair-faced one, O Supreme Goddess, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the limbs of the fire: the supreme placement ending with "namas" for the heart, [using the mantra] *sahasrārciṣe hṛdayāya namas*. (17.77)
This mantra is remembered as ending with "svāhā" for the head, beginning with "svasti pūrṇāya.
Also, "uttiṣṭha puruṣāya" is for the tuft (śikhā), ending with "vaṣaṭ. (17.78)
"O beautiful one, [the mantra] 'hum' is for the armor that pervades the smoke;
O beloved, 'vauṣaṭ' is for the three eyes of the seven-tongued one."
One should assign the limbs with the mantra: "To the archer, to the weapon, Phaṭ!
O daughter of the mountain, listen now to the mantra for the invocation.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, then [the word] Vaiśvānara, then Jātavedas, Lohitākṣa, and after that, Ihāvaha. (17.82)
"Accomplish all rites," ending with the wife of Vahni (svāhā)—having worshipped with this mantra, one should meditate upon Vahni with a concentrated mind. (17.83)
Listen, O Maheśānī, to the description of meditation, for through meditation one attains omniscience:
[the deity] resembles the bandhūka flower and has the luster of well-refined gold. (17.84)
Holding a lotus in his hand, possessing mighty arms, adorned with two faces,
having hands composed of the seven meters, and embodying the three abodes.

Having understood in three ways the meaning of the three feet, which carries the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, and which is adorned by the four horns consisting of the Brahman, Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, and Hotṛ priests; (86)
The Pañcarātra, the Pāśupata, the great doctrine of the gods, the Buddhist, and the Vedic—these are the six [systems] with tawny eyes. (17.87)
His ears were the fourfold expanse of the Vedas' meaning, and his voice was the sound consisting of hymns and liturgical recitations;
he was like the sun within the hollow of a jewel bound to the matted locks of the subterranean realm.
Adorned with golden ornaments and decorated with golden earrings, he stands in the midst of a red lotus, seated upon a svastika throne. (17.89)
He wears crimson garments and holds in his three left arms a golden vessel filled with ghee that hangs down from his back.
It was constantly resounding and increasing in its own splendor;
there was a lance, a palm-leaf fan, and a golden vessel for clarified butter.
One should thus meditate upon the great fire, which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life, with its face turned away and copper-colored, and filled with seven tongues of flame.

O beautiful one, having first worshipped the seven tongues of flame in the directions beginning with the east, O Goddess, one should then worship Brāhmī and the others for the sake of accomplishing one's own tasks, O beloved. (17.93)
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, as well as Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā, O beautiful one. (17.94)
O Maheśānī, O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Mahālakṣmī;
furthermore, Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī [should be worshipped] in the outer region. (17.95)
O beautiful one, O Great Goddess, one should worship Rati, Prīti, Kīrti, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi in the outer region.
O Maheśānī, the wise one should worship Brahmā upon the girdles;
and he should encircle all the girdles with bundles of *darbha* grass. (17.97)
Then one should offer oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* into the pit fashioned in three rows;
having heated the *sruva* ladle three times, O Great Goddess, one should sprinkle it with water.
O beautiful one, having heated them again with both the left and right hands,
O Supreme Goddess, one should place the *sruva* and *sruk* ladles on the right side.
O Goddess of the gods, one should sprinkle the vessel of clarified butter with the weapon-mantra;
then, having cast the purifier into it, one should indeed throw it into the fire. (17.100)

O Supreme Goddess, O Great Queen, having taken clarified butter from that vessel with the *sruva* ladle while reciting [the mantra] ending with the heart-mantra, one should offer it into the fire, O Great Queen. (17.101)
O Great Goddess, [one should offer] to Agni and then to Soma;
O Beloved, the words *agnīṣoma*, ending in the locative case (ṅe), extend up to the wife of Vahni (the fire-syllable svāhā).
One should take the excellent clarified butter from the left, the right, and the middle;
one should offer it with "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods.
O Maheśānī, O Maheśvarī, with the seed-syllable of Māyā ending with the heart-mantra, I perform the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and so forth, O Maheśvarī. (17.104)
O Supreme Goddess, one should offer seven oblations for each of the others;
having declared the group of rites ending with marriage, one should perform the consecration.
O Maheśānī, a person should worship the Goddess in that fire;
having meditated upon the oneness of that fire with one's own self, one should perform the ritual visualization.
Then, one should offer sixteen oblations with the root mantra,
using karavīra flowers mixed with sesame seeds, anointed with the three sweets, and combined with blood.
O Maheśvarī, one should offer oblations to Mahādevī with the root mantra either one thousand and eight times or likewise one hundred and eight times.
O Maheśānī, having separated [the deities], one should perform the oblation for the enclosure and so forth;
first uttering the Praṇava, [one offers] "to Agni" and likewise this very same [mantra]. (17.109)
"svāhā to the great earth"—this is remembered as the end of this mantra;
likewise, "bhuvaḥ to Vāyu and indeed to the intermediate space. (17.110)
O Maheśānī, the mantra ends with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā) and is used for [offering] to Dyu;
likewise, O Dear One, it is used for Svarga, Sūrya, and Candramas.
O Maheśānī, the mantra [for the constellations] consists of the names of the *nakṣatras* ending with the wife of Fire (*svāhā*).
At its conclusion, O fair-faced one, one should perform the great preliminary rite (*pūrvāṅga*). (17.112)
The wise one should protect that fire according to the ritual rules and to the best of his ability;
O Goddess, honored by the gods, he should perform the oblation with the hand turned downward. (17.113)
O Supreme Goddess, if one performs the fire-oblation with the palm turned upwards, then the merit produced thereby shall not exist.
Thus has been described to you the divine delineation of the sacrificial pits and other implements;
O Supreme Goddess, these must be prepared with great care for the performance of the fire-oblation (homa).
Now I shall speak, O Maheśānī; listen with full attention.
On the seventh lunar day (saptamī) that occurs in the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha— || 17-116 ||
On that night, one should worship the Great Goddess,
the Supreme Sovereign, who has four arms, is exceedingly fierce, and dwells in the cremation ground.
The Supreme Goddess holds a severed head, the gesture of fearlessness, a sword, and a boon-granting mudrā;
she is adorned with a garland of severed heads and endowed with three eyes.
When the first watch has passed, until the end of the third watch,
one should worship the Supreme Goddess with extensive displays of great magnificence.
O Goddess, one should worship Kālarātrikā with the aforementioned worship;
O lady of pure smiles, one should perform the recitation (japa) to the measure of a thousand.
O Supreme Goddess, O Great Mistress, one should perform the oblation according to what was previously stated;
O Beloved, the supreme food offering, O Goddess, consists of fried grains and other such substances.
One should give a most beloved object that is dear to Mahāmāyā;
by failing to do so, one goes to hell—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Maheśvarī.
Now, O Supreme Goddess, I shall describe to you the procedure for the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana): having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and facing the east during the day.
At night, one should perform this most excellent daily rite facing north;
know it, O Pārvatī, to be the destroyer of the heaps of sins of others. (17.124)
The killing of an embryo, the drinking of liquor, the theft of gold,
as well as approaching the wife of one's teacher, and whatever other evil deed has been committed— (17.125)
This [goddess], assuming the form of Mahābhairava, purifies all this;
she has two arms, wears yellow garments, and is adorned with various ornaments. (17.126)
She is red in color, slender-limbed, radiant with the three folds [of skin] upon her waist,
and auspicious, holding a supreme, divine book in her right hand.
One should visualize the goddess Sandhyā as wearing a silken garment, possessing three eyes, and holding a training-sutra (śikṣāsūtra) in her left hand. (17.128)
Thus has this divine meditation been described to you, O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods;
by meditating especially upon the twilight [devotion], the destruction of all sins shall occur.

Then likewise, the sipping of water (ācamana) and the invocation of the sacred ford (tīrtha), followed by breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the supreme ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa). || 17-130 ||
Having taken water in the palm of the hand and recited the mantra five times,
O Goddess, one should consecrate the head with the dripping water.
O Supreme Goddess, having taken that water in the right hand,
O Beloved, one should draw that water, which is of the nature of light, through the *iḍā* [nāḍī].
Having washed away the impurity within the body, one should exhale through the Piṅgalā;
then one should perform the washing of the hands and offer the arghya water to the Sun.
O Goddess of the gods, one should offer the *arghya* to Mahādevī by repeating [the mantra] three times;
immediately thereafter, one should recite the Gāyatrī while joined with meditation.
Then, having gratified the gods, one should satisfy the chosen deity three times.
Having offered the recitation (japa), O Goddess of Devas, one should then mutter the root mantra. (17.135)
Having recited the supreme mantra one hundred and eight times,
and then having offered the recitation, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff.

O Maheśvarī, one should perform the six-limbed breath control (prāṇāyāma) at the conclusion [of the rite] on the new moon day, the full moon day, and likewise on the day of a śrāddha ceremony. (17.137)
O Supreme Goddess, at the time of the transit [of the sun] one should perform the twilight ritual;
O Pārvatī, the fourfold rites are for the sake of the gods.

Know that the scripture is likewise [authoritative], since the performance of the eternal rite of the twilight (sandhyā) should be carried out even on the twelfth lunar day and other such occasions, O beloved. (17.139)
"By failing to do so, one indeed goes to hell; for my word alone is authoritative.
Thus has this supreme, divine daily conduct been described to you.
O Supreme Goddess, the best of practitioners should perform [this] at the three junctions of the day;
he who has no regard for this is not called a Brāhmaṇa. (17.141)
When the Blessed Lady is enraged, she indeed destroys his desired objects of pleasure.
O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, listen now to the procedure for worship in brief.
First is the placement of the ṛṣi and so forth; after that, the purification of the hands; then the pervasive placements on the fingers and the placement beginning with the heart. (17.143)
Three claps of the hands, the binding of the directions, breath control (prāṇāyāma), meditation, worship, and recitation—this is the sequence in all tantras. (17.144)
The offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna) should likewise be performed according to the rules by those who know the tantras;
one should worship Bhairava, Durgā, and likewise Maheśvarī.
One should worship Vṛṣabha and Nandin with great effort;
the wise man, proficient in all the scriptures, should sacrifice to Mahākāla.
Having worshipped the Cakrarāja, one becomes the master of all siddhis;
O Śivā, at the outset, one should worship the Liṅga, the Great God (Mahādeva), with diligence.
And at that very time, one should worship one's own chosen deity;
therefore, one should take the flower-offering (nirmālya) with a spirit of devotion. || 17-148 ||
The use of the *nirmālya* from a [different] *liṅga* is forbidden unless one has performed the desired worship [to that specific deity].

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Meditation on Kālī and Other Forms of Worship, the Determination of the Fire-pit, the Girdle, and the Yoni, and the Description of the Fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) and so forth," in the glorious *Bṛhannīlatantra*, within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. 17.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
The Holy Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O cause of creation, preservation, and destruction!
In the course of conversation with the Great Goddess, this has been related by me in detail.
O Supreme Lord, O Great Ruler, please grant me the favor of hearing the thousand names of the goddess Nīlasarasvatī;
tell them to me, O Mahādeva, if I am dear to you. (18.2)
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Well asked, O Great Goddess! This [list], hidden in all the tantras, cannot be fully recounted—even the thousand names of Tārā. (18–3)
Through disclosure, there shall be a loss of accomplishment and one is deprived of prosperity;
he who reveals [the teaching] out of delusion shall meet death within six months. (18.4)
It is unspeakable, O Supreme Goddess; it is indeed unspeakable, O Beautiful One.
Forgive me, O Bestower of Boons, if you have affection for me. (18.5)
"Listen, O Goddess, best among those who know all the scriptures [O Śivā, according to the Kha manuscript]:
this essence of wealth, O Great Goddess, must be guarded, O Supreme Sovereign. (18.6)
One's lifespan should be guarded, and the secrets of one's home should be guarded; thus one shall not partake in sin.
O Supreme Goddess, these must be well-guarded; through such guarding, one attains perfection.
Through manifestation there would be the loss of the effect, and through manifestation there would be dissolution;
therefore, O auspicious Maheśānī, this must never be made manifest.
Having heard these words of the god, the goddess, the most beautiful one, the supreme sovereign lady, became astonished and despondent there. (18-9)
Listen, O Supreme Lord, who have reached the further shore of the ocean of compassion!
O Mahādeva, it is certain that you have no affection for me here. (18.10)
Thinking, "Blessings, blessings, O Mahādeva," Maheśvarī,
the auspicious daughter of the mountain, turned her face away and remained there, O Lord of Gods.
Beholding the Goddess turned away, Mahādeva Maheśvara laughed and embraced his beloved, the Supreme Sovereign, as he spoke these words.
O Maheśvarī, right there he spoke to Mahādevī:
"O daughter of the mountain, know that you are my own essential nature. (18.13)
"O Great Goddess, without you I shall have the form of a corpse as previously described.
Forgive me, O Supreme Bliss; forgive me, O Daughter of the Mountain. (18.14)
Just as the vital breath dwells within the body, O Maheśānī, O beautiful one, so do you, O Primordial One of the worlds; I have fallen at your feet. (18.15)
Thinking thus, O Great Goddess, protect me, your servant.
Then the Goddess Maheśānī, Śivā, who deludes the three worlds— 18.16.
Embracing Mahādeva, she spoke with a voice faltering with emotion:
"O Supreme Lord, I am eternally the nature of the body, and you are the embodied one. (18.17)
Nevertheless, you speak such pleasant words to me in order to deceive me;
Mahādeva spoke again, O Bhairavī, O beloved of my life. (18.18)
"You wish to hear the thousand names of Tārā in their entirety.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"O Supreme Lord, the Thousand Names of Tārā have not been heard by me."
Tell me, O illustrious one, the truth that is most beautiful.
(Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Īśāna, O Omniscient One, how do practitioners always attain the supreme siddhi? Tell me that, O Beautiful One. (18–20)
Because there is no hymn superior to this, as is certain in the tantras;
it is divine, the remover of all sins, and the warder-off of all calamities. (18–21)
This hymn produces all-encompassing knowledge and merit, is endowed with every auspiciousness, is equal to hundreds of preparatory rites (puraścaryā), and brings delight to all. (18–22)
O Lord of the Gods, please recite the thousand names of Tārā, which bestow subjugation, bring about death, and grant great eradication.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"The thousand names of Tārā shall come forth through the recitation of this hymn.
I shall proclaim the thousand names of Tārā in their entirety. (18–24)
Listen, O Goddess, with constant devotion, to that which is the supreme benefit for devotees: the fruit that is obtained without the need for ritual offerings or recitation. (18–25)

O Goddess, I shall describe that entire fruit; listen to it. Oṃ. Of this *Sahasranāma* hymn of the venerable goddess Tārā, named *Bhaktikulasarvasva*, Akṣobhya is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *Bṛhatī* and *Uṣṇih* are the meters (*chandas*), and the venerable Ugratārā is the deity (*devatā*).
The deity is the illustrious Ekajaṭā, the illustrious Nīlasarasvatī; the application is for the sake of attaining the four aims of human life.
Tārā, Rātri, Mahārātri, Kālarātri, Mahāmati; [Kapālinī according to the Kha manuscript];
Kālikā, Kāmadā, Māyā, Mahāmāyā, Mahāsmṛti; [Mahotsavā according to the Kha manuscript]. || 18–26 ||
Delighting in great gifts, adorned with sacrifices and sacrificial festivals;
moon-faced, [vajra-faced], with eyes like those of the cakora bird, possessing beautiful eyes and lovely vision. (18–27)
The great goddess is three-eyed, with eyes like those of a deer, and enchanting;
she is Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Jyotsnā, Cārukeśī, and Sumūrdhajā. (18–28)
Vārāhī, Vāruṇī, Vidya, Mahāvidyā, Maheśvarī, Siddhā, Piṅgā, Kuñcitakeśā, and she whose form is the Great Sacrifice. (18–29)
Gaurī is the color of the campaka flower, slender-limbed, and the enchantress of Śiva;
