she is the embodiment of all bliss and the sole remover of every peril.
She is composed of the bliss of knowledge, she is Nandā, she is Bhadrakālī in her true form;
she is Gāyatrī and Sucaritrā, devoted to the Kaula vow.
Hiraṇyagarbhā, Bhūgarbhā, Mahāgarbhā, Sulocanī, Himavat-tanayā, Divyā, and Mahāmegha-svarūpiṇī. || 18-32 ||
The Mother of the World, the Sustainer of the World, the Benefactress of the Worlds;
she who is Aindrī, Saumyā, and Ghorā; Yāmyā, Vāruṇī, and Mādhavī; Āgneyī, Vainateyī, Nairṛtī, Aiśānī, and she whose essence is Caṇḍikā.
The daughter of Sumeru is eternal and beneficial to all. || 18-34 ||
With a trembling tongue and lotus-like eyes, adorned with a garland of severed heads and pearls, she consists of all bliss, is everything, and has the nature of universal bliss. (18.35)
Fortitude, Intelligence, as well as Lakṣmī, Faith, she who moves upon the serpent,
Rukmiṇī, Jānakī, Durgā, Ambikā, Satyavatī, and Rati; Kāmākhyā, the Giver of Desires, Nandā, Nārasiṃhī, and Sarasvatī.
Devoted to Mahādeva, Caṇḍī is the shatterer of fierce, staff-like arms.
She with long hair, she with beautiful hair, she with tawny hair, and she with great locks;
Bhavānī, the consort of Bhava, the virtuous Satī who removes the fear of Bhava. || 18-38 ||
Likewise, she is Paurandarī, the wife of Viṣṇu, and Māheśvarī;
she is the mother of all, the eternal Vidyā, Cārvaṅgī, and the destroyer of the Daityas.
O Maheśānī, you who possess every form, O passionate one of excellent complexion;
you are the Great Vidyā, the Great Māyā, the Great Wisdom, and the Great Festival. (18.40)
Virūpā, Viśvarūpā, Mṛḍānī, and Mṛḍavallabhā;
she who resembles ten million moons and who shines with the brilliance of a hundred suns.
The daughter of Jahnu, the most formidable, Pārvatī who deludes the universe, she who can assume any form at will, the Great Sovereign, eternally energetic, and high-minded. (18.42)
She is the consort of the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, the enchantress of Śaṅkara,
the daughter of Kaśyapa, Kamalā, Kṛṣṇā, she who is the very form of Kṛṣṇa, and Kālinī.
She was Māheśvarī, mounted upon a bull, causing wonder to all;
she was venerable, possessed of pride, pure, and likewise the daughter of the Himālaya mountain.
Aparṇā, with eyes like lotus petals, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
bearing a great conch, the beloved and enchanting daughter of the mountain.
She is Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, the consort of Śambhu, Gaṅgā, Jaleśvarī, Bhāgīrathī, Manas, Buddhi, Nityā, and likewise Vidyāmayī. || 18-46 ||
The beloved of Hara, the daughter of the Mountain, the wife of Hara, the ascetic;
the Goddess who removes great diseases, possessing a most formidable form. (18.47)
She possesses the radiance of great merit, she is formidable, the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
she holds a conch, she wields a thunderbolt, she is the sustainer, and likewise she holds a book.
Cāmuṇḍā, Capalā, Tuṅgā, the slayer of the demon Śumbha, Śānti, Nidrā, Mahānidrā, Pūrṇanidrā, and Reṇukā. (18.49)
Kaumārī, Kulajā, Kuntī [Kānti, KHA], devoted to the Kaula vow, Vanadurgā, Sadācārā, Draupadī, and Drupadātmajā. || 18-50 ||
She is glorious, the source of glory, the sustainer of glory, and the bestower of glory;
she is the form of creation, the great Gaurī, the destroyer of Niśumbha’s life.
Padminī (200), Vasudhā, Pṛthvī, Rohiṇī, Vindhyavāsinī, Śivaśakti, Mahāśakti, Śaṅkhinī, and Śaktinirgatā [Nāśinī in manuscript kha]. || 18.52 ||
The Goddess who takes away the life of the Daityas, the protector of all, she who is forbearance, the bringer of security, and who is the form of intelligence and possesses great wealth. (18.53)
Śrīvidyā, Bhairavī, the auspicious one, Bhavānī, the destroyer of worldly existence;
Tāpinī, Bhāvinī, Sītā, whose nature is sharp radiance. (18.54)
The giver, devoted to charity, Kālī, Durgā, adorned by the Daityas, the bestower of great merit, the formidable one, the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha. || 18-55 ||
Padmā, Padmāvatī, Kṛṣṇā, Tuṣṭā, Puṣṭā, as well as Urvaśī, Vajriṇī, Vajrahastā, and likewise Nārāyaṇī and Śivā.
She who possesses a sword, who holds a sword in her hand, and who bears a sword and a skull-bowl;
she is a celestial woman, a daughter of the gods, the venerable mother of the gods, born of Puloma.
She is blissful, the bestower of heaven, and the increaser of all happiness;
she is virtuous, possessed of virtue, subtle, of subtle form, and the granter of boons.
The venerable Speech is the bestower of boons, ever wise and the giver of knowledge;
she is Ugrakālī, Mahākālī, Bhadrakālī, and Dakṣiṇā. (18.59)
Born from the lineage of Bhṛgu, she is Bhārgavī, the beloved of Bhṛgu;
she bears a trident, holds a trident in her hand, and carries a knife and a skull-bowl.
Born from a great lineage, she has a magnificent peacock as her vehicle;
she is devoted to the great conch, is red in color, and holds a red skull-cup.
Clad in red garments, the beautiful woman, the mistress of the gods, the bestower of liberation and of auspiciousness, dark-hued, and slow with the intoxication of amorous play. (18.62)
Jyeṣṭhā, who bestows supreme bliss, is served by hosts of yoginīs;
as well as Sārā, Jāmbavatī, Satyabhāmā, and the daughter of the mountain (Pārvatī).

Fierce, possessing fierce strength, terrible, having Rudra as her essence and being of a reddish nature, she is of the form of Rudra, the Great Fierce One, the destroyer of the fierce Daityas. || 18-64 ||
Kaumārī, Kauśikī, Caṇḍā, the Vidyā who destroys the Daitya Kāla, the consort of Śambhu, she who delights in Śambhu, the wife of Śambhu, and Mahodarī. (18.65)
She is the wife of Śiva, devoted to Śiva, the consort of Śiva, and beloved by Śiva; she is the wife of Hara, devoted to Hara, the consort of Hara, and beloved by Hara.
She is the beloved of Madanāntaka, the consort of Madanāntaka;
she is Girijā, the daughter of the mountain, and the beloved of the Lord of the Mountain.
She is the past, the future, and the present; she is manifest, purifying, and the protector of others;
she is invisible yet possesses a manifest form, and she increases both the desired and the undesired. || 18-68 ||
The imperishable one whose life-force has departed, the lady who is the sovereign of Indra,
she who is born from the ocean of waters, the sustainer, and the firmly established one.
Udbhavā, Kṣobhaṇā, Kṣemā, Śrīgarbhā, Parameśvarī, Kamalā, Puṣpadehā, Kāminī, and Kañjalocanā. || 18-70 ||
She who is the refuge, the lotus-like one, the beloved, the increaser of stainless bliss;
she who wears her hair in a braided knot, the formidable one, the stainless one, and she whose form is divine.
The auspicious army of the gods has its ornaments raised aloft; it is Mahodarī, Śrīmatī, Śiśirā, Navya, Nandā, and Śiśirācalakanyakā. (18.72)
She who is highly honored, the best among the gods, the eldest, the mistress of life,
the steadfast, the destroyer of darkness, the dispeller of gloom, the self-restrained, and the devoted wife.
She is the illuminator, mounted upon her chariot, the light of all the worlds;
she is the wise one of great heroism, the female swan who carries one across the cycle of existence.
She who removes the suffering of prostrate living beings, the destroyer of the Daityas,
the goddess Ḍākinī and Śākinī, who bears an excellent khaṭvāṅga staff.
Kaumudī, Kumudānandā, Kaulikā, Kulajāmarā, Garvitā, Guṇasaṃpannā, Nagajā, and Khagavāhinī. (18.76)
Moon-faced, most formidable, and beautiful with lovely hair;
charming, delightful, venerable, worthy of honor by the virtuous, and a friend to all. (400) 18-77.
Jyeṣṭhā, Śreṣṭhā, Maghā, Puṣyā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Pūrvaphālgunī;
she is the slayer of Raktabīja and the destroyer of Raktabīja.
She is the slayer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, the destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa;
she is the wielder of the sword, the remover, the excellent wielder, and the bearer of the stainless and pure.
Vimalā, Bhāskarī, Vīṇā, Mahiṣāsuraghātinī, Kālindī, Yamunā, Vṛddhā, Surabhi, Yuvati, Bālikā, and Satī. (18.80)
She is Kauśalyā, Kaumudī, Maitrī incarnate, and Arundhatī;
she is the consort of the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva), Pūrṇā, and the embodiment of perfect bliss.
She was the wife of Puṇḍarīkākṣa and the beloved of Puṇḍarīkākṣa;
her face was like the full moon, and her radiance was equal to the young moon.
Revatī, Ramaṇī, Citrā, adorned with variegated garments and ornaments, Sītā, Vīṇāvatī, Yaśodā, and the beloved Vijayā. || 18.83 ||
Born from fresh flowers, she is the festival of the festival of fresh flowers;
she is a garland of wreaths of fresh flowers, adorned with ornaments of blossoms.
Her vital breath is equal to that of a fresh flower; she is fond of festivals of fresh flowers;
standing in the midst of the circle of the deceased, Śivā is beautiful in all her limbs. (18.85)
The sixth [form] consists of fresh flowers, adorned with a mandala of flower clusters;
endowed with the qualities of fresh flowers, she is beloved by Bhairava in the cremation ground. (18.86)
She is the lamp of the Kula scriptures, the promoter of the Kula path;
she is Śmaśānabhairavī, Kālī, Bhairavī, and the beloved of Bhairava.
Ānandabhairavī is to be meditated upon; she is Bhairavī, Kurubhairavī, the one who delights Mahābhairava, and the enchantress of the Bhairavī lineage. (18.88)
Śrīvidyābhairavī, Nītibhairavī, Guṇabhairavī, Saṃmohabhairavī, Puṣṭibhairavī, and Tuṣṭibhairavī. || 18-89 ||
Saṃhārabhairavī, Sṛṣṭibhairavī, Sthitibhairavī, Ānandabhairavī, Vīrā, Sundarī, and Sthitisundarī. (18.90)
She is the embodiment of bliss through her qualities, the beautiful one who takes the form of Time;
she is the illustrious Māyāsundarī, the gentle Sundarī, and the Beauty of the World.
Śrīvidyāmohinī is the intellect whose nature is great wisdom;
she is Mallikā, the connoisseur of necklaces, beautiful with her support of a necklace. 18.92
She has the color of a blue lotus and is adorned with *nāgakeśara* flowers;
she resembles the *japā* flower and is beautified by *japā* flowers.
She is the beloved of Viṣṇu, the doer of what is dear to him, the destroyer of the lords of the Dānavas;
she is the sovereign of knowledge, the giver of knowledge, and the bestower of the bliss of knowledge.
Endowed with the weight of virtues, possessed of virtue and moral conduct, she is perfected in beauty and youth, and adorned with beauty and youth. (18.95)
She is the locus of virtues, devoted to virtues, beautiful through her reverence for virtue,
intoxicated by the fragrance of wine, and adorned with a pair of earrings.
The Goddess resides at the foot of a tree, she rests upon the branches of a tree;
she dwells in the middle and the top of a palm tree, and she inhabits the interior of a tree. || 18.97 ||
Resembling the self-arisen flower, bearing the self-arisen flower, delighted by the self-arisen flower, and graced by the self-arisen flower. || 18-98 ||
She delights in the flowers of the Self-Arisen One; she is naked, meditative, and nectar-like.
She is fond of semen (or white, according to the Kha manuscript), devoted to semen, and intent on immersing herself in semen.
Pūrṇaparṇā, Suparṇā, Niṣparṇā, and Pāpanāśinī;
Madirāmodasaṃpannā and Madirāmodadhāriṇī. || 18-100 ||
She is the support of all, the possessor of all virtues, the bearer of the Joy of Nanda; she is born from the flower of womanhood, and her festival is the festival of the flower of womanhood.
The doe has a life-force equal to that of a woman’s flower, delights in the woman’s flower, is fond of whatever arises at all times, and celebrates whatever arises at all times. (18.102)
She may have four arms, ten arms, or eighteen arms;
likewise, she may have two or six arms. She is pleased, adorned with a red lotus. (18.103)
Kauberī, Kauravī, Kauryā, Kurukullā, Kapālinī; she whose shanks are like very long plantain trees, Rambhorū, and Rāmavallabhā. || 18-104 ||
She is the night-walker, the very form of night, possessing a radiance equal to the moon of night;
she belongs to the moon, she is a digit of the moon, she is the moon itself, and her face resembles the beautiful moon.
She who possesses streams, she who flows, the destroyer of all miserable states;
the support of all, consisting of all, whose very nature is universal bliss. (18.106)
The sovereign of all wheels, she who is everything, composed of all mantras, and auspicious;
she whose life-force is the thousand-eyed one, and who is beloved by the thousand-eyed one. (18.107)
She has a thousand heads, is perfectly beautiful, possesses deception, and devours all things;
she is the staff, stationed upon the wheel of the staff, and bestows the fruits of the six groups.
She resides in the center of the twenty-sixth lotus, situated in the midst of the twenty-six families; she dwells within the color of the syllable *hūṃ* and is adorned with the letter *hūṃ*.
She whose abode is the letter *ha*, who is adorned with the syllable *ha*;
she who is captivating, encircled by necklaces, and adorned with necklaces and diamonds.
Accompanied by the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, adorned with *hrīṃ*-syllables, she is the digit of Kandarpa, the *Kundā* who is *Kaulinī*, proud of her lineage. (600) 18.111
Her life-breath is the ketakī flower; she has made the ketakī her ornament;
she is attached to the ketakī flower; she is adorned by the ketakī. (18.112)
Mahāmāyā Maheśvarī has a face filled with camphor;
she is Kalā, Keli, Kriyā, and Kīrṇā, longing for the Kadamba flower.
She was like a bank of clouds, possessing the gait of an elephant's trunk [the reading "karigatiḥ" is found in manuscript *kha*], walking with the stride of a lordly elephant;
she was short in stature, with eyes as pleasant as those of the *khañjana* bird, and adorned by a pair of *khañjana* birds.
Like a firefly, she is difficult to perceive; like a firefly, she is flickering.
She is the Great Illusion, the mother of the world, fond of song and instrumental music, and Rati herself.
Goddess of the hosts, worshipped by the hosts, adored for her virtues, bestower of virtues;
rich in virtues, endowed with virtues, giver of virtues, whose very essence is virtue. || 18-116 ||
She is the venerable one, the most venerable, the fair-complexioned Gaurī, who bestows the fruit of lordship over the Gaṇas;
she is the Great Knowledge, the Great Intelligence, the weigher, and the enchantress of the hosts.
She is the capable one, she who loves worldly existence, she who is to be contemplated, she who is to be meditated upon, and she whose essence is worldly existence;
she is the gurgling one, the one with a terrible countenance, and the destroyer of the fierce Daityas.
Ghorā, Ghoravatī, Ghoṣyā [Ghoṣā, kha], Ghoraputrī, Ghanācalā [Ghanālayā, kha], Carcarī, Cārunayanā, Cāruvaktrā, and Caturguṇā. || 18-119 ||
Caṇḍī consists of the four Vedas; she has a face like the moon and four faces;
her eyes are like moving cakora birds and her eyes are like moving khañjana birds.
Her abode is the moving lotus; she is adorned with moving lotuses [the variant reading *locanā* (having eyes) is found in manuscript *kha*];
she possesses an umbrella, she is fond of the umbrella, she is the umbrella itself, and she is adorned with the umbrella and the chowrie.
With severed covering, severed head, and severed nose;
consisting of deceit, abounding in deceit, terrified by deceit, having the form of deceit, and stable in deceit. (18.122)
She whose abode is the letter *cha*, she who is enriched by the letter *cha*, she who is fond of guile;
she who is disguised, she who delights in deception, and she who dwells within deceit and fraud.
She is beloved by Jagannātha, she is considered the life-force of all beings, and she is regarded as the one who grants liberation to the world.
She is the ancient one, the consort of Jīmūta, and she is adorned by clouds.
Jāmātṛvaradā, Jambhā, Jamalārjunabhañjinī, Jharjharī, Jhākṛti, Jhallī, Jharī, and likewise Jharjharikā. (18.125)
She who produces the sound "ṭaṅkāra," she who produces every "ṭaṅkāra" sound;
she whose limbs resound with "ṭhaṃ," she who holds the hand-drum (ḍamaruka), she who is the form of the ḍākinīs, and she who is fond of the hand-drum. || 18.126 ||
She is the constant resonance of the ḍhakkā drum, adorned with jewels as tulasī;
she is the balance, the crossing, she who has crossed over, the star, and likewise the savior.
Tantravijñā, Tantrarata, Tantravidyā, and Tantradā;
Tāntrikī, Tantrayogyā, Tantrasārā, and Tantrikā. (18.128)
She is the upholder of the Tantras, the creator of the Tantras, and the embodiment of all Tantras;
her face is like the cool-rayed moon, and her radiance is equal to that of the cool-rayed moon.
Her limbs are like a mass of frost, beautiful as the source of frost;
she is the essence of the Tantras, the hand of the Tantras, and the very embodiment of the essence of the Tantras.
Her face is like the abode of frost, her radiance equal to the moon;
she is the daughter of the snowy mountain, the one who rides Tārkṣya, whose limbs are stars, and who is beautiful as a palm tree. (18.131)
Accompanied by the *tāra* sound, she is adorned with the *tāra* sound;
her abode is the peak syllable *tha*, and she is garlanded with the letter *tha*.
Compassionate, devoted to the miserable, she is the destroyer of suffering and poverty;
she is the shatterer of the pain of misfortune and the eradicator of the state of ill-fortune.
She is the daughter, the kinswoman of the distressed, and the destroyer of the lords of the Dānavas;
she is the worthy recipient of gifts, devoted to giving, and satisfied by the honor of charity. || 18.134 ||
She is served by those who have subdued their senses; she is the self-subdued one, compassion itself, and beloved of Damodara.
She is the bestower of boons upon Dadhīci, the contented one, and the crusher of the lords of the Dānavas.
Long-eyed, long-haired, and long-nosed is Dīrghikā;
she is the destroyer of the suffering of poverty and the eradicator of the pain of indigence.
She is the deceptive one, the jagged-toothed, the guileful, and the bestower of boons upon the demon Dambhāsura;
she is the giver of wealth and grain, the auspicious one, and the bestower of the riches of the Lord of Wealth. || 18-137 ||
She is the lawful wife, devoted to dharma, the destroyer of both dharma and adharma [the increaser, kha];
she is the possessor of dharma, the one who acts according to dharma, the one worthy of dharma, and the increaser of both dharma and adharma. || 18-138 ||
Dhaneśvarī, devoted to dharma, increasing the bliss of dharma;
the presiding deity of wealth, fond of wealth, rich in wealth, and satisfied by wealth. || 18-139 ||
She is the wise one, the courageous one, the radiant one, resembling a white lotus;
she is the supporter, the sustainer, the nurse, the leader, the earth, and the bearer. (800) || 18-140 ||
She is righteous, endowed with Dharma, and free from those who revile the Dharma;
she is ever-new, born of the mountain, lowly, possessing a deep navel, and the sovereign of mountains.
She whose eyes are like fresh lotuses, beautiful as a new lotus, the refined lady, the eldest in the city, the daughter of the king of mountains, and the mountain itself. (18.142)
She who is pleased by the Naga kings, adorned by the Naga kings, the Mistress of the Nagas, mounted upon a Naga, the Sovereign of the family of the Naga kings. || 18-143 ||
She is the crescent of the new moon, the auspicious benediction, and the beloved of Nandikeśvara;
she is born from the lotus, has lotus-like eyes, and possesses eyes like a pair of lotuses.
Her speech is water-born, her body is as pure as water;
she is enriched by a serpent as a sacred thread, wearing a serpent as her sacrificial cord.
She is satisfied by *nāgakesara* flowers, she wears garlands of *nāgakesara*,
and she is adorned with fresh *ketakī*, *kunda*, *mallikā*, and lotuses.
The heroine is beloved by the hero, adorned with the hero’s love, accompanied by the hero’s love, and permeated by the hero’s love. || 18-147 ||
She is the abode that delights the leaders, she who brings joy to the leaders;
she is eternally devoted to playful activities and bestows the fruits of those playful activities.
She delights in playful acts, she is playful, she is the abode of those who perform playful acts;
she finds joy in play, she is devoted to play, and she is intent on meditation upon play. || 18-149 ||
Beloved by Pūṣan, worshipped with flowers, adorned with garlands of blossoms, the giver of merit, the full moon of the month of Pauṣa is complete and bestows the fruit of ten million merits. (18.150)
She is hidden by the Purāṇas and Āgamas, protected by the Purāṇas and Āgamas;
she is the domain of the Purāṇas, full, primordial, mature, and playful. || 18.151 ||
She who dwells in the heart of Prahlāda, bringing him joy; she whose conduct is meritorious;
she who belongs to the month of Phālguna; she who is beloved by Phālguna (Arjuna); and she who bears the name of Phālguna.
She who bestows the love of Phālguna, adorned by the king of serpents, having a serpent-girdle, beloved by serpents, and adorned with a serpent-necklace. || 18.153 ||

She whose every limb is adorned by the Lord of Serpents, she who wears serpents as ornaments, she who is beloved by the serpents, she who delights in serpents, and she who wears serpents as bracelets. || 18-154 ||

She who bestows the fruit [of liberation] is Triphalā; she is capable and adorned with the ornament of fruits. Her every limb is composed of the syllable *pha*, and she increases the joy of Phālguna. (18.155)
Devoted to Vāsudeva, she is wise and causes the discernment of the wise; she possesses a lute, is filled with power, and shines with the nectar of youth.
Bālāvasumatī, Vidyā adorned with the necklace of knowledge, Vidyāvatī who delights in the state of a physician, Vaivasvatī, and Bali. || 18-157 ||
Balividhvaṃsinī, Varāṅgasthā, Varānanā, she who dwells upon the chest of Viṣṇu, Vāgvatī, and Vindhyavāsinī. || 18.58 ||
She who bestows fear, who grants terror, whose radiance is equal to the web of rays of the sun;
she who is the object of worship for Bhṛgu, worthy of honor by Bhṛgu, and saluted by Bharadvāja. (18.159)
She is the giver of fear, the destroyer of fear, of terrifying form, and yet beautiful; she possesses illusory power, delights in honor, and is intent upon the respect accorded by the mind.
She bestows bliss upon Mādhava; she is the honey-sweet wine that gladdens the eyes;
she is endowed with the qualities of a great festival; she is vast and possesses great virtues. (18.161)
Delighting in the fragrance of wine, devoted to immersion in wine, Yaśodharī is the science of fame who increases the joy of Yaśoda. (18.162)
White as camphor with her fame, adorned with the river Yaśodā, she is the beloved sister of Yamarāja; she increases the bliss of the path of yoga.
She is Yama’s sister Yamunā, who increases the path of yoga;
she is the bringer of joy to the Yādavas and the enhancer of the Yādava delight.
Delighted by sacrifice, consisting of sacrifice, adorned with the performance of sacrifice;
delighted by Rāma, devoted to Rāma, and intent upon pleasing Rāma. (18.165)
She is the queen, the one worshipped in the royal court, the sovereign lady of the kings of gods, the goddess Ramā;
she is the delightful woman, the source of pleasure, the beautiful one, and the bestower of bliss upon Rāma.
Her face is like the full moon, her eyes are like red lotuses;
she is satisfied by the love of Lāṅgalin and fond of the affection of Lāṅgalin. (18.167)
She who is crimson as lac, the woman, the play, the graceful one, the dissolution;
she who delights in the virtues of the Lord of Laṅkā, and who bestows boons upon the Lord of Laṅkā. || 18-168 ||
She who delights in clove blossoms, who is eager for a garland of clove flowers;
she is the creator, the wife of Vivasvat, and the bearer of love for Vivasvat.
Seated upon a corpse, resting upon the chest of a corpse, the protector of those who have come for refuge, the worthy refuge, Śrī, possessing the qualities of autumn. (18.170)

Residing in the very center of the six-cornered [mandala], she is cultivated for the sake of attaining perfection; the Goddess takes the form of the syllable *HŪṂ*, adorned with the appearance of the syllable *HŪṂ*. (18.171)
Kṣemaṅkarī, as well as Kṣemā, Kṣemadhāmavivardhinī, Kṣemāmnāyā, as well as Ājñā, Iḍā, and Īśvaravallabhā. || 18-172 ||
Likewise, Ugradakṣā and Ugrā arise from the vowels beginning with *a*;
they abide in the phoneme-cluster of the letter *ṛ* and are adorned with the vowel *ṝ*. (18.173)
She is the letter *e* and likewise the one who is *e*; she is perfumed by the syllable *e*. She is desired (*aiṣṭā*) and likewise *oṣā*, bearing the syllable *au*.
And she whose essential nature is the syllables *aṃ* and *aḥ*, who is well-concealed by all the Āgamas—(1000) this, O Goddess, is what has been told as the Thousand Names of Tārā. || 18-175 ||
Whoever recites this hymn every day with a spirit of devotion, whether by day or by night, or during both the twilights; || 18-176 ||
By the recitation of this King of Hymns, a king becomes a servant;
he shall be honored in all scriptures, and in every tantra, he is Hara himself. (18.177)
Whether he recites or even listens to this in a shrine of Śiva, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, or at a crossroads, he is a yogi; of this there is no doubt. (18.178)
Whatever names of the Enemy of Mura exist in this context, those auspicious ones should be taken up, and never any others whatsoever. (18.179)
One should not fail to chant the name of Hari, nor should one fail to touch a leaf of Tulasī;
one should never entertain thoughts of anything else, nor ever engage in the censure of others. (18.180)
For one who worships with devotion using red flowers such as sindūra and karavīra, there is nothing whatsoever that is unattainable.

By the recitation of this hymn, one indeed brings about the paralysis of wind, the paralysis of water, the paralysis of the movement of the sun, and the paralysis of fire [the reading *śaityaṃ* appears in manuscript *kha*]. One may swiftly attract prosperity, and freedom from debt arises by force.
Just as fire would burn grass, so too shall he crush his enemies in an instant. || 18-183 ||
He who should always recite or even listen with a one-pointed mind would enchant the wives of kings and bring even the gods under his control. (18.184)
He shall be long-lived, happy, and eloquent, and his speech shall be authoritative;
he obtains the fruit that comes from bathing at all sacred fords and from performing ancestral rites at Gayā.
He who recites this with one-pointed mind truly obtains that fruit—those who have faith in its propitiation and those who are intent upon accomplishing it. (18.186)
All their creative power shall belong to her, O Goddess, and she is the supreme goal;
having stayed in a bower of seasonal creepers, one should strike with a staff.
Having recited [the mantra] and offered praise with devotion, one shall indeed go to the state of Tāriṇī;
especially on the eighth, the fourteenth, the ninth, and on Saturday.
O Goddess of gods, for one who worships at the time of the sun’s transit, within the mandala, at night, and on the new moon day—
extending throughout the year— the supernatural powers (siddhis) remain under their control.
A woman who is bereft of sons, afflicted by misfortune and disease, or a woman who is barren, or one who has only one child, or one whose fetuses die; || 18-190 ||
O Great Goddess, even she who is destitute of wealth and grain, and who is overwhelmed by disease and grief, should likewise have this written on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*). (18–191)
One should bind it on the left arm, and one shall become possessed of all happiness;
likewise, even a man who is generally tormented by suffering [shall find relief]. (18–192)
In an assembly, in terrible calamity, in dispute, in danger from an enemy, in a fourfold army, as well as in battle, and everywhere when oppressed by misfortune; || 18-193 ||
O auspicious one, by mere remembrance, [impurities] go far away to their destruction;
she should be worshipped with effort in an empty house or a temple of Śiva.

At the root of a bilva tree, in a cremation ground, on a riverbank, or within a kula-maṇḍala, [one should offer] cooked rice mixed with sugar and fermented liquor, along with milk and milk-rice (pāyasa). || 18-195 ||
With offerings such as cakes mixed with flour and other appropriate oblations,
whatever substance has been presented should be consumed according to the prescribed rule.
If that [offering] is not consumed out of delusion, the deities do not wish to partake;
yet, by this very procedure, he who worships the Supreme Goddess— || 18-197 ||
O Goddess, on that circle of the earth he is the manifest Lord, of this there is no doubt;
O Queen of the Gods, all rites such as recitation and the like should be performed with the Great Conch.
Thus have I described the power of the Kulasarvasvaka;
it cannot be fully recounted even in hundreds of millions of years.
O Supreme Goddess, whatever has been spoken by me out of impulsiveness cannot be fully described even in a thousand future births.
It should be given to one of noble birth who is devoted to Tārā;
it must not be given to one devoted to another deity, especially not to a Vaiṣṇava. (18–201)
It should always be given to one of noble birth, who has great aspirations, who is devoted to faith, who is high-souled, and whose virtues have been thoroughly tested.
It must not be given to one who is not a devotee, nor to one intent on other paths; it should not be given, O Goddess of the God of Gods, for it is to be kept secret in all the Āgamas. (18–203)
One should never show this hymn to one who is devoid of worship and recitation, nor to one who reviles women and the gods; by showing it to such a person, one becomes a slayer of Śiva.
O Goddess, this should always be recited at all times and in all circumstances.

O Mistress of the Kula, that man who daily recites this hymn with devotion shall become equal to the Lord of Wealth in his accumulation of riches, and like the Lord of Speech through the pride of his learning.
In beauty he was the god of love incarnate, in fame he was Nārāyaṇa, and in power he was indeed Śaṅkara; by his happiness, valor, and majesty, he was truly the lord of the earth, and not otherwise.
Thus has this secret Thousand Names of Tārā been told to you;
it is certain that there is no hymn superior to this among the tantras. (18–206)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Thousand Names of Tārā," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī within the glorious Bṛhannīlatantra. || 18 ||
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
The venerable Bhairava said:
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the most wonderful armor (kavaca), by knowing which all practitioners will certainly attain liberation. (19-1)
Listen to this supreme secret armor (*kavaca*) spoken from my own mouth;
for by reciting it, all auspiciousness arises—of this there is no doubt. (19.2)
O Great Goddess, that which was not to be revealed has been revealed out of affection for you;
it is the supreme essence, extracted from the essences of all essences. (19.3)
He who wears this armor or recites it with a spirit of devotion is Śiva himself, he is a Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa), and he is a yogi; of this there is no doubt. (19.4)
O Goddess, O Beloved, for one who worships the supreme Tāriṇī without the armor-mantra (kavaca),
no success arises even in a hundred crores of kalpas.
May the root protect the seed of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
and may that very root of power protect the *liṅga* with effort. (19-6)
May the seed-syllable of Vadhū always protect Maṇipūra in its entirety;
may the seed-syllable of Varma protect Anāhata for me everywhere and in every way. (19.7)
May the weapon and the rest always protect the pure region of the throat;
may the remainder indeed eternally protect my command-center, which has two petals. (19.8)
May Tārā always protect my head; may Jaṭā always protect my face;
and may Nīlāsarasvatī always protect my heart once again. (19.9)
May Mahānīlasarasvatī always protect the mūlādhāra;
may Akṣobhya protect all the limbs, and may Bṛhatī protect the forehead.
May the deity Ugratārā protect my conch at all times;
may the seed-syllable Hrīṃ protect my ears forever in their entirety. || 19-11 ||
May Hūṃ-Śakti, the destroyer of obstacles, always protect my two breasts;
and may the eternal Goddess Lakṣmī always protect my tongue. (19.12)
May Sarasvatī always protect the tip of my tongue with diligence;
may Rati always protect my seed, and may Prīti always protect my face. (19.13)
May Kīrti always protect Kīrti; may Śānti always protect Śānti;
may Puṣṭi protect my prosperity, and may Tuṣṭi always protect contentment. (19.14)
May Vairocana always protect [my head], and Śaṅkhapāṇḍura my conch-shell;
may Pāṇḍura always protect my secret organ at all times and in every way. (19.15)
May Padmanābha always protect my ten-petalled navel;
may Asitāṅga protect the genitals, and Nāmaka protect the two ears.
May Māmaka protect my arms; may Maheśvarī protect my hands.
May Tārā always protect my back, and Padmāntaka protect mine.
And may Yamāntaka and Vighnāntaka always protect my sides.
May those two feet, which bring an end to obstacles and to hell, always protect me.
"May Tārā, the Supreme Goddess, constantly protect my eight limbs.
Thus, O Goddess, this armor (kavaca), spoken from my own mouth, has been declared. (19.19)
O Supreme Goddess, due to negligence, this must never be disclosed; otherwise, the Yoginīs would slay [the offender], and she herself would become a bringer of her own destruction. (19–20)
O Goddess, if it is obtained by the best of practitioners through the power of fortune, then, O Goddess, great accomplishment will certainly arise for him. (19–21)
It must never be given to those who are forbidden, nor should it ever be revealed.
If one should give it to those who are forbidden, then one will meet with death. (19–22)
One should bestow it upon a disciple who is peaceful, endowed with the tantra and mantra, and possessed of devotion to the guru; therein lies the unsurpassed accomplishment. (19–23)
The entire secret has been told, which bestows infinite fruit;
it must be guarded, O Supreme Goddess, and never revealed. (19–24)
O Goddess, she who worships the auspicious Tāriṇī without the armor-mantra (kavaca) is certainly devoured by that most fierce one along with the Yoginīs. (19–25)
Thus, O Goddess, this secret armor has been told to you, which is difficult to obtain. Now, O Maheśānī, I shall speak of that which must be guarded with great effort. (19–26)
O lotus-faced one, listen to the secret mantra and the secret recitation;
having extracted the Great Power, the Supreme Goddess Mātaṅgī. (19–27)
O Maheśānī, the seed-syllable of fire is declared to be the third seed-syllable;
this mantra, consisting of three seed-syllables, bestows all eloquence. (19–28)
Eleven thousand repetitions are prescribed for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa);
one should perform the fire oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that number, and the libation (tarpaṇa) likewise with a tenth part.
For the consecration, one should feed ten Brahmins with a tenth part [of the offerings], O Maheśvarī; they should be given honey, milk-rice, and great clarified butter.
One should perform the oblation with a spirit of devotion; this is hidden in all tantras.
By means of this king of mantras, one should accomplish the auspicious Tāriṇī. (19–31)
Then, O Great Goddess, O Maheśvarī, one certainly becomes perfected;
for, O beautiful one, having placed the hand upon the region of the young woman's womb. (19-32)
Facing north, O Maheśānī, one should mentally contemplate the most beautiful Tāriṇī, who deludes even the god of love, O Goddess. (19-33)
O Maheśvarī, O Supreme Goddess, having honored [the deity] within the center of the womb,
one should bring the face there and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
O Maheśānī, one becomes a master of accomplished mantras; of this there is no doubt.
By practicing for five days, one becomes like Kubera. (19-35)
Having become endowed with all sovereign powers, one should roam upon the circle of the earth;
the mantra should be recited one hundred and eight times, preceded by the massaging of the breasts.
One should thrust the *liṅga* into the cavity of the *yoni*, with the head [of the *liṅga*] placed lightly upon the crown [of the *yoni*].
By means of repeated striking, O Goddess of Devas, O beautiful one, the semen is emitted. (19.37)
If one places it in the left hand and applies a tilaka-mark, one becomes possessed of all prosperity and rejoices upon the surface of the earth. (19.38)
Even kings enter into servitude; what then of other people?
For him, the pair of lotus-feet is the ornament upon the crowns of [all] kings.
O Goddess, he becomes like another Bṛhaspati in the assembly hall.
Thus has been told to you this secret recitation of the mantra, which is of great value. (19–40)
O Great Goddess, O Daughter of the Mountain, this king of mantras has been told;
it must always be kept secret from the uninitiated, O Śivā, even though it is a perfected mantra. (19.41)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Armor of Tārā and the Secret Mantra," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī within the glorious Bṛhannīlatantra. || 19 ||
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
The Goddess said:
O God, O Maheśvara, this entire hundred names has been indicated;
O Mahādeva, it was not revealed to me through hundreds of efforts. (20.1)
"O Supreme Lord, by reciting this, the practitioner attains perfection through force;
O Mahādeva, please tell me the hundred names in brief. (20.2)
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which brings benefit to devotees;
by knowing which, all practitioners have attained liberation while living. (20–3)
For they, having accomplished their purpose, go of their own accord to the city of the Goddess;
I shall proclaim the hundred names which, through recitation, bestow omniscience. (20.4)
Abandoning the thousand names, the wise person should recite the hundred names.
O Maheśānī, in the Kali age there is no other recourse; in the Kali age there shall be no other way.
Listen, O virtuous lady of beautiful hips, to this ancient hundred names which grants all perfections to men and bestows happiness upon practitioners.
She is the Savior (Tāriṇī) through her union with the Savior (Tāra), whose very nature is the Great Savior (Mahātāra);
she is the one who takes away the life of the stars (Tāraka) and whose nature is the bliss of Tārā.
Mahānīlā, Maheśānī, Mahānīlasarasvatī, Ugratārā, Satī, Sādhvī, Bhavānī, and the liberator from worldly existence (Bhavamocinī). || 20-8 ||
She who delights in the great conch, the formidable one, the consort of Śaṅkara, and the beloved of Śaṅkara;
she who delights in great giving, the fierce Caṇḍī, the destroyer of the fierce Asuras. || 20-9 ||
With a face like the moon and possessing the beautiful luster of the moon,
she has a single braid of hair, eyes like those of a deer, and bestows boons and fearlessness.
Mahākālī, the Great Goddess, Guhyakālī, the bestower of boons; she who delights in Mahākāla, the virtuous one, the granter of great sovereignty. || 20-11 ||
Bestower of liberation, giver of heaven, gentle, of gentle form, slayer of the enemies of the gods, the knower of the deceitful, of great sound, Kamalā—such is Bagalāmukhī. (20.12)
Kālī, the bestower of great liberation, whose nature is that of Kālarātri;
Sarasvatī, the most excellent of rivers, the celestial Gaṅgā who dwells in heaven.
The daughter of the Himalaya, delighting in the form of a maiden,
sat upon a corpse, adorned with a garland of severed heads.
She is naked, devoted to her husband, and eager for inverted union;
she is menstruating, delights in passion, and is fond of the flower of the Self-Existent One.
Her life-breath is the Svayambhū-flower; she is eager for the Svayambhū-flower. Her life-breath is Śiva; she delights in Śiva; she is the giver of Śiva; her seat is Śiva. || 20-16 ||
Aṭṭahāsā is of terrible form, whose nature is eternal bliss;
Meghavarṇā is a young maiden with the breasts of a youth anointed with saffron. (20.17)
Dwarfish, beloved by dwarfish people, adorned with ornaments of jewels,
accompanied by the sound of tinkling bells, she dances with blood-red eyes.
She has a slender body, is fond of *kṛsara*, and is eager for the bow;
she carries a skull-bowl and a mendicant’s bowl, and wears a garland of fifty skulls.

She is the giver of offerings to gods and ancestors, contentment, and nourishment; she is the most excellent woman, peace, forbearance, mind, and intellect, and her nature is that of the seed of all things.
The fierce one who carries others across, she who has herself crossed over and possesses a multitude of virtues;
the mistress of Rāma, the delightful woman, the beautiful one whose very nature is the bliss of Rāma.
"Filled with the essence of the night moon, with eyes like red lotuses—thus, O Maheśvarī, have these one hundred divine names been told to you. (100) 20–22.
One should recite with a spirit of devotion this unsurpassed hymn, capable of delivering one across [the ocean of existence], which is praised by the great roar of all the asuras. (20–23)
O Supreme Goddess, within six months one obtains great sovereignty;
O Beloved, by one desiring land, it should be recited, and after a year one shall obtain it.
One seeking wealth shall obtain wealth; one seeking liberation shall obtain liberation;
and one seeking a wife shall obtain a wife, as proclaimed by all the scriptures. (20–25)
And if a person recites it one hundred times on the eighth lunar day, O Goddess of gods, truth is accomplished; there is no doubt whatsoever. (20–26)
Thus, O Maheśvarī, this is the truth, again the truth, the truth, the truth;
there is no doubt that among all hymns, there is none superior to this. (p. 227) 20–27.
One should recite the hundred names as a mantra, chanting them with a spirit of devotion;
O Goddess, one should recite them every day if one desires one's own welfare. (20–28)
Now I shall describe the origin of the Vidyā, O fair-faced one, by the mere knowledge of which one becomes victorious on earth. (20–29)
O fair-faced one, at midnight, having consecrated unctuous water by reciting the "yoni-bīja" mantra three times, one hundred and eight times; 20–30.
O Goddess, if one drinks that water while reciting [the mantra] for six months,
having become composed of all knowledge, one rejoices upon the surface of the earth.
Listen, O daughter of the mountain, to the Great Goddess who is the embodiment of Śakti:
whether one follows the Vaiṣṇava path, the Śaiva path, the Śākta path, or even the Gāṇapa [Gāṇapatya] path. (20–32)
Nevertheless, O Bhairavasundarī, hear of the preeminence of Śakti [derived] from the Supreme Lord, who is the totality (sakala) and whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
From that, Śakti arose; from Śakti, Nāda; after that, Bindu.
Then, from the Bindu-self, which is of the nature of the Bindu-kalā in the form of Time (kāla)... [20.34]
And from him the entire world, consisting of both the stationary and the moving, is born;
he alone is indeed to be heard, to be reflected upon, and to be meditated upon. (20.35)
And it is to be realized directly, O Goddess Śivā, through various Āgamas;
it is to be heard from the statements of the Vedas, and it is to be reflected upon through means such as contemplation. (20.36)
This very one should be meditated upon through successive births according to the instructions of the Guru;
then, at that moment, He who is the Self of all becomes directly manifest in an instant.
O Goddess of gods, O Supreme Sovereign, listen while that is manifest before you;
O Goddess, through manifold dispositions, even there one is led by disposition. (20-38)

O Beloved, just as there is but one single taste in cows, yet it assumes diversity when combined with various vessels and milk products for the sake of devotees, so too does that [taste] attain manifoldness through its association with what is called milk. (20.39)
O Goddess, from grass the juice is produced, and from that, the supreme juice; from that comes curd, from that the sacrificial oblation, and from that, the arising of the [divine] essence. (20.40)
That very [cause] is the cause therein, and that effect is perceived as such;
yet, O Mahādeva, the effect is seen without the cause.
In the very same way, this very self is born in various forms of birth;
therefore, once born, the distinction of time is indeed perceived.
He is born, he dies; he is bound, he is liberated; he is the man who experiences happiness;
he is the old man and he is the learned one; he is neither woman, nor man, nor neuter.
O Śivā, through the conjunction with various superimpositions, that very Self is born as the individual soul;
yet that one and only Self is eternal and exists in all forms. (20.44)
It is both unmanifest and manifest; it is certainly known through its inherent nature (prakṛti).
Therefore, without connection to that nature, it is never known anywhere. (20.45)
Just as a jar is not perceived without its connection to "jar-ness," so too, even while being distinguished from others, it undergoes differentiation. (20.46)
Without me, no distinction whatsoever arises in the Puruṣa;
neither through ritual applications, nor through forms of knowledge, nor through sacred revelation, nor through the lineages of gurus. (20.47)
Neither by ablutions nor by libations, nor ever by gifts, is the Self known;
for the Self is known through primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and the person is dissolved by primordial nature.
Everything is presided over by Prakṛti; the entire world is deceived by Prakṛti.
Through Prakṛti it attains differentiation, and through Prakṛti it may attain non-differentiation. (20.49)
The individual soul (nara) is neither Prakṛti nor Puruṣa; he is the Supreme Lord.
Thus has this reality, the essence of all things and most delightful, been told to you.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Essence of Reality: The Hundred Names of Tārā," in the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī within the illustrious *Bṛhannīlatantra*.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the ancient essence of reality (tattvasāra), by the mere knowledge of which one becomes like Kubera. (21-1)
Having carefully prepared this copper, lead, and even brass,
the practitioner should indeed dig a pit measuring four cubits in size.
One should reduce it to fine ash, avoiding any admixture of charcoal;
then, having mixed it with half-dry cow-dung, it should be filled over a copper vessel.
One should heat it for exactly seven days, O Supreme Goddess;
thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should carefully lift it up, O Śivā.
O Goddess Maheśvarī, having taken that [substance] in an iron vessel,
O Goddess, one should heat it intensely with charcoal embers from a firebrand.
O beautiful one, when the copper has been liquefied in such a way that it becomes pure,
one should, with a disciplined mind, add mercury equal to half of that amount into it.
Maheśvarī should prepare [the ointment] combined with the juice of *vijāvara*, the juice of *aṭarūṣa*, and the juice of *siṃhikā*. (21.7)
And then, O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods, gold shall truly arise;
through the recitation of the root mantra, it is certainly accomplished—of this there is no doubt. (21.8)
By reciting the mantra ten thousand times, one certainly attains success; there is no doubt.
This is accomplished either with the aforementioned mercury or with purified mercury. (21.9)
Having removed [the impurities], one should add lead there, and it will turn into silver.
Thus I have told you everything that bestows all eloquence. (21.10)
O Goddess, O fair-faced one, he shall truly, truly become worthy of the practice.
Now listen, O lady of beautiful limbs, to [the description of] the ash of mercury (sūtabhasma) as well. (21.11)
O Dear One, by which mere consciousness the accomplishment of the mantra occurs, the preceptor, having dug a pit measuring one and a half cubits, [should proceed]. (21.12)
Then, O Supreme Goddess, one should smear it with turmeric and cow dung;
thereafter, one should reduce it to ash with elephant urine according to the prescribed rite.
O Goddess of gods, one should reduce it to ashes according to the prescribed rite by means of the root of the *vaijayantī* plant, as well as with *siddharasa* and dried cow dung.
Taking pure mercury on an auspicious day at night,
and placing salt above and below it, it is reduced to ashes at that very moment.
O Supreme Goddess, when combined with the sprouts of the Aśvattha tree, it indeed becomes the ash of mercury; O Sovereign Lady, there is no doubt in this matter. (21-16)
O Goddess of gods, by means of Aśvadanta and indeed Vājimāra,
that chariot situated there is reduced to ashes at that very moment.
O beautiful one, when that is joined with the mineral element (dhātu), it becomes bound;
by means of the nectar of the underworld (pātālarasaka) alone, it shall become the most excellent gold. (21.18)
Having first bound the pill, one should afterwards strike it with mercury;
then, O you who are honored by the assembly of gurus, the binding indeed occurs—this is the truth. (21.19)
O lady of pure smiles, one should perform the recitation according to the rite for three nights;
thereafter, O Goddess of gods, the application is perfected—of this there is no doubt. (21–20)
The yogi who is a great poet shall be endowed with the essence of creative contemplation;
O auspicious Goddess, the determination of *bhāva* has thus been declared.
But existence, O Goddess, is threefold according to the sequence of the divine, the heroic, and the animal;
likewise, the gurus are to be known as threefold, as are the deities of the mantra. (21–22)
O Great Goddess, the first state is the most excellent among all the scriptures;
the second is declared to be middling, and the third is censured by all.
O Goddess, without devotion, mantra and vidyā do not bestow their fruit, despite extensive recitation, fire-offerings, and various forms of physical austerity. (21–24)
What is the use of hundreds of thousands of heroic rites (*vīrasādhana*), or what use are those crowded with noble lineages?
What use is the worship of sacred seats (*pīṭha*) alone, or what use are the feeding of virgins and such? (21–25)
What is the use of giving gifts for the pleasure of one's own wife, and likewise,
what is the use of subduing the senses or performing the duties of family tradition?
If one who is devoted to the family were not pure in being,
one attains liberation through being, and through being, the increase of the family.
Through the state of being (bhāva), there shall be the increase of the lineage (gotra); through the state of being, the accomplishment of the family (kula).
What is the use of elaborate ritual deposits (nyāsa), and what is the use of elaborate purifications of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi)?
What is the use of such worship alone if the state [of realization] does not arise?
The remaining state, O Mahādeva, brings happiness to all actions. || 21-29 ||
O Goddess of the gods, with that state one should worship the Supreme Goddess;
having attained the causeless [state], Maheśvara is filled with agitation.
Wherever one may go on a Tuesday to a cremation ground,
there one shall obtain the fruit of worship equivalent to that performed for seven days.
If one goes there on the fourteenth day, one obtains the fruit of the merit of an entire fortnight;
but if one does not go, nor worship at that place, one is undoubtedly a mere beast.
"O God, there should be no one else superior [to me]," thus intent on such thoughts, when the practitioner falls into agitation, my own agitation arises. (21.33)
Therefore, the excellent hero should always strive to be endowed with enjoyments;
through enjoyment he attains liberation, and through enjoyment he [unites with] the beautiful lady of the Kula. (21.34)
Having encountered one who is without cause, Maheśvara becomes agitated;
he would perform neither mental worship, nor meditation, nor contemplation. (21.35)
Whatever one speaks, whatever one sleeps, whatever one does, and whatever one worships—all that is the form of the Kula; having meditated thus, the wise one should conduct himself.
Therefore, having eaten and drunk, one should worship the Supreme Goddess;
in this matter, there is no fault regarding the violation of sacred tradition, nor any defect such as transgression.
Alone in a desolate region, in a cremation ground, on a mountain, in a forest,
in an empty house, or on a riverbank, he should always wander without fear.
For heroes, the time for recitation is praised as being at all times;
the propitiation of the Kula should be performed in every place and at every sacred seat (pīṭha). (21.39)
Having understood this, O Goddess of gods, O lady of beautiful countenance, one should perform everything;
what is the use of saying much more here? What else shall I tell you? (21.40)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Alchemy and the Essence," in the illustrious Bṛhannīlatantra, within the dialogue between Bhairavī and Bhairava. || 21 ||
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, the thousand names of Kālī were previously indicated;
O Mahādeva, speak them if you have affection for me. (22-1)
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Parameśānī, listen with a one-pointed mind, O Goddess, to this Thousand Names of Kālī within this Tantra, which increases the devotion of the faithful. (22-2)
(Oṃ. Of this Thousand-Name Hymn of the Mantra of the Goddess Śrī Kālī, Mahākālabhairava is the seer;
Anuṣṭubh is the meter; Śrī Kālī is the deity; Krīṃ is the seed-syllable; Hūṃ is the power; Hrīṃ is the pin;
the application is for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. [Perform] the ritual placements (nyāsa) and so forth.
Kalikā, Kāmadā, Kullā, Bhadrakālī, Gaṇeśvarī; Bhairavī, beloved of Bhairava, Bhavānī, the liberator from worldly existence. || 22-3 ||
She is Kālarātri, Mahārātri, and the deluding Moharātri;
she delights in Mahākāla, is subtle, and is devoted to the Kaula vow.
She was of delicate limbs yet possessed formidable limbs; she was a lovely woman of excellent form, her body anointed with fragrant sandalwood paste—a virtuous, chaste, and devoted wife.
Kākinī is of beautiful form and color, the consort of Mahākāla;
she is the destroyer of desire, the art of desire, the knower of desire, and of great exaltation.
Mahālakṣmī is of beautiful form, having the nature of Mahākāla;
she is of noble lineage, the essence of all lineages, and the one who reveals the path of the Kula.
She whose form is the lineage, the cakora-eyed Śrī Durgā, the destroyer of difficulties;
she who is the maiden, the virgin, the fair-complexioned Gaurī, yet whose body is black and whose mind is great. (22.8)
She has a dark body and a blue form, with tawny hair and a slender waist;
she has tawny eyes, is fond of lotuses, and is Kālī, possessing the prowess of Time.
The Goddess beloved of the Lord of Kalās, Kulakāntā, Aparājitā, Ugratārā, Mahogrā, and likewise the auspicious Ekajaṭā. (22.10)

She is blue, dense, possessing cranes, the giver at the time of death, composed of the subtle arts, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, subtle, the bestower of boons, and affectionate toward her devotees. || 22-11 ||
She has beautiful hips, possesses great arrows, is a young maiden, a youthful woman, and chaste;
she has long limbs, long hair, and likewise wears human skulls.
Wearing a garland of human heads, bearing corpses, skulls, and bones,
with blood-red eyes and wide-open gaze, she is the Earth adorned with vermilion.
The terrible night, the great night, the horrific destroyer of the end;
the lioness of Nara, the most fierce, blue-hued, and seated upon a bull.
Vilocanā, Virūpākṣī, Raktotpalavilocanā, Pūrṇenduvadanā, Bhīmā, and likewise Prasannavadanā. (22.15)
She has lotus-like eyes and large, expansive eyes; she is filled with the splendor of the autumnal moonlight;
her eyes possess the beauty of a full-blown white lotus; she is the destroyer of fear.
She of the loud laughter, she of the great breath, the destroyer of great obstacles;
she with sunken eyes, the slender-necked one, the one who perfects the sacred sites of the Kula.
With a face as serene as a family well, she is a great ornament to her lineage;
she possesses the nectar-like essence of many words and is intensely swift in her fierce form.
Vegadarpā, Viśālaindrī, Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā, as well as Caṇḍikā, Kālavadanā, and Sutīkṣṇanāsikā. || 22-19 ||
She has long hair and beautiful locks; her body is tawny and she is deep red in hue.
She delights in ornaments of the *preta*s, and she possesses small bells upon the staff-like arms of the *preta*s. (22.20)
She who possesses the conch, she whose mudrā is the conch, she who resounds with the sound of the conch;
she who dwells in the cremation ground, she who is full, she whose face is like the full moon, the auspicious one.
She who is beloved by Śiva, who delights in Śiva, and who rests upon the seat of Śiva;
she is the abode of merit, the greatly meritorious one, the giver of merit, and the beloved of merit.
She bears human skulls, she is terrifying, the destroyer of the fearsome Asuras;
she is the sacrificial fee (Dakṣiṇā), pleased by the sacrificial fee, and wears a serpent as her sacred thread.
Digaṃbarī Mahākālī is peaceful, with full and elevated breasts;
she sits upon a formidable seat, possesses a terrifying form, and lets blood flow from the corners of her mouth.
She is the great sound, attached to Śiva; she is the great resonance, the large-bellied one;
she is afflicted by desire, attached to desire, intoxicated, and whose contemplation is fixed on Śiva.
The goddess whose abode is the ocean, beloved by great intoxicated folk;
she who draws forth, delights in drawing forth, and effects the summoning of all. || 22-26 ||
Delighting in musical instruments, fond of great songs, she dwells among the *pretas*;
she is celebrated as wearing a garland of human skulls and is adorned with floral wreaths.
Four-armed and most fierce, ten-handed and fond of her beloved, she is the Mother of the World, the Sustainer of the World, the Supreme One who bestows liberation upon the world. (22–28)
The sustainer of the world, the protector of the world, the cause of joy for the world;
consisting of the life-force of the world, the daughter of Himavat, Māyā, she of the great tresses.
She has the limbs of a serpent, her body is coiled, and she rests upon a serpent-bed;
she is the terrible Night of Doom, blazing with the heat of the sun and moon. (200) 22-30 ||
Nāgendranandinī, Devakanyā, Śrīmanoramā, Vidyādharī, Vedavidyā, Yakṣiṇī, and Śivamohinī. (22–31)
The Rākṣasī, the Ḍākinī, the one composed of the gods, the conqueror of the entire world;
she who is the form of the Vedas, likewise the fiery one, the great liberation, and the sovereign of beings. (22–32)
Devoted to her husband, intent upon her husband, and dedicated to devotion to her husband;
she is the bestower of success, the giver of accomplishments, and likewise beloved by the perfected ones (siddhas).
She has a handmaid in her hand, is mounted upon Śiva, is of the form of Śiva, and has a corpse as her seat;
she is known as Tamisrā, Tāmasī, Vijñā, and Mahāmeghasvarūpiṇī.
She was beautiful and variegated, of lovely complexion, and adorned with beautiful hair;
she possessed graceful limbs, was restless and fickle, and was devoted to the customs of China.
Devoted to the conduct of China, modest, life-giving, and sinless;
likewise Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, and Mahānīlasarasvatī. (22–36)
Most venerable, devoted to Dharma, the destroyer of both merit and demerit;
distinguished, great, garlanded, and likewise fond of sacrifices with Soma. || 22-37 ||
Bestower of fear, delighting in fear, beloved by terrifying folk; she whose form is speech, Chinnamastā, who is eternally fond of the severed Asura.

Sāvitrī is the form of the Ṛgveda; she is endowed with passion (rāga), she is characterized by the quality of rajas, she delights in rajas, she is stained by rajas, and she increases the association with rajas. || 22-39 ||
She is immersed in passion (rajas), abundant in passion, and adorned with locks of hair;
she wears earrings, is fond of earrings, and is likewise beautified by earrings.
Revatī, Revataprītā, Revā, the auspicious Airāvatī, Śaktinī, Cakriṇī, Padmā, and Mahāpadmanivāsinī. || 22-41 ||
Padmālayā, Mahāpadmā, Padminī, Padmavallabhā, Padmapriyā, Padmaratā, and Mahāpadmasuśobhitā. || 22-42 ||
Śūlahastā, Śūlaratā, Śūlinī, Śūlasaṅgikā, Piṇākadhāriṇī, Vīṇā, as well as Vīṇāvatī and Maghā. (22.43)
Rohiṇī, who delights in the *bahula* constellation, likewise increases [the power of] vehicles;
she rejoices in battle, is devoted to battle, and is the destroyer of the Asuras in combat. || 22.44 ||
She who stands at the forefront of battle, Rāṇā, Raṇāgrā, and Raṇapaṇḍitā;
she who is endowed with matted locks, Jaṭāpiṅgā, as well as Vajriṇī and Śūlinī.
She who is fond of pleasure, devoted to pleasure, dedicated to pleasure, and overcome by pleasure;
she who fears pleasure, has attained pleasure, and is the destroyer of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
She who drinks blood, she who delights in blood, she who is called "Blood," she who is adorned with blood;
she whose form is blood, she who has entered into blood, she who carries a skull-bowl filled with blood. || 22-47 ||
Adorned with a necklace of human heads dripping with blood,
she is seated upon a bull, delights in the bull, and has made her abode upon the bull-throne.
Clad in tiger-skin, she is fierce; likewise, she is garlanded with tiger-skin.
She possesses the limbs of desire, she is supremely delighted, and she is the devourer of the life-breaths of enemies.
She is young, possessing youthful vitality, and likewise the crusher of the young;
she bestows youthful love, yet is aged, and is the virtuous one dear to the aged.
Svapnāvatī, Svapnaratā, Nārasiṃhī, Mahālayā, Amoghā, Rundhatī, Ramyā, Tīkṣṇā, and Bhogavatī are always [present]. (22.51)
Mandākinī, Mandaratā, Mahānandā, Varapradā;
Mānadā, Māninī, Mānyā, Mānanīyā, Madāturā.
Madirā, Madironmādā, Madirākṣī, Madālayā, Sudīrghā, Madhyamā, Nandā, and Vinatāsuranirgatā. (22.53)
Bestower of victory, devoted to victory, invincible, destroyer of asuras;
slayer of wicked daityas and annihilator of evil asuras. || 22-54 ||
She is the giver of happiness, the giver of liberation, liberation itself, and the bestower of great liberation;
she is fame, the renowned one, the ornament, the object of adornment, and the beloved of the Lord of Beings.

Beyond qualities, yet delighted by qualities, colored by qualities, and having qualities as her very essence; possessed of qualities and yet devoid of qualities—Sītā is established as the ultimate goal and the supreme limit.
Dhaniṣṭhā, the giver of wealth, the auspicious, the bestower of riches, the brilliantly radiant;
the venerable, the most venerable, the daughter of Dhaumya, the destroyer of the demons of Dhaumya. (400) || 22-57 ||

She is free from desire yet the giver of wealth; she fulfills desires and lives for the sake of those with desires; she is the wish-fulfilling gem, the celestial wish-granting creeper, and likewise the bearer of Śaṅkara.

She who brings auspiciousness, she who is devoted to Śaṅkara, and likewise she who deludes Śaṅkara; Bhavānī, the bestower of existence, the auspicious one, she who is fond of Bhava, and whose abode is Bhava.
The beloved of Mahādeva, the delightful one, the charming woman beautiful as desire,
possessing the splendor of plantain trunks, she who dwells upon a stainless seat.
Māthurī, Mathurā, Māyā, as well as Surabhivardhinī—she who is manifest and unmanifest, possessing manifold forms, the abode of all holy fords, and auspicious. (22.61)
She is the embodiment of sacred fords (tīrtha), she of great form; likewise, she is the wife of Agastya, Śivānī, she who delights in moss (śaivala), and she who dwells in moss.
Kuntalā, Kuntalaprītā, and likewise Kuntalaśobhitā;
Mahākacā, Mahābuddhi, Mahāmāyā, and Mahāgadā.
She has the nature of a great cloud, as well as being the enchantress Kaṅkaṇamohinī;
she is worshipped by the gods, devoted to the gods, a young woman, and the embodiment of all auspiciousness.
She makes everyone dear, she is the object of enjoyment, the embodiment of enjoyment, and has the form of the *bhaga*.
She is pleased by the *bhaga*, is devoted to the *bhaga*, and is always delighted by love for the *bhaga*.
Delighting in the friction of the vulva, seated upon the vulva,
skilled in the vulva, pervaded by the vulva, she is the increaser of the fortune of the vulva.
The daughter of Dakṣa, the highly capable, the all-capable, the fierce Pracaṇḍikā; she who loves the staff, who delights in the staff, and who is intent upon striking with the staff.
Fearing punishment, having entered into punishment, and delighting in the suppression of punishment,
she stands in the midst of well-known punishment, embodying the worlds of Bhuḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
The first is Durgā, Jayā, Sūkṣmā, Sūkṣmarūpā, Jayākṛti, Kṣemaṅkarī, Mahāghūrṇā, Ghūrṇanāsā, and Vaśaṅkarī. || 22-69 ||
She has expansive limbs, is cloud-like, adorned with three folds, and auspicious;
she is intoxicated with passion, devoted to the joy of love, and the destroyer of the arrogant Asuras.
She is the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the crusher of the demon Niśumbha;
she is Caṇḍarūpā, Mahācaṇḍī, Caṇḍikā, and Caṇḍanāyikā.
Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍavarṇā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍāvatī, and Śivā;
Nīlākārā, Nīlavarṇā, and she whose eyes are like blue lotuses.
With sword in hand and delicate limbs, likewise bearing a skull-bowl;
she is Bhīmā, with a terrifying face, most formidable and fearsome.
She is auspicious, blessed, pure, and likewise supremely wondrous; she is the supreme abider, devoted to the highest, higher than the highest, and transcendent.
She whose nature is supreme bliss, whose form is eternal bliss;
she who is eternal, eternally beloved, free from sloth, Bhavānī, the beauty of existence.
She who deludes the three worlds, she who is perfected, likewise she who is dear to the perfected ones; she who is Bhairavī, she who is beloved by Bhairava, and likewise she who deludes Bhairava.
Mātaṅgī, Kamalā, Lakṣmī, Ṣoḍaśī, Viṣayāturā, Viṣamagnā, Viṣaratā, Viṣarakṣā, and Jayadrathā. (22.77)
Always wearing the side-locks of a youth, she causes wonder in all;
she holds a mace, is full of desire, and is adorned with a garland of swords and severed heads.
The mistress of yogis, the mother of yoga, whose very nature is the bliss of yoga;
she is Ānandabhairavī, Nandā, and likewise the one dear to the people of Nanda.
Nalinī is a beautiful woman, radiant and adorned with a bright face;
she has a quivering tongue, blue feet, and likewise a beautiful mouth and right side. (22.80)
She who partakes of offerings, who delights in offerings, who enjoys offerings, and who is supremely passionate;
she who enjoys fruits, whose essence is the fruit, who bestows fruits, and who is fond of the *śrīphala* fruit. || 22-81 ||
She who possesses fruit, she who is the thunderbolt of fruit, she who wards off fruitlessness;
she who delights in fruit, she who has attained fruit, she who binds together the bonds of fruit.
She is oriented toward the fruit, she is the Great Being, and she is composed of sattva;
she possesses all forms, delights in all things, and dwells within all sentient beings. (22.83)
She of great form, of great fortune, whose nature is like a great cloud;
the destroyer of fear, devoted to the Gaṇas, pleased with the Gaṇas, and of great course.
She is the auspicious one who leads to a good state of existence, who is honored, who is well-eyed, and who resides upon the corpse-seat;
she is the Gaṅgā who deludes the three worlds, the celestial Gaṅgā, and the dweller of heaven.
She is Great Bliss, Eternal Bliss, whose nature is both eternal and non-eternal;
she possesses the fragrance of truth, consists of the hosts of truth, is the embodiment of truth, and is of great form.
Śmaśānabhairavī, Kālī, as well as Bhayavimardinī, Tripurā, Parameśānī, Sundarī, and Purasundarī. || 22-87 ||
Tripureśī is the fifteenth, Puravāsinī the fifth;
Mahāsaptadaśī is the sixth, and likewise Saptamī and Aṣṭamī are the seventh and eighth.
The ninth is Daśamī, beloved by the gods; the tenth is Śivā;
the twelfth is the supreme, divine [form]; and the thirteenth is Nīlarūpā.
The fourteenth day, the full moon, the Queen of the Kings of Queens,
as well as Tripurā, Tripureśī, and Tripuramardinī.
Beautiful in all her limbs, she is red in hue, wearing red garments and a sacred thread;
she holds a chowrie, is fond of the chowrie, and is the crusher of the demon Camara.
She is pleasing to the mind, beautiful, delightful, a female swan with a charming smile;
she has shapely hips, is richly endowed with hips, and is graced by the weight of her hips. (22.92)
Clad in silken garments, wearing fine silk, she is beautiful;
her face is like camphor and the moon, and she is adorned with liquid saffron. || 22-93 ||
She is the Earth, she who possesses vast forms, and she who brings about the destruction of the lords of the earth;
she is the altar of jewels, the sovereign of the gods, the queen of the gods, and the enchantress of the gods.
The crest-jewel, the jewel-necked one, adorned with precious gems;
Urvaśī, the pacifier, Kālī, whose nature is that of Mahākāla.
Sarvarūpā, Mahāsattvā, Rūpāntaravilāsinī, Śivā, Śaivā, Rudrāṇī, and likewise Śivaninādinī. (22.96)
Mātaṅginī, Bhrāmarī, and likewise Anaṅgamekhalā;
Yoginī, Ḍākinī, and likewise the supreme Maheśvarī. (22.97)
Alambuṣā and Bhavānī, who are endowed with the flood of great vidyās; she who has the form of a vulture, the source of Brahman, the one of great bliss, and the one of great prosperity.
Virūpākṣā, Mahānādā, Caṇḍarūpā, Kṛtākṛti, Varārohā, Mahāvallī, and Mahātripurasundarī. || 22-99 ||
She whose essence is the *bhaga*, who takes the form of the support of the *bhaga*, who is garlanded with *bhagas*;
the Goddess who designates the *liṅga*, the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), the Great Memory (*mahāsmṛti*). || 22.100 ||
She of great intelligence, greatly peaceful, of tranquil form, and with a beautiful face;
she who wears a garland of *liṅgas*, whose ornament is the *liṅga*, and who is adorned with a garland of *bhagas*.

Delighting in the nectar of the bhaga and liṅga, having the nature of the nectar of the bhaga and liṅga, rejoicing in the worship of the bhaga and liṅga, and having the very form of the bhaga and liṅga. || 22-102 ||
Delighted by the flowers of the Self-Existent One, she has the flowers of the Self-Existent One as her seat;
she delights in the flowers of the Self-Existent One and is intent on embracing the creeper.
She feeds on liquor, delights in liquor, and is crushed by the essence of liquor;
she is extremely fierce through the drinking of liquor and is censured by all the scriptures. || 22-104 ||
Always delighted by the *kuṇḍa* and *gola*, she always delights in the *golapuṣpa*;
she is pleased by that which arises from the *kuṇḍa* and *gola*, and her very essence consists of that which arises from the *kuṇḍa* and *gola*.
Self-existent, auspicious, the sustainer, the purifier, the sanctifier of the world;
the Great Lakṣmī, the Great Sovereign, she who possesses the splendor of Mahāviṣṇu. (22.106)
She who is dear to Viṣṇu, she who delights in Viṣṇu, she who is devoted to devotion for Viṣṇu;
she who dwells upon the chest of Viṣṇu, she who has the form of Viṣṇu—she is indeed Vaiṣṇavī.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, and likewise Rohiṇī;
Dhṛti, Medhā, Tuṣṭi, and Puṣṭirūpā, as well as Citā and Citi. (22–108)
She is the form of consciousness, whose nature is pure awareness, the eternal embodiment of knowledge;
she is Gaurī, the conqueror of all the wise, fair-complexioned, Śacī, and Śivā.
Bhavarūpā, Bhavaparā, Bhavānī, Bhavamocinī, Punarvasu, Puṣyā, Tejasvinī, and Sindhuvāsinī. (22.110)

The daughter of Puloma is the consumer of semen, the enjoyer of semen, intent upon the emission of semen, worthy of worship by semen, venerable to semen, and the object of enjoyment for semen. (22.111)
Worshipped by Śukra, satisfied by Śukra, she bestows liberation from all that is Śukra;
she is the embodiment of Śukra, whose body is Śukra, whose limbs are Śukra, and who deludes with Śukra.
Worshiped by the gods, delighting in the gods, she is a young woman who is all-auspicious;
she brings joy to all, is the object of enjoyment, the very form of enjoyment, and the embodiment of fortune.
Delighting in the vulva, devoted to the vulva, and likewise intent on love for the vulva;
she delights in the friction of the vulva and is settled upon the vulva. (22.114)
She who possesses fortune, who is pervaded by fortune, who increases fortune and auspiciousness;
she who is the daughter of Dakṣa, the highly capable, the all-capable, and the destroyer of all obstacles. (22.115)
She is fond of punishment, devoted to punishment, intent on striking with punishment;
she is terrified of punishment, subject to punishment, and delights in the crushing of punishment.
Standing in the center of the sacrificial altar-mandala, she is the embodiment of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ;
she is the primordial Durgā, Jayā, the Subtle One, whose form is subtle and whose appearance is victorious.

She brings security, she is greatly trembling, her nose quivers, and she brings others under her control; her limbs are expansive, she is pure, adorned with three folds [on her belly], and auspicious.
Intoxicated by wine, delighting in wine, she is the maddened celestial courtesan;
she is the slayer of the demons Madhu and Kaiṭabha and the crusher of the demon Niśumbha.
Caṇḍarūpā, Mahācaṇḍā, Caṇḍikā, Caṇḍanāyikā, Caṇḍogrā, Caturvargā, as well as Caṇḍāvatī and Śivā. (22.120)
She has a blue body, is blue in color, and has eyes like blue lotuses;
she is fond of both the eternal and the non-eternal, the auspicious one, Bhavānī, the beauty of worldly existence.
Bhairavī, Bhairavaprītā, as well as Bhairavamohinī, Mātaṅgī, Kamalā, Lakṣmī, Ṣoḍaśī, and Bhīṣaṇāturā. (22-122)
Immersed in poison, delighting in poison, and consuming poison, she is likewise victorious;
she always wears the feathers of a crow and causes wonder in all.
She who holds a mace, she who is full of desire, she who bears a sword, adorned with a garland of severed heads;
the Mistress of Yoga, devoted to yoga, whose very nature is the bliss of yoga.
Ānandabhairavī, Nandā, likewise Ānandajanapriyā, Nalinī, Lalanā, Śubhrā, and she who is resplendent with a beautiful face. (22.125)
Lolling-tongued, blue-footed, likewise facing south, fond of offerings, delighting in offerings, the enjoyer of offerings, and greatly passionate. (22.126)
She who is to be enjoyed as the fruit, whose essence is the fruit, the giver of fruit, who is fond of fruit;
she who possesses fruit, who is deeply attached to fruit, and who wards off both fruit and non-fruit. || 22.127 ||

Delighting in the fruit, abiding in the fruit, and possessing the bond of connection to the fruit; facing toward the fruit, she is the Great Being for all beings, and she is the virtuous one. (22.128)
She who possesses all forms, who delights in all things, and who dwells within all sentient beings;
she of great form, of great fortune, whose nature is like a great cloud. || 22-129 ||
She is the destroyer of fear, devoted to the Gaṇas, praised by the Gaṇas, and the great refuge;
she is the true goal, the embodiment of honor, manifest, ever-seated upon her throne, and auspicious.
She who deludes the three worlds, the Gaṅgā, the celestial Gaṅgā, the dweller in heaven;
she is great bliss, eternal bliss, the perpetual, whose nature is truth. (22.131)
She who bathes in semen, the producer of semen, she who is served by semen, the exceedingly seminal; the one of great semen, devoted to semen, and the ordainer of the emission of semen. || 22-132 ||

Sāradā is the life-breath of the practitioner, the increaser of the practitioner’s love, the eternal bestower of the practitioner’s desired objects, and she who is served by the love of the practitioner. (22.133)
She is the all-in-all of the practitioner’s love, the drinker of the blood of the practitioner’s devotees;
she is Mallikā, Mālatī, Jāti, Saptavarṇā, and Mahākacā.
She consists of all things, she is entirely pure, and likewise the bestower of lordship over the Gaṇas;
she is the sky, she delights in the sky, and likewise she dwells in the sky.

The beloved of Gaṇanātha, the auspicious one, the worship of Bhava, she who is all-auspiciousness (Sarvamaṅgalā), Guhyakālī, Bhadrakālī, whose form is Śiva, and the refuge of the virtuous. || 22-136 ||
Sad-bhaktā, Sat-parā, Setu, Sarvāṅga-sundarī, Maghā, Kṣīṇodarī, Mahāvega, and Vegānanda-svarūpiṇī. || 22-137 ||
Rudhirā, Rudhiraprītā, and Rudhirānandaśobhanā; Pañcamī, who delights in the fifth [note], and likewise she whose ornament is the fifth. || 22-138 ||
She is perfected through the recitation of the fifth [vowel], she delights in the sacrifice of the fifth;
she has the form of the letter *ka*, and her nature is the syllable *ka*.

Delighting in the fifth [syllable] *ma*, having the five [objects] beginning with *ma* as her domain, she originates from the form of the vowel *ṛ*; she is the vowel *ṛ* and possesses all forms. (22.140)
She who is the consort of Śarva, the abode of all, the source of the essence of all, the sovereign of all, the quintessence of all, the desire of all, and the enchantress of all. || 22-141 ||
Ganesha’s mother, Durga, Mahamaya, Maheshvari;
the mother of Mahesha, Moha, Vidyā, Vidyotanī, and Vibhā. (22.142)
She is steadfast and of steady mind, perfectly firm, and delighting in the Dharma;
she is the embodiment of the Dharma, devoted to the Dharma, and intent upon the practice of the Dharma.
She is the context for the performance of dharma, beautiful in all her manifestations;
she is the utterances *svadhā*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *śrauṣaṭ*, and *vauṣaṭ*, whose very essence is *svadhā*.
She is the Brahmanī, connected with Brahman, dwelling in the abode of Brahman;
she is the lotus-born, seated upon a lotus, and the bestower of the fruits of the four aims of life.
Four-armed and joined with Śiva, she enters the Śiva-liṅga;
she is Mahābhīmā, possessing beautiful hair, and resides on Mount Gandhamādana. (1000) || 22-146 ||
The goddess honored by the Gandharvas, the fragrant one, honored by the gods, devoted to the Gandharvas, Surabhi, and likewise Sugandhā. (22.147)
She who has the fragrance of a lotus, the great fragrance, whose scent perfumes the quarters of the sky;
she who is smeared with black pigment, who delights in black, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
She is Vidyā and Vidyāvatī, the Mistress of Knowledge (Vidyeśā) born from the wise;
she is the Great Speech who bestows knowledge, possessing the form of Mahābhairava.
She is devoted to love for Bhairava, delights in Mahākāla, and is auspicious; she is Māheśvarī, mounted upon an elephant, and likewise possesses the gait of a lordly elephant.
She is the consort of Yajñendra, the fierce Caṇḍī, who rests upon the back of an elephant;
she moves with the slow gait of a lordly elephant, the Great Vidyā, most brilliantly radiant.
She who carries the *bagalā* [weapon], she who is aged and yet young, appearing in the form of a child;
the girl devoted to children’s play, the destroyer of the demon Bala. || 22-152 ||
Kālī, Kṛṣṇadurgā, and Sarasvatī abide in childhood, abide in youth, are fully possessed of great youth, and possess distinguished youth. (22.153)
Kātyāyanī and Cāmuṇḍā, the slayer of the demon Caṇḍāsura; the Goddess who bears Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
